faqs.question: Why are ostrich feathers used in dusters?
faqs.answer: Ostrich feathers have soft, fine barbs that build static and hold dust rather than just pushing it around.

faqs.question: Who invented the feather duster?
faqs.answer: Susan Hibbard received a US patent for a feather duster in 1876.

faqs.question: How do you clean a feather duster?
faqs.answer: Shake it outside, and occasionally wash it gently in lukewarm water with mild soap and let it air-dry.

image.alt: An ostrich feather duster with a wooden handle

name: Fire screen

place_of_invention.notes: Screens to shield people from the heat of open fires and guards to stop sparks became common household items in early modern Europe; exact origin unknown.

short_description: A panel or mesh placed in front of a fireplace to block sparks or heat.
description: Pole screens and panel screens in 18th-century homes shielded faces from the fierce heat of open fires, important when wax-based cosmetics could melt. Mesh spark guards stop embers from flying onto floors. Fire screens are still standard accessories for open fireplaces.
why_unchanged: A barrier between fire and room is all that is needed, so the form has not changed.

faqs.question: What was a pole screen?
faqs.answer: It was a small adjustable panel on a pole used to shield a person's face from the heat of the fire.

faqs.question: Why are mesh fire screens important?
faqs.answer: They stop sparks and embers from flying out and starting fires or burning carpets.

faqs.question: Do fire screens need to be fire-proof?
faqs.answer: Yes; modern spark guards are made of metal mesh or tempered glass to withstand heat.

image.alt: A metal fire screen in front of a fireplace

name: Fire tongs

place_of_invention.notes: Tongs were used by metalworkers from the Bronze Age, and hearth tongs for handling fuel appear in Greek and Roman households; no single origin can be given.

short_description: Hinged metal tongs used to pick up and arrange logs or coals in a fire.
description: Smiths used tongs to handle hot metal since the Bronze Age, and similar tongs were adopted for household hearths. Fire tongs let you lift and place logs or coals safely without touching them. They are part of standard fireplace tool sets today.
why_unchanged: Two hinged arms grip securely at a distance from the heat, which cannot be simplified.

faqs.question: What are fire tongs used for?
faqs.answer: They pick up and move logs, coals and burning pieces to arrange the fire safely.

faqs.question: Are fire tongs the same as blacksmith tongs?
faqs.answer: They share the same principle, but blacksmith tongs are heavier and made to hold hot metal firmly.

faqs.question: What does 'go at it hammer and tongs' mean?
faqs.answer: It means doing something with great energy, from the vigorous work of a blacksmith.

image.alt: A pair of iron fireplace tongs

name: Fireplace poker

place_of_invention.notes: Iron rods for stirring fires are as old as the hearth; the poker as part of a fireplace tool set became standard after wall fireplaces with chimneys spread in medieval Europe.

short_description: A metal rod used to stir and arrange burning logs or coals.
description: A poker lets you move burning fuel safely, breaking up coals and adding air to revive a fire. With the spread of wall fireplaces in medieval Europe, iron pokers became standard hearth tools. Many have a hook or spike near the tip for moving logs.
why_unchanged: A long iron rod keeps hands away from the heat, which is all the job requires.

faqs.question: Why does a poker have a hook?
faqs.answer: The hook lets you pull logs toward you, while the point pushes them away.

faqs.question: What is 'Wittgenstein's poker'?
faqs.answer: It refers to a 1946 Cambridge argument in which philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein reportedly brandished a poker at Karl Popper.

faqs.question: What else comes in a fireplace tool set?
faqs.answer: Typical sets include a poker, tongs, shovel and brush on a stand.

image.alt: A wrought-iron fireplace poker by a hearth

name: Flat iron

place_of_invention.notes: Pan-shaped irons filled with hot coals were used in Han-dynasty China (from around the 1st century BCE), and smoothing stones earlier; solid flat irons heated on the fire were common in Europe by the 17th century.

short_description: A heavy iron with a flat sole, heated on a stove and used to press clothes.
description: Flat irons, also called sad irons, were solid metal blocks with a handle that were heated on a stove or fire and pushed over damp fabric. Households kept several irons heating in rotation. Electric irons later replaced the fire, but the flat heated sole and handle are unchanged.
why_unchanged: Heat plus weight on a smooth sole is exactly what smooths fabric fibres.

faqs.question: Why was it called a 'sad iron'?
faqs.answer: 'Sad' was an old word for solid or heavy, describing the dense metal iron.

faqs.question: How did people know when the iron was hot enough?
faqs.answer: They often spat on it or flicked water on the sole and listened for a sizzle.

faqs.question: Who improved the flat iron with a removable handle?
faqs.answer: Mary Florence Potts patented a design with a detachable wooden handle in 1870s America, so the handle stayed cool while irons were swapped.

image.alt: An antique cast-iron flat iron

name: Flint and steel

place_of_invention.notes: Fire-making by striking flint against iron pyrite is much older (Ötzi the Iceman carried such a kit around 3300 BCE); steel strikers appear once iron working spread in the Iron Age.

short_description: A fire-starting kit in which a steel striker is struck against flint to throw sparks onto tinder.
description: When a piece of hard steel is struck against sharp flint, tiny shavings of metal fly off and ignite as sparks. Caught on charred cloth or tinder, they can be blown into a flame. Flint and steel was the standard way to make fire until matches arrived in the 19th century, and it is still used by bushcraft enthusiasts.
why_unchanged: Steel striking hard stone reliably makes sparks, so the kit needs no improvement.

faqs.question: Is it the flint or the steel that sparks?
faqs.answer: The sparks are tiny particles of steel shaved off by the sharp flint, which burn as they fly.

faqs.question: What is char cloth?
faqs.answer: It is cloth heated without oxygen until charred, which catches sparks easily and glows.

faqs.question: How did people make fire before steel?
faqs.answer: They struck flint against iron pyrite or used friction methods such as the bow drill.

image.alt: A steel fire striker and a piece of flint

name: Fly swatter

place_of_invention.notes: Robert R. Montgomery patented a 'fly-killer' in 1900; the name 'fly swatter' was popularized around 1905 by Kansas health official Samuel Crumbine.

short_description: A flat perforated paddle on a handle used to kill flies.
description: Robert R. Montgomery patented a wire-mesh 'fly-killer' in 1900. In 1905 Dr. Samuel Crumbine of Kansas, campaigning against flies as disease carriers, popularized the name 'fly swatter', inspired by a baseball chant of 'swat the ball'. Plastic swatters keep the same mesh paddle and long handle.
why_unchanged: Holes in the paddle let air pass so the fly feels no warning, and the long handle adds speed.

faqs.question: Why does a fly swatter have holes?
faqs.answer: The holes reduce air resistance and pressure, so the fly doesn't sense the swatter coming.

faqs.question: Who named the fly swatter?
faqs.answer: Kansas public health official Samuel Crumbine popularized the name around 1905.

faqs.question: Why is it hard to swat flies?
faqs.answer: Flies process visual motion very quickly and can plan an escape jump in a fraction of a second.

image.alt: A plastic fly swatter

name: Fly whisk

place_of_invention.notes: Fly whisks of animal hair on handles appear in ancient Egyptian art and were used across Africa and Asia; they likely arose in many places.

short_description: A tuft of animal hair or fibre on a handle, waved to drive away flies.
description: Fly whisks were used in ancient Egypt, where they also became symbols of royal authority. In many African and Asian cultures they remain both practical tools and signs of status or religious office. The tuft-on-a-handle design has never changed.
why_unchanged: A light tuft on a handle waves insects away without harming anything.

faqs.question: Why are fly whisks symbols of power?
faqs.answer: In ancient Egypt and many African cultures, fly whisks were carried by rulers and elders as signs of authority.

faqs.question: What is a chowrie?
faqs.answer: A chowrie is a South Asian fly whisk, often of yak tail, used in religious and royal ceremonies.

faqs.question: Do people still use fly whisks?
faqs.answer: Yes; they are used in hot regions and by riders and herders to drive off flies.

image.alt: A horsehair fly whisk with a wooden handle

name: Flypaper

place_of_invention.notes: Sticky fly-catching papers were sold in Europe and the US in the 19th century; the Thum family's 'Tanglefoot' brand, launched in Grand Rapids in the 1880s, made it widespread. No single inventor is clearly credited.

short_description: A strip or sheet of paper coated with sticky material that traps flies.
description: Before screens and sprays, sticky paper hung from ceilings or laid on tables was one of the main ways to control flies. In the 1880s the Thum brothers of Grand Rapids sold 'Tanglefoot' sticky flypaper widely. Hanging spiral flypaper ribbons are still sold today.
why_unchanged: A sticky surface catches insects without chemicals or mechanism.

faqs.question: How does flypaper attract flies?
faqs.answer: It is coated with a sticky mixture, often with a sweet scent, that lures flies who then get stuck.

faqs.question: Is flypaper toxic?
faqs.answer: Modern flypaper is generally non-toxic, relying on stickiness rather than poison, though early versions sometimes contained arsenic.

faqs.question: Where should flypaper be hung?
faqs.answer: Near windows, lights or places where flies gather, away from where people walk.

image.alt: A strip of flypaper hanging from a ceiling

name: Folding chair

place_of_invention.notes: Folding stools with crossed legs are known from Middle Kingdom Egypt; a Bronze Age folding stool from Guldhøj, Denmark (c. 1400 BCE) shows the idea spread widely.

short_description: A portable chair that collapses flat for storage.
description: Ancient Egyptians made folding stools with X-shaped crossed legs, sometimes inlaid with ivory, and similar ones were used by Roman magistrates as the 'sella curulis'. Folding seating spread through medieval Europe for travelling nobles and clergy. Modern metal and wooden folding chairs use the same scissor principle.
why_unchanged: Hinged crossed legs collapse flat and lock open under weight, a design that needs no improvement.

faqs.question: Why did Roman officials use folding chairs?
faqs.answer: The curule seat was a folding chair that magistrates could carry with them, and it became a symbol of authority.

faqs.question: What is a faldstool?
faqs.answer: A faldstool is a medieval folding seat used by bishops and kings, related to the word 'fauteuil'.

faqs.question: How old is the folding chair?
faqs.answer: Folding stools are known from ancient Egypt about 4,000 years ago.

image.alt: A folding chair, open and ready to use

name: Folding screen

place_of_invention.notes: Folding screens are recorded in China by the Han dynasty, and possibly earlier; they spread to Japan, Korea and later Europe.

short_description: A free-standing screen of hinged panels used to divide a room or block drafts.
description: Folding screens were developed in China, where hinged panels of wood, lacquer or silk divided spaces and blocked drafts. They spread to Japan as byōbu, often painted by leading artists, and reached Europe in the 17th and 18th centuries. Today they still serve as room dividers and dressing screens.
why_unchanged: Hinged panels stand by themselves in a zigzag and fold flat, a design that cannot be simplified.

faqs.question: What is a byōbu?
faqs.answer: A byōbu is a Japanese folding screen, often decorated with paintings or gold leaf.

faqs.question: How does a folding screen stand up?
faqs.answer: Its panels are set at angles in a zigzag, which keeps it stable without any base.

faqs.question: Why were folding screens used in Western bedrooms?
faqs.answer: They provided privacy for dressing and blocked cold drafts.

image.alt: A painted Chinese folding screen

name: Footstool

place_of_invention.notes: Footstools are well known from Egyptian royal burials, including Tutankhamun's tomb; they were used across the ancient Near East.

short_description: A low stool on which to rest the feet while sitting.
description: Footstools in ancient Egypt raised the feet of rulers seated on high thrones, and Tutankhamun's footstools are decorated with images of defeated enemies. Through history they kept feet off cold floors and improved comfort. Footstools remain common household furniture.
why_unchanged: A low platform for the feet is too simple to need redesign.

faqs.question: Why did kings have footstools?
faqs.answer: Thrones were tall, so footstools supported the feet and symbolized power over subjects or enemies.

faqs.question: Are footstools good for posture?
faqs.answer: A footrest can help shorter people sit with their feet supported and knees at a comfortable angle.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a footstool and an ottoman?
faqs.answer: A footstool is usually small and on legs, while an ottoman is larger and upholstered, often doubling as a seat.

image.alt: A small upholstered footstool

name: Four-poster bed

place_of_invention.notes: Beds with tall corner posts supporting a canopy and curtains became fashionable in late medieval and Tudor Europe; earlier canopy beds existed in antiquity.

short_description: A bed with four tall corner posts, often supporting a canopy and curtains.
description: In late medieval and Tudor homes, four-poster beds held heavy curtains that kept out drafts and gave privacy in shared rooms. They were among the most valuable items in a household. Four-poster beds are still made as decorative statement pieces.
why_unchanged: Four posts supporting a frame overhead is the simplest way to hang curtains around a bed.

faqs.question: Why did four-poster beds have curtains?
faqs.answer: Curtains kept out drafts in cold houses and gave privacy when several people shared a room.

faqs.question: What is the Great Bed of Ware?
faqs.answer: It is a huge carved oak four-poster bed from about 1590, now in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London.

faqs.question: Is a canopy bed the same as a four-poster?
faqs.answer: A canopy bed has a cloth covering on top; most four-posters can support a canopy, but not all have one.

image.alt: A carved oak four-poster bed

name: Friction match

place_of_invention.notes: John Walker, a chemist, discovered the friction match in 1826 but did not patent it; others soon copied and sold the idea.

short_description: A small stick with a chemical head that ignites when struck against a rough surface.
description: John Walker, a chemist in Stockton-on-Tees, found that a stick coated with chemicals burst into flame when scraped. He sold his 'friction lights' from 1827 but never patented them. Strike-anywhere matches still follow the same principle.
why_unchanged: A combustible head that ignites by friction is all a match needs; nothing has proved simpler.

faqs.question: Who invented the friction match?
faqs.answer: English chemist John Walker discovered it in 1826 in Stockton-on-Tees.

faqs.question: Why didn't John Walker patent his match?
faqs.answer: He reportedly felt it should benefit the public, so he never patented it.

faqs.question: What is a 'strike anywhere' match?
faqs.answer: It is a match whose head contains all the chemicals needed to ignite on any rough surface.

image.alt: A box of wooden strike-anywhere matches

name: Futon

place_of_invention.notes: Japanese bedding laid on the floor developed over centuries; padded cotton futon mattresses became common during the Edo period as cotton cultivation spread. Dating is approximate.

short_description: A padded mattress laid on the floor for sleeping and folded away by day.
description: Traditional Japanese bedding consists of a shikibuton mattress and a kakebuton quilt laid on tatami mats at night. Cotton-filled futons became widespread during the Edo period, and they are folded and stored in a cupboard each morning to free the room. Western 'futons' adapted the idea to sofa beds, but the Japanese form is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A foldable floor mattress makes one room serve for living and sleeping, which remains valuable.

faqs.question: Why are futons aired in the sun?
faqs.answer: Hanging futons in sunlight dries out moisture and helps keep them fresh and fluffy.

faqs.question: Is a Japanese futon the same as a Western futon?
faqs.answer: No; a Japanese futon is a thin floor mattress, while a Western futon is often a thick mattress on a convertible sofa frame.

faqs.question: What is a shikibuton?
faqs.answer: It is the bottom mattress of a Japanese futon set, laid directly on tatami.

image.alt: A Japanese futon laid out on tatami mats

name: Hammock

place_of_invention.notes: Used by the Taíno and other Indigenous peoples long before European contact; the age is uncertain because fibre hammocks rarely survive. Europeans first recorded them in 1492.

short_description: A sling of fabric or netting hung between two points for sleeping or resting.
description: Indigenous peoples of the Caribbean and the Amazon slept in hammocks woven from plant fibres, which kept them off damp ground and away from insects and snakes. Columbus's crews described them in 1492, and the Taíno word 'hamaka' entered European languages. Navies adopted hammocks for sailors' sleeping quarters by the 16th century.
why_unchanged: A net or cloth slung between two anchor points needs no frame and conforms naturally to the body.

faqs.question: Why did sailors sleep in hammocks?
faqs.answer: Hammocks swing with the ship's motion, take little space and can be rolled up during the day to free the deck.

faqs.question: How should you lie in a hammock?
faqs.answer: Lying diagonally across a wide Brazilian- or Mayan-style hammock lets you lie almost flat.

faqs.question: Where does the word 'hammock' come from?
faqs.answer: It comes via Spanish 'hamaca' from the Taíno word for this sleeping net.

image.alt: A woven hammock hanging between two trees

name: Hand brush

place_of_invention.notes: Short-handled sweeping brushes for hearths, tables and floors were common household tools in Europe by the 18th century; no single origin is known.

short_description: A short-handled brush used with a dustpan to sweep up small amounts of dirt.
description: The hand brush lets debris be swept precisely into a dustpan or off tables and hearths. Hearth brushes and hand brushes of bristle or horsehair were standard in early modern households. Plastic and wood versions are used the same way today.
why_unchanged: Bristles on a short handle give control for small sweeping jobs, so the design endures.

faqs.question: What is a whisk broom?
faqs.answer: It is a small hand broom of stiff fibres used for brushing clothes, furniture or small areas.

faqs.question: What bristles are best for a hand brush?
faqs.answer: Soft bristles like horsehair suit fine dust, while stiff ones work better on coarse debris.

faqs.question: How do you clean a hand brush?
faqs.answer: Comb out debris and wash it in warm soapy water, then let it dry.

image.alt: A hand brush lying on a dustpan

name: High chair

place_of_invention.notes: Tall children's chairs that let infants sit at the family table were made in Europe and colonial America by the 18th century; some earlier examples are claimed. Origins are uncertain.

short_description: A tall chair for a baby or toddler, often with a tray, used at mealtimes.
description: High chairs raised small children to the height of the family table so they could eat with adults. Early versions were tall wooden chairs with long legs and a bar across the front. Modern versions add trays and straps but keep the same tall seat on splayed legs.
why_unchanged: Lifting a child to table height with a safe seat and wide legs is an unchanged need.

faqs.question: When can a baby use a high chair?
faqs.answer: Usually when they can sit up on their own, often around six months.

faqs.question: Why do high chairs have splayed legs?
faqs.answer: Wide-set legs make the tall chair more stable and less likely to tip.

faqs.question: Do high chairs need a harness?
faqs.answer: Safety standards recommend using the restraint system to prevent falls.

image.alt: A wooden child's high chair

name: Ironing board

place_of_invention.notes: Boards laid across tables or chairs were used earlier; a folding ironing table was patented in the US by W. Vandenburg and J. Harvey in 1858, and Sarah Boone patented an improved narrow board for sleeves in 1892.

short_description: A padded folding board on legs on which clothes are ironed.
description: Clothes were once ironed on tables or planks set across chairs. In the mid-19th century inventors patented folding ironing tables, and in 1892 Sarah Boone patented a narrow, curved board that made ironing sleeves and bodices easier. Modern ironing boards keep the padded, tapered top on folding legs.
why_unchanged: A narrow padded surface with a tapered end fits garments perfectly and folds away.

faqs.question: Who was Sarah Boone?
faqs.answer: Sarah Boone was an African American inventor who patented an improved ironing board in 1892.

faqs.question: Why is one end of an ironing board pointed?
faqs.answer: The narrow end lets you slip sleeves, collars and trouser legs over it.

faqs.question: Why does an ironing board cover have a reflective surface?
faqs.answer: A reflective cover bounces heat back into the fabric, which can speed ironing.

image.alt: A folding ironing board with an iron

name: Kerosene lamp

place_of_invention.notes: Ignacy Łukasiewicz built a practical kerosene lamp in Lviv in 1853, after distilling kerosene from petroleum; Abraham Gesner had earlier produced kerosene from coal.

short_description: A lamp that burns kerosene through a flat wick, shielded by a glass chimney.
description: Polish pharmacist Ignacy Łukasiewicz distilled kerosene from crude oil and, in 1853, built a lamp to burn it, lighting a hospital operation in Lviv. Kerosene lamps quickly replaced whale-oil lamps and candles worldwide. The fuel tank, adjustable wick and glass chimney are still produced today.
why_unchanged: An adjustable wick and glass chimney give a bright, steady flame with no further refinement needed.

faqs.question: Who invented the kerosene lamp?
faqs.answer: Ignacy Łukasiewicz built the first practical kerosene lamp in Lviv in 1853.

faqs.question: What does the glass chimney do?
faqs.answer: It creates an updraft that feeds air to the flame and shields it from drafts, making it bright and steady.

faqs.question: Are kerosene lamps still used?
faqs.answer: Yes, in areas without electricity and as emergency or decorative lighting.

image.alt: A vintage kerosene lamp with glass chimney

name: Kilim

place_of_invention.notes: Flat-woven rugs are very old in Anatolia, Persia and Central Asia, but few early examples survive and the date of origin is disputed.

short_description: A flat-woven rug with no pile, made by tightly interweaving coloured wefts.
description: Kilims are made on a loom by tightly packing coloured weft threads to hide the warps, creating a flat, reversible rug. They have been woven for centuries by nomadic and village weavers in Anatolia, Persia, the Caucasus and Central Asia. Traditional patterns and techniques are still passed down today.
why_unchanged: Flat tapestry weaving produces a durable, lightweight rug with only a simple loom.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a kilim and a carpet?
faqs.answer: A kilim is flat-woven with no pile, while a carpet has a raised surface of knotted tufts.

faqs.question: Why do kilims have slits?
faqs.answer: Many are woven with a slit-tapestry technique, leaving small gaps where colour areas meet.

faqs.question: Are kilims reversible?
faqs.answer: Yes; most kilims look nearly the same on both sides.

image.alt: A colourful Turkish kilim rug

name: Lantern

place_of_invention.notes: Romans used lanterns with panes of thin horn or bladder; paper and silk lanterns were developed independently in China.

short_description: A portable enclosed light with transparent sides and a carrying handle.
description: A lantern surrounds a flame with a protective case so it can be carried in wind and rain. Romans used lanterns with translucent horn panes, and glass panels became common later. Candle and oil lanterns are still used for camping and decoration, along with electric versions in the same shape.
why_unchanged: A shielded flame with a handle solves wind and portability in one simple design.

faqs.question: Why were lanterns once called 'lanthorns'?
faqs.answer: In English the word was often spelled 'lanthorn' because the panes were made of thin, translucent horn.

faqs.question: What is a hurricane lantern?
faqs.answer: It is a lantern with a glass chimney and air flow design that keeps the flame burning in strong wind.

faqs.question: Why are lanterns important in festivals?
faqs.answer: Lanterns symbolize light and hope in many cultures, such as the Chinese Lantern Festival.

image.alt: An old metal and glass lantern with a candle

name: Lint roller

place_of_invention.notes: Nicholas McKay is credited with inventing the adhesive lint roller in 1956; it was later marketed under the Helmac brand.

short_description: A handled roller covered with sticky paper that lifts lint and hair from clothing.
description: Nicholas McKay devised the lint roller in 1956, wrapping a roller in adhesive tape with the sticky side out. As each layer fills with lint, it is peeled off to reveal a fresh one. The design is still essentially the same.
why_unchanged: A rolling sticky surface with tear-off layers is the fastest way to lift lint from fabric.

faqs.question: Who invented the lint roller?
faqs.answer: Nicholas McKay is credited with inventing it in 1956.

faqs.question: Does a lint roller remove pet hair?
faqs.answer: Yes; it is one of the most popular tools for removing pet hair from clothes and furniture.

faqs.question: Is there a reusable lint roller?
faqs.answer: Yes; some use washable sticky silicone or fabric brushes instead of disposable sheets.

image.alt: A lint roller being used on a jacket

name: Mattress

place_of_invention.notes: Layers of plant bedding about 77,000 years old found at Sibudu Cave are the oldest known; stuffed mattresses on frames came much later in Egypt, Persia and Rome.

short_description: A padded pad on which a person sleeps.
description: The oldest known bedding, found at Sibudu Cave in South Africa, consisted of layers of sedges and rushes, some containing insect-repelling leaves. Later cultures stuffed cloth bags with straw, wool, feathers or horsehair. Modern mattresses with springs or foam keep the same idea of a thick padded layer.
why_unchanged: A padded layer between body and hard surface is all a sleeper needs.

faqs.question: What is the oldest known bedding?
faqs.answer: About 77,000-year-old layers of plant bedding were found at Sibudu Cave in South Africa.

faqs.question: Why did ancient bedding include aromatic leaves?
faqs.answer: Leaves from plants such as Cape laurel contain chemicals that repel mosquitoes and other insects.

faqs.question: How often should you replace a mattress?
faqs.answer: Many experts suggest every seven to ten years, depending on comfort and wear.

image.alt: A mattress on a bed frame

name: Mop

place_of_invention.notes: The English word 'mop' is recorded from the 15th century, and cloths on sticks were likely used earlier. Later improvements include Thomas W. Stewart's 1893 US mop patent with a wringing mechanism.

short_description: A bundle of absorbent fibres or cloth on a handle, used to wash floors.
description: Mops made of rags or yarn tied to a stick were used on ships' decks and floors for centuries. In the 19th century inventors added clamping heads and wringers, but the core idea of absorbent strands on a pole remained. String mops and flat mops are still standard cleaning tools.
why_unchanged: Absorbent strands on a long handle lift water off the floor without the user kneeling.

faqs.question: Why are sailors sometimes called 'swabbies'?
faqs.answer: Sailors cleaned, or 'swabbed', the decks with mops called swabs, so the nickname stuck.

faqs.question: How often should a mop head be replaced?
faqs.answer: Many cleaners recommend washing mop heads after each use and replacing them every few months to avoid spreading bacteria.

faqs.question: What is a 'mop-up' operation?
faqs.answer: It means finishing off remaining tasks, from the idea of mopping up the last of a spill.

image.alt: A cotton string mop next to a bucket

name: Mosquito coil

place_of_invention.notes: Eiichiro Ueyama developed pyrethrum incense sticks in the 1890s; the spiral coil, which burns longer, was introduced around 1902, an idea attributed to his wife Yuki.

short_description: A spiral of insect-repellent paste that smoulders slowly to keep mosquitoes away.
description: Japanese businessman Eiichiro Ueyama made incense sticks containing pyrethrum, a natural insecticide from chrysanthemum flowers. Around 1902 the spiral shape was introduced so the coil could burn for hours in a compact form. Mosquito coils are still widely used in Asia, Africa and Latin America.
why_unchanged: A spiral packs a long burn into a small space and needs no electricity.

faqs.question: Why is a mosquito coil shaped like a spiral?
faqs.answer: The spiral lets a long strip burn for hours while staying compact and stable.

faqs.question: What is in a mosquito coil?
faqs.answer: Traditionally pyrethrum powder from chrysanthemum flowers, though many modern coils use synthetic pyrethroids.

faqs.question: Are mosquito coils safe indoors?
faqs.answer: Their smoke can irritate lungs, so they are best used outdoors or in well-ventilated spaces.

image.alt: A green mosquito coil burning on a stand

name: Murphy bed

place_of_invention.notes: William Lawrence Murphy developed the wall bed in San Francisco around 1900 and founded the Murphy Wall Bed Company; earlier folding beds existed, but his name became the generic term.

short_description: A bed hinged at one end that folds up into a wall or cabinet when not in use.
description: According to company history, William Lawrence Murphy designed a bed that folded into a closet so his one-room apartment could double as a parlor. The design spread through apartments and hotels in the early 20th century. Murphy beds still use the same pivot-and-counterbalance principle.
why_unchanged: A hinged bed balanced by springs or pistons hides away easily, so the idea has not changed.

faqs.question: Who invented the Murphy bed?
faqs.answer: William Lawrence Murphy of San Francisco developed it around 1900.

faqs.question: Is a Murphy bed safe?
faqs.answer: Modern Murphy beds use counterbalance systems and must be properly anchored to the wall to be safe.

faqs.question: Why are Murphy beds popular in small apartments?
faqs.answer: Folding the bed away frees floor space so one room can serve as both bedroom and living room.

image.alt: A Murphy bed folding into a wall cabinet

name: Oil lamp

place_of_invention.notes: Carved stone lamps burning animal fat have been found at Lascaux and other Paleolithic caves; clay lamps later became widespread across the Near East and Mediterranean.

short_description: A vessel holding oil or fat with a wick that burns to give light.
description: Paleolithic people burned animal fat in hollowed stones, and lamps found at Lascaux in France lit cave painters' work. Clay lamps with a spout for the wick spread across the ancient Near East, Greece and Rome. Oil lamps are still used in religious ceremonies such as Diwali and in places without electricity.
why_unchanged: A reservoir of fuel feeding a wick is the simplest steady flame, unchanged for millennia.

faqs.question: What fuel did ancient oil lamps use?
faqs.answer: They burned animal fat, olive oil, sesame oil and other plant oils depending on the region.

faqs.question: What is a diya?
faqs.answer: A diya is a small clay oil lamp used in South Asia, especially during the festival of Diwali.

faqs.question: Were the lamps of Aladdin real oil lamps?
faqs.answer: Yes, the story imagines a typical Middle Eastern oil lamp with a spout for the wick.

image.alt: An ancient clay oil lamp

name: Ottoman

place_of_invention.notes: The name and form were inspired by low cushioned seating in the Ottoman Empire, which became fashionable in Europe in the late 18th century.

short_description: A low, padded, backless seat or footrest, often with storage inside.
description: Ottomans take their name from the Ottoman Empire, where low cushioned seating was common. Europeans adopted the form in the late 18th century, first as long divans and later as padded footrests and seats. Today's ottomans, often with hidden storage, follow the same simple padded design.
why_unchanged: A padded block is a versatile seat, footrest and table in one simple piece.

faqs.question: Why is it called an ottoman?
faqs.answer: It is named after the Ottoman Empire, whose cushioned seating inspired it.

faqs.question: What is a storage ottoman?
faqs.answer: It is an ottoman with a hinged or removable top concealing a storage space inside.

faqs.question: Can an ottoman replace a coffee table?
faqs.answer: Yes; with a tray on top, a firm ottoman often serves as a coffee table.

image.alt: A leather upholstered ottoman

name: Paper lantern

place_of_invention.notes: Paper lanterns followed the development of papermaking in Han China; the exact date of the first paper lantern is uncertain, and silk lanterns may have come first.

short_description: A lantern made of paper stretched over a frame of bamboo or wire.
description: After papermaking was refined in Han dynasty China, paper stretched over bamboo frames was used to shield and diffuse candle flames. Lanterns became central to festivals such as the Lantern Festival marking the end of Chinese New Year. Paper lanterns are still made the same way and used for decoration around the world.
why_unchanged: Paper on a light frame diffuses light beautifully and folds flat, needing no improvement.

faqs.question: What is the Lantern Festival?
faqs.answer: It is a Chinese festival held on the 15th day of the first lunar month, marking the end of New Year celebrations.

faqs.question: Are paper lanterns safe with candles?
faqs.answer: Real flames can ignite paper, so LED lights are commonly used today.

faqs.question: What is a chōchin?
faqs.answer: A chōchin is a traditional Japanese collapsible paper lantern, often hung outside shops and shrines.

image.alt: Red Chinese paper lanterns hanging

name: Paper towel

place_of_invention.notes: The Scott Paper Company sold 'Sani-Towels' for public washrooms from 1907; kitchen rolls followed in 1931.

short_description: A disposable sheet of absorbent paper, usually torn from a perforated roll.
description: The Scott Paper Company introduced paper towels in 1907 as a more hygienic alternative to shared cloth towels in schools and washrooms. A perforated kitchen roll followed in 1931 and became a household staple. Paper towels still come as perforated rolls of absorbent paper.
why_unchanged: A roll of absorbent, tear-off sheets is about as convenient as cleaning up a spill can get.

faqs.question: Why were paper towels invented?
faqs.answer: To replace shared cloth roller towels, which spread germs in schools and public washrooms.

faqs.question: When did paper towels come to kitchens?
faqs.answer: Scott Paper launched a kitchen roll in 1931, and it became common after World War II.

faqs.question: Are paper towels recyclable?
faqs.answer: Usually not, because the fibers are short and often contaminated, but used ones can be composted.

image.alt: A roll of white paper towels on a holder

name: Peg rail

place_of_invention.notes: Wooden pegs set into wall boards are much older; the Shakers made the continuous peg rail a signature feature of their buildings from the late 18th century.

short_description: A wooden board with a row of turned pegs, mounted on a wall for hanging things.
description: The Shakers, a religious community in the United States, lined their rooms with peg rails to hang clothes, tools and even chairs off the floor for cleaning. The simple board of turned wooden pegs became an icon of practical design. Peg rails are still popular in hallways and kitchens.
why_unchanged: A row of pegs on a board is maximally simple and endlessly adaptable storage.

faqs.question: Why did the Shakers hang chairs on the wall?
faqs.answer: Hanging chairs on peg rails cleared the floor for sweeping, reflecting their emphasis on order and cleanliness.

faqs.question: What are Shaker pegs made of?
faqs.answer: Traditionally turned hardwoods such as maple or cherry.

faqs.question: Where are peg rails used today?
faqs.answer: They are common in entryways, mudrooms, kitchens and children's rooms.

image.alt: A wooden Shaker peg rail with hanging items

name: Picture frame

place_of_invention.notes: Painted borders and carved surrounds were integral to many earlier panels, and a framed Roman-era Fayum portrait from Egypt is known; frames made separately from the picture became standard in 15th-century Europe.

short_description: A border that surrounds and protects a picture, photograph or artwork.
description: Early panel paintings often had frames carved from the same piece of wood as the painting surface. In the 15th century, frames began to be made separately and attached, allowing them to be changed with fashion. Today's frames still use the same moulding, glazing and backing structure.
why_unchanged: A rigid border that protects the edges and sets the image apart from the wall needs no reinvention.

faqs.question: Why are many old frames gilded?
faqs.answer: Gold leaf reflected candlelight and signalled the value of the painting and its owner.

faqs.question: What is a mat or passe-partout?
faqs.answer: It is a card border placed between the frame and artwork that adds space and keeps the image from touching the glass.

faqs.question: Should picture frame glass be UV-protective?
faqs.answer: For valuable or light-sensitive works, UV-filtering glazing helps slow fading.

image.alt: An ornate gilded picture frame

name: Pile rug

place_of_invention.notes: The Pazyryk carpet, found frozen in a Scythian burial mound, is the oldest known knotted-pile carpet; the technique may have originated in Central Asia or Persia.

short_description: A floor covering with a soft surface made of knotted yarn tufts.
description: Knotted-pile rugs are made by tying short lengths of yarn around the warp threads of a loom, creating a dense, soft surface. The Pazyryk carpet from about the 4th century BCE shows that the technique was already highly refined. Hand-knotted rugs from Persia, Anatolia and the Caucasus are still made the same way.
why_unchanged: Hand-knotting yields a durable, insulating surface, and the loom process has no better manual alternative.

faqs.question: What is the oldest known carpet?
faqs.answer: The Pazyryk carpet, discovered in Siberia in 1949 and dating from about the 4th century BCE, is the oldest known knotted-pile carpet.

faqs.question: How is a rug different from a carpet?
faqs.answer: A rug usually covers part of a floor and is movable, while a carpet often covers a whole room.

faqs.question: Why are hand-knotted rugs expensive?
faqs.answer: A single rug can contain hundreds of thousands of individually tied knots and take months to make.

image.alt: A hand-knotted Persian rug

name: Pillow

place_of_invention.notes: Frequently cited as early Mesopotamian stone headrests, though the dating and identification are not firmly established. Soft stuffed pillows were later used by Greeks, Romans and Chinese.

short_description: A cushioned support for the head during sleep.
description: Early head supports in Mesopotamia, Egypt and China were often hard, made of stone, wood or ceramic, and kept the head raised and hair tidy. Greeks and Romans used soft pillows stuffed with feathers, straw or reeds. The stuffed fabric pillow has stayed essentially the same ever since.
why_unchanged: A soft, filled bag that supports the neck works for every sleeper and needs no mechanism.

faqs.question: Why did ancient people use hard pillows?
faqs.answer: Hard headrests kept the head off the ground, away from insects, and protected elaborate hairstyles.

faqs.question: How often should pillows be replaced?
faqs.answer: Many sleep experts suggest replacing pillows every one to two years as they lose support and collect allergens.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a pillow and a cushion?
faqs.answer: A pillow usually supports the head in bed, while a cushion is for seating or decoration.

image.alt: Two white pillows on a bed

name: Plunger

place_of_invention.notes: The rubber force cup spread with indoor plumbing; no single inventor is reliably documented.

short_description: A rubber suction cup on a stick used to clear blocked drains and toilets.
description: The plunger appeared alongside indoor plumbing and vulcanized rubber in the late 19th century. Pushing and pulling the cup creates pressure and suction that dislodge a blockage in the pipe. Flanged versions for toilets were added later, but the basic cup-on-a-handle is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A flexible cup that seals over a drain and pumps pressure into it clears most clogs without tools or chemicals.

faqs.question: How does a plunger work?
faqs.answer: The cup seals over the drain, and pushing and pulling it alternates pressure and suction, which loosens the clog.

faqs.question: Why are there different plunger shapes?
faqs.answer: A flat cup suits sinks and tubs, while a flanged plunger has an extra lip that fits into a toilet's curved drain.

faqs.question: Who invented the plunger?
faqs.answer: No single inventor is reliably credited; the rubber force cup spread in the late 19th century with indoor plumbing.

image.alt: A red rubber plunger with a wooden handle

name: Quilt

place_of_invention.notes: Quilting as a technique is much older (a quilted textile from Noin-Ula, Mongolia, dates to around the 1st century BCE); the Tristan Quilts from Sicily are among the oldest surviving quilted bedcovers.

short_description: A bed covering made of layers of fabric and padding stitched together.
description: A quilt sandwiches a layer of batting between two fabrics and holds them together with lines of stitching. The Tristan Quilts, made in Sicily in the late 14th century, are among the earliest surviving quilted bedcovers. Patchwork quilting later became a celebrated folk art, especially in North America.
why_unchanged: Stitching layers together keeps the filling evenly spread, a solution that cannot be bettered with thread and cloth.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a quilt and a duvet?
faqs.answer: A quilt is stitched through all its layers and usually thinner, while a duvet is a loosely filled bag typically used inside a removable cover.

faqs.question: What is a quilting bee?
faqs.answer: It is a social gathering where people work together on a quilt, a tradition especially strong in 19th-century America.

faqs.question: Are quilts only for beds?
faqs.answer: No; quilted fabric is also used in clothing, wall hangings and historically as padding under armour.

image.alt: A colourful patchwork quilt

name: Rocking chair

place_of_invention.notes: Rocking chairs appear in England and the American colonies in the early 1700s, likely by adding rockers to existing chairs; the popular claim that Benjamin Franklin invented it is not supported by evidence.

short_description: A chair mounted on curved rockers so that it rocks back and forth.
description: Rocking chairs emerged in the early 18th century, possibly by fitting cradle-style rockers to ordinary chairs. They became especially popular in North America, with styles such as the Boston rocker. The curved rockers and chair body are still the same today.
why_unchanged: Two curved runners turn any chair into a soothing rocker, a design that needs nothing more.

faqs.question: Did Benjamin Franklin invent the rocking chair?
faqs.answer: That is a popular myth; rocking chairs existed in the early 18th century, but there is no solid evidence that Franklin invented them.

faqs.question: Is rocking good for you?
faqs.answer: Gentle rocking can be calming and is used in some care settings for people with dementia.

faqs.question: What is a Boston rocker?
faqs.answer: It is a popular 19th-century American rocking chair with a spindle back and a curved seat.

image.alt: A wooden rocking chair on a porch

name: Safety match

place_of_invention.notes: Gustaf Erik Pasch patented the idea of putting red phosphorus on the striking surface in 1844; Johan Edvard Lundström improved and mass-produced safety matches in Jönköping from the 1850s.

short_description: A match that lights only when struck on a special surface on its box.
description: Early matches used toxic white phosphorus and lit too easily. In 1844 Swedish chemist Gustaf Erik Pasch separated the chemicals, putting red phosphorus on the striking strip, and the Lundström brothers of Jönköping made the design a commercial success. The safety match and its striking box are unchanged today.
why_unchanged: Splitting the chemistry between head and box made matches safe without adding complexity.

faqs.question: Why are they called safety matches?
faqs.answer: They only light when struck on the box's special strip, so they rarely ignite by accident.

faqs.question: Why was white phosphorus dangerous?
faqs.answer: It was toxic and caused 'phossy jaw', a disease of match factory workers, and was later banned.

faqs.question: Where were safety matches mass-produced first?
faqs.answer: In Jönköping, Sweden, which became famous worldwide for its match industry.

image.alt: A matchbox with safety matches

name: Scrub brush

place_of_invention.notes: Brushes of plant fibre or animal hair are very old; the stiff-bristled block brush for scrubbing floors and laundry was a standard household tool in Europe by the 18th century. Precise origin unknown.

short_description: A handheld brush with stiff bristles set in a block, used for scrubbing surfaces.
description: Scrub brushes have a wooden or plastic block filled with stiff bristles, sometimes shaped to fit the hand. They were essential for cleaning wooden floors, stone steps and laundry before machines took over. They are still used for tough cleaning jobs everywhere.
why_unchanged: A block of stiff bristles concentrates hand pressure into scrubbing power, and that physics has not changed.

faqs.question: What bristles do scrub brushes use?
faqs.answer: Traditional brushes used plant fibres such as tampico or animal hair; modern ones mostly use nylon or polypropylene.

faqs.question: Why do some scrub brushes have a pointed end?
faqs.answer: The pointed tip reaches into corners and along edges where a rectangular brush cannot.

faqs.question: How do you clean a scrub brush?
faqs.answer: Rinse it thoroughly, soak it in hot soapy water or diluted vinegar, and let it dry bristles-down.

image.alt: A wooden scrub brush with stiff bristles

name: Shelf

place_of_invention.notes: Stone 'dressers' with shelves at Skara Brae are among the oldest surviving examples; wall ledges and niches were likely used even earlier.

short_description: A flat horizontal board fixed to a wall or frame for holding objects.
description: At the Neolithic village of Skara Brae in Orkney, each house had a stone dresser with shelves facing the entrance, probably to display important possessions. Wooden shelves on brackets became common in later homes, shops and libraries. The form is still a horizontal plank held level.
why_unchanged: A level board at a convenient height is the most direct way to store items off the floor.

faqs.question: What is the oldest known shelf?
faqs.answer: The stone dressers at Skara Brae in Scotland, built around 3100 BCE, are among the oldest surviving shelved furniture.

faqs.question: How much weight can a wall shelf hold?
faqs.answer: It depends on the brackets and anchoring; shelves screwed into wall studs can hold far more than those held only by drywall plugs.

faqs.question: What does 'on the shelf' mean?
faqs.answer: It means set aside or no longer in use, from the idea of something stored away on a shelf.

image.alt: A wooden wall shelf holding books

name: Shoji screen

place_of_invention.notes: Sliding paper-covered doors developed in Japanese architecture from the Heian period onward; the familiar latticed shoji became widespread with the shoin style of the Muromachi period. Dating is approximate.

short_description: A sliding door or panel made of translucent paper on a wooden lattice.
description: Shoji are sliding panels of washi paper stretched over a light wooden grid, used in traditional Japanese homes as doors, windows and room dividers. The paper diffuses soft daylight into the room while giving privacy. Modern shoji are made in the same way, sometimes with tougher synthetic paper.
why_unchanged: Paper on a wooden lattice is light, translucent and slides easily, which is exactly what is needed.

faqs.question: What is the difference between shoji and fusuma?
faqs.answer: Shoji use translucent paper to let light through, while fusuma are opaque sliding panels used between rooms.

faqs.question: How do you repair a torn shoji?
faqs.answer: Small tears can be patched with paper, or the whole panel can be re-papered with rice glue.

faqs.question: Why do shoji slide instead of swing?
faqs.answer: Sliding panels save space and let rooms be opened up or divided flexibly.

image.alt: Japanese shoji sliding doors with paper panels

name: Spring clothespin

place_of_invention.notes: David M. Smith patented the spring-hinged clothespin in 1853; one-piece wooden pegs without springs are older.

short_description: Two wooden or plastic levers joined by a coiled spring that clamp laundry to a line.
description: Before the spring clothespin, laundry was held with one-piece split wooden pegs. In 1853 David M. Smith of Springfield, Vermont, patented a design with two levers and a spring that grips firmly. The familiar form, refined in the late 19th century, is still made by the millions.
why_unchanged: Two levers and a spring give a strong one-handed clamp with almost no material.

faqs.question: Who invented the spring clothespin?
faqs.answer: David M. Smith of Springfield, Vermont, received a patent for it in 1853.

faqs.question: What did people use before spring clothespins?
faqs.answer: They used one-piece wooden pegs with a slot cut into them, often made by hand.

faqs.question: Is there a giant clothespin sculpture?
faqs.answer: Yes, Claes Oldenburg's 'Clothespin' (1976) is a 45-foot steel sculpture in Philadelphia.

image.alt: Wooden spring clothespins on a line

name: Spring mousetrap

place_of_invention.notes: William C. Hooker received a US patent for a spring-loaded snap trap in 1894; James Henry Atkinson patented the similar 'Little Nipper' in Britain in 1897.

short_description: A wooden base with a spring-loaded bar that snaps shut when a mouse takes the bait.
description: William C. Hooker of Abingdon, Illinois, patented the spring-loaded snap trap in 1894, and James Henry Atkinson's British 'Little Nipper' followed in 1897. Despite thousands of later mousetrap patents, the classic wooden snap trap remains the best seller. It became a byword for a design that is hard to improve.
why_unchanged: A spring, a bar and a trigger kill quickly and cheaply, so countless 'better mousetraps' have failed to replace it.

faqs.question: Who invented the snap mousetrap?
faqs.answer: William C. Hooker patented it in the US in 1894, and James Henry Atkinson patented a similar British design in 1897.

faqs.question: What is the best bait for a mousetrap?
faqs.answer: Peanut butter or chocolate often work better than cheese because they are sticky and aromatic.

faqs.question: What does 'build a better mousetrap' mean?
faqs.answer: It means creating an improved version of a common product, a phrase often attributed to Ralph Waldo Emerson.

image.alt: A classic wooden spring mousetrap

name: Squeegee

place_of_invention.notes: Simple rubber-bladed squeegees were used on ships' decks earlier; Ettore Steccone patented the lightweight single-blade window squeegee in 1936, the design used by window cleaners ever since.

short_description: A rubber blade on a handle used to wipe water from windows and smooth surfaces.
description: Window washers once used heavy, multi-bladed squeegees. In 1936, Italian-born Ettore Steccone in Oakland, California, patented a light brass squeegee with a single replaceable rubber blade. His design remains the professional standard for cleaning glass.
why_unchanged: A single straight rubber edge wipes water cleanly off glass, a solution that cannot be bettered.

faqs.question: Who invented the modern window squeegee?
faqs.answer: Ettore Steccone patented the single-blade window squeegee in 1936.

faqs.question: How do professionals avoid streaks?
faqs.answer: They use a clean, sharp blade and wipe the edge between strokes, often in an S-shaped motion.

faqs.question: Where else are squeegees used?
faqs.answer: They are used in screen printing, on shower glass and for clearing water from floors.

image.alt: A window squeegee on a wet window

name: Stool

place_of_invention.region: Ancient Egypt and the Near East
place_of_invention.notes: Stools are among the oldest documented furniture in Egyptian tombs, but simple stools were almost certainly used earlier and in many places independently.

short_description: A backless, armless seat on legs or a solid base.
description: The stool is one of the oldest forms of furniture, found in ancient Egyptian tombs and depicted in Mesopotamian art. Three-legged stools were valued because they sit steadily on uneven floors. Today stools serve as kitchen seating, workshop seats and milking stools.
why_unchanged: A flat seat on legs is the minimal possible piece of seating, so there is nothing to simplify or improve.

faqs.question: Why do milking stools have three legs?
faqs.answer: Three legs always touch the ground at once, so a three-legged stool cannot wobble on an uneven barn floor.

faqs.question: Is the stool older than the chair?
faqs.answer: Most historians believe so, since the stool is simpler and appears very early in Egyptian burials, but both are ancient.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a stool and an ottoman?
faqs.answer: A stool is a hard raised seat on legs, while an ottoman is a low upholstered seat or footrest, usually without visible legs.

image.alt: A wooden three-legged stool

name: Table

place_of_invention.notes: Raised tables for offerings and dining appear in Egyptian and Mesopotamian art; earlier low platforms likely existed elsewhere.

short_description: A flat raised surface supported by legs.
description: Ancient Egyptians used small tables to hold food, offerings and objects, often low to the ground. Greeks and Romans used small tables placed beside dining couches, while large communal tables spread in medieval Europe. The basic form of a flat top on legs has barely changed.
why_unchanged: A flat top held at working height by legs is the simplest way to lift objects off the floor.

faqs.question: Why do we say 'set the table'?
faqs.answer: Many medieval tables were loose boards laid on trestles and set up for meals, then taken down afterwards.

faqs.question: What is the standard height of a dining table?
faqs.answer: Most dining tables are about 72 to 76 cm (28 to 30 inches) high, matched to standard chair seat heights.

faqs.question: Did ancient Romans eat at tables?
faqs.answer: Wealthy Romans reclined on couches around small low tables rather than sitting upright at a large one.

image.alt: A wooden table with four legs

name: Tatami mat

place_of_invention.notes: Tatami began as movable mats for sitting and sleeping in aristocratic Heian homes and later covered whole floors; the standardized room-covering tatami spread from the Muromachi period.

short_description: A thick rectangular floor mat of rice straw covered with woven rush.
description: Tatami mats were originally portable seats and beds for Japanese nobility, then became fixed floor coverings in whole rooms. Each mat has a rice-straw core covered with woven igusa rush and bound with cloth edges. Japanese rooms are still measured in numbers of tatami.
why_unchanged: A firm, cushioned, breathable rectangle that tiles a room is ideal for floor living.

faqs.question: How big is a tatami mat?
faqs.answer: Sizes vary by region, but a typical mat is about 1.8 by 0.9 metres, a 2:1 ratio.

faqs.question: Why are Japanese rooms measured in tatami?
faqs.answer: Rooms were laid out to fit whole mats, so a room's size is described as a number of mats, such as six-mat room.

faqs.question: Should you wear shoes on tatami?
faqs.answer: No; tatami are walked on with bare feet or socks to protect the delicate rush surface.

image.alt: A Japanese room covered with tatami mats

name: Torch

place_of_invention.notes: Traces of torch use have been found in Paleolithic caves in Europe; flaming brands were used worldwide and have no single origin.

short_description: A stick with a burning end, carried as a source of light.
description: Prehistoric people carried burning sticks and bundles of resinous wood to light caves, and soot marks on cave walls show where torches were tapped. Later torches were wrapped in cloth soaked with pitch or fat. Flaming torches are still used in ceremonies, the Olympic torch relay and outdoor lighting.
why_unchanged: A fuel-soaked stick is the most portable fire possible, needing no container.

faqs.question: How did prehistoric people use torches in caves?
faqs.answer: They carried burning sticks or bundles to light their way and the walls, leaving soot marks archaeologists still find.

faqs.question: Why is a flashlight called a 'torch' in Britain?
faqs.answer: When electric flashlights arrived, British English simply kept the old word for a handheld light.

faqs.question: When did the Olympic torch relay start?
faqs.answer: The modern torch relay began at the 1936 Berlin Olympics.

image.alt: A burning wooden torch

name: Trestle table

place_of_invention.notes: Boards laid on trestles were used in antiquity and became the standard dining table in medieval European halls; no single origin is known.

short_description: A table made of a board resting on separate supports called trestles.
description: In medieval halls, tables were often boards laid on trestles for meals and cleared away afterwards so the space could be used for other purposes. Later trestle tables had fixed supports joined by a stretcher. Folding trestles and boards are still used for markets, events and workshops.
why_unchanged: A top on two detachable supports is easy to build, carry and store.

faqs.question: Why were medieval tables taken apart?
faqs.answer: Great halls served many functions, so tables were dismantled after meals to clear the floor.

faqs.question: What is a trestle?
faqs.answer: A trestle is a supporting frame, often with splayed legs, used in pairs to hold up a board.

faqs.question: Are trestle tables still made?
faqs.answer: Yes; folding trestle tables are common for events, and fixed trestle-base dining tables are popular in farmhouse style.

image.alt: A wooden trestle table

name: Vase

place_of_invention.notes: Decorative pottery vessels were made in many early civilizations; using a vase specifically to display cut flowers is documented in ancient Egypt and became widespread in China and later Europe.

short_description: An open decorative vessel, often used to hold cut flowers.
description: Ancient potters in Mesopotamia, Egypt and China made ornamental vessels, and Egyptians placed flowers in vessels for offerings and decoration. Greek painted vases and Chinese porcelain later became celebrated art forms. The tall, open-mouthed vessel holding flowers in water is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A narrow-necked open vessel holds water and supports stems, so its form needs no improvement.

faqs.question: How do you keep cut flowers fresh in a vase?
faqs.answer: Use clean water, trim stems at an angle and change the water every couple of days.

faqs.question: Why are Ming vases so famous?
faqs.answer: Ming dynasty porcelain, especially blue-and-white ware, is prized for its quality, and rare pieces sell for millions.

faqs.question: What is the Portland Vase?
faqs.answer: It is a Roman cameo-glass vase from around the 1st century CE, now in the British Museum.

image.alt: A ceramic vase holding fresh flowers

name: Venetian blind

place_of_invention.notes: Slatted blinds were advertised in London in the 18th century and patented by Edward Bevan in 1841; the name links them to Venice, though Persian origins are also claimed. Origins are disputed.

short_description: A window blind of horizontal slats that can be tilted or raised with cords.
description: Venetian blinds have horizontal slats linked by cords or tapes, so they can be tilted to control light or drawn up completely. They were sold in 18th-century London and America, and Edward Bevan patented an improved version in 1841. Modern aluminium, wooden and vinyl blinds work the same way.
why_unchanged: Tiltable slats offer fine control of light and privacy with simple cords.

faqs.question: Why are they called Venetian blinds?
faqs.answer: The name suggests they reached Europe via Venetian traders, though the exact origin is uncertain.

faqs.question: How do you clean venetian blinds?
faqs.answer: Close the slats and wipe with a damp cloth or use a duster, then reverse and repeat.

faqs.question: Are corded blinds safe for children?
faqs.answer: Looped cords can be a strangulation hazard, so safety devices or cordless designs are recommended in homes with small children.

image.alt: A window with venetian blinds

name: Wall sconce

place_of_invention.notes: Wall brackets holding torches, candles or lamps were used in castles and churches throughout the Middle Ages; no single origin is known.

short_description: A light fixture attached to a wall, originally holding a candle or torch.
description: Medieval castles and churches used iron brackets on walls to hold torches and candles, saving floor and table space. Later sconces had a reflective backplate to amplify candlelight. Electric sconces today keep the same wall-mounted form.
why_unchanged: Mounting a light on the wall frees space and spreads light, a need that has not changed.

faqs.question: What does 'sconce' mean?
faqs.answer: It comes from an Old French word for a lantern, derived from Latin 'absconsa', meaning hidden or covered.

faqs.question: Why did old sconces have mirrors?
faqs.answer: A mirrored or polished backplate reflected candlelight, making the room brighter.

faqs.question: Where are sconces used today?
faqs.answer: They are common in hallways, bathrooms and on either side of beds or mirrors.

image.alt: A brass candle wall sconce

name: Wardrobe

place_of_invention.notes: Large upright cupboards for hanging or storing clothes, such as the French armoire, developed from medieval chests and cupboards; no single inventor or place is known.

short_description: A tall cupboard with doors for hanging and storing clothes.
description: In the Middle Ages clothes were kept folded in chests, and a 'wardrobe' was a room where garments were stored. By the 17th century, tall freestanding cupboards such as the French armoire became fashionable for storing clothes upright. Built-in and freestanding wardrobes today keep the same tall, door-fronted form.
why_unchanged: A tall box with doors and a rail stores clothes hanging and dust-free in a small footprint.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a wardrobe and an armoire?
faqs.answer: An armoire is a type of tall, often ornate wardrobe, originally French; today the words are used almost interchangeably.

faqs.question: Why was a wardrobe originally a room?
faqs.answer: Medieval households kept clothing and valuables in a 'garderobe' or wardrobe room, and the name later passed to the furniture.

faqs.question: Which famous book features a wardrobe?
faqs.answer: C. S. Lewis's 'The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe' (1950), in which children enter Narnia through one.

image.alt: A tall wooden wardrobe with two doors

name: Warming pan

place_of_invention.notes: Covered pans filled with embers for warming beds were common in Europe by the 16th and 17th centuries; exact origin unknown.

short_description: A covered metal pan on a long handle, filled with hot coals and passed between bed sheets to warm them.
description: Before central heating, beds could be icy, so households filled a lidded brass or copper pan with embers and moved it between the sheets before bedtime. The long handle kept the user's hands away from the heat. Warming pans are now mostly decorative, but the design is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A lidded pan on a long handle carries heat safely into a bed with nothing more required.

faqs.question: How was a warming pan used?
faqs.answer: It was filled with embers, closed, and slid back and forth between the sheets to avoid scorching them.

faqs.question: What replaced the warming pan?
faqs.answer: Hot water bottles, and later electric blankets, became safer alternatives.

faqs.question: Why do warming pans have holes in the lid?
faqs.answer: The holes let a little air reach the embers so they keep glowing.

image.alt: An antique brass warming pan with a long handle

name: Washboard

place_of_invention.notes: Ridged wooden boards for washing clothes were used in Europe in the 18th century; Stephen Rust received a US patent for an improved washboard in 1833. The exact origin is unknown.

short_description: A ridged board on which wet clothes are rubbed to clean them.
description: Clothes are soaped and rubbed up and down the ridged surface of a washboard, forcing water and soap through the fibres. Wooden boards were later fitted with corrugated metal or glass surfaces in the 19th century. Washboards are still used for hand laundry and as instruments in folk and zydeco music.
why_unchanged: Corrugated ridges plus friction is the simplest effective way to scrub fabric by hand.

faqs.question: Are washboards still used for laundry?
faqs.answer: Yes, in many places without washing machines and by travellers or campers doing hand laundry.

faqs.question: How is a washboard used as an instrument?
faqs.answer: Players scrape the ridges with thimbles or spoons to create rhythm, especially in zydeco, skiffle and jug band music.

faqs.question: Why did some washboards have glass surfaces?
faqs.answer: Glass was smooth, rust-proof and gentle on fabric, and was used when metal was scarce in wartime.

image.alt: A vintage wooden and metal washboard

name: Wind chime

place_of_invention.notes: Bronze bells hung to ring in the wind were used in ancient China, and Romans hung bronze tintinnabula; the idea likely arose independently in several cultures.

short_description: A set of hanging tubes, rods or bells that ring when moved by the wind.
description: Wind bells were hung from the eaves of Chinese temples and pagodas to ring in the breeze, and Romans hung bronze chimes believed to ward off evil. Today wind chimes made of metal tubes, bamboo or glass hang in gardens and porches. Their form remains simple hanging sounding pieces.
why_unchanged: Free-hanging pieces struck by a central clapper make music from any breeze, with nothing to improve.

faqs.question: How are wind chimes tuned?
faqs.answer: The length, thickness and material of each tube determine its pitch, so tubes are cut to specific lengths.

faqs.question: What is a fūrin?
faqs.answer: A fūrin is a Japanese glass or metal wind bell, traditionally hung in summer for its cooling sound.

faqs.question: Why did Romans hang wind chimes?
faqs.answer: Roman tintinnabula were believed to ward off evil spirits and bring good luck.

image.alt: A metal wind chime hanging from a porch

name: Window shutter

place_of_invention.notes: Greek and Roman buildings used wooden or stone shutters; similar solid window covers were developed independently elsewhere.

short_description: A hinged panel that closes over a window to block light, weather or intruders.
description: Before glass was common, solid shutters were the main way to close a window opening against weather and thieves. Ancient Greek and Roman buildings used wooden or marble shutters, and louvred shutters later let air in while blocking sun. Hinged shutters remain popular in Mediterranean and colonial-style homes.
why_unchanged: A hinged panel over an opening is the most direct way to seal or shade it.

faqs.question: What are louvred shutters for?
faqs.answer: Angled slats let air circulate while blocking direct sunlight and rain, ideal for hot climates.

faqs.question: Why do many houses have shutters that don't close?
faqs.answer: Over time shutters became mostly ornamental, and many modern ones are fixed to the wall only for looks.

faqs.question: What are plantation shutters?
faqs.answer: They are interior shutters with wide adjustable louvres, associated with homes in the American South.

image.alt: Wooden shutters on a house window

name: Windsor chair

place_of_invention.notes: The Windsor chair developed in the early 18th century in England, possibly named after the town of Windsor, through which many were shipped; the precise origin is uncertain.

short_description: A wooden chair with a solid seat into which spindles and legs are fitted.
description: Windsor chairs have a thick, carved wooden seat into which the legs and the back spindles are separately socketed. They were made in England from the early 18th century and became immensely popular in colonial America. Windsor chairs are still made by hand and machine in the same way.
why_unchanged: Socketing every part into a solid seat makes a light, strong chair that needs no further refinement.

faqs.question: Why is it called a Windsor chair?
faqs.answer: It is thought to be named after Windsor, England, from where the chairs were shipped to London, though this is not certain.

faqs.question: What makes a Windsor chair distinctive?
faqs.answer: Its solid seat into which legs and spindles are fitted separately, rather than a frame structure.

faqs.question: Were Windsor chairs used by America's founders?
faqs.answer: Yes; Windsor chairs were used in Independence Hall in Philadelphia during the 18th century.

image.alt: A wooden Windsor chair with spindle back

name: Wire coat hanger

place_of_invention.notes: O. A. North received an 1869 US patent for a clothes hanger, and Albert J. Parkhouse is often credited with the bent-wire hanger in 1903 at the Timberlake Wire and Novelty Company in Jackson, Michigan; the attribution is disputed.

short_description: A shaped wire frame with a hook, used to hang clothes on a rail.
description: The familiar wire hanger, a triangle of bent wire with a hook on top, spread in the early 20th century. Albert J. Parkhouse is popularly said to have bent one from wire in 1903 when his workplace lacked coat hooks, but earlier patents exist. Wooden and plastic hangers use the same shoulder-shaped form.
why_unchanged: A shoulder-shaped frame with a hook keeps clothes wrinkle-free using a single piece of wire.

faqs.question: Who invented the wire coat hanger?
faqs.answer: It is often credited to Albert J. Parkhouse in 1903, but earlier hanger patents, such as O. A. North's in 1869, mean the credit is disputed.

faqs.question: Why do dry cleaners use wire hangers?
faqs.answer: They are cheap, light and can be recycled or returned for reuse.

faqs.question: Are wire hangers bad for clothes?
faqs.answer: Thin wire can leave marks and stretch shoulders on heavy garments, so wider wooden or padded hangers are often preferred.

image.alt: Several wire coat hangers on a rail

name: Woven mat

place_of_invention.notes: Impressions of woven mats in early Near Eastern settlements suggest great antiquity; mat-making from reeds and grasses arose independently in many cultures.

short_description: A flat floor covering woven from reeds, grass, rushes or other plant fibre.
description: Mats woven from plant materials are among the oldest household textiles, used for sitting, sleeping and covering earth floors. Traces of mats appear in early farming settlements of the Near East, and mat weaving was practised from Africa to Asia and the Americas. Woven reed, rush and palm-leaf mats are still made by hand around the world.
why_unchanged: Over-under weaving of local plant fibres is the simplest way to make a flat, durable surface.

faqs.question: What are traditional woven mats made from?
faqs.answer: Common materials include reeds, rushes, palm leaves, bamboo, seagrass and jute.

faqs.question: How do you clean a reed or seagrass mat?
faqs.answer: Vacuum regularly and spot-clean with a damp cloth; avoid soaking, since natural fibres can warp or rot.

faqs.question: Are woven mats used for prayer?
faqs.answer: Yes; mats are used in many traditions, and woven prayer mats are common in Muslim households.

image.alt: A hand-woven reed floor mat

name: Apple corer

place_of_invention.notes: Hand corers carved from bone or made of metal were in use in the 18th century; origins are not documented.

short_description: A tube-shaped blade pushed through an apple to remove its core.
description: Simple apple corers, sometimes carved from bone, were used in 18th-century homes. A round, sharpened tube is pushed through the fruit and twisted out, taking the seeds and core with it. Wedger-corers that also slice the fruit are a later addition, but the basic tube is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A sharpened tube removes a core in one push, so the basic tool needs no change.

faqs.question: How do you use an apple corer?
faqs.answer: Center it over the stem, push down through the apple and twist to pull out the core.

faqs.question: Can it be used on other fruit?
faqs.answer: Yes, it works on pears and can hollow out vegetables like zucchini for stuffing.

faqs.question: What were old apple corers made from?
faqs.answer: Some 18th- and 19th-century corers were carved from sheep bone.

image.alt: An apple corer pushed through an apple

name: Apple peeler

place_of_invention.notes: Moses Coates received a US patent for an apple parer in 1803; many crank parers were patented later in the century.

short_description: A hand-cranked machine that peels, and often cores and slices, an apple as it turns.
description: Moses Coates of Pennsylvania patented an apple parer in 1803, and inventors filed many improved crank designs throughout the 19th century. The apple is speared on a fork and turned by a crank while a blade rides along its surface. Cast-iron and modern clamp-on versions still work the same way.
why_unchanged: Turning the fruit against a fixed blade peels it in seconds, and the gearing needs no modern help.

faqs.question: Who invented the apple peeler?
faqs.answer: Moses Coates received a US patent for an apple parer in 1803.

faqs.question: Can it core and slice too?
faqs.answer: Many models peel, core and spiral-slice the apple in one turn of the crank.

faqs.question: Will it work on potatoes?
faqs.answer: Yes, many apple peelers also peel firm, round potatoes.

image.alt: A hand-cranked apple peeler with an apple

name: Baker's peel

place_of_invention.notes: Long-handled peels were used in Roman bakeries such as those at Pompeii; similar tools existed elsewhere.

short_description: A flat, shovel-like paddle used to slide bread and pizza into and out of an oven.
description: Roman bakers used long-handled paddles to load and unload bread from deep wood-fired ovens, as at Pompeii. The flat blade slides under a loaf and the long handle keeps the baker away from the heat. Pizzerias and bakeries still use the same peels of wood or metal.
why_unchanged: A flat blade on a long handle is the only practical way to reach into a deep hot oven.

faqs.question: Why is it called a peel?
faqs.answer: The word comes from the Latin pala, meaning spade.

faqs.question: Should I use a wooden or metal peel?
faqs.answer: Wood releases raw dough more easily, while thin metal slides under baked items better.

faqs.question: How do I stop dough sticking to the peel?
faqs.answer: Dust the peel with flour, semolina or cornmeal before placing the dough.

image.alt: A wooden peel sliding pizza into an oven

name: Bamboo steamer

place_of_invention.notes: Ceramic steaming vessels appear in Neolithic China; woven bamboo steamers developed later and their date is uncertain.

short_description: Stackable round baskets of woven bamboo placed over boiling water to steam food.
description: Steaming has deep roots in China, where Neolithic potters made steamer vessels with perforated bases thousands of years ago. Stackable bamboo baskets with woven lids became the classic form, absorbing excess moisture so food stays dry on the surface. They are indispensable for dumplings, buns and dim sum.
why_unchanged: Bamboo is light, cheap and absorbs condensation, so stacking baskets over water remains ideal.

faqs.question: Why use bamboo instead of metal?
faqs.answer: Bamboo absorbs condensation, so drips do not fall back onto food and make it soggy.

faqs.question: How do you stop food sticking?
faqs.answer: Line the basket with parchment, cabbage leaves or a cloth before adding dumplings.

faqs.question: Can several layers cook at once?
faqs.answer: Yes, baskets stack so different foods steam together; the bottom layer cooks fastest.

image.alt: Stacked bamboo steamer baskets with dumplings

name: Banneton

place_of_invention.notes: Woven proofing baskets are traditional in French and German baking; their exact origin is not documented.

short_description: A woven cane or wicker basket used to support bread dough while it rises.
description: Bannetons, called Gärkörbchen in German, support soft dough during its final rise so it keeps its shape. Flour dusted inside the basket leaves a distinctive spiral pattern on the loaf. Artisan bakers still use the same rattan or cane baskets.
why_unchanged: Woven cane wicks moisture and holds shape perfectly, so bakers have never needed an alternative.

faqs.question: What is a banneton for?
faqs.answer: It holds shaped dough during proofing so the loaf keeps its form.

faqs.question: How do I prevent sticking?
faqs.answer: Dust the basket generously with rice flour, which absorbs less moisture than wheat flour.

faqs.question: Do I bake bread in the banneton?
faqs.answer: No, the dough is turned out onto a peel or tray before baking.

image.alt: A rattan banneton with sourdough dough

name: Baster

place_of_invention.notes: Bulb basters became common in the 20th century; earlier cooks used spoons and ladles. Inventor not documented.
