description: Clipboards developed in the late 19th century from simple writing boards, adding a spring clip to keep paper in place. They let people write while standing, from inspectors and coaches to doctors on ward rounds. The board-and-clip design has not changed.
why_unchanged: A stiff board and a spring clip provide a portable desk with nothing more to add.

faqs.question: Who invented the clipboard?
faqs.answer: Several patents were filed in North America in the late 1800s, and no single inventor is clearly credited.

faqs.question: Why does a clipboard make people look official?
faqs.answer: It is associated with inspections and surveys, so carrying one signals that someone is working.

faqs.question: What is a storage clipboard?
faqs.answer: A clipboard with a shallow box behind the board for keeping extra forms and pens.

image.alt: A clipboard holding a sheet of paper

name: Codex

place_of_invention.notes: The Roman poet Martial mentions parchment codices in the late 1st century CE; the format was adopted early by Christians and had largely replaced the scroll by the 4th-5th century.

short_description: A book made of stacked sheets folded and bound along one edge, the form of all modern books.
description: The codex developed in the Roman world from bound wax tablets and parchment notebooks and gradually replaced the scroll between the 1st and 5th centuries. Its pages can be turned to any place, written on both sides and protected by covers. Every printed book today keeps the same basic structure.
why_unchanged: Pages bound at one edge allow random access and compact storage, which is why the form has lasted two thousand years.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a codex and a scroll?
faqs.answer: A codex has separate pages bound at one edge, while a scroll is a continuous rolled strip.

faqs.question: Why did the codex replace the scroll?
faqs.answer: It was more compact, used both sides of the page and allowed readers to jump to any passage.

faqs.question: What is the oldest complete codex of the Bible?
faqs.answer: Codex Sinaiticus, from the 4th century CE, contains the oldest complete New Testament.

image.alt: An open medieval codex with handwritten pages

name: Colored pencil

place_of_invention.notes: Coloured drawing pencils were made by several European manufacturers in the late 19th and early 20th centuries; no single inventor or firm is reliably credited.

short_description: A pencil with a core of pigment bound in wax or oil instead of graphite.
description: Coloured pencils became widely available from European pencil makers in the early 20th century, using pigments bound in wax or oil and encased in wood like an ordinary pencil. They became a standard tool for children, illustrators and mapmakers. The form is identical to the graphite pencil, with only the core changed.
why_unchanged: It borrows the proven wood-cased pencil form, which needs no change to carry colour.

faqs.question: How are colored pencils different from crayons?
faqs.answer: Colored pencils have a thin, harder core encased in wood, allowing fine detail, while crayons are solid wax sticks.

faqs.question: Can colored pencils be erased?
faqs.answer: Lightly applied colour can often be lifted with a plastic eraser, but heavy wax-based layers are hard to remove.

faqs.question: What are watercolor pencils?
faqs.answer: They have water-soluble cores, so colour laid down dry can be blended with a wet brush.

image.alt: A row of sharpened colored pencils

name: Composition notebook

place_of_invention.notes: Sewn notebooks with marbled covers were sold for school compositions in the 19th century; marbled paper itself was introduced to Europe from the Middle East and Turkey. No inventor is documented.

short_description: A sewn notebook with stiff black-and-white marbled covers.
description: The composition notebook takes its name from its use for school compositions in the 19th century. Its pages are sewn and glued along the spine, so they cannot easily be removed, making it a trusted record for lab notes and diaries. The black-and-white marbled cover is a design classic.
why_unchanged: Sewn pages in a stiff cover make a durable permanent record, so the format has not changed.

faqs.question: Why is the cover marbled?
faqs.answer: Marbled covers imitate traditional marbled paper used in bookbinding and help hide wear.

faqs.question: Why do scientists use composition notebooks?
faqs.answer: Their sewn pages cannot be removed without trace, making them good permanent records.

faqs.question: What does the name mean?
faqs.answer: They were originally used for writing compositions, or essays, in school.

image.search_query: black and white marbled composition notebook
image.alt: A black-and-white marbled composition notebook

name: Correction fluid

place_of_invention.notes: Bette Nesmith Graham, a secretary, created a white tempera-based correction fluid in 1956, sold as Mistake Out and later Liquid Paper.

short_description: An opaque white fluid painted over typing or writing mistakes to cover them.
description: Typist Bette Nesmith Graham began painting over her errors with white tempera paint in the 1950s and founded a company to sell it, later renamed Liquid Paper. The small bottle with a brush in the cap became a staple of offices. Pen-style and tape versions followed, but the bottle-and-brush form remains.
why_unchanged: A small bottle with a cap brush covers mistakes quickly and precisely, so it never needed a new design.

faqs.question: Who invented correction fluid?
faqs.answer: Bette Nesmith Graham, a Texas secretary, invented it in 1956.

faqs.question: Is there a fun fact about its inventor?
faqs.answer: Bette Nesmith Graham's son was Michael Nesmith of the band The Monkees.

faqs.question: What is correction fluid made of?
faqs.answer: It is mostly white titanium dioxide pigment mixed with a quick-drying solvent and resins.

image.alt: A bottle of white correction fluid with its brush applicator

name: Crayon

place_of_invention.notes: Wax-based drawing crayons were made in Europe in the 19th century; Binney & Smith of New York launched Crayola crayons in 1903, which popularised them for children. No single inventor is credited.

short_description: A stick of coloured wax used for drawing.
description: Coloured wax crayons developed in 19th-century Europe, and in 1903 Binney & Smith in the United States introduced Crayola crayons, an affordable non-toxic box for children. Pigment is mixed into paraffin wax, moulded into sticks and wrapped in paper labels. The paper-wrapped wax stick has not changed in over a century.
why_unchanged: A paper-wrapped wax stick is cheap, safe and robust for small hands, so its form has stayed the same.

faqs.question: What are crayons made of?
faqs.answer: Most are paraffin wax mixed with coloured pigment, with a paper wrapper for grip.

faqs.question: When did Crayola crayons first appear?
faqs.answer: Binney & Smith sold the first box of eight Crayola crayons in 1903.

faqs.question: How do you remove crayon from walls?
faqs.answer: A damp cloth with a little baking soda or a gentle eraser sponge usually lifts wax marks.

image.alt: A box of colourful wax crayons

name: Dip pen

place_of_invention.notes: Metal nibs date back to antiquity, but mass production of cheap steel nibs began in Birmingham in the 1820s with makers such as John Mitchell, Josiah Mason and Joseph Gillott; no single inventor is credited.

short_description: A pen with a replaceable metal nib on a holder, dipped in ink to write.
description: Steel nibs pressed by machine in Birmingham in the 1820s made dip pens cheap, and they rapidly replaced quills for everyday writing in the 19th century. The nib is slotted into a wooden or plastic holder and dipped into an inkwell, holding enough ink for a few words. Calligraphers, illustrators and comic artists still use the same design.
why_unchanged: A slit metal nib on a simple holder gives fine line control that artists still prefer.

faqs.question: Why do artists still use dip pens?
faqs.answer: Flexible nibs produce lines that vary in width with pressure, and they work with inks that would clog fountain pens.

faqs.question: Where were steel nibs made?
faqs.answer: Birmingham, England, was the world centre of steel nib production in the 19th century.

faqs.question: How often must you dip the pen?
faqs.answer: Typically every few words or lines, depending on the nib size and the ink.

image.alt: A dip pen with a steel nib beside a bottle of ink

name: Drafting compass

place_of_invention.notes: Euclid's geometry (c. 300 BCE) relies on compass constructions, and bronze compasses survive from Roman sites such as Pompeii. Earlier use is likely.

short_description: A hinged two-legged instrument for drawing circles and arcs.
description: The compass was a basic tool of ancient Greek geometry, used with a straightedge to construct figures in Euclid's Elements, and Roman bronze examples survive from Pompeii. One sharp leg is fixed at the centre while the other, holding a pencil or pen, sweeps around it. Every school geometry set still includes one.
why_unchanged: Two hinged legs fixing a radius is the simplest possible way to draw a perfect circle.

faqs.question: How old is the compass for drawing circles?
faqs.answer: It was used in classical Greek geometry by around 300 BCE, and Roman examples survive.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a compass and dividers?
faqs.answer: A compass has a pencil or pen on one leg to draw, while dividers have two points for measuring and transferring distances.

faqs.question: Why is it sometimes called 'a pair of compasses'?
faqs.answer: Like scissors, it has two matching legs, so in British English it is traditionally called a pair.

image.alt: A metal drafting compass drawing a circle on paper

name: Dust jacket

place_of_invention.notes: The earliest known surviving dust jacket, found in the Bodleian Library in 2009, is from the gift book Friendship's Offering, dated 1829.

short_description: A removable paper cover wrapped around a hardback book.
description: Dust jackets began as plain paper wrappers to protect fine bindings until purchase; the earliest known example dates from 1829. In the 20th century they became printed marketing tools with cover art and blurbs. The folded paper wrapper with flaps remains standard on hardback books.
why_unchanged: A folded paper wrapper protects the binding and advertises the book, so its form persists.

faqs.question: What is the oldest dust jacket?
faqs.answer: The oldest known surviving one, from 1829, was found in Oxford's Bodleian Library in 2009.

faqs.question: Why do collectors care about dust jackets?
faqs.answer: A first edition with its original jacket can be worth many times more than one without.

faqs.question: What are the flaps for?
faqs.answer: The flaps hold the jacket in place and often carry a summary and author biography.

image.alt: A hardcover book wrapped in a printed dust jacket

name: Envelope

place_of_invention.notes: Clay envelopes enclosed Mesopotamian tablets around 3500 BCE, and folded paper wrappers were used for centuries. Commercially made paper envelopes appeared in Britain in the 1830s, and envelope-folding machines followed in the 1840s.

short_description: A flat folded paper container with a sealable flap for letters.
description: Letters were long folded and sealed on themselves, but pre-cut paper envelopes became widespread in Britain in the 1830s and 1840s, especially after the cheap postal rates of 1840. Machines invented in the 1840s could fold and glue them in bulk. The diamond-cut folded paper envelope with a gummed flap is still standard.
why_unchanged: A single folded sheet with a gummed flap protects a letter cheaply and simply, so the form has stayed the same.

faqs.question: What came before the envelope?
faqs.answer: Letters were folded and sealed with wax, and in ancient Mesopotamia clay tablets were enclosed in clay envelopes.

faqs.question: Why did envelopes become common in the 1840s?
faqs.answer: Britain's postal reform of 1840 made postage cheap and paid by weight, encouraging the use of separate envelopes.

faqs.question: What are envelope sizes like C5 and DL?
faqs.answer: They are international standard sizes; C5 fits A5 or folded A4, and DL fits A4 folded in three.

image.alt: A plain white paper envelope with its flap open

name: Eraser

place_of_invention.notes: In 1770 Joseph Priestley noted that natural rubber could rub out pencil marks, and London instrument maker Edward Nairne is credited with selling cubes of rubber for the purpose. Before that, bread crumbs were used.

short_description: A block of rubber or vinyl used to remove pencil marks from paper.
description: Before rubber, people erased pencil marks with lumps of bread. In 1770 Joseph Priestley recorded that a gum from South America could rub out marks, giving the material the English name 'rubber', and instrument maker Edward Nairne sold small cubes of it. Vulcanized rubber in the 19th century made erasers durable, and synthetic vinyl erasers followed in the 20th century, but the simple handheld block is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A soft block that lifts graphite by friction needs no mechanism, so only its material has evolved.

faqs.question: Why is rubber called rubber?
faqs.answer: In English the material got its name in 1770 because it could 'rub out' pencil marks.

faqs.question: What did people use before erasers?
faqs.answer: Bread crumbs were commonly used to remove pencil marks, and wax tablets could simply be smoothed over.

faqs.question: How does an eraser work?
faqs.answer: The eraser's material is stickier than paper, so as you rub it picks up graphite particles and carries them away in crumbs.

image.alt: A pink rubber eraser beside pencil marks on paper

name: Felt-tip marker

place_of_invention.notes: Lee Newman patented a felt-tipped marking pen in 1910 and Sidney Rosenthal's Magic Marker of 1952 popularised the form; Yukio Horie of Pentel introduced the fine fibre-tip pen in 1962. Credit varies by type.

short_description: A pen with a porous felt or fibre tip that draws ink from a reservoir.
description: Felt-tipped markers combine an ink reservoir with a porous tip that wicks ink to the surface. Sidney Rosenthal's Magic Marker of 1952 made them popular for signs and art, and Japan's Pentel introduced the fine-tip version in 1962. The capped barrel with a fibre nib is unchanged in today's markers.
why_unchanged: A wick tip fed from a reservoir delivers bold, even colour with no moving parts.

faqs.question: Who invented the marker?
faqs.answer: Lee Newman patented an early felt-tip pen in 1910, Sidney Rosenthal popularised it as the Magic Marker in 1952, and Pentel created the fine-tip pen in 1962.

faqs.question: Why do markers dry out?
faqs.answer: The ink's solvent evaporates through the porous tip, so the cap must be replaced after use.

faqs.question: What is a permanent marker?
faqs.answer: A marker using alcohol-based, water-resistant ink that bonds to many surfaces.

image.alt: A set of colourful felt-tip markers

name: File folder

place_of_invention.notes: Folders of manila card developed with vertical filing systems in American offices in the 1890s; Edwin Grenville Seibels is credited with promoting vertical filing in 1898. No inventor of the folder itself is documented.

short_description: A folded sheet of card with a tab, used to hold loose papers in a filing system.
description: As offices grew in the late 19th century, papers moved from bound books and pigeonholes into vertical filing cabinets organised with folders. The folded manila folder with a labelled tab became the standard unit of office record-keeping. Its form has not changed, and it even inspired the folder icon on computers.
why_unchanged: A folded card with a tab holds and labels papers at almost no cost, so nothing has replaced it.

faqs.question: Why are file folders often beige?
faqs.answer: They were traditionally made of manila paper, originally from Manila hemp fibres.

faqs.question: What are folder tabs for?
faqs.answer: Tabs stick up above other folders so labels can be read at a glance in a drawer.

faqs.question: Is the computer folder icon based on this?
faqs.answer: Yes, the folder icon on computers imitates the paper file folder.

image.alt: Manila file folders with labelled tabs

name: Fountain pen

place_of_invention.notes: Reservoir pens existed much earlier, including one reported for the Fatimid caliph al-Mu'izz in 973 and Petrache Poenaru's 1827 French patent. Lewis Waterman's 1884 patent for an improved capillary feed is widely seen as producing the first reliable fountain pen.

short_description: A nib pen with an internal ink reservoir that feeds ink by capillary action.
description: Inventors experimented with self-filling pens for centuries, but early models leaked or skipped. In the 1880s improved feeds, notably Lewis Waterman's 1884 design, regulated ink flow with air channels and made the fountain pen practical. The basic parts, a nib, a feed and a reservoir in a capped barrel, are unchanged in modern pens.
why_unchanged: A nib, feed and reservoir balance ink and air perfectly, so later changes only affected filling systems and materials.

faqs.question: Who invented the fountain pen?
faqs.answer: Many people contributed; Petrache Poenaru patented one in 1827, and Lewis Waterman's 1884 feed made it reliable.

faqs.question: How does a fountain pen work?
faqs.answer: Capillary action draws ink through narrow channels in the feed to the nib, while air enters to replace the ink used.

faqs.question: Why do fountain pen nibs have a hole?
faqs.answer: The breather hole ends the slit, lets air in, and helps the nib flex without cracking.

image.alt: A fountain pen nib writing in cursive on paper

name: French curve

place_of_invention.notes: Templates of curved edges were used by draughtsmen in 19th-century Europe; German mathematician Ludwig Burmester designed widely used sets in the late 1800s. The origin of the name is unclear.

short_description: A flat template with smoothly varying curves for drawing irregular curves.
description: A French curve is a template cut with a variety of curves so a draughtsman can find a portion matching any smooth line. Shipbuilders, engineers and fashion designers have used them to draw curves that compasses cannot make. Transparent plastic versions are still used in pattern-making and art.
why_unchanged: A single cut template already contains countless curve segments, so the idea needed no improvement.

faqs.question: Why is it called a French curve?
faqs.answer: The origin of the name is uncertain; it has been used in English since at least the 19th century.

faqs.question: What is a French curve used for?
faqs.answer: It helps draw smooth irregular curves in technical drawing, pattern-making and illustration.

faqs.question: How do you use one?
faqs.answer: Slide and rotate the template until an edge matches several points of the curve, then trace that section and repeat.

image.alt: A set of transparent French curve templates

name: Globe

place_of_invention.notes: The Erdapfel made by Martin Behaim and collaborators in 1492 is the oldest surviving terrestrial globe; the Greek scholar Crates of Mallus is reported to have built a globe around 150 BCE, but none survives.

short_description: A spherical model of the Earth mounted on an axis.
description: Ancient Greek scholars understood that the Earth was round, and Crates of Mallus reportedly made a globe in the 2nd century BCE. The oldest surviving example is Martin Behaim's Erdapfel of 1492, made just before Columbus reached the Americas. Desk globes tilted on a stand have kept the same form for centuries.
why_unchanged: A sphere is the only map without distortion, so the globe cannot be improved in form.

faqs.question: What is the oldest surviving globe?
faqs.answer: The Erdapfel, made in Nuremberg in 1492 under Martin Behaim.

faqs.question: Why are globes tilted?
faqs.answer: The axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees to match the Earth's tilt relative to its orbit.

faqs.question: Why do globes show no distortion?
faqs.answer: Only a sphere can represent the Earth's surface with correct shapes, areas and distances at once.

image.alt: A tilted desk globe on a wooden stand

name: Glue stick

place_of_invention.notes: Wolfgang Dierichs, a researcher at Henkel, devised the glue stick after watching someone apply lipstick; Henkel launched it as Pritt in 1969.

short_description: Solid glue in a twist-up tube, applied by rubbing.
description: Henkel researcher Wolfgang Dierichs came up with the idea of solid glue in a lipstick-style tube, and the Pritt stick launched in 1969. It is clean, quick-drying and safe for children. Glue sticks are made worldwide in the same twist-up form.
why_unchanged: A twist-up solid glue is mess-free and portable, so its form has not changed.

faqs.question: Who invented the glue stick?
faqs.answer: Wolfgang Dierichs of Henkel, inspired by lipstick; it launched as Pritt in 1969.

faqs.question: Why do glue sticks dry out?
faqs.answer: If the cap is left off, the water in the glue evaporates.

faqs.question: Is glue stick safe for children?
faqs.answer: Yes, most are non-toxic and washable, which is why they are popular in schools.

image.alt: An open glue stick with its cap beside it

name: Graph paper

place_of_invention.notes: The first commercially published graph paper is generally attributed to a Dr Buxton of England in 1794; details of the attribution are uncertain.

short_description: Paper printed with a fine grid of squares for drawing graphs and diagrams.
description: Graph paper appeared at the end of the 18th century as scientists and engineers began plotting data visually. Its regular grid allows accurate plotting of points, scale drawings and patterns. Students, engineers, and knitting or embroidery designers still use it every day.
why_unchanged: A printed grid is the simplest aid to plotting and scaling, so it has not changed.

faqs.question: When was graph paper first sold?
faqs.answer: The first commercial graph paper is usually attributed to Dr Buxton of England in 1794.

faqs.question: What types of graph paper exist?
faqs.answer: Common types include square grid, isometric, polar and logarithmic paper.

faqs.question: Why is graph paper used in bullet journals?
faqs.answer: The faint grid or dot pattern helps draw neat layouts and tables by hand.

image.alt: A sheet of graph paper with a pencil

name: Guillotine paper cutter

place_of_invention.notes: Guillaume Massiquot patented a paper-cutting machine in France in 1844, and Thirault built an earlier model around 1837; the lever-arm desk trimmer developed from these.

short_description: A board with a hinged blade arm for cutting straight edges through paper.
description: Paper-cutting guillotines appeared in France in the 1830s-1840s for trimming printed sheets; in France such cutters are still called 'massicots' after Guillaume Massiquot. The office version, a gridded board with a hinged blade arm, cuts clean straight lines through several sheets. It remains common in schools, offices and print shops.
why_unchanged: A hinged blade against a straight edge gives clean, square cuts with one motion.

faqs.question: Why is it called a guillotine?
faqs.answer: Its falling or hinged blade resembles the guillotine used for executions in France.

faqs.question: What is a massicot?
faqs.answer: It is the French name for a paper cutter, after inventor Guillaume Massiquot.

faqs.question: How do you use one safely?
faqs.answer: Keep fingers behind the guard, hold the paper with the clamp, and lock the blade down when not in use.

image.alt: A desktop paper guillotine with a blade arm

name: Hand-crank pencil sharpener

place_of_invention.notes: John Lee Love patented a portable crank-operated sharpener with a shavings receptacle in 1897. Desk-mounted crank sharpeners with rotating cutters became common in the early 20th century, and attributions for the exact design vary.

short_description: A desk-mounted sharpener in which a crank turns cutters around an inserted pencil.
description: Crank-operated sharpeners appeared in the late 19th century; in 1897 John Lee Love patented a portable model that caught shavings in a receptacle. The classic school and office version, screwed to a desk or wall, uses two helical cutters that rotate around the pencil as the handle is turned. Its basic layout has been used in classrooms for more than a century.
why_unchanged: Rotating helical cutters give a quick, even point with no skill required, so the crank mechanism has endured.

faqs.question: How does a crank sharpener work?
faqs.answer: Turning the handle spins one or two spiral-edged cutters around the pencil, shaving the wood and graphite into a cone.

faqs.question: Who was John Lee Love?
faqs.answer: He was an African American inventor from Fall River, Massachusetts, who patented a portable pencil sharpener in 1897.

faqs.question: Why are crank sharpeners mounted on walls in schools?
faqs.answer: Fixing them in place lets many students use them quickly and keeps shavings in one container.

image.alt: A metal crank pencil sharpener mounted on a wall

name: Highlighter

place_of_invention.notes: The Carter's Ink Company introduced the Hi-Liter in 1963; Frank Honn is sometimes named as the developer, but sources vary.

short_description: A broad-tipped marker with translucent fluorescent ink used to mark text.
description: The highlighter was introduced in 1963 by the Carter's Ink Company as the Hi-Liter, a felt-tip pen with transparent ink that marked text without obscuring it. Fluorescent inks made it brighter in the 1970s. The chisel-tip marker in yellow remains one of the most familiar study tools.
why_unchanged: A wide chisel tip and see-through ink do one job perfectly, so the design has stayed the same.

faqs.question: Why is yellow the most popular highlighter colour?
faqs.answer: Yellow is bright and does not obscure text, and it does not show up when photocopied.

faqs.question: Why do highlighters glow?
faqs.answer: Their fluorescent dyes absorb ultraviolet light and re-emit it as visible light, making the colour look brighter.

faqs.question: Does highlighting help you study?
faqs.answer: Research suggests highlighting alone is a weak study technique; it works better combined with summarising or self-testing.

image.alt: A yellow highlighter marking a line of printed text

name: Hole punch

place_of_invention.notes: Friedrich Soennecken filed a patent for a paper hole punch in Germany in November 1886; ticket punches and other perforators existed earlier, and Benjamin Smith's 1885 US conductor's punch is sometimes cited.

short_description: A lever-operated device that punches holes in paper for filing in binders.
description: German office supplies maker Friedrich Soennecken patented his paper punch in 1886, alongside the ring binder that it served. A lever pushes hollow steel punches through a stack of paper, and the punched discs collect in a removable tray. The two-hole and three-hole desk punches used today work the same way.
why_unchanged: A lever and hollow punch cut clean holes in many sheets at once, so the mechanism has endured.

faqs.question: Who invented the hole punch?
faqs.answer: Friedrich Soennecken of Germany patented a paper punch in 1886, though simpler punches existed earlier.

faqs.question: Why do hole punches differ between countries?
faqs.answer: Europe commonly uses two holes 80 mm apart, while North America typically uses three holes for ring binders.

faqs.question: What are the punched paper dots called?
faqs.answer: They are called chads, a word that became famous during the disputed 2000 US election count.

image.alt: A two-hole office paper punch

name: Index card

place_of_invention.notes: Carl Linnaeus is often credited with using standardised paper slips for his botanical records in the 1760s; scholars such as Conrad Gessner used slips earlier, and Melvil Dewey's library supplies standardised card sizes in the 1870s.

short_description: A small card of heavy paper used to record and sort information.
description: Scholars long used loose slips of paper for notes, and Carl Linnaeus is often credited with a system of uniform slips for organising plant data in the 1760s. In the 19th century libraries adopted index cards for catalogues, with Melvil Dewey promoting standard sizes. The 3-by-5-inch card is still used for notes, recipes and flashcards.
why_unchanged: A uniform card can be sorted and rearranged endlessly, a flexibility that needs no improvement.

faqs.question: Who invented the index card?
faqs.answer: Carl Linnaeus is often credited with using uniform slips in the 1760s, though earlier scholars used similar systems.

faqs.question: What is the most common size?
faqs.answer: The 3-by-5-inch card, standardised for library catalogues in the 19th century.

faqs.question: How are index cards used for studying?
faqs.answer: Writing a question on one side and the answer on the other turns them into flashcards for self-testing.

image.alt: A stack of white ruled index cards

name: Ink brush

place_of_invention.notes: The oldest surviving Chinese writing brushes date to the Warring States period; painted Neolithic pottery suggests brushes were used much earlier. The legend crediting general Meng Tian is not historical.

short_description: A brush of animal hair set in a bamboo handle, used for East Asian calligraphy and painting.
description: The ink brush is one of the 'Four Treasures of the Study' in Chinese tradition, along with ink, paper and inkstone. Surviving examples date back to around the 4th century BCE, and brushes shaped Chinese characters for over two millennia. Calligraphers in China, Japan and Korea still use the same bamboo-handled brush.
why_unchanged: A tapered hair tip gives endless variation of line, which calligraphers do not want to change.

faqs.question: What are the Four Treasures of the Study?
faqs.answer: In Chinese tradition they are the brush, inkstick, paper and inkstone.

faqs.question: What hair is used in calligraphy brushes?
faqs.answer: Goat hair gives a soft brush, while weasel (called wolf) hair is springier; many brushes mix both.

faqs.question: Did Meng Tian invent the brush?
faqs.answer: Legend credits him, but archaeological brushes are older than his time.

image.alt: A bamboo calligraphy brush resting on an inkstone

name: Ink pad

place_of_invention.notes: Ink pads were developed to accompany rubber stamps in the late 19th century; no inventor is reliably documented.

short_description: A shallow box containing a pad of absorbent material soaked in ink, used to ink stamps.
description: As rubber stamps became widespread in the late 19th century, the ink pad provided an even, convenient supply of ink. A fabric or foam pad saturated with ink sits in a lidded tin or plastic case to keep it from drying out. The design is still used with hand stamps and fingerprinting.
why_unchanged: A saturated pad in a closing case inks a stamp evenly every time, so nothing needed changing.

faqs.question: How do you re-ink an ink pad?
faqs.answer: Drip refill ink evenly over the pad and let it soak in before use.

faqs.question: What is an ink pad used for besides stamps?
faqs.answer: It is used for fingerprinting, crafts and printing small designs.

faqs.question: Why does an ink pad have a lid?
faqs.answer: The lid stops the ink drying out between uses.

image.alt: An open black stamp ink pad

name: Inkstick

invention.display: Han dynasty (c. 2nd century BCE to 2nd century CE)

place_of_invention.notes: Solid ink made from soot and binder was moulded into sticks in China by the Han dynasty; earlier inks were used as pellets or liquids.

short_description: A solid stick of soot and glue that is ground with water on an inkstone to make ink.
description: Chinese ink makers combined pine or oil soot with animal glue and moulded it into sticks, which were ground against a wet inkstone to produce fresh ink. The process, known by the Han dynasty, allowed the writer to control the ink's thickness. Calligraphers still prepare ink this way.
why_unchanged: A dry stick keeps for centuries and makes ink on demand, so it has not changed.

faqs.question: How do you use an inkstick?
faqs.answer: Grind it in circles on a wet inkstone until the water becomes ink of the desired darkness.

faqs.question: Why is it called India ink in English?
faqs.answer: The name came from ink imported via India, though the technique originated in China.

faqs.question: Do inksticks improve with age?
faqs.answer: Many calligraphers believe aged inksticks produce smoother ink, and antique sticks are collected.

image.alt: A decorated black Chinese inkstick

name: Inkstone

place_of_invention.notes: Stone grinding slabs for ink are known from Han dynasty tombs; earlier grinding stones may have been used for pigments.

short_description: A flat stone slab with a well, used to grind an inkstick with water.
description: The inkstone provides a slightly abrasive surface on which an inkstick is ground with water to make ink. It became one of the Four Treasures of the Study, and fine stones such as Duan stone are prized by collectors. Calligraphers still use the same flat slab with a reservoir.
why_unchanged: A flat abrasive stone with a well is the ideal surface for grinding ink, so it has not changed.

faqs.question: What is an inkstone used for?
faqs.answer: It is used to grind an inkstick with water to make fresh ink for calligraphy.

faqs.question: What is Duan stone?
faqs.answer: A fine volcanic stone from Guangdong, China, prized for inkstones since the Tang dynasty.

faqs.question: Why does an inkstone have a well?
faqs.answer: The well holds water and the ground ink so the brush can be loaded easily.

image.alt: A carved Chinese inkstone with ground ink

name: Inkwell

place_of_invention.notes: Ink containers are known from ancient Egypt and China; Roman bronze and ceramic inkwells are found widely across the empire. The date given reflects Roman examples, not the first ink container.

short_description: A small container for holding ink into which a pen is dipped.
description: Inkwells have been used wherever people wrote with dipped pens, from Roman scribes to Victorian schoolchildren. Typical designs have a narrow opening to limit spills and evaporation and a heavy base to prevent tipping. Many old school desks had a hole to hold one, and inkwells remain in use with dip pens and calligraphy.
why_unchanged: A small, stable, narrow-mouthed pot is all a dip pen needs, so its form has not changed.

faqs.question: Why did old school desks have holes?
faqs.answer: The hole held a ceramic inkwell so pupils could dip their pens without knocking the ink over.

faqs.question: What is a non-spill inkwell?
faqs.answer: It has an inward-sloping funnel at the top so ink does not pour out if the well is tipped.

faqs.question: Are inkwells still made?
faqs.answer: Yes, they are made for calligraphers and dip-pen artists as well as decorative desk sets.

image.alt: A glass inkwell on a wooden desk

name: Legal pad

place_of_invention.notes: Tradition credits Thomas W. Holley, a paper-mill worker who bound scrap paper into pads around 1888; the story is popular but poorly documented.

short_description: A pad of yellow ruled paper with a wide left margin, glued at the top.
description: According to tradition, Thomas Holley began binding scrap sheets into pads at a Holyoke paper mill around 1888. The pad later gained its characteristic left margin line, said to be added at a judge's request, and is often yellow. Lawyers, students and writers still use legal pads in the same form.
why_unchanged: A top-glued pad with ruled lines is portable and tears off cleanly, so it has stayed the same.

faqs.question: Why are legal pads yellow?
faqs.answer: There is no definitive answer; yellow may have hidden the uneven colour of recycled paper and is thought to be easy on the eyes.

faqs.question: What makes a pad 'legal'?
faqs.answer: Traditionally a 1.25-inch left margin line; the size is often letter or legal format.

faqs.question: Who invented the legal pad?
faqs.answer: Tradition credits Thomas Holley of Holyoke, Massachusetts, around 1888, though the story is not well documented.

image.alt: A yellow legal pad with a pen

name: Letter opener

place_of_invention.notes: Paper knives were used to slit the uncut folded pages of books and to open sealed letters; they became common desk items as letter writing grew in the 18th and 19th centuries. No inventor is known.

short_description: A blunt, knife-shaped blade used to slit open envelopes.
description: Letter openers descend from paper knives used to cut the folded edges of newly printed books and to open sealed letters. With the boom in mail in the 19th century they became standard desk accessories, often made of silver, ivory or brass. The blunt blade with a pointed tip is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A blunt blade slides into a flap and cuts paper cleanly without damaging the contents.

faqs.question: Why is a letter opener blunt?
faqs.answer: It only needs to slit paper along a fold, and a blunt edge avoids cutting the letter or the user.

faqs.question: What is a paper knife?
faqs.answer: An older term for a similar tool used to cut the uncut page folds of new books.

faqs.question: How do you open an envelope neatly?
faqs.answer: Slip the tip under a corner of the flap and slide the blade along the top fold.

image.alt: A silver letter opener beside an envelope

name: Lever arch file

place_of_invention.notes: Louis Leitz is widely associated with the lever arch mechanism in 1896, building on Friedrich Soennecken's 1886 binder; some sources credit Soennecken with the lever itself. Leitz added the characteristic finger hole in the spine in 1911.

short_description: A stiff box file with a lever-operated two-ring mechanism for holding large amounts of punched paper.
description: The lever arch file developed in Germany in the 1890s, when a lever was added to open and close large arched rings, a development closely associated with Louis Leitz. The thick spine with a finger hole lets it be pulled from a shelf easily. It remains the standard archive file in Europe.
why_unchanged: A lever-operated arch holds hundreds of pages securely and opens with one hand, so it has not been bettered.

faqs.question: Who invented the lever arch file?
faqs.answer: Louis Leitz of Stuttgart is most associated with it from 1896, building on Friedrich Soennecken's earlier binder.

faqs.question: What is the hole in the spine for?
faqs.answer: The finger hole, added in 1911, lets you pull the file off a shelf easily.

faqs.question: How many sheets does a lever arch file hold?
faqs.answer: A standard 75-80 mm file holds roughly 500 sheets of ordinary paper.

image.alt: Lever arch files standing on an office shelf

name: Map

place_of_invention.notes: Among the oldest known maps is the Ga-Sur clay tablet from near Kirkuk, about 2300 BCE; the Babylonian Map of the World dates to the 6th century BCE. Older carvings have been proposed as maps but are disputed.

short_description: A flat drawing of an area showing places, routes and features.
description: Some of the earliest maps were drawn on clay tablets in Mesopotamia over 4,000 years ago, showing land, rivers and settlements. Greek, Chinese and later European mapmakers developed scale, coordinates and projections. The folded or flat paper map remains a basic tool for travel and learning.
why_unchanged: A scaled drawing of space is the clearest way to show where things are, so its basic form persists.

faqs.question: What is the oldest known map?
faqs.answer: The Ga-Sur clay tablet from Mesopotamia, about 2300 BCE, is among the oldest widely accepted maps.

faqs.question: Why is north usually at the top?
faqs.answer: It is a convention popularised by European mapmakers; many older maps put east or south at the top.

faqs.question: What is a map projection?
faqs.answer: It is a method of showing the curved Earth on a flat surface, which always distorts size, shape or distance.

image.alt: An unfolded paper map of a region

name: Mechanical pencil

place_of_invention.notes: Sampson Mordan and John Isaac Hawkins patented a propelling pencil in 1822. Lead holders existed earlier, including one described by Conrad Gessner in 1565 and an example recovered from HMS Pandora, which sank in 1791.

inventor: Sampson Mordan and John Isaac Hawkins
short_description: A pencil whose thin lead is advanced through a metal or plastic barrel by a mechanism.
description: Sampson Mordan and John Isaac Hawkins patented a propelling pencil in London in 1822, and Mordan's company made elegant silver versions for decades. The core idea is a refillable lead pushed forward by a screw or click mechanism, so the pencil never needs sharpening. Modern push-button versions with fine leads follow the same principle.
why_unchanged: A refillable barrel that advances a constant-width lead solves the sharpening problem completely.

faqs.question: Who invented the mechanical pencil?
faqs.answer: The first patent for a propelling pencil was granted to Sampson Mordan and John Isaac Hawkins in Britain in 1822, though simpler lead holders existed before.

faqs.question: Why use a mechanical pencil instead of a wooden one?
faqs.answer: It keeps a consistently fine line, never needs sharpening and stays the same length.

faqs.question: What lead sizes are common?
faqs.answer: The most common widths are 0.5 mm and 0.7 mm, with 0.3 mm and 0.9 mm also widely available.

image.alt: A mechanical pencil with a thin lead extended

name: Paper

place_of_invention.notes: Archaeological finds such as the Fangmatan map show paper in China by the 2nd century BCE; court official Cai Lun is traditionally credited with improving papermaking in 105 CE.

short_description: A thin sheet made of matted plant fibres, used for writing, printing and wrapping.
description: Paper was developed in China from pulped plant fibres such as hemp and bark, with archaeological examples from the 2nd century BCE; Cai Lun's refinements in 105 CE are traditionally celebrated as its invention. The technique spread via the Islamic world to Europe by the 12th century. Paper today is made by machine, but the sheet of matted fibres is the same.
why_unchanged: A thin sheet of matted fibres is cheap, light and writable, so its form has not changed.

faqs.question: Who invented paper?
faqs.answer: Paper existed in China by the 2nd century BCE; Cai Lun is traditionally credited with improving the process in 105 CE.

faqs.question: How did paper reach Europe?
faqs.answer: It spread through the Islamic world, with paper mills in Spain by the 11th to 12th century.

faqs.question: What is the difference between paper and papyrus?
faqs.answer: Papyrus is made from strips of a plant laid crosswise, while paper is made from fibres pulped and matted together.

image.alt: A stack of plain white paper sheets

name: Paper clip

place_of_invention.notes: The double-loop 'Gem' design appeared in Britain in the late 19th century, apparently from the Gem Manufacturing Company; its designer is unknown. The popular claim that Norwegian Johan Vaaler invented it is a myth: his 1899/1901 patents describe a different, less practical clip. William Middlebrook's 1899 US patent covered a machine for making Gem-style clips.

short_description: A bent loop of steel wire that holds sheets of paper together by friction and spring tension.
description: The familiar double-oval Gem clip spread from Britain to the United States around the turn of the 20th century and quickly displaced pins and ribbons for fastening papers. It works by gripping the sheets between its loops, so nothing is pierced and the clip can be removed and reused. Despite countless patented alternatives, the Gem shape remains the standard worldwide.
why_unchanged: A single twisted wire already provides grip, reusability and near-zero cost, so no redesign has improved on it.

faqs.question: Who invented the paper clip?
faqs.answer: No single inventor can be credited. The Gem-style clip appeared in Britain in the 1890s, and the often-repeated story that Norway's Johan Vaaler invented it is a myth, since his patented design was different.

faqs.question: Why does a paper clip have two loops?
faqs.answer: The inner and outer loops press against opposite sides of the paper, creating spring tension that holds the sheets without tearing them.

faqs.question: Is there a fun fact about paper clips?
faqs.answer: During World War II, some Norwegians wore paper clips on their lapels as a quiet symbol of resistance and unity, which helped spread the myth of a Norwegian inventor.

image.search_query: silver paper clips on white paper
image.alt: A few silver Gem paper clips lying on a sheet of paper

name: Paper spindle

place_of_invention.notes: Spikes for holding papers were widely used in 19th-century offices, shops and newspapers; no inventor or place of origin is documented.

short_description: An upright metal spike on a weighted base onto which receipts and notes are impaled.
description: The paper spindle, or spike, was a standard fixture in offices, restaurants and newsrooms for collecting receipts, orders and rejected copy. Papers are simply pushed down onto the point and kept in order of arrival. Its use gave rise to the newsroom phrase 'spiked' for a story that was rejected.
why_unchanged: A pointed rod on a base is the simplest way to stack papers in order, so its form has never changed.

faqs.question: What does it mean when a story is spiked?
faqs.answer: In newspaper slang a rejected story was impaled on the editor's spike, so 'spiked' came to mean killed or not published.

faqs.question: Where are paper spindles still used?
faqs.answer: They are common in restaurant kitchens and shops for holding order tickets and receipts.

faqs.question: Are paper spindles safe?
faqs.answer: Their sharp point has caused hand injuries, so many modern versions have a bent tip or a guard.

image.search_query: receipt spike paper spindle on desk
image.alt: A metal paper spike holding a stack of receipts

name: Paperback book

place_of_invention.notes: Paper-covered books existed earlier, such as the Tauchnitz editions from 1841 and Albatross Books from 1932; Allen Lane's Penguin Books, launched in 1935, made the mass-market paperback widespread.

short_description: A book bound in flexible card covers, usually glued at the spine.
description: Cheap paper-covered books were sold in the 19th century, but the launch of Penguin Books in 1935 by Allen Lane made good literature available in sixpenny paperbacks sold even at railway stations. The glued spine and card cover made books affordable and portable. Paperbacks remain the most common book format.
why_unchanged: A glued spine and card cover make books cheap and light, a balance that has not needed changing.

faqs.question: When did paperbacks become popular?
faqs.answer: Mass-market paperbacks took off after Penguin Books launched in Britain in 1935.

faqs.question: What is perfect binding?
faqs.answer: It is the method of gluing pages directly to the spine, used for most paperbacks.

faqs.question: Why were early Penguin paperbacks colour-coded?
faqs.answer: Orange covers meant fiction, green crime and blue biography, making genres easy to spot.

image.alt: A stack of well-read paperback books

name: Paperweight

place_of_invention.notes: Pietro Bigaglia of Venice exhibited glass millefiori paperweights in 1845; French makers such as Baccarat, Clichy and Saint-Louis produced them soon after. Plain weights to hold down papers are older.

short_description: A heavy object placed on papers to keep them from blowing away.
description: Any heavy object can hold papers down, but decorative glass paperweights became a fashion in the 1840s, starting in Venice and then France. Their golden age ran from about 1845 to 1860, and they are still made by glass artists today. The smooth heavy dome is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A heavy, stable shape with a flat base holds papers down perfectly, so only its decoration varies.

faqs.question: When were glass paperweights first made?
faqs.answer: Decorative glass paperweights appeared in Venice in the mid-1840s and quickly spread to France.

faqs.question: What is millefiori?
faqs.answer: Italian for 'a thousand flowers', it is a technique of slicing patterned glass rods to make flower-like designs.

faqs.question: Are antique paperweights valuable?
faqs.answer: Fine French paperweights from 1845-1860 can sell for thousands of dollars at auction.

image.alt: A glass millefiori paperweight on a desk

name: Pencil

place_of_invention.notes: A large graphite deposit discovered at Borrowdale, Cumbria, in the mid-16th century supplied the first graphite pencils. Conrad Gessner described a wood-encased writing instrument in 1565; the wood-cased design was developed in Italy and Germany, and Nicolas-Jacques Conté's 1795 clay-graphite process created the modern lead.

short_description: A writing instrument with a core of graphite encased in wood.
description: The pencil arose after pure graphite was discovered at Borrowdale in England in the 16th century and sticks of it were wrapped in string or wood. The familiar wooden casing with a glued-in core became standard in Europe, and in 1795 Nicolas-Jacques Conté's method of mixing graphite with clay allowed hardness grades. The hexagonal or round wood-cased pencil has remained essentially the same since.
why_unchanged: A cheap graphite core protected by sharpenable wood writes anywhere and erases easily, which no redesign has bettered.

faqs.question: Is pencil lead made of lead?
faqs.answer: No. It is a mixture of graphite and clay; the name comes from early users who mistook graphite for a form of lead.

faqs.question: What do HB and 2B mean on a pencil?
faqs.answer: H stands for hard and B for black; more clay makes a harder, lighter pencil, while more graphite makes a softer, darker one.

faqs.question: Why are many pencils painted yellow?
faqs.answer: In the late 19th century, high-quality Chinese graphite was marketed in yellow pencils as a sign of quality, and the colour became a convention in North America.

image.alt: Several sharpened wooden pencils in a row

name: Pencil sharpener

place_of_invention.notes: Bernard Lassimonne patented a pencil sharpener in France in 1847, and the familiar small prism-shaped handheld sharpener is often attributed to Theodor Paul Möbius in Germany around 1908. Attributions vary between sources.

short_description: A small device with an angled blade into which a pencil is twisted to sharpen it.
description: Pencils were once sharpened with knives, until 19th-century inventors in France patented devices with a conical blade guide. The compact handheld version, a block with a tapered hole and a single screwed-on blade, became common in the early 20th century. The same design is sold in millions today, often with a shavings container added.
why_unchanged: A conical hole and a single blade sharpen a pencil perfectly with nothing but a twist of the wrist.

faqs.question: Who invented the pencil sharpener?
faqs.answer: Several 19th-century French inventors patented sharpeners, including Bernard Lassimonne in 1847; the small handheld prism form is often credited to Germany around 1908.

faqs.question: How do you keep a sharpener working well?
faqs.answer: Empty the shavings, keep the blade free of graphite, and replace or tighten the blade when it becomes dull.

faqs.question: Why do some sharpeners have two holes?
faqs.answer: The larger hole fits thick pencils such as coloured or carpenter's pencils, while the smaller fits standard ones.

image.search_query: metal handheld pencil sharpener with shavings
image.alt: A small metal pencil sharpener with wood shavings

name: Pencil with attached eraser

place_of_invention.notes: Hymen Lipman received a US patent in 1858 for a pencil with an eraser attached; the patent was later ruled invalid in 1875 as a mere combination of existing items.

short_description: A wooden pencil with a rubber eraser held at the end by a metal band.
description: Hymen Lipman patented the idea of fixing a piece of rubber to the end of a pencil in 1858. The design was soon held in place by a crimped metal ferrule, the form still sold today. The US Supreme Court invalidated the patent in 1875, which allowed every manufacturer to adopt it.
why_unchanged: Putting the eraser where the hand already holds it is so convenient that the combination has never been redesigned.

faqs.question: Who put the eraser on the pencil?
faqs.answer: Hymen Lipman of Philadelphia patented the pencil with an attached eraser in 1858.

faqs.question: What is the metal band on a pencil called?
faqs.answer: It is called a ferrule; it is crimped onto the wood to hold the eraser in place.

faqs.question: Why are pencils in Europe often sold without erasers?
faqs.answer: Many European schools and artists prefer separate erasers, which are larger and do not wear down unevenly, so the eraser-tipped pencil is mainly a North American habit.

image.search_query: pencil with pink eraser and metal ferrule
image.alt: Close-up of a pencil's pink eraser and metal ferrule

name: Postage stamp

place_of_invention.notes: The Penny Black, issued in May 1840, was the first adhesive postage stamp, part of postal reforms proposed by Rowland Hill. Scotsman James Chalmers is also claimed by some as the stamp's originator.

short_description: A small adhesive paper label showing that postage has been paid.
description: The Penny Black, bearing a profile of Queen Victoria, went on sale in Britain in May 1840 as part of Rowland Hill's reform introducing cheap, prepaid postage. Other countries quickly adopted adhesive stamps. Perforations were added in the 1850s, but the small gummed paper label remains the same.
why_unchanged: A small prepaid label is the simplest proof of payment, so its form has not changed.

faqs.question: What was the first postage stamp?
faqs.answer: The British Penny Black, issued in May 1840.

faqs.question: Why do British stamps not show the country's name?
faqs.answer: As the first country to issue stamps, Britain never needed a name and instead uses the monarch's profile.

faqs.question: When were perforations added to stamps?
faqs.answer: Perforated sheets were introduced in Britain in the 1850s; before that, stamps were cut with scissors.

image.alt: The Penny Black postage stamp with Queen Victoria's profile

name: Postcard

place_of_invention.notes: Austria-Hungary issued the first official postal card in October 1869, following a proposal by economist Emanuel Herrmann; Heinrich von Stephan had suggested a similar idea in Germany in 1865.

short_description: A rectangular card sent through the mail without an envelope.
description: Austria-Hungary introduced the first official postcard, the Correspondenz-Karte, in 1869 at the suggestion of Emanuel Herrmann, offering a cheaper way to send short messages. Picture postcards became a craze around 1900. The card with a message side and an address side is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A card with room for an address, a stamp and a short message is all the format requires.

faqs.question: Where was the first postcard issued?
faqs.answer: Austria-Hungary issued the first official postal card in 1869.

faqs.question: Why do postcards have a divided back?
faqs.answer: From about 1902, the back was split so senders could write a message beside the address, leaving the front for a picture.

faqs.question: What is a postcard collector called?
faqs.answer: A deltiologist.

image.alt: A stack of vintage picture postcards

name: Protractor

place_of_invention.notes: Thomas Blundeville described a protractor for navigation in 1589; graduated semicircles for measuring angles were developed by several European instrument makers in the 16th and 17th centuries.

short_description: A semicircular or circular measuring tool marked in degrees for drawing and measuring angles.
description: The protractor developed among European navigators, surveyors and mathematicians in the 16th century as a way to lay out and measure angles on charts. Its semicircle marked from 0 to 180 degrees became a standard part of every school geometry set. The design is unchanged apart from today's transparent plastic.
why_unchanged: A graduated semicircle measures any angle directly, so it has never needed another form.

faqs.question: Where does the word protractor come from?
faqs.answer: It comes from the Latin protrahere, 'to draw forth', referring to drawing out lines at given angles.

faqs.question: How do you use a protractor?
faqs.answer: Place its centre point on the angle's vertex, line the baseline up with one side, and read where the other side crosses the scale.

faqs.question: Why are protractors usually transparent?
faqs.answer: Clear plastic lets you see the lines underneath, making it easier to align and read angles.

image.alt: A transparent semicircular protractor showing degree markings

name: Push pin

place_of_invention.notes: Edwin Moore invented the push pin with a handle in 1900 and founded the Moore Push-Pin Company.

short_description: A pin with a cylindrical handle used to fix papers to boards.
description: Edwin Moore invented the push pin in 1900, describing it as a pin with a handle, and built a successful company selling them. The raised head makes it easy to push in and pull out. Push pins remain a fixture of noticeboards and maps.
why_unchanged: A handle on a pin makes it easy to insert and remove, so the design is complete.

faqs.question: Who invented the push pin?
faqs.answer: Edwin Moore of Philadelphia invented it in 1900.

faqs.question: Why are push pins used on maps?
faqs.answer: Their coloured heads are easy to see and grip, making them ideal for marking locations.

faqs.question: How is a push pin different from a thumbtack?
faqs.answer: A push pin has a raised handle, while a thumbtack has a flat head.

image.search_query: colorful push pins in cork board
image.alt: Colourful push pins in a cork board

name: Quill pen

place_of_invention.notes: Isidore of Seville (early 7th century) is often cited for an early written reference to bird-feather pens; quills may have been used earlier, and they dominated European writing until the 19th century.

short_description: A pen made from a large bird feather whose hollow shaft is cut to a writing point.
description: Quill pens, usually cut from goose flight feathers, replaced reed pens in Europe during the early Middle Ages and were used to write most medieval manuscripts and documents such as the Magna Carta and the US Declaration of Independence. The shaft is hardened, cut to a slit nib and dipped in ink. Calligraphers still cut and use quills in the traditional way.
why_unchanged: A hollow feather shaft already holds ink and flexes like a nib, so its natural form needed no improvement.

faqs.question: Which feathers make the best quills?
faqs.answer: Primary flight feathers from geese were most common, with swan feathers prized for their size and crow feathers used for fine lines.

faqs.question: Where does the word pen come from?
faqs.answer: It comes from the Latin penna, meaning feather.

faqs.question: Why do we have penknives?
faqs.answer: Small folding knives were originally made to cut and re-sharpen quill pens, which is how the penknife got its name.

image.alt: A white feather quill pen resting in an inkwell

name: Reed pen

place_of_invention.notes: Egyptian scribes used rush brushes from about 3000 BCE; the split-nib reed pen (Greek kalamos) came into use in Greco-Roman Egypt around the 3rd century BCE. Reed styluses for cuneiform are a separate tool.

short_description: A pen cut from a hollow reed stem with a split nib, dipped in ink to write.
description: The reed pen was the main writing instrument of the Greco-Roman world, used on papyrus and later parchment. A length of reed is cut at an angle and split at the tip so ink flows to the writing edge. It is still used for Arabic calligraphy, where it is called a qalam.
why_unchanged: A hollow reed naturally carries ink and can be cut to any nib width, so it needs no redesign.

faqs.question: What is a qalam?
faqs.answer: It is the Arabic name for the reed pen, still used by calligraphers to write Arabic script.

faqs.question: How is a reed pen cut?
faqs.answer: The reed is cut at an angle with a knife, its tip shaped and split with a slit so ink is drawn down to the writing edge.

faqs.question: Did the ancient Egyptians use reed pens?
faqs.answer: Early Egyptian scribes used rush stems chewed into brushes; the split reed pen became common in Egypt in the Greco-Roman period.

image.alt: A cut reed pen beside Arabic calligraphy

name: Ring binder

place_of_invention.notes: Friedrich Soennecken is credited with inventing the ring binder in 1886, together with his hole punch.

short_description: A folder with metal rings that open and close to hold punched sheets of paper.
description: Friedrich Soennecken introduced the ring binder in Germany in 1886, allowing loose sheets to be filed, added and removed in any order. Metal rings spring open and snap shut through punched holes in the paper. Ring binders remain a standard of schools and offices worldwide.
why_unchanged: Opening rings let pages be added or rearranged freely, which no other binding does as simply.

faqs.question: Who invented the ring binder?
faqs.answer: Friedrich Soennecken of Germany invented it in 1886.

faqs.question: What is the difference between O-ring and D-ring binders?
faqs.answer: D-ring binders hold more paper and let pages lie flatter because the straight side of the ring is fixed to the spine.

faqs.question: Why are ring binders used for loose-leaf notes?
faqs.answer: Pages can be inserted, removed or reordered at any time without damaging the rest.

image.alt: An open ring binder holding punched paper

name: Rocker blotter

place_of_invention.notes: Curved blotters with a handle became common desk accessories in the 19th century, when dip pens were widely used; no inventor is documented.

short_description: A curved block with a handle, covered in blotting paper, rocked over wet ink to dry it.
description: The rocker blotter holds a sheet of blotting paper over a curved base, so it can be rolled across a page to soak up ink without smudging. It became a standard part of Victorian desk sets. Fountain-pen users still use it in the same form.
why_unchanged: The curved base presses evenly across a page, so its form remains ideal for drying ink.

faqs.question: How do you use a rocker blotter?
faqs.answer: Place it on wet writing and rock it from one end to the other, so the paper soaks up excess ink.

faqs.question: Why is it curved?
faqs.answer: The curve lets it apply even pressure across the page without smearing the ink.

faqs.question: How do you replace the paper?
faqs.answer: Unscrew the top handle, clip a fresh sheet of blotting paper around the base, and screw it back on.

image.alt: A wooden rocker blotter on a writing desk

name: Rollerball pen

place_of_invention.notes: The Japanese company Ohto is generally credited with introducing the first rollerball pen using water-based ink in 1963.

short_description: A pen with a ballpoint-style tip that uses liquid, water-based ink.
description: The rollerball uses the same rolling-ball tip as a ballpoint, but with thinner water-based or gel ink that flows more freely. It was introduced by the Japanese firm Ohto in 1963 and later popularised worldwide. It writes with less pressure and a smoother, darker line.
why_unchanged: It keeps the proven ball-in-socket tip, changing only the ink.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a rollerball and a ballpoint?
faqs.answer: Both use a rolling ball, but a rollerball uses liquid water-based ink rather than thick oil-based ink, so it writes more smoothly.

faqs.question: Do rollerball pens dry out?
faqs.answer: Yes, liquid ink evaporates faster, so rollerballs usually have caps that must be replaced.

faqs.question: Is a gel pen a rollerball?
faqs.answer: Gel pens are a type of rollerball that use a pigmented gel ink.

image.alt: A capped rollerball pen beside handwritten notes

name: Rolodex

place_of_invention.notes: Arnold Neustadter designed the Rolodex with engineer Hildaur Neilsen and launched it in 1956.

short_description: A rotating card file for storing contact details.
description: Arnold Neustadter introduced the Rolodex in 1956: slotted cards that clip onto a rotating cylinder so contacts can be flipped through by turning a knob. It became a symbol of business networking. Although contacts went digital, Rolodexes are still made in the same form.
why_unchanged: Slotted cards on a rotating drum make browsing contacts fast, so the mechanism has not changed.

faqs.question: Who invented the Rolodex?
faqs.answer: Arnold Neustadter, with engineer Hildaur Neilsen, launched it in 1956.

faqs.question: Where does the name come from?
faqs.answer: It combines 'rolling' and 'index'.

faqs.question: What does 'a big Rolodex' mean?
faqs.answer: It means having an extensive network of professional contacts.

image.alt: A rotary Rolodex card file on a desk

name: Rubber band

place_of_invention.notes: Stephen Perry of Messrs Perry and Co patented rubber bands on 17 March 1845, made possible by the vulcanization of rubber in the early 1840s.

short_description: A loop of elastic rubber used to hold objects together.
description: Stephen Perry, a London manufacturer of stationery, patented the rubber band in 1845 as a way to hold papers and envelopes together. Vulcanized rubber made the bands durable and elastic. They are now used for everything from bundling mail to holding vegetables together, unchanged in form.
why_unchanged: A loop of elastic material grips any shape, so nothing about it needs changing.

faqs.question: Who invented the rubber band?
faqs.answer: Stephen Perry patented it in London in 1845.

faqs.question: Why do rubber bands become brittle?
faqs.answer: Oxygen, heat and ultraviolet light break down the rubber over time.

faqs.question: Who uses the most rubber bands?
faqs.answer: Postal services are among the largest users, bundling letters for delivery.

image.alt: A pile of colourful rubber bands

name: Rubber stamp

place_of_invention.notes: The rubber stamp developed in the US after vulcanized rubber became available; L. F. Witherell and James Orton Woodruff are both named as inventors around 1866, and credit is disputed.

short_description: A block with a raised rubber design that prints when inked and pressed onto paper.
description: After vulcanized rubber made it possible to mould fine details, rubber stamps appeared in the United States in the 1860s. A raised rubber die mounted on a wooden or plastic handle is pressed onto an ink pad and then onto paper. Offices, post offices and crafters still use stamps of the same design.
why_unchanged: A raised rubber image on a handle prints reliably and endlessly, so it has not changed.

faqs.question: Who invented the rubber stamp?
faqs.answer: Credit is disputed between Americans L. F. Witherell and James Orton Woodruff, both around 1866.

faqs.question: What does 'rubber stamp' mean figuratively?
faqs.answer: It describes approving something automatically without real consideration.

faqs.question: How are rubber stamps made?
faqs.answer: Traditionally the design is moulded or laser-engraved into rubber, which is mounted on a block.

image.search_query: wooden rubber stamp and ink pad
image.alt: A wooden rubber stamp next to an ink pad

name: Ruler

place_of_invention.notes: A copper-alloy cubit rod from Nippur (Mesopotamia) is dated to roughly 2650 BCE, and graduated shell and ivory rulers have been found at Indus Valley sites such as Mohenjo-daro and Lothal.

short_description: A straight strip marked with units of length, used for measuring and drawing straight lines.
description: Graduated measuring rods were among the tools of the first cities: a cubit rod from Nippur and finely marked rulers from the Indus Valley show standardised units in use over 4,000 years ago. The ruler serves two jobs, measuring lengths and guiding a pen along a straight edge. Only its units and materials have changed since.
why_unchanged: A rigid straight edge with marked units does its job completely, leaving nothing to redesign.

faqs.question: How old is the ruler?
faqs.answer: Graduated rulers and cubit rods date back to at least the mid-3rd millennium BCE in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley.

faqs.question: Why do some rulers start a little after the edge?
faqs.answer: A small gap protects the zero mark from wear, keeping measurements accurate as the end gets damaged.

faqs.question: Why is a ruler called a rule?
faqs.answer: Both words come from the Latin regula, a straight stick or guide.

image.alt: A wooden ruler with centimetre markings

name: Scroll

place_of_invention.notes: The oldest known papyrus roll, blank, was found in the tomb of the official Hemaka at Saqqara, dating to about 2900 BCE.

short_description: A long roll of papyrus, parchment or paper wound around itself or on rods.
description: Scrolls of papyrus were the main form of written record in ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome, read by unrolling from one side to the other. The Torah is still written and read as a parchment scroll, and East Asian hanging and hand scrolls remain an art form. The rolled format is unchanged since antiquity.
why_unchanged: Rolling a long sheet protects and stores it compactly, so the form has endured for ritual and art.

faqs.question: How old is the oldest scroll?
faqs.answer: A blank papyrus roll from the tomb of Hemaka in Egypt dates to about 2900 BCE.

faqs.question: Are scrolls still used?
faqs.answer: Yes, Torah scrolls are used in synagogues, and Chinese and Japanese scroll paintings are still made.

faqs.question: Where does the word volume come from?
faqs.answer: It comes from the Latin volumen, meaning a rolled scroll.

image.alt: A partially unrolled parchment scroll

name: Sealing wax

place_of_invention.notes: Beeswax-based mixtures were used for seals throughout the Middle Ages; harder shellac-based sealing wax, often coloured red with vermilion, became common in Europe from the 16th century.

short_description: A wax that is melted to seal letters and documents and take the impression of a seal.
description: Before envelopes had gummed flaps, letters were folded and closed with a blob of wax stamped with a seal, proving they had not been opened. Medieval seals used beeswax mixtures, while shellac-based sealing wax spread in the 16th century and became the familiar red stick. It is still used for invitations, certificates and decorative mail.
why_unchanged: Melted wax that hardens and takes an impression provides a seal and a signature at once.

faqs.question: Why was sealing wax used?
faqs.answer: It closed letters and showed by the seal's impression who had sent them and that they were unopened.

faqs.question: Why is sealing wax often red?
faqs.answer: Traditional sealing wax was coloured with vermilion, and red became the conventional colour.

faqs.question: Can sealing wax go through the post?
faqs.answer: Modern flexible sealing wax is designed to bend without cracking, so it can survive mail sorting.

image.search_query: red sealing wax stick and seal
image.alt: A stick of red sealing wax beside a wax-sealed letter

name: Set square

place_of_invention.notes: Right-angle squares were used by builders in ancient Egypt and Rome; flat triangular set squares for technical drawing became common in Europe as drafting developed in the 18th century. No inventor is known.

short_description: A flat triangle with a right angle, used to draw perpendicular and angled lines.
description: The set square is a flat triangle, usually with 45-45-90 or 30-60-90 degree angles, used alongside a straight edge or T-square in technical drawing. It descends from builders' squares used since antiquity. It remains part of every school geometry set.
why_unchanged: A rigid triangle with fixed angles gives accurate lines instantly, so it has no need to change.

faqs.question: Why do set squares come in two shapes?
faqs.answer: One has 45-45-90 degree angles and the other 30-60-90 degrees, so together they can draw many common angles.

faqs.question: What is a set square called in American English?
faqs.answer: It is usually called a triangle.

faqs.question: How is a set square used with a ruler?
faqs.answer: Sliding the set square along a fixed straight edge lets you draw parallel lines at a constant angle.

image.alt: Two transparent plastic set squares

name: Slide rule

place_of_invention.notes: William Oughtred created the slide rule around 1622 by placing two logarithmic scales (developed from Edmund Gunter's scale) side by side; he described it in print in 1632.

short_description: A calculating device made of sliding logarithmic scales for multiplication and division.
description: Soon after John Napier invented logarithms, William Oughtred realised that sliding two logarithmic scales against each other could multiply and divide numbers. The slide rule became the engineer's essential tool for 350 years, used to design bridges, aircraft and the Apollo missions. Electronic calculators replaced it in the 1970s, but its form never changed while in use.
why_unchanged: Two sliding logarithmic scales calculate directly, so later versions only added scales.

faqs.question: How does a slide rule multiply numbers?
faqs.answer: Adding lengths on logarithmic scales is equivalent to multiplying the numbers they represent.

faqs.question: Who invented the slide rule?
faqs.answer: William Oughtred, an English mathematician, around 1622.

faqs.question: Did astronauts use slide rules?
faqs.answer: Yes, Apollo astronauts carried small slide rules as a backup for calculations.

image.alt: A vintage wooden slide rule with its cursor

name: Spiral notebook

place_of_invention.notes: Spiral and coil binding was developed in the 1920s; various patents were filed in the US and Germany, and no single inventor is clearly credited.

short_description: A notebook whose pages are held by a wire coil threaded through punched holes.
description: Spiral binding appeared in the 1920s, letting notebooks open completely flat and fold back on themselves. Pages are punched along one edge and a wire or plastic coil is threaded through them. The spiral-bound notebook became a classroom staple and has not changed since.
why_unchanged: A coil through punched holes lets pages lie flat or fold back, which nothing else does so cheaply.

faqs.question: Why are spiral notebooks popular?
faqs.answer: They lie flat and can fold back on themselves, making them easy to write in on any surface.

faqs.question: How do you remove pages cleanly?
faqs.answer: Many notebooks have perforations near the spiral so pages tear out without ragged edges.

faqs.question: What is the difference between spiral and wire-O binding?
faqs.answer: A spiral is a single continuous coil, while wire-O uses double loops that close into rings.

image.alt: An open spiral-bound notebook with lined pages

name: Staple

place_of_invention.notes: Wire staples for paper developed alongside staplers in the United States in the 1860s-1890s; George McGill's patented brass fasteners and staple presses were early examples.

short_description: A small U-shaped piece of wire driven through paper to bind sheets together.
description: Paper staples appeared in the late 19th century as machines were developed to drive and bend small wire fasteners. Strips of pre-formed staples glued together made loading easy and became standard in the 20th century. The U-shaped wire has remained unchanged.
why_unchanged: A bent wire that pierces and folds is the cheapest permanent paper binding possible.

faqs.question: How are staples held together in a strip?
faqs.answer: They are lightly glued side by side so the strip can be loaded into a stapler and snapped off one at a time.

faqs.question: What is the best way to remove a staple?
faqs.answer: Use a staple remover, whose jaws lift both legs at once without tearing the paper.

faqs.question: Are all staples the same size?
faqs.answer: No, sizes vary by wire gauge and leg length, such as the common 26/6 and 24/6 office staples.

image.alt: A strip of silver office staples

name: Stapler

place_of_invention.notes: Several US patents of the 1860s-1870s contributed, including George McGill's 1879 staple press and Henry R. Heyl's 1877 device that inserted and clinched staples. The story of a stapler made for King Louis XV of France is unverified.

short_description: A hand-operated device that drives a wire staple through paper and bends its ends.
description: Staplers developed in the United States in the 1870s, when inventors such as Henry Heyl and George McGill patented machines that pushed a wire staple through papers and folded it closed. Later designs added a magazine of pre-formed staples, creating the familiar desktop stapler of the 20th century. Its hinged head and anvil layout has not changed since.
why_unchanged: A hinged arm pressing staples against a shaped anvil binds papers in one motion, leaving little to improve.

faqs.question: Who invented the stapler?
faqs.answer: Several American inventors in the 1870s contributed, including Henry R. Heyl and George McGill; no single person is solely credited.

faqs.question: What is the anvil on a stapler?
faqs.answer: The metal plate under the head that bends the staple legs; rotating it lets staples bend outward for temporary pinning.

faqs.question: Why is the Swingline stapler famous?
faqs.answer: A red Swingline stapler featured in the 1999 comedy film Office Space and became a pop culture icon.

image.alt: A black desktop stapler on an office desk

name: Sticky note

place_of_invention.notes: 3M chemist Spencer Silver developed a low-tack adhesive in 1968, and colleague Art Fry had the idea of using it for bookmarks in 1974; the product launched as Post-it Notes in 1980.

short_description: A small square of paper with a strip of reusable adhesive on the back.
description: Spencer Silver created a weak, reusable adhesive at 3M in 1968 but found no use for it until Art Fry used it in 1974 to make bookmarks that would stay in his hymnbook. The resulting Post-it Notes launched nationally in 1980. The yellow square with a sticky strip is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A strip of repositionable glue on paper does exactly what is needed, so the design has stayed the same.

faqs.question: Who invented the sticky note?
faqs.answer: Spencer Silver created the adhesive and Art Fry the idea for the notes, both at 3M.

faqs.question: Why are sticky notes yellow?
faqs.answer: The original prototype paper happened to be yellow scrap from a neighbouring lab.

faqs.question: Why can sticky notes be restuck?
faqs.answer: The adhesive is made of tiny spheres that touch the surface only at points, so it grips lightly and releases cleanly.

image.alt: Yellow sticky notes stuck to a desk

name: Stylus

place_of_invention.notes: Reed styluses were used to impress cuneiform signs into clay tablets in Sumer from the late 4th millennium BCE; metal and bone styluses for wax tablets followed in Greece and Rome.

short_description: A pointed stick used to write by pressing or scratching into a surface.
