faqs.answer: Combs are thousands of years old; carved examples from Predynastic Egypt date to around 3900 BCE and similar tools were made independently worldwide.

faqs.question: Why do some combs have fine and wide teeth?
faqs.answer: Wide teeth detangle thick or knotted hair, while fine teeth smooth hair and remove small debris.

faqs.question: Are wooden combs better than plastic ones?
faqs.answer: Some people prefer wood because it creates less static, but both work; the main thing is smooth, burr-free teeth.

image.alt: A simple plastic hair comb

name: Condom

place_of_invention.notes: The anatomist Gabriele Falloppio described a linen sheath against syphilis in a work published in 1564; earlier use is debated. Rubber condoms followed vulcanization in the 1850s, and latex in the 1920s.

short_description: A thin sheath worn during sex to prevent pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections.
description: The first undisputed description of a condom comes from the Italian anatomist Gabriele Falloppio, who recommended a linen sheath to prevent syphilis. Later condoms were made of animal gut, then vulcanized rubber in the 19th century and latex from the 1920s. The thin sheath remains one of the most effective and widely used means of protection.
why_unchanged: A thin, close-fitting sheath is the simplest effective barrier, so only materials have changed.

faqs.question: When were condoms first described?
faqs.answer: Gabriele Falloppio described a linen sheath for preventing syphilis in a work published in 1564.

faqs.question: When did latex condoms appear?
faqs.answer: Latex condoms appeared in the 1920s and were thinner, stronger and longer-lasting than rubber ones.

faqs.question: Do condoms expire?
faqs.answer: Yes; materials degrade over time, so it is important to check the expiry date and store them away from heat.

image.alt: A sealed condom packet

name: Cotton swab

place_of_invention.notes: Leo Gerstenzang is credited with creating the product after seeing his wife wrap cotton on toothpicks; it was sold as 'Baby Gays' and later 'Q-tips'.

short_description: A short stick with a wad of cotton wrapped around one or both ends.
description: Leo Gerstenzang reportedly got the idea after watching his wife wrap cotton around toothpicks to clean their baby. His company began making ready-made swabs in the 1920s, later sold under the name Q-tips. Paper and wooden sticks have replaced plastic in many places, but the design is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A stick tipped with soft cotton is ideal for precise, gentle application and cleaning.

faqs.question: Who invented the cotton swab?
faqs.answer: Leo Gerstenzang created the first commercially made cotton swabs in the US in the 1920s.

faqs.question: What does the 'Q' in Q-tips stand for?
faqs.answer: It stood for 'quality'; the brand was first named Q-tips Baby Gays.

faqs.question: Should you clean your ears with cotton swabs?
faqs.answer: Manufacturers and doctors advise against inserting them into the ear canal, as this can push wax deeper or damage the eardrum.

image.alt: A handful of cotton swabs

name: Crutch

place_of_invention.notes: A carving from an Egyptian tomb dated to about 2830 BCE is often cited as the earliest depiction of a crutch; simple forked sticks were surely used earlier.

short_description: A long support placed under the arm to take weight off an injured leg.
description: The underarm crutch is one of the oldest medical aids, with an ancient Egyptian carving showing a man using one nearly 5,000 years ago. For most of history it was a forked stick or a pole with a padded crosspiece. Modern aluminum crutches are adjustable, but the underarm pad, hand grip and shaft are the same.
why_unchanged: A padded top under the arm and a handgrip transfer weight from leg to arms, which is all a crutch must do.

faqs.question: How old is the crutch?
faqs.answer: An Egyptian tomb carving from around 2830 BCE shows a person using a crutch.

faqs.question: Should a crutch press into the armpit?
faqs.answer: No; the pad should rest against the side of the chest, with weight carried by the hands, to avoid nerve damage.

faqs.question: How do you climb stairs on crutches?
faqs.answer: A common rule is 'up with the good, down with the bad': lead with the uninjured leg going up and the crutches going down.

image.alt: A pair of aluminum underarm crutches

name: Cupping cup

place_of_invention.notes: The Ebers Papyrus is often cited as an early reference to cupping; the practice was also used in ancient China and Greece, and its true origin is uncertain.

short_description: A small cup applied to the skin with suction, used in traditional cupping therapy.
description: Cupping therapy uses cups to create suction on the skin, traditionally by heating the air inside. It appears in ancient Egyptian, Greek and Chinese medicine and in Islamic medicine as hijama. Glass, bamboo and silicone cups of the same basic shape are still used today, though scientific evidence for benefits is limited.
why_unchanged: A rounded cup that holds suction on the skin is the whole device, so it never changed.

faqs.question: What is cupping?
faqs.answer: It is a traditional therapy that creates suction on the skin with cups, often leaving round marks.

faqs.question: Does cupping work?
faqs.answer: Scientific evidence is limited and mixed; some people report relief, but it is not proven for most claims.

faqs.question: Why does cupping leave circular marks?
faqs.answer: The suction pulls blood to the skin's surface, causing bruise-like marks that fade over days.

image.alt: Glass cupping cups

name: Curling tongs

place_of_invention.notes: Heated tongs for hair were used in antiquity (the Roman calamistrum), but the clamping tongs used for 'Marcel waves' were introduced by the hairdresser Marcel Grateau in 1872.

short_description: A heated rod with a clamp, used to curl or wave hair.
description: Heated rods for curling hair go back to ancient Rome, but the hinged clamp-and-barrel design took off when the Paris hairdresser Marcel Grateau popularized his 'Marcel wave' in 1872. The tongs were originally heated over a flame; electric versions arrived in the 20th century. The barrel-and-clamp form remains standard.
why_unchanged: A heated barrel with a clamp that holds hair around it is the simplest way to set a curl.

faqs.question: Who invented curling tongs?
faqs.answer: Heated hair tongs are ancient, but the Paris hairdresser Marcel Grateau introduced the clamping tongs used for Marcel waves in 1872.

faqs.question: How were curling tongs heated before electricity?
faqs.answer: They were warmed over a gas flame, spirit lamp or stove and tested on paper to avoid scorching hair.

faqs.question: What is the difference between curling tongs and a curling wand?
faqs.answer: Tongs have a clamp to hold the hair against the barrel, while a wand has no clamp and the hair is wrapped by hand.

image.alt: A pair of curling tongs

name: Dental floss

place_of_invention.notes: Parmly recommended waxed silk thread for cleaning between teeth in 1815; the first floss patent went to Asahel Shurtleff in 1874 and commercial silk floss followed in 1882.

short_description: A thin thread used to clean between teeth and below the gumline.
description: In 1815 the New Orleans dentist Levi Spear Parmly advised patients to clean between their teeth with waxed silk thread. Commercial floss appeared later in the 19th century, and Johnson & Johnson began selling it in 1898. Nylon replaced silk in the 1940s, but floss is still simply a thread pulled between the teeth.
why_unchanged: A thin, strong thread is the only practical shape that fits into the tight gap between two teeth.

faqs.question: Who invented dental floss?
faqs.answer: The American dentist Levi Spear Parmly is credited with recommending silk thread for cleaning between teeth in 1815.

faqs.question: What was floss made of originally?
faqs.answer: Early floss was silk thread, often waxed; nylon replaced it during the 1940s when silk became scarce.

faqs.question: Should you floss before or after brushing?
faqs.answer: Either works, but many dentists suggest flossing first so the fluoride in toothpaste can reach the spaces you have just cleared.

image.alt: A strand of dental floss pulled from its dispenser

name: Dental mirror

place_of_invention.notes: Small mouth mirrors were in use by dentists by the mid-19th century; no single inventor or date is documented.

short_description: A small angled mirror on a long handle used to see inside the mouth.
description: The dental mirror lets a dentist see the back and inner surfaces of teeth and reflect light into the mouth. It became a standard instrument as dentistry professionalized in the 19th century. Today's versions use front-surface mirrors and disposable heads, but the round mirror on a thin handle is the same.
why_unchanged: A small mirror at an angle on a slim handle is the simplest way to look around corners inside the mouth.

faqs.question: Why is a dental mirror angled?
faqs.answer: The angle lets the dentist view tooth surfaces that face away from them, such as the backs of the front teeth.

faqs.question: What else is a dental mirror used for?
faqs.answer: Dentists also use it to reflect light onto teeth and to gently hold back the cheek or tongue.

faqs.question: Why do some dental mirrors not produce a double image?
faqs.answer: Front-surface mirrors put the reflective coating on top of the glass, avoiding the faint second reflection of ordinary mirrors.

image.alt: A dental mirror on a metal handle

name: Ear pick

place_of_invention.notes: Small ear scoops are known from Roman and Chinese archaeological contexts and from many other cultures; no single origin can be identified.

short_description: A small spoon-ended stick used to remove earwax.
description: Small scoops for cleaning ears appear in Roman toilet sets, often on the same ring as tweezers and nail cleaners, and similar tools are ancient in China. In East Asia the ear pick (mimikaki in Japanese) remains a common household item, often with a fluffy tuft at the other end. It is still a thin stick with a tiny scoop at the tip.
why_unchanged: A tiny scoop on a slender handle is all that the ear canal allows.

faqs.question: Is it safe to clean ears with an ear pick?
faqs.answer: Doctors generally advise against putting objects in the ear canal because they can push wax deeper or injure the eardrum.

faqs.question: Why is the ear pick common in East Asia?
faqs.answer: Many East Asians have dry, flaky earwax, which a scoop removes more easily than the wet wax common elsewhere.

faqs.question: What is the fluffy ball on some ear picks?
faqs.answer: In Japan many ear picks have a down tuft (bonten) at the other end for sweeping out loose flakes.

image.alt: A bamboo ear pick with a tiny scoop

name: Emery board

place_of_invention.notes: Emery-coated cardboard files are often credited to Flowery Manicure Products of the US around 1910; other accounts cite a 19th-century origin. Sources disagree.

short_description: A disposable nail file made of cardboard coated with emery or another abrasive.
description: The emery board is a cheap, flexible nail file made by gluing abrasive grit to a thin strip of card. It became widely available in the early 20th century and quickly became a standard handbag and bathroom item. Many now use synthetic abrasives, but the double-sided strip is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A light, disposable abrasive card costs almost nothing and does the job perfectly.

faqs.question: What is emery?
faqs.answer: Emery is a dark, naturally occurring rock rich in corundum, ground into a powder for use as an abrasive.

faqs.question: Why do emery boards have two sides?
faqs.answer: One side usually has a coarser grit for shaping and the other a finer grit for smoothing.

faqs.question: Can emery boards be shared?
faqs.answer: Because they cannot be fully sanitized, many salons give each client a new board for hygiene.

image.alt: Several emery boards

name: Exfoliating mitt

place_of_invention.notes: The kese, a coarse washing mitt used in the hammam, is part of the Ottoman bathing tradition, which inherited Roman and Byzantine bathhouse practices. Precise dating is not documented.

short_description: A coarse glove used to scrub away dead skin in the bath.
description: In the Turkish hammam, an attendant scrubs bathers with a kese, a rough mitt that removes dead skin in visible rolls. Similar mitts are used in Moroccan and Korean bathhouses. The simple coarse-weave glove is unchanged and widely sold today.
why_unchanged: A rough glove lets the whole hand act as a scrubber, which is all exfoliation needs.

faqs.question: What is a kese?
faqs.answer: A kese is the traditional scrubbing mitt of the Turkish bath, made of coarse woven fabric.

faqs.question: How do you use an exfoliating mitt?
faqs.answer: After soaking in warm water to soften the skin, scrub firmly in long strokes; dead skin comes away in small rolls.

faqs.question: Do other cultures use similar mitts?
faqs.answer: Yes; Korean bathhouses use the Italy towel and Moroccan hammams use a kessa glove.

image.alt: A coarse exfoliating bath mitt

name: Eye bath

place_of_invention.notes: Eye baths in glass, ceramic and silver were common in Britain from the 18th–19th centuries; earlier origins are not documented.

short_description: A small cup shaped to fit the eye socket, used to rinse the eye.
description: Eye baths are small cups with a rim shaped to fit around the eye, filled with a rinsing solution and held against the eye while blinking. They were widely produced in Britain in glass, pottery and silver from the 18th century, and many antique examples survive. Plastic eye baths are still sold in pharmacies.
why_unchanged: A cup shaped to seal around the eye is the simplest way to bathe it.

faqs.question: How do you use an eye bath?
faqs.answer: Fill it with sterile solution, press it gently around the eye, tilt the head back and blink several times.

faqs.question: Are eye baths still recommended?
faqs.answer: Some doctors prefer sterile single-use eyewash, because reused eye baths can spread infection if not kept clean.

faqs.question: Are antique eye baths collectible?
faqs.answer: Yes; glass and ceramic eye baths from the 18th–20th centuries are popular with collectors.

image.alt: A glass eye bath cup

name: Eye patch

place_of_invention.notes: Covering an injured or lost eye with cloth is ancient and universal; no specific origin can be documented.

short_description: A small pad or shield worn over one eye, held with a strap or adhesive.
description: People have covered injured or missing eyes with cloth since ancient times. In the 20th century eye patches also became a medical treatment for amblyopia (lazy eye), forcing the weaker eye to work. The simple fabric patch on a strap is still common.
why_unchanged: A small shield on a strap covers one eye completely, which is the whole purpose.

faqs.question: Why are eye patches used for lazy eye?
faqs.answer: Covering the stronger eye forces the brain to use the weaker eye, helping its vision develop.

faqs.question: Did pirates really wear eye patches?
faqs.answer: Some sailors who lost eyes wore patches, but the image is largely a literary and film stereotype.

faqs.question: Are adhesive eye patches better for children?
faqs.answer: Adhesive patches are harder for children to remove, which can make amblyopia treatment more effective.

image.alt: A black fabric eye patch

name: Eyebrow pencil

place_of_invention.notes: Wood-cased cosmetic pencils became common in the early 20th century; earlier people darkened brows with burnt matches, soot or kohl. No single inventor is documented.

short_description: A wood-cased or retractable pencil with a soft colored core for filling in brows.
description: People have darkened their eyebrows with soot, kohl and burnt cork for centuries. In the early 20th century cosmetic makers adapted the wood-cased writing pencil to hold soft, waxy pigment, creating the eyebrow pencil. It is still sharpened and used in the same way.
why_unchanged: A pencil gives fine, controllable lines and a built-in protective casing, so the format needed no change.

faqs.question: What did people use before eyebrow pencils?
faqs.answer: Common substitutes included burnt matches, cork, soot, kohl and charcoal.

faqs.question: Can an eyebrow pencil be used as eyeliner?
faqs.answer: Some can, but eyeliner formulas are usually softer and tested for use near the eye.

faqs.question: Why do some brow pencils have a spoolie?
faqs.answer: The spiral brush blends the pencil strokes and brushes brow hairs into place.

image.alt: An eyebrow pencil

name: Eyedropper

place_of_invention.notes: Glass droppers with rubber bulbs came into use after vulcanized rubber became widely available; no inventor is credited.

short_description: A glass or plastic tube with a rubber bulb used to dispense liquid one drop at a time.
description: The eyedropper combines a narrow glass tube with a squeezable rubber bulb, letting users draw up liquid and release it drop by drop. It became common in pharmacies and homes in the late 19th century. Plastic versions are now common, but the bulb-and-tube design is unchanged.
why_unchanged: Squeezing a bulb on a narrow tube gives precise drop control with no moving parts.

faqs.question: How does an eyedropper work?
faqs.answer: Squeezing the bulb pushes air out; releasing it creates suction that draws liquid into the tube.

faqs.question: Why is it called an eyedropper?
faqs.answer: It was widely used to put medicated drops into the eyes.

faqs.question: What is a pipette?
faqs.answer: A pipette is a related lab instrument designed for measuring precise liquid volumes.

image.alt: A glass eyedropper with a rubber bulb

name: Eyeglasses

place_of_invention.notes: A 1306 sermon by Giordano da Pisa said spectacles had been invented about twenty years earlier; the inventor is unknown, and claims for Salvino degli Armati are considered a hoax.

short_description: A pair of lenses held in a frame in front of the eyes to correct vision.
description: Eyeglasses were invented in northern Italy around 1286, initially as convex lenses for reading, held on the nose without arms. Concave lenses for nearsightedness followed in the 15th century, and side arms resting on the ears became common in the 18th century. The two-lenses-in-a-frame design has remained basically the same.
why_unchanged: Two lenses held in front of the eyes is the simplest way to correct vision, so only frames and materials evolved.

faqs.question: Who invented eyeglasses?
faqs.answer: Nobody knows for certain; a sermon from 1306 dates their invention to about 1286 in Italy.

faqs.question: When did glasses get arms?
faqs.answer: Temple arms over the ears became widespread in the 18th century; before that glasses were perched on the nose or held.

faqs.question: Who invented bifocals?
faqs.answer: Benjamin Franklin is often credited with bifocals in the 1780s, though the claim is debated.

image.alt: A pair of eyeglasses on a table

name: Eyelash curler

place_of_invention.notes: William Beldue McDonnell is credited with developing the Kurlash eyelash curler in the 1920s; the company later became Kurlash Co.

short_description: A hand-held clamp that bends eyelashes upward.
description: The mechanical eyelash curler appeared in the US in the 1920s, when the Kurlash company introduced a scissor-handled clamp with a curved pad. It quickly became a staple of cosmetics kits. Modern curlers look almost identical, with a rubber pad and hinged frame.
why_unchanged: A curved clamp shaped to the eyelid presses lashes evenly, which is all a curl requires.

faqs.question: When was the eyelash curler invented?
faqs.answer: It was introduced in the US in the 1920s under the Kurlash brand.

faqs.question: Should you curl lashes before or after mascara?
faqs.answer: Usually before; curling lashes coated in mascara can make them brittle or stick to the pad.

faqs.question: How often should the rubber pad be replaced?
faqs.answer: Every few months, or when it shows grooves or cracks that could crimp the lashes.

image.alt: A metal eyelash curler

name: Facial tissue

place_of_invention.notes: Kimberly-Clark introduced Kleenex in 1924 as a makeup remover; it was marketed as a disposable handkerchief from around 1930.

short_description: A soft, disposable paper sheet for wiping the nose or face.
description: Kimberly-Clark developed a soft creped paper from a material used as a filter in First World War gas masks. It launched Kleenex in 1924 as a cold-cream remover, but customers used it to blow their noses, so it was rebranded as a disposable handkerchief. The interfolded pop-up box followed in the late 1920s, and tissues have barely changed since.
why_unchanged: A soft, disposable sheet in a pop-up box is about as simple and hygienic as it gets.

faqs.question: What were tissues first sold for?
faqs.answer: Kleenex was originally marketed in 1924 for removing makeup and cold cream.

faqs.question: Why are tissues interfolded in the box?
faqs.answer: Interfolding means pulling out one tissue lifts the next, so they pop up one at a time.

faqs.question: Why does 'Kleenex' mean tissue?
faqs.answer: The brand became so dominant that its name turned into a generic word, much like 'aspirin'.

image.alt: A tissue pulled from a box

name: Folding fan

place_of_invention.notes: The folding fan is traditionally credited to Japan, where wooden-slat hiōgi date to around the Nara–Heian periods; it later spread to China and Europe.

short_description: A hand-held fan made of pleated material on ribs that fold together.
description: The folding fan is generally believed to have originated in Japan, where early versions were made of thin wooden slats. It spread to China and, via trade, to Europe, where it became a fashionable accessory in the 17th and 18th centuries. Folding fans are still made with the same ribs and pleated leaf.
why_unchanged: Ribs that fan out and fold flat make a fan that is compact to carry and easy to use.

faqs.question: Where was the folding fan invented?
faqs.answer: Most historians credit Japan with inventing the folding fan, around the 8th–9th century.

faqs.question: Was there a 'language of the fan'?
faqs.answer: Nineteenth-century booklets described a fan language for flirting, but historians consider it largely a playful invention rather than a real code.

faqs.question: How do you fold a fan correctly?
faqs.answer: Close it gently along its existing pleats, guard sticks outermost, to avoid tearing the leaf.

image.alt: An open paper folding fan

name: Forearm crutch

place_of_invention.notes: Anders Lofstrand Jr. patented an adjustable forearm crutch in the 1940s, and the type is often called a 'Lofstrand crutch'; similar elbow crutches existed earlier in Europe.

short_description: A crutch with a cuff that wraps around the forearm and a handgrip.
description: The forearm or elbow crutch uses a cuff around the forearm instead of an underarm pad, giving more freedom of movement for long-term users. Anders Lofstrand Jr. patented an adjustable version in the 1940s, and his name is still used for the type. Modern forearm crutches keep the same cuff-and-grip design.
why_unchanged: A cuff and grip let users release the handle without dropping the crutch, so the design stayed.

faqs.question: What is the difference between underarm and forearm crutches?
faqs.answer: Forearm crutches use a cuff around the forearm and are typically used for long-term mobility, while underarm crutches suit short-term injuries.

faqs.question: Why are they called Lofstrand crutches?
faqs.answer: They are named after Anders Lofstrand Jr., who patented an adjustable forearm crutch.

faqs.question: Are forearm crutches harder to use?
faqs.answer: They require more upper-body strength and balance, but they are more maneuverable once mastered.

image.alt: A pair of forearm crutches

name: Gua sha scraper

place_of_invention.notes: Gua sha is a long-standing folk practice in China and Southeast Asia; the date of origin and the earliest tools are not well documented.

short_description: A smooth-edged tool used to scrape the skin in traditional Chinese practice.
description: Gua sha involves scraping lubricated skin with a smooth-edged tool, traditionally of horn, jade or even a ceramic spoon or coin. It is a folk remedy in China and Southeast Asia and has become popular in facial skincare. The tool is still a flat, curved plate.
why_unchanged: A smooth curved edge glides over the skin, so the tool has remained a simple shaped plate.

faqs.question: What does 'gua sha' mean?
faqs.answer: It roughly translates as 'scraping sand', referring to the red marks scraping can raise.

faqs.question: Is facial gua sha the same as traditional gua sha?
faqs.answer: Facial gua sha is much gentler and aims to massage, while body gua sha uses firm strokes.

faqs.question: Is gua sha scientifically proven?
faqs.answer: Evidence is limited; some small studies suggest short-term pain relief, but more research is needed.

image.alt: A jade gua sha scraper

name: Hair roller

place_of_invention.notes: People curled hair with rags, paper and heated rods for centuries; cylindrical rollers became common in the 20th century and no single inventor is clearly credited.

short_description: A small cylinder around which hair is wound to set curls.
description: Hair has long been set by winding it around rags, clay or sticks and letting it dry. Cylindrical rollers of metal, then foam and plastic, became common in the 20th century, especially from the 1950s when the set-and-dry hairstyle was everyday routine. They remain popular for heatless curling.
why_unchanged: A cylinder of the right diameter is all that is needed to shape a curl as hair dries.

faqs.question: How do hair rollers work?
faqs.answer: Hair is wound around the roller while damp and left to dry, setting it in the curved shape.

faqs.question: What size roller should I use?
faqs.answer: Larger rollers give volume and loose waves, while smaller ones create tighter curls.

faqs.question: Do rollers damage hair?
faqs.answer: Heatless rollers are generally gentler than hot tools, though winding too tightly can stress hair.

image.alt: Several plastic hair rollers

name: Hair stick

place_of_invention.notes: Hair sticks (ji) appear in early Chinese archaeology and many other cultures used similar pins; precise origins are uncertain.

short_description: A single straight stick pushed through a bun to hold long hair in place.
description: Hair sticks have long been used in China, Japan, Korea and elsewhere to secure long hair in a knot or bun. In ancient China the hairpin was tied to coming-of-age rituals, and Japanese kanzashi became elaborate decorative forms. The basic tool is still a single tapered rod, now often made of wood, metal or acrylic.
why_unchanged: One tapered rod twisted through a bun locks hair in place with no moving parts.

faqs.question: How do you use a hair stick?
faqs.answer: Twist the hair into a bun, push the stick in at the top, turn it to catch the base of the bun, then push it through to anchor.

faqs.question: Are hair sticks only Asian?
faqs.answer: They are strongly associated with East Asia, but straight hair pins were used in many ancient cultures, including Rome and Egypt.

faqs.question: What is a kanzashi?
faqs.answer: Kanzashi are traditional Japanese hair ornaments, many of which are decorated hair sticks.

image.alt: A wooden hair stick holding a bun

name: Hairbrush

invention.display: Date uncertain; common by the 18th century

place_of_invention.notes: Bristle hairbrushes were in use in Europe by the 17th–18th centuries, but earlier precursors are poorly documented. Lyda Newman patented an improved, easier-to-clean hairbrush in 1898.

short_description: A brush with a handle and bristles used to detangle, smooth and style hair.
description: Bristle hairbrushes became common in Europe in the early modern period, often with boar bristles set into wooden or ivory backs. In the 19th century manufacturers developed cushioned and air-vented designs, and in 1898 the African American inventor Lyda Newman patented a brush designed for easy cleaning. Today's brushes use plastic and nylon but keep the paddle or round head on a handle.
why_unchanged: A handle with a field of bristles distributes the hair's natural oils and detangles efficiently, so the design stayed.

faqs.question: Who invented the hairbrush?
faqs.answer: No single person invented it; brushes evolved over centuries. Lyda Newman received a notable 1898 US patent for an improved, hygienic hairbrush.

faqs.question: Why are boar-bristle brushes popular?
faqs.answer: Boar bristles are thought to spread the scalp's natural oils along the hair, adding shine.

faqs.question: Should you brush wet hair?
faqs.answer: Wet hair is more fragile, so stylists usually recommend a wide-tooth comb or a brush designed for wet hair.

image.alt: A paddle hairbrush with bristles

name: Hairnet

place_of_invention.notes: Well-preserved Nordic Bronze Age burials such as Borum Eshøj contained hairnets made by sprang technique; hairnets were also known in ancient Greece and Rome.

short_description: A fine, loosely knotted net worn over the hair to keep it in place.
description: Hairnets are surprisingly old: Bronze Age burials in Denmark contained finely worked hairnets more than 3,000 years old, and Greek and Roman women wore them too. They later became fashionable accessories and, in the 20th century, a hygiene requirement in kitchens and factories. Modern nylon hairnets keep the same open mesh form.
why_unchanged: An open mesh that holds hair while staying light and breathable is already the ideal form.

faqs.question: How old is the hairnet?
faqs.answer: Hairnets from Nordic Bronze Age burials date to roughly 1400 BCE.

faqs.question: Why do food workers wear hairnets?
faqs.answer: They keep loose hairs from falling into food and are required by many food safety regulations.

faqs.question: What is sprang?
faqs.answer: Sprang is an ancient textile technique that twists threads stretched on a frame, producing a stretchy net-like fabric used in early hairnets.

image.alt: A fine hairnet

name: Hairpin

place_of_invention.notes: Bone and metal pins used to fasten hair are found in many ancient cultures; prehistoric examples may be older.

short_description: A long pin, often U-shaped, used to hold hair in place.
description: Pins to secure hair have been found in ancient Egyptian, Mesopotamian, Greek, Roman and Chinese contexts, made from bone, ivory, bronze and precious metals. The two-pronged U-shaped hairpin became the standard for holding buns and updos. Modern hairpins are made of thin steel wire but keep the same open U form.
why_unchanged: A two-pronged pin slides into hair and grips by friction, which needs no further refinement.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a hairpin and a bobby pin?
faqs.answer: A hairpin is an open U-shape that holds hair loosely, while a bobby pin has two prongs pressed tightly together to clamp hair.

faqs.question: How old are hairpins?
faqs.answer: Hairpins of bone and metal date back thousands of years and appear in ancient Egyptian and Mesopotamian sites.

faqs.question: How do you use a hairpin in a bun?
faqs.answer: Insert the pin facing outward, then turn it and push it into the bun so the prongs anchor against the base of the hair.

image.alt: Several metal U-shaped hairpins

name: Hammam bowl

place_of_invention.notes: The hammam bowl (tas) is a traditional part of Turkish bathing; ornate metal examples survive from the Ottoman period, but earlier origins are undocumented.

short_description: A shallow metal bowl used to pour water over the body in a Turkish bath.
description: In a traditional hammam, bathers sit beside a marble basin and pour warm water over themselves with a shallow bowl called a tas. Ottoman examples were often hammered copper or silver with engraved decoration. The same bowls are still used in hammams and sold as souvenirs.
why_unchanged: A shallow, hand-sized bowl is the simplest way to scoop and pour bath water.

faqs.question: What is a tas?
faqs.answer: Tas is the Turkish word for the shallow bowl used to pour water in the hammam.

faqs.question: Why is there no shower in a traditional hammam?
faqs.answer: Bathers use running water from a basin and a bowl instead, a practice tied to the hammam's flowing-water tradition.

faqs.question: Why are hammam bowls often copper?
faqs.answer: Copper is easy to hammer and decorate, and it was the traditional metal of Ottoman bathware.

image.alt: An engraved copper hammam bowl

name: Hand fan

place_of_invention.notes: Rigid fans of feathers and leaves appear in early Egyptian art and tombs; hand fans were probably used independently in many hot regions much earlier.

short_description: A fixed, flat fan on a handle waved to create a cooling breeze.
description: Rigid hand fans of palm leaf, feathers or woven fibers are depicted in ancient Egyptian art, and ceremonial ostrich-feather fans were found in Tutankhamun's tomb. Similar fans developed independently in China, India and elsewhere. Simple palm and paper fans of the same flat, handled form are still common in hot climates.
why_unchanged: A flat surface on a handle moves air efficiently, and no part of it needs improving.

faqs.question: How old is the hand fan?
faqs.answer: Rigid fans appear in ancient Egyptian art and burials, and probably existed even earlier.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a hand fan and a folding fan?
faqs.answer: A rigid hand fan has a fixed blade, while a folding fan collapses along its ribs.

faqs.question: Are fans used in ceremonies?
faqs.answer: Yes; large feather fans were status symbols in ancient Egypt and are still used in some religious and royal ceremonies.

image.alt: A woven palm-leaf hand fan

name: Hand mirror

place_of_invention.notes: Handled mirrors of polished copper and later bronze were common in ancient Egypt; similar mirrors appear in Mesopotamia, China and the Etruscan world.

short_description: A small mirror with a handle, held in the hand for grooming.
description: Ancient Egyptians used round polished copper and bronze mirrors on decorative handles, many found in tombs. Handled mirrors were also used by the Etruscans, Greeks, Romans and Chinese. Today's hand mirrors use glass but keep the same disc-on-a-handle shape.
why_unchanged: A round reflective face on a handle is the most natural form for checking your appearance up close.

faqs.question: Why did Egyptian mirrors have such ornate handles?
faqs.answer: Mirrors were luxury goods, and handles were often shaped like papyrus stems, deities or figures with symbolic meaning.

faqs.question: How do you use a hand mirror to see the back of your head?
faqs.answer: Stand with your back to a wall mirror and hold the hand mirror in front of you, angled to show the reflection behind.

faqs.question: Were ancient mirrors clear?
faqs.answer: Polished metal gave a softer, slightly tinted reflection compared with modern glass mirrors.

image.alt: A round hand mirror with a handle

name: Hot water bottle

place_of_invention.notes: Warming pans and stone bottles were used earlier; Eduard Penkala is credited with the rubber hot water bottle around 1903.

short_description: A flexible rubber bag filled with hot water and used for warmth or pain relief.
description: People warmed beds with heated stones, copper bed warmers and stoneware bottles for centuries. Around 1903 the Croatian inventor Eduard Penkala developed a rubber hot water bottle, which was soft and safe to hold against the body. The ribbed rubber bottle with a screw stopper has changed little since.
why_unchanged: A flexible rubber bag with a screw stopper holds heat safely, so there was nothing to fix.

faqs.question: Who invented the rubber hot water bottle?
faqs.answer: The Croatian engineer Eduard Penkala is credited with inventing it around 1903.

faqs.question: Why should you not use boiling water?
faqs.answer: Boiling water can damage the rubber and cause burns; manufacturers recommend hot, not boiling, water.

faqs.question: Do hot water bottles expire?
faqs.answer: Many are stamped with a manufacture date; a common guideline is to replace them every two to three years.

image.alt: A red rubber hot water bottle

name: Hypodermic syringe

place_of_invention.notes: Alexander Wood (Edinburgh) and Charles Pravaz (Lyon) independently developed hypodermic syringes with hollow needles in 1853; syringes without needles are much older.

short_description: A plunger-and-barrel device with a hollow needle for injecting fluids into the body.
description: Simple syringes for irrigation existed in antiquity, but the hypodermic syringe was developed in 1853 by Alexander Wood in Scotland and Charles Pravaz in France. Glass syringes became standard, and disposable plastic syringes appeared in the mid-20th century. The barrel, plunger and needle form has remained the same.
why_unchanged: A plunger in a graduated barrel attached to a hollow needle gives precise dosing in a simple form.

faqs.question: Who invented the hypodermic syringe?
faqs.answer: Alexander Wood and Charles Pravaz independently developed it in 1853.

faqs.question: When did disposable syringes appear?
faqs.answer: Disposable plastic syringes became widespread in the mid-20th century, reducing infection risks.

faqs.question: Why are needles measured in gauges?
faqs.answer: Gauge indicates diameter; a higher gauge number means a thinner needle.

image.alt: A plastic syringe with a needle

name: Kohl applicator

place_of_invention.notes: Kohl and its applicator sticks are well documented from early dynastic Egypt; kohl use was also widespread in the Near East, North Africa and South Asia.

short_description: A slender rod, often with a rounded tip, used to apply kohl around the eyes.
description: Ancient Egyptians lined their eyes with kohl, made from minerals such as galena, both for beauty and reportedly to protect against eye ailments and sun glare. They applied it with small sticks of wood, ivory or metal dipped into a kohl pot. Similar applicators, such as the surma salai in South Asia, are still used today.
why_unchanged: A slim rod with a rounded tip is the safest and most precise way to line the eyelid.

faqs.question: What is kohl made of?
faqs.answer: Traditional kohl was made from ground minerals such as galena (lead sulfide) or stibnite, sometimes with soot and oils.

faqs.question: Is traditional kohl safe?
faqs.answer: Some traditional kohl contains lead, so health agencies warn against products that are not certified lead-free.

faqs.question: Why did Egyptians wear kohl?
faqs.answer: It was cosmetic and symbolic, and it was also believed to protect the eyes from disease and glare.

image.alt: An ancient Egyptian kohl pot with applicator

name: Lice comb

place_of_invention.notes: An ivory comb from Lachish bearing an early alphabetic inscription about lice is a famous example; double-sided lice combs were also used in ancient Egypt and are probably older.

short_description: A very fine-toothed comb designed to remove head lice and their eggs.
description: Lice have plagued people throughout history, and fine-toothed combs to remove them appear in many ancient sites, sometimes with lice still trapped in their teeth. A small ivory comb from Lachish carries one of the earliest known alphabetic sentences, a wish to root out lice. Modern nit combs are made of metal or plastic but use the same tightly spaced teeth.
why_unchanged: Only very closely spaced teeth can catch tiny eggs, so the design is dictated by the size of the louse.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a lice comb and a normal comb?
faqs.answer: A lice comb has teeth set so close together, often under 0.3 mm apart, that they trap lice and nits that slip through ordinary combs.

faqs.question: What does the ancient Lachish comb say?
faqs.answer: Its short inscription, in an early alphabet, expresses a wish that the comb root out the lice of the hair and beard.

faqs.question: Does combing alone get rid of lice?
faqs.answer: Regular wet combing with a nit comb can remove lice, and health agencies often recommend it alongside or instead of chemical treatments.

image.alt: A fine-toothed metal lice comb

name: Lipstick tube

place_of_invention.notes: James Bruce Mason Jr. patented the swivel-up lipstick tube in 1923; sliding metal lipstick cases had appeared around 1915 (often credited to Maurice Levy).

short_description: A cylindrical case with a twist mechanism that raises and lowers a stick of lipstick.
description: Lip color is ancient, but for centuries it was sold in pots or wrapped in paper. Metal push-up cases appeared in the 1910s, and in 1923 James Bruce Mason Jr. patented the swivel mechanism that raises the stick by twisting the base. Nearly every lipstick today still uses this twist-up tube.
why_unchanged: A twist mechanism inside a capped tube protects the stick and dispenses it neatly, so there was no need for change.

faqs.question: Who invented the twist-up lipstick tube?
faqs.answer: James Bruce Mason Jr. of Nashville patented the swivel lipstick tube in 1923.

faqs.question: How was lipstick sold before tubes?
faqs.answer: It was sold in small pots, as paper-wrapped sticks or in slide-up metal cases.

faqs.question: Why do lipstick tips come in different shapes?
faqs.answer: Bullet, slanted and flat tips give different control over lining and filling in the lips.

image.alt: An open lipstick in a metal tube

name: Loofah

place_of_invention.notes: The luffa plant is native to Asia and its dried fruit has been used as a scrubber for a long time; firm early dates are not documented.

short_description: A natural scrubbing sponge made from the dried fibrous fruit of the luffa plant.
description: The loofah is the fibrous skeleton of a ripe luffa gourd, a vine of the cucumber family native to tropical Asia. Once dried and peeled, it becomes a rough, springy scrubber used for exfoliating skin and cleaning dishes. It is still grown and used in the same natural form.
why_unchanged: The plant itself grows the scrubber; drying and cutting it is all the processing required.

faqs.question: Is a loofah a sea sponge?
faqs.answer: No; it is the dried fiber skeleton of a gourd-like fruit, not a marine animal.

faqs.question: Can you eat luffa?
faqs.answer: Young luffa fruits are eaten as a vegetable in many Asian cuisines; only mature ones become fibrous.

faqs.question: How often should a loofah be replaced?
faqs.answer: Because it stays damp and can harbor bacteria, it is commonly replaced every few weeks.

image.alt: A dried natural loofah

name: Magnifying glass

place_of_invention.notes: Roger Bacon described using lenses to magnify writing in the 1260s; lenses and reading stones were known earlier, and no single inventor is credited.

short_description: A convex lens, usually in a frame with a handle, used to enlarge small details.
description: The magnifying power of curved glass was known in antiquity, and the 11th-century scholar Ibn al-Haytham studied lenses in detail. In the 13th century Roger Bacon described using a lens segment to make letters appear larger. The handled magnifying glass became a familiar tool and remains unchanged.
why_unchanged: A convex lens on a handle magnifies by pure optics, so there is nothing to redesign.

faqs.question: How does a magnifying glass work?
faqs.answer: Its convex lens bends light rays so that an object appears larger when viewed within the lens's focal length.

faqs.question: Can a magnifying glass start a fire?
faqs.answer: Yes; it can focus sunlight into a hot point, a technique used since antiquity, so it should not be left in the sun.

faqs.question: Why is the magnifying glass a symbol of detectives?
faqs.answer: Sherlock Holmes popularized it as a tool for examining clues closely.

image.alt: A handled magnifying glass

name: Makeup brush

place_of_invention.notes: Ancient Egyptians applied cosmetics with sticks and simple brushes; the evidence for brushes specifically is limited, and modern cosmetic brushes evolved from artists' brushes.

short_description: A soft-bristled brush used to apply powder, blush and other cosmetics.
description: Cosmetics were widely used in ancient Egypt and the Mediterranean, applied with fingers, sticks and simple brushes. The modern makeup brush, with soft natural or synthetic fibers held in a metal ferrule, follows the design of artists' paintbrushes. A wide variety of shapes exists, but the basic brush construction is unchanged.
why_unchanged: Bristles, a ferrule and a handle already give fine, even application of powder or color.

faqs.question: Why are there so many shapes of makeup brush?
faqs.answer: Different shapes suit different tasks: large fluffy brushes for powder, angled ones for contour and fine ones for eyeliner.

faqs.question: Are synthetic brushes better than natural hair?
faqs.answer: Synthetic fibers work well with liquids and creams, while natural hair is often preferred for powders.

faqs.question: How often should makeup brushes be cleaned?
faqs.answer: Many dermatologists suggest washing them weekly to avoid buildup of oils and bacteria.

image.alt: A set of makeup brushes

name: Mascara wand

place_of_invention.notes: Helena Rubinstein's 'Mascara-Matic' (1957) is widely cited as the first tube with a built-in spiral wand; earlier mascara came in cakes applied with a small brush.

short_description: A small spiral brush attached to the cap of a mascara tube.
description: For decades mascara was sold as a solid cake that had to be moistened and applied with a tiny brush. In 1957 Helena Rubinstein's company introduced a tube of liquid mascara with a built-in spiral wand. Bristle shapes vary, but the wand-in-tube format has remained standard ever since.
why_unchanged: A spiral brush that stores inside its own tube coats lashes evenly and stays clean, so the format endures.

faqs.question: How was mascara applied before the wand?
faqs.answer: It came as a pressed cake that was moistened, often with water, and applied with a small brush.

faqs.question: Why are mascara wands twisted?
faqs.answer: The wire is twisted around the bristles to hold them firmly and create a spiral that catches and separates lashes.

faqs.question: How long does mascara last once opened?
faqs.answer: Most guidelines suggest replacing it after about three months to reduce the risk of eye infection.

image.alt: A mascara wand with a spiral brush

name: Menstrual cup

place_of_invention.notes: Earlier menstrual cup patents date from the 1860s, but the American actress Leona Chalmers patented the design closest to modern cups in 1937.

short_description: A flexible, reusable cup worn internally to collect menstrual fluid.
description: Leona Chalmers patented a bell-shaped reusable rubber cup in 1937. Rubber shortages during the Second World War and social taboos limited its success, and the idea was revived in the late 1980s. Today's medical-grade silicone cups keep the same bell shape with a short stem.
why_unchanged: A soft bell-shaped cup forms a seal and holds fluid, so later improvements were only in materials.

faqs.question: Who invented the menstrual cup?
faqs.answer: Leona Chalmers patented the modern design in 1937, though earlier patents for similar devices exist.

faqs.question: How long can a menstrual cup be worn?
faqs.answer: Most manufacturers say up to 12 hours, depending on flow.

faqs.question: How long does a menstrual cup last?
faqs.answer: With proper care, a silicone cup can last several years.

image.alt: A silicone menstrual cup

name: Mirror

place_of_invention.notes: Polished obsidian mirrors from Neolithic Anatolia are among the oldest known; polished metal mirrors followed in Egypt, Mesopotamia and China, and silvered glass mirrors spread from the 16th century onward.

short_description: A smooth reflective surface used to see one's own reflection.
description: The oldest known manufactured mirrors are polished obsidian discs from Neolithic Anatolia, around 8,000 years old. Polished copper and bronze mirrors were used in ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia and China, and Venetian glassmakers perfected glass mirrors in the Renaissance. In 1835 Justus von Liebig developed a chemical silvering process that made glass mirrors cheap, and the flat reflective surface has stayed the same.
why_unchanged: A flat reflective surface does its job by definition, so only the materials ever changed.

faqs.question: What were the first mirrors made of?
faqs.answer: The earliest known mirrors were polished obsidian, a natural volcanic glass, from Neolithic Anatolia.

faqs.question: How are modern mirrors made?
faqs.answer: A thin layer of silver or aluminum is deposited on the back of glass and protected with paint.

faqs.question: Why does a mirror flip left and right?
faqs.answer: It actually reverses front to back; we interpret this as a left-right swap because we imagine ourselves turning around.

image.alt: A round mirror reflecting light

name: Miswak

place_of_invention.notes: Chew sticks were used across Africa, the Middle East and Asia; Babylonian use is commonly cited but the precise origin is unknown.

short_description: A natural toothbrush made from a twig of the Salvadora persica (arak) tree.
description: The miswak is a chewing stick whose end is chewed or cut until the fibers splay into a soft brush. Chew sticks were used in many ancient societies, and the miswak became especially widespread in the Islamic world, where its use is recommended in religious tradition. It is still sold and used daily in parts of Africa, the Middle East and South Asia.
why_unchanged: A frayed twig already combines bristles and handle in one piece, and the plant's natural compounds made it effective without modification.

faqs.question: How do you use a miswak?
faqs.answer: You peel back about a centimeter of bark, chew the exposed end until the fibers separate, then brush the teeth with it; the worn end is cut off and refreshed every day or so.

faqs.question: Does the miswak actually clean teeth?
faqs.answer: Studies have found it can remove plaque comparably to a toothbrush when used properly, and the wood contains natural compounds such as fluoride and silica.

faqs.question: Is the miswak the same as a chew stick?
faqs.answer: It is one kind of chew stick; other cultures used twigs of neem, licorice or other trees in the same way.

image.alt: Several miswak sticks with frayed ends

name: Monocle

place_of_invention.notes: The antiquarian Philipp von Stosch is said to have used a single lens in the early 18th century; the monocle became fashionable in the 19th century in Germany, Britain and elsewhere.

short_description: A single corrective lens held in place by the muscles around one eye.
description: Single lenses held to the eye were used by scholars in the 18th century, and the monocle as a lens held by the eye socket became fashionable in 19th-century Prussia and Britain. It became a symbol of the upper class and military officers. Though rare today, monocles are still made in the same round form.
why_unchanged: A single lens gripped by the eye socket has no frame to improve.

faqs.question: How does a monocle stay in place?
faqs.answer: It is held between the cheek and brow by the muscles around the eye, sometimes with a ridged rim for grip.

faqs.question: Why was the monocle associated with aristocrats?
faqs.answer: In the 19th century it was fashionable among upper-class men and officers, especially in Prussia and Britain.

faqs.question: Are monocles still made?
faqs.answer: Yes, a few opticians still make prescription monocles, mostly for enthusiasts.

image.alt: A monocle on a chain

name: Mosquito net

place_of_invention.notes: Herodotus described Egyptians sleeping under nets to avoid gnats; nets were probably used in many regions earlier.

short_description: A fine mesh curtain hung around a bed to keep out mosquitoes.
description: The Greek historian Herodotus wrote that people in Egypt slept under nets to protect themselves from biting insects. Nets of fine fabric have been used across Asia, Africa and the Mediterranean ever since. Today insecticide-treated nets are a key tool against malaria, but the hanging mesh canopy is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A fine mesh canopy blocks insects while letting air through, which is exactly what is needed.

faqs.question: How do mosquito nets help prevent malaria?
faqs.answer: They stop mosquitoes, which bite mostly at night, from reaching people while they sleep; insecticide-treated nets also kill mosquitoes.

faqs.question: What is an insecticide-treated net?
faqs.answer: It is a net treated with a long-lasting insecticide, making it more effective than an untreated barrier.

faqs.question: How old are mosquito nets?
faqs.answer: Herodotus described nets being used against biting insects in Egypt in the 5th century BCE.

image.alt: A white mosquito net over a bed

name: Nail brush

place_of_invention.notes: Small stiff-bristled brushes for cleaning nails were part of European toilet sets by the 18th century; precise origins are undocumented.

short_description: A small stiff-bristled brush for scrubbing dirt from under and around fingernails.
description: The nail brush became a common washstand item in Europe as handwashing and grooming routines developed. It is a compact block with dense stiff bristles, sometimes on both sides. Surgeons adopted scrub brushes for hand hygiene, and the same simple design is used at home today.
why_unchanged: A small block of stiff bristles reaches under nails effectively with no need for refinement.

faqs.question: Why use a nail brush?
faqs.answer: It removes dirt and bacteria from under the nails, where ordinary handwashing often misses.

faqs.question: Do surgeons still use nail brushes?
faqs.answer: Many surgical scrub protocols now favor sponges or alcohol rubs, though nail cleaners and brushes are still used in some.

faqs.question: How do you keep a nail brush clean?
faqs.answer: Rinse it, let it dry bristles-down, and replace it when the bristles soften or splay.

image.alt: A wooden nail brush with stiff bristles

name: Nail buffer

place_of_invention.notes: Chamois-covered nail buffers were part of Victorian manicure sets; no inventor or exact date is recorded.

short_description: A padded tool, traditionally covered in chamois, used to polish nails to a shine.
description: Before nail polish became common in the 1920s, a shine was achieved by rubbing the nails with a buffer and a polishing paste. Victorian buffers were often ornate, with silver or ivory handles and chamois pads. Modern buffers are blocks or files with polishing surfaces, but the rub-to-shine principle remains.
why_unchanged: A soft pad rubbed over the nail generates a shine through friction alone.

faqs.question: What did people use before nail polish?
faqs.answer: They buffed their nails with powders or pastes and a chamois buffer to create a natural shine.

faqs.question: Does buffing damage nails?
faqs.answer: Gentle, occasional buffing is fine, but heavy buffing thins the nail plate.

faqs.question: What is a four-sided buffer block?
faqs.answer: It has progressively finer surfaces, from filing and smoothing to final polishing.

image.alt: A vintage chamois nail buffer

name: Nail clippers

place_of_invention.notes: Several US patents for fingernail clippers were issued in the 1870s–1890s, and the lever-type clipper was refined around 1900; credit for the design is spread across these patents.

short_description: A small lever-operated cutter with curved jaws for trimming nails.
description: Before clippers, people trimmed nails with knives or small scissors. In the late 19th century US inventors patented compact clippers, and the familiar lever design that folds over the cutting jaws became widespread in the early 20th century. Modern clippers are nearly identical in shape and action.
why_unchanged: A folding lever gives strong, precise force to two curved blades in a pocket-sized tool.

faqs.question: Who invented nail clippers?
faqs.answer: No single inventor is credited; several Americans patented clipper designs between the 1870s and 1890s.

faqs.question: Why are nail clipper blades curved?
faqs.answer: The curve follows the natural shape of the fingertip, giving a smooth, rounded cut.

faqs.question: Should toenails be cut straight?
faqs.answer: Yes, podiatrists recommend cutting toenails straight across to reduce the risk of ingrown nails.

image.alt: A pair of steel nail clippers

name: Nail file

place_of_invention.notes: People have abraded nails with stones and rough materials since antiquity; the steel nail file became common in 19th-century Europe, but no inventor or exact date is documented.

short_description: A thin, rough-surfaced strip used to shape and smooth fingernails.
description: Before dedicated tools, nails were shaped with pumice, stones or knives. Slim steel files with a cross-hatched surface became standard parts of 19th-century manicure sets, alongside emery boards and later glass files. The basic flat, slender file remains the same.
why_unchanged: A flat abrasive strip is the most direct way to wear down and smooth a nail edge.

faqs.question: Which way should you file nails?
faqs.answer: Filing gently in one direction, rather than sawing back and forth, helps prevent splitting and peeling.

faqs.question: Are glass nail files better than metal ones?
faqs.answer: Glass files have a very fine grit that tends to seal the nail edge smoothly and can be washed easily.

faqs.question: Can you file wet nails?
faqs.answer: It is best to file dry nails, since wet nails are softer and more prone to tearing.

image.alt: A metal nail file

name: Nail scissors

place_of_invention.notes: Small curved scissors for nails appear in European toilet and manicure sets by the 18th–19th centuries; no inventor is recorded.

short_description: Small scissors with short, curved blades for trimming nails.
description: Small scissors were used for nails long before clippers, and the curved-blade version became a standard part of European manicure sets. The curve lets the blades follow the round edge of the nail. They are still sold in the same form, often for babies and precise trimming.
why_unchanged: Short curved blades already match the shape of a nail, so there was nothing to change.

faqs.question: Why are nail scissors curved?
faqs.answer: The curved blades follow the shape of the nail so it can be trimmed in a smooth arc.

faqs.question: Are nail scissors better than clippers for babies?
faqs.answer: Many parents prefer round-tipped nail scissors for babies because they give more control over tiny nails.

faqs.question: Can nail scissors be used on cuticles?
faqs.answer: Cuticle scissors are a separate, finer type; regular nail scissors are too large for safe cuticle trimming.

image.alt: A pair of curved nail scissors

name: Neti pot

place_of_invention.notes: Nasal rinsing (jala neti) is part of traditional yoga and Ayurvedic practice; the age of the practice and of the vessel is uncertain.

short_description: A small spouted pot used to rinse the nasal passages with salt water.
description: Jala neti, rinsing the nose with salt water, is a traditional cleansing practice in yoga and Ayurveda. The small teapot-like vessel lets water pour into one nostril and out the other. It became popular in the West from the 2000s as a remedy for allergies and sinus congestion, in the same form.
why_unchanged: A small pot with a spout that fits the nostril is all that nasal rinsing needs.

faqs.question: How do you use a neti pot?
faqs.answer: Tilt your head over a sink, pour saline into the upper nostril and let it flow out the lower one, breathing through the mouth.

faqs.question: Can you use tap water in a neti pot?
faqs.answer: No; health authorities advise using distilled, sterile or boiled-and-cooled water to avoid dangerous infections.

faqs.question: What does a neti pot help with?
faqs.answer: Saline rinses can ease nasal congestion, allergies and sinus symptoms.

image.alt: A ceramic neti pot

name: Orange stick

place_of_invention.notes: A chiropodist named Sitts is often said to have introduced the orangewood stick for manicures around 1830; this attribution is not well documented.

short_description: A slim stick of orangewood with a beveled end used to push back cuticles and clean nails.
description: Orange sticks are made from orangewood, which is hard but fine-grained, and are cut with a pointed end and a slanted flat end. They became standard in manicures in the 19th century as a gentler alternative to metal instruments. They are still sold cheaply and are often discarded after one use.
why_unchanged: A slim wooden stick with one pointed and one beveled end covers every cuticle task it needs to.

faqs.question: Why are they made of orangewood?
faqs.answer: Orangewood is fine-grained and dense, so it holds a smooth edge without splintering.

faqs.question: What is the slanted end for?
faqs.answer: The angled end gently pushes back softened cuticles, while the pointed end cleans under the nail.

faqs.question: Can an orange stick be reused?
faqs.answer: Because wood is porous, it is hygienic to use a new stick for each person.

image.alt: Several orangewood cuticle sticks

name: Pacifier

place_of_invention.notes: Rag 'sugar teats' and coral teethers were used for centuries; rubber pacifiers appeared in the late 19th century, and a 1900 US patent for a 'baby comforter' is often cited as an early modern design.

short_description: A rubber or silicone teat on a shield and handle, given to babies to suck.
description: For centuries babies were soothed with sugar teats, cloth bundles filled with sweetened bread or sugar. Rubber pacifiers with a nipple, a shield and a ring handle appeared in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Modern pacifiers use silicone and orthodontic shapes, but the three-part design is the same.
why_unchanged: A soft teat with a shield that cannot be swallowed and a handle to grip meets every need.

faqs.question: What did babies use before pacifiers?
faqs.answer: Parents used sugar teats, cloth knots filled with sugar or bread, and teethers of coral or ivory.

faqs.question: Why does a pacifier have air holes in the shield?
faqs.answer: The holes let air flow if the shield gets pressed against the face, and are a safety requirement in many countries.

faqs.question: Do pacifiers affect teeth?
faqs.answer: Long-term use beyond toddlerhood can affect tooth alignment, so dentists often recommend weaning by age two to four.

image.alt: A baby pacifier

name: Perfume atomizer

place_of_invention.notes: Dr. Allen DeVilbiss developed a squeeze-bulb atomizer for medical use in the late 19th century; his son Thomas DeVilbiss adapted it for perfume in the early 20th century.

short_description: A bottle fitted with a squeeze bulb or pump that sprays perfume in a fine mist.
description: The DeVilbiss family of Toledo, Ohio, first made atomizers to spray medicine into the throat and nose. The design was adapted for perfume in the early 20th century, letting users apply a fine mist instead of dabbing. Many modern fragrances use pump sprays, but the bulb atomizer is still made in the same form.
why_unchanged: Squeezing a bulb to push air through a narrow tube is a simple, reliable way to turn liquid into mist.

faqs.question: How does an atomizer work?
faqs.answer: Air from the squeezed bulb rushes across the top of a narrow tube, drawing up liquid and breaking it into tiny droplets.

faqs.question: Was the atomizer invented for perfume?
faqs.answer: No; it was first designed to spray medicines into the throat and nose.

faqs.question: Why does a spray use less perfume than dabbing?
faqs.answer: The fine mist spreads a small amount of fragrance over a wider area.

image.alt: A vintage perfume atomizer with a tasseled bulb

name: Perfume bottle

place_of_invention.notes: Core-formed glass vessels for scented oils appear in Egypt and Mesopotamia in the mid-2nd millennium BCE; perfume containers of stone and clay are older.

short_description: A small stoppered bottle for holding perfume or scented oil.
description: Ancient Egyptians and Mesopotamians stored scented oils in small vessels of stone, clay and, from about 1500 BCE, core-formed glass. Glassblowing, developed in the Roman world, made small perfume flasks cheaper and more common. Today's perfume bottles are often elaborate designer objects, but they remain small stoppered glass vessels.
why_unchanged: A small sealed glass vessel protects volatile scent from air and light, which is all that is required.

faqs.question: Why are perfume bottles usually glass?
faqs.answer: Glass does not react with the fragrance and seals well, preserving the scent.

faqs.question: Why are some perfume bottles dark?
faqs.answer: Tinted glass protects fragrances from light, which can break down their ingredients.

faqs.question: Are vintage perfume bottles collectible?
faqs.answer: Yes; bottles made by companies such as Lalique and Baccarat are highly sought after by collectors.

image.alt: A glass perfume bottle

name: Plaster cast

place_of_invention.notes: Antonius Mathijsen, a Dutch army surgeon, introduced plaster of Paris bandages in 1851; plaster had been used with fractures before, but his rolled bandage method became the standard.

short_description: A hard shell of plaster-soaked bandage molded around a broken limb.
description: In 1851 Dutch military surgeon Antonius Mathijsen introduced bandages impregnated with plaster of Paris, which could be wetted, wrapped and left to harden around a broken limb. The method spread rapidly across Europe. Fiberglass casts now often replace plaster, but the technique of wrapping and setting a rigid shell is the same.
why_unchanged: Wrapping a wet bandage that sets hard produces a custom-fitted immobilizer, so the principle stayed.

faqs.question: Who invented the plaster cast?
faqs.answer: Dutch army surgeon Antonius Mathijsen introduced plaster of Paris bandages in 1851.

faqs.question: Why do some people get fiberglass casts?
faqs.answer: Fiberglass is lighter, stronger and more water-resistant than plaster, and dries faster.

faqs.question: Why does a cast itch?
faqs.answer: Skin under the cast sheds and sweats without being washed, which can cause itching; doctors warn against poking objects inside.

image.alt: A plaster cast on an arm

name: Powder puff

place_of_invention.notes: Puffs of swansdown were used to apply face and wig powder in 18th-century Europe; no inventor is recorded.

short_description: A soft pad used to apply loose powder to the face and body.
description: In the 18th century, when powdered faces and wigs were fashionable, powder was applied with soft puffs of swansdown. Puffs became a standard item in cosmetic compacts in the 20th century, made from velour or cotton. The soft round pad remains essentially the same.
why_unchanged: A soft, airy pad picks up powder and lays it down evenly with a light touch.

faqs.question: What were powder puffs originally made of?
faqs.answer: Early puffs were often made of swan's down, the fine soft feathers under the outer plumage.

faqs.question: How do you use a powder puff?
faqs.answer: Press it into loose powder, tap off the excess and press or roll it onto the skin to set makeup.

faqs.question: Why does a puff have a ribbon on the back?
faqs.answer: The band lets you slip your fingers through for better control.

image.alt: A round velour powder puff

name: Pumice stone

place_of_invention.notes: Pumice was used as an abrasive for skin and hair removal in ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome; the volcanic Aegean islands were an important source. Exact dating is uncertain.

short_description: A light, porous volcanic rock used to smooth rough skin.
description: Pumice forms when frothy lava cools rapidly, trapping gas bubbles. Ancient Egyptians, Greeks and Romans used it to smooth skin, remove hair and polish surfaces. Today it is still a staple for softening calluses on the feet, often in its natural form.
why_unchanged: Nature provides a light, abrasive stone that is already the ideal shape and texture.

faqs.question: Why does pumice float?
faqs.answer: It is full of trapped gas bubbles, which make it lighter than water.

faqs.question: How do you use a pumice stone?
faqs.answer: Soak the skin and stone in warm water, then rub the stone gently over calluses in circular motions.

faqs.question: Is pumice used in other products?
faqs.answer: Yes; ground pumice is used in some toothpastes, hand cleaners, and to stone-wash denim.

image.alt: A gray pumice stone

name: Razor strop

place_of_invention.notes: Leather strops have accompanied steel razors for centuries; no specific origin is documented.

short_description: A strip of leather used to straighten and polish the edge of a razor.
description: A strop is a flat strip of leather, sometimes paired with canvas, on which a straight razor is drawn spine-first to realign its edge before shaving. Strops were a fixture of barbershops and home bathrooms as long as straight razors were common. They are still made in the same hanging or paddle form.
why_unchanged: Drawing a blade along flexible leather realigns its edge, a task the plain strip already does perfectly.

faqs.question: What does stropping do?
faqs.answer: It straightens the microscopic edge of the blade, which bends during use, and polishes it to a keen finish.

faqs.question: Is stropping the same as sharpening?
faqs.answer: No; sharpening on a stone removes metal, while stropping only realigns and polishes the existing edge.

faqs.question: Why do you strop with the spine leading?
faqs.answer: Leading with the spine prevents the sharp edge from cutting into the leather.

image.alt: A leather razor strop hanging on a hook

name: Reading stone

place_of_invention.notes: Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics (c. 1021) discussed magnification by curved glass; polished glass or crystal domes used for reading are associated with medieval Europe. Dating is approximate.

short_description: A dome-shaped lens laid directly on text to magnify it for reading.
description: Reading stones were hemispheres of polished crystal or glass that, placed on a page, enlarged the letters. They are associated with medieval monks and scholars whose eyesight was failing. Glass dome magnifiers based on the same idea are still sold for reading and stamp collecting.
why_unchanged: A dome that sits directly on the page stays in focus without being held, so the design is complete.

faqs.question: What is a reading stone?
faqs.answer: It is a hemisphere of glass or crystal placed on text to magnify it, an early form of magnifier.

faqs.question: Who used reading stones?
faqs.answer: They are associated with medieval monks and scholars who needed help reading as their eyesight weakened.

faqs.question: Are dome magnifiers still used?
faqs.answer: Yes; acrylic dome magnifiers are popular with people with low vision and with collectors.

image.alt: A glass reading stone on a page of text

name: Reflex hammer

place_of_invention.notes: John Madison Taylor introduced the tomahawk-shaped Taylor reflex hammer in 1888; other designs, such as the Queen Square and Trömner hammers, came later.

short_description: A small rubber-headed hammer used to test tendon reflexes.
description: Testing tendon reflexes became part of neurological examinations in the 1870s, initially with fingers or percussion hammers. In 1888 John Madison Taylor introduced a hammer with a triangular rubber head, now called the Taylor hammer. It remains a standard tool in doctors' offices.
why_unchanged: A weighted rubber head on a handle delivers a quick, controlled tap, which is all reflex testing needs.

faqs.question: Who invented the reflex hammer?
faqs.answer: John Madison Taylor introduced the classic triangular-headed reflex hammer in 1888.

faqs.question: What does the knee-jerk test show?
faqs.answer: It checks the patellar reflex, which helps assess the nerves and spinal cord segments involved.

faqs.question: Why are there different reflex hammer shapes?
faqs.answer: Designs like the Queen Square or Trömner hammer offer different weights and tip sizes for testing various reflexes.

image.alt: A Taylor reflex hammer

name: Roll-on deodorant

place_of_invention.notes: Bristol-Myers launched Ban roll-on in 1952, inspired by the ballpoint pen; Helen Barnett Diserens is often credited with developing it, but sources vary.

short_description: A bottle with a rotating ball at the top that rolls liquid deodorant onto the skin.
description: Roll-on deodorant was introduced in the US in 1952 under the Ban brand, borrowing the rolling-ball principle of the newly popular ballpoint pen. The ball picks up liquid from the bottle and spreads a thin, even layer. The roll-on remains a major format today with essentially the same mechanism.
why_unchanged: A rolling ball in the bottle's neck applies an even layer without spills, so the mechanism was never changed.

faqs.question: What inspired roll-on deodorant?
faqs.answer: It was inspired by the ballpoint pen, which uses a rolling ball to spread ink.

faqs.question: What is the difference between deodorant and antiperspirant?
faqs.answer: Deodorant masks or neutralizes odor, while antiperspirant reduces sweating, usually using aluminum salts.

faqs.question: Why should roll-on dry before dressing?
faqs.answer: Letting it dry prevents marks on clothing and helps the product work effectively.

image.alt: A roll-on deodorant bottle

name: Roller bandage

place_of_invention.notes: Linen bandages for wounds and mummification are documented in ancient Egypt; Hippocratic writings describe detailed bandaging techniques.

short_description: A long strip of fabric rolled up and wound around a body part to dress or support it.
description: Ancient Egyptians were expert bandagers, using linen strips both for the dead and for wounds. Greek physicians described rolled bandages and techniques such as the spiral and figure-of-eight. Gauze and elastic bandages are now standard, but the rolled strip is used exactly as before.
why_unchanged: A long rolled strip can be wrapped to fit any limb, so the form is universal.

faqs.question: How old are bandages?
faqs.answer: Linen bandages were used in ancient Egypt thousands of years ago.

faqs.question: What is a figure-of-eight bandage?
faqs.answer: It is a wrapping pattern that crosses over itself in an 8 shape, often used around joints like the ankle.

faqs.question: How tight should a bandage be?
faqs.answer: Snug but not tight; numbness, tingling or pale skin beyond the bandage mean it should be loosened.

image.alt: A rolled gauze bandage

name: Safety razor

place_of_invention.notes: Earlier safety razors existed (e.g. the Kampfe brothers' 1880 design), but King C. Gillette's double-edged disposable-blade razor, patented in 1904, defined the lasting form.

short_description: A razor with a guard that holds a thin, replaceable double-edged blade.
description: King Camp Gillette and the engineer William Nickerson developed a razor that clamped a thin, disposable double-edged blade between a handle and a guard. Patented in 1904, it made home shaving safer and cheaper, and it was issued to millions of US soldiers in the First World War. Double-edge razors of essentially the same design are still made today.
why_unchanged: Clamping a cheap, replaceable blade behind a guard solved both safety and sharpening at once.

faqs.question: Who invented the safety razor?
faqs.answer: Several designs existed earlier, but King C. Gillette's disposable double-edged blade razor of 1901–1904 became the standard.

faqs.question: Why are safety razors popular again?
faqs.answer: Blades are inexpensive and recyclable, and many people find the shave closer than with cartridge razors.

faqs.question: Can you take a safety razor blade on a plane?
faqs.answer: Loose razor blades are generally prohibited in carry-on luggage, though rules vary by country.

image.alt: A chrome double-edged safety razor

name: Sauna ladle

place_of_invention.notes: Throwing water on hot stones is central to the Finnish sauna, whose origins are ancient but undated; the long-handled ladle has accompanied it throughout.

short_description: A long-handled scoop for throwing water onto hot sauna stones.
description: The Finnish sauna relies on löyly, the burst of steam produced when water is thrown on heated stones. A ladle with a long handle lets bathers do this without burning their hands. Wooden and metal ladles of the same scoop-on-a-pole design are still found in nearly every sauna.
why_unchanged: A cup on a long, heat-safe handle is exactly what tossing water onto hot stones requires.

faqs.question: What is löyly?
faqs.answer: Löyly is the Finnish word for the steam created when water hits the hot sauna stones.

faqs.question: Why is the handle so long?
faqs.answer: It keeps the hand away from the scalding steam and hot stove.

faqs.question: Is it okay to add scents to sauna water?
faqs.answer: Many people add a few drops of birch or tar scent, but only products intended for saunas should be used.

image.alt: A wooden sauna ladle and bucket

name: Sauna whisk

place_of_invention.notes: Leafy birch whisks (Finnish vihta or vasta, Russian venik) are part of long-standing Finnish and Slavic bathing traditions; precise dating is not possible.

short_description: A bundle of leafy birch twigs used to gently beat the skin in a sauna or banya.
description: In Finnish saunas and Russian banyas, bathers lightly slap themselves with a bundle of fresh or dried leafy twigs, usually birch. The practice is said to improve circulation and releases a fresh scent. Whisks are still tied by hand in early summer from young branches, exactly as they always were.
why_unchanged: A bundle of leafy twigs is the tool itself, and tradition has kept it exactly that.

faqs.question: What is a vihta or vasta?
faqs.answer: Both are Finnish names for the leafy birch whisk; the term used depends on the region.

faqs.question: Why do people hit themselves with branches in a sauna?
faqs.answer: The gentle beating is believed to boost circulation, relax muscles and spread the heat and scent of the leaves.

faqs.question: Can a sauna whisk be stored?
faqs.answer: Yes; whisks can be dried or frozen and soaked in water before use.

image.alt: A leafy birch sauna whisk

name: Scrunchie

place_of_invention.notes: Rommy Hunt Revson filed a patent for the fabric-covered elastic hair tie in 1986 (granted 1987); fabric-covered hair elastics were sold earlier, in the 1960s.

short_description: A fabric-covered elastic band used to tie hair into a ponytail.
description: The scrunchie is an elastic hair tie wrapped in gathered fabric, which is gentler on hair than a bare rubber band. Rommy Hunt Revson patented the design in the late 1980s and named it the 'Scunci' after her poodle. It was a defining accessory of the late 1980s and 1990s and has returned to fashion since.
why_unchanged: Gathered fabric around elastic already balances grip and gentleness, so the product has been revived rather than redesigned.

faqs.question: Who invented the scrunchie?
faqs.answer: Rommy Hunt Revson patented the scrunchie in the 1980s and sold it under the name Scunci.

faqs.question: Why did people say the scrunchie is gentler on hair?
