faqs.answer: The fabric covering reduces friction and the pulling that bare elastics can cause, which helps limit breakage.

faqs.question: Where does the name Scunci come from?
faqs.answer: Revson reportedly named it after her pet poodle.

image.alt: A velvet scrunchie

name: Shaving brush

place_of_invention.notes: Shaving brushes are commonly said to have appeared in France in the mid-18th century; documentation is limited.

short_description: A round brush used to whip shaving soap into lather and apply it to the face.
description: The shaving brush is traditionally dated to 18th-century France, when lathering soap became part of the shaving routine. Brushes were made from badger, boar or horsehair set in handles of wood, horn or bone. Synthetic fibers are now common, but the dense, round knot on a short handle is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A dense, round knot of bristles holds water and builds lather perfectly, so there was no need to change it.

faqs.question: Why use a shaving brush instead of fingers?
faqs.answer: A brush whips soap into a rich lather, lifts the hairs and gently exfoliates the skin before shaving.

faqs.question: What is the best hair for a shaving brush?
faqs.answer: Badger hair is traditional and holds water well, boar is stiffer and cheaper, and synthetic fibers dry quickly and are animal-free.

faqs.question: How do you care for a shaving brush?
faqs.answer: Rinse it thoroughly, shake out the water and let it dry bristles-down or in open air.

image.alt: A badger-hair shaving brush on a stand

name: Shaving mug

place_of_invention.notes: Personalized shaving mugs became common in barbershops in the 19th century; no single origin is recorded.

short_description: A mug used to hold shaving soap and work it into lather.
description: Shaving mugs became popular in the 19th century, when customers in American barbershops kept their own personalized mugs on the shop's shelf. Many had a separate compartment for soap and water. Wet shavers still use similar mugs or bowls to build lather with a brush.
why_unchanged: A sturdy cup to hold a puck of soap and a wet brush already does exactly what is required.

faqs.question: Why did barbershops keep customers' own mugs?
faqs.answer: Personal mugs, often painted with the owner's name or trade, were thought to reduce the spread of skin infections.

faqs.question: What is a scuttle?
faqs.answer: A scuttle is a shaving mug with a double wall filled with hot water to keep lather warm.

faqs.question: Do I need a shaving mug?
faqs.answer: Not strictly; lather can be built in a bowl or on the face, but a mug holds the soap puck conveniently.

image.alt: A ceramic shaving mug with a brush

name: Snellen chart

place_of_invention.notes: Herman Snellen published his eye chart in 1862; it remains the most widely recognized chart for testing visual acuity, alongside later charts like LogMAR.

short_description: A wall chart of rows of letters in decreasing sizes, used to test eyesight.
description: Dutch ophthalmologist Herman Snellen developed his chart in 1862, using specially designed letters called optotypes on a grid. The size of each row corresponds to a standard viewing distance. Variants exist, but the classic Snellen chart with a large E at the top is still used worldwide.
why_unchanged: Rows of standardized letters shrinking in size measure acuity simply and reliably, so the chart stuck.

faqs.question: Who invented the eye chart?
faqs.answer: Herman Snellen created it in Utrecht in 1862.

faqs.question: What does 20/20 vision mean?
faqs.answer: It means you can read at 20 feet what a person with normal vision can read at 20 feet; 20/40 means you need to be at 20 feet to see what others see at 40.

faqs.question: Why does the chart start with a big E?
faqs.answer: Many Snellen charts begin with a single large letter, often E, which tests the lowest level of acuity.

image.alt: A Snellen eye chart

name: Splint

place_of_invention.notes: Splints of wood and bark wrapped in linen were found on Egyptian mummies from the Fifth Dynasty; splinting was described by Hippocrates and probably practiced earlier.

short_description: A rigid support bound to an injured limb to keep it still.
description: Splints are among the oldest medical devices; archaeologists found bark and wooden splints bound with linen on Egyptian mummies over 4,500 years old. Hippocrates described splinting fractures in ancient Greece. Modern splints use aluminum, plastic or padded foam, but the idea of binding a rigid support along a limb is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A rigid support bound along a limb is the simplest way to stop movement, so it never needed redesign.

faqs.question: How old are splints?
faqs.answer: Splints have been found on Egyptian mummies from around 2750 BCE.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a splint and a cast?
faqs.answer: A splint supports one side and can be adjusted for swelling, while a cast wraps the limb completely.

faqs.question: Can you improvise a splint?
faqs.answer: In first aid, rolled newspapers, boards or sticks padded and tied along the limb can serve as a temporary splint.

image.alt: An arm splint

name: Stethoscope

place_of_invention.notes: René Laennec invented the monaural wooden-tube stethoscope in 1816; the binaural form with two earpieces, which defines the modern instrument, was developed in the 1850s (notably by George Cammann in New York).

short_description: An instrument for listening to sounds inside the body, especially the heart and lungs.
description: In 1816 the French physician René Laennec rolled paper into a tube to listen to a patient's heart, then developed a wooden tube he called the stethoscope. In the 1850s binaural versions with flexible tubes and two earpieces appeared, establishing the form used today. Modern stethoscopes add diaphragms and better acoustics, but the layout is unchanged since then.
why_unchanged: A chest piece, tubing and earpieces carry body sounds directly to the ears, and the design has proved hard to beat.

faqs.question: Who invented the stethoscope?
faqs.answer: René Laennec invented it in Paris in 1816.

faqs.question: Why did Laennec invent it?
faqs.answer: He felt it was inappropriate to put his ear directly to a young woman's chest, so he rolled paper into a tube and found it amplified the heartbeat.

faqs.question: What is the difference between the bell and the diaphragm?
faqs.answer: The diaphragm picks up high-pitched sounds like breathing, while the bell picks up low-pitched sounds like certain heart murmurs.

image.alt: A stethoscope on a table

name: Straight razor

place_of_invention.notes: Bronze and copper razors are known from ancient Egypt, but the folding steel straight razor is usually dated to Sheffield in the late 17th century.

short_description: A single steel blade that folds into its handle, used for shaving.
description: People shaved with sharpened stone, bronze and copper blades for thousands of years. The folding steel straight razor, with a blade that pivots into a protective handle, is generally traced to Sheffield cutlers around 1680. It was the main shaving tool until the 20th century and is still used by barbers and enthusiasts.
why_unchanged: A sharp blade that folds into its handle is both safe to carry and simple to maintain.

faqs.question: Why is it called a 'cut-throat' razor?
faqs.answer: The nickname comes from the exposed blade, which can cause serious cuts if handled carelessly.

faqs.question: How do you keep a straight razor sharp?
faqs.answer: It is honed on a stone occasionally and stropped on leather before each shave to realign the edge.

faqs.question: Do barbers still use straight razors?
faqs.answer: Many do, though often with disposable-blade versions called shavettes for hygiene reasons.

image.alt: An open straight razor with a horn handle

name: Stretcher

place_of_invention.notes: Carrying the sick or wounded on litters or poles is ancient and universal; organized military stretcher-bearing developed in the 18th–19th centuries.

short_description: A frame with fabric stretched between two poles for carrying a person who cannot walk.
description: Two poles with a sheet of fabric between them have been used to carry the injured since antiquity. In the Napoleonic era Baron Dominique-Jean Larrey organized battlefield ambulance services that improved casualty transport. Folding and wheeled versions exist, but the classic pole stretcher is still used in first aid and the military.
why_unchanged: Two poles and a fabric bed are light, strong and easy to carry, so the design endures.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a stretcher and a gurney?
faqs.answer: A stretcher is carried by people, while a gurney has wheels and an adjustable frame.

faqs.question: How many people carry a stretcher?
faqs.answer: At least two, and four is often recommended over long distances or rough ground.

faqs.question: Can you improvise a stretcher?
faqs.answer: Yes; two poles threaded through buttoned jackets or a folded blanket can make an emergency stretcher.

image.alt: A canvas folding stretcher

name: Tampon

place_of_invention.notes: Absorbent plugs were used for menstruation in antiquity; Earle Haas filed the patent for the modern applicator tampon in 1931 (granted 1933), later sold as Tampax.

short_description: A small plug of absorbent material inserted to absorb menstrual flow.
description: Absorbent inserts for menstruation have been made from papyrus, wool and other materials since ancient times. In 1931 the Colorado physician Earle Haas designed a compressed cotton tampon with a cardboard applicator tube and a removal string. He sold the patent to Gertrude Tendrich, who founded Tampax, and the design is still standard.
why_unchanged: A compressed absorbent core with an applicator and string solved insertion, absorption and removal together.

faqs.question: Who invented the modern tampon?
faqs.answer: Dr. Earle Haas designed the applicator tampon in 1931, patented in 1933 and sold as Tampax.

faqs.question: What is toxic shock syndrome?
faqs.answer: It is a rare but serious bacterial illness linked to tampon use; changing tampons every 4–8 hours reduces the risk.

faqs.question: Were tampons used in ancient times?
faqs.answer: Ancient medical texts describe inserted absorbent materials, though how commonly they were used is uncertain.

image.alt: A wrapped tampon

name: Teething ring

place_of_invention.notes: Teethers of coral, ivory and bone, often set in silver rattles, were common in early modern Europe; simple rings for chewing are likely older.

short_description: A ring that a teething baby can safely chew to soothe sore gums.
description: Wealthy European families gave babies coral or ivory teethers, often attached to silver whistles and bells, which were thought to have protective powers. Simpler rings of bone and wood were used by others. Modern teething rings are made of rubber or silicone, sometimes chilled, but they keep the same ring shape.
why_unchanged: A ring is easy for tiny hands to hold and safe to chew, so the shape has stayed.

faqs.question: Why are teething rings ring-shaped?
faqs.answer: A ring is easy for a baby to grasp and has no small parts that could break off.

faqs.question: Why were old teethers made of coral?
faqs.answer: Coral was believed to ward off evil and illness, as well as being smooth and hard.

faqs.question: Is it okay to freeze a teething ring?
faqs.answer: Chilling in the fridge is fine, but health advice usually warns against freezing because it can become hard enough to hurt gums.

image.alt: A silicone teething ring

name: Toilet paper roll

place_of_invention.notes: Paper for hygiene was used in China centuries earlier, and Joseph Gayetty sold flat packaged sheets in 1857; Seth Wheeler patented wrapping paper on a roll in 1871 and perforated rolls in 1891.

short_description: A long strip of soft paper wound on a cardboard core and perforated into sheets.
description: Paper for personal hygiene is recorded in China as early as the 6th century, and in 1857 Joseph Gayetty sold flat 'medicated paper' in the US. Seth Wheeler of Albany patented paper on a roll in 1871 and the perforated roll in 1891. The perforated roll on a core is still the standard worldwide.
why_unchanged: A perforated roll dispenses one sheet at a time from a compact holder, which is hard to improve.

faqs.question: Who invented the toilet paper roll?
faqs.answer: Seth Wheeler of Albany, New York, patented rolled and perforated toilet paper in 1871 and 1891.

faqs.question: Should toilet paper hang over or under?
faqs.answer: Wheeler's 1891 patent drawings show the paper hanging over the front of the roll.

faqs.question: What did people use before toilet paper?
faqs.answer: Methods varied widely: leaves, moss, corn cobs, sponges on sticks, water and old newspapers.

image.alt: A roll of toilet paper

name: Tongue depressor

place_of_invention.notes: Metal tongue depressors were used by 19th-century physicians; disposable wooden ones became standard in the 20th century. No single inventor is clearly credited.

short_description: A thin, flat, rounded stick used to press the tongue down to examine the mouth and throat.
description: Doctors began using flat instruments to hold the tongue down for throat examinations in the 19th century, often made of metal. Disposable wooden tongue depressors became the norm in the 20th century for hygiene reasons. The plain flat stick with rounded ends is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A smooth flat stick does the job perfectly and is cheap enough to discard after one use.

faqs.question: Why do doctors use a tongue depressor?
faqs.answer: It holds the tongue down so they can see the throat and tonsils clearly.

faqs.question: Why do tongue depressors make people gag?
faqs.answer: Touching the back of the tongue can trigger the gag reflex, which is why doctors press near the middle.

faqs.question: What else are tongue depressors used for?
faqs.answer: They are also used as craft sticks, for applying ointments and as makeshift finger splints.

image.alt: Wooden tongue depressors

name: Tongue scraper

place_of_invention.notes: Tongue scraping is described in Ayurvedic tradition; exact dating is uncertain. Ornate tongue scrapers were also common in Victorian Britain.

short_description: A curved strip or loop used to scrape coating off the surface of the tongue.
description: Tongue scraping is a long-standing part of the Ayurvedic daily routine in India, where U-shaped scrapers of copper, silver or other metals are still used. Tongue scrapers were also fashionable in Europe, particularly in 18th- and 19th-century Britain. The simple bow shape held at both ends has stayed the same, now often made of stainless steel or plastic.
why_unchanged: A smooth curved edge pulled from back to front is all that is needed to clear the tongue's surface.

faqs.question: Why do people scrape their tongues?
faqs.answer: Scraping removes bacteria, food debris and dead cells from the tongue, which can help reduce bad breath.

faqs.question: Is a tongue scraper better than brushing the tongue?
faqs.answer: Some studies suggest a scraper removes tongue coating slightly more effectively than a toothbrush, though both help.

faqs.question: Why are traditional tongue scrapers made of copper?
faqs.answer: Copper is the traditional Ayurvedic material and is valued for its antimicrobial properties, though stainless steel works equally well for scraping.

image.alt: A U-shaped copper tongue scraper

name: Toothbrush

place_of_invention.notes: Bristle toothbrushes are recorded in China under the Hongzhi Emperor (1498); earlier Chinese bristle brushes may exist. William Addis began mass production in England around 1780.

short_description: A small brush with a handle and a head of bristles for cleaning teeth.
description: The bristle toothbrush, with coarse hog bristles fixed into a bone or bamboo handle, is recorded in China at the end of the 15th century. Travelers brought the idea to Europe, and in about 1780 William Addis of England began manufacturing toothbrushes commercially. Nylon bristles replaced animal hair in 1938, but the handle-and-bristle-head layout remained the same.
why_unchanged: A straight handle with a tuft of bristles at the end reaches every tooth surface, so later changes affected only materials and ergonomics.

faqs.question: Who invented the toothbrush?
faqs.answer: The bristle toothbrush first appears in Ming-dynasty China in 1498; no single inventor is known. William Addis is credited with the first mass-produced toothbrushes in England around 1780.

faqs.question: When did toothbrushes get nylon bristles?
faqs.answer: Nylon bristles were introduced in 1938, replacing the hog, horse or badger hair used before.

faqs.question: How often should you replace a toothbrush?
faqs.answer: Dental associations generally recommend replacing it every three to four months, or sooner if the bristles are frayed.

image.alt: A manual toothbrush on a white background

name: Toothpaste tube

place_of_invention.notes: Sheffield's company is usually credited with the first collapsible toothpaste tube; Colgate adopted the format in 1896. The collapsible metal tube itself was patented for artists' paint by John Goffe Rand in 1841.

short_description: A squeezable, collapsible tube that dispenses toothpaste.
description: Before the 1890s toothpaste and tooth powder were sold in jars, which were messy and unhygienic. The dentist Washington Sheffield adapted the collapsible metal tube, previously used for oil paints, to hold toothpaste. Plastic and laminate tubes replaced lead and tin in the 20th century, but the squeeze-and-cap format is unchanged.
why_unchanged: Squeezing paste out of a sealed tube keeps the contents clean and dispenses just the right amount, so the format never needed rethinking.

faqs.question: Who first put toothpaste in a tube?
faqs.answer: Dr. Washington Sheffield of Connecticut is generally credited with selling toothpaste in a collapsible tube in 1892.

faqs.question: What did toothpaste come in before tubes?
faqs.answer: It was sold as powder or paste in jars and tins, into which everyone dipped their brush.

faqs.question: What do the colored squares on the bottom of tubes mean?
faqs.answer: They are printing registration marks read by machines during manufacturing; despite a popular myth, they say nothing about the ingredients.

image.alt: A squeezed tube of toothpaste

name: Toothpick

place_of_invention.notes: Grooves on fossil hominin teeth suggest tooth-picking long predates any surviving tool; early metal picks are known from Mesopotamian sites. Almost certainly used independently by many cultures.

short_description: A small, thin stick used to remove food from between the teeth.
description: The toothpick is one of humanity's oldest grooming habits, with wear marks on ancient teeth showing that people probed between them with twigs or grass stalks. Ornate picks of bronze, silver and gold were carried by the wealthy in antiquity and the Middle Ages. Mass-produced wooden toothpicks spread in the 19th century, especially after machines were developed in the United States to cut them from birch.
why_unchanged: A thin, pointed stick is already the simplest shape that fits between teeth, so there was nothing to improve.

faqs.question: How old is the toothpick?
faqs.answer: Wear grooves on fossil teeth suggest early humans picked their teeth with sticks long before written history. Metal toothpicks have been found in ancient Mesopotamian contexts.

faqs.question: Why do some toothpicks have grooves near one end?
faqs.answer: The decorative grooves on many European-style toothpicks let you snap off the end and use it as a small rest, so the used tip does not touch the table.

faqs.question: Are toothpicks good for your teeth?
faqs.answer: They can dislodge trapped food, but dentists generally recommend floss or interdental brushes for routine cleaning because a stiff pick can irritate the gums.

image.alt: A pile of wooden toothpicks

name: Towel

place_of_invention.notes: Flat-woven Turkish bath towels (peshtemal) are traditionally linked to Bursa; looped terry towels were inspired by Ottoman weaving and mass-produced in England in the 1850s. Earlier drying cloths existed everywhere.

short_description: A piece of absorbent fabric for drying the body.
description: Cloths for drying the body have existed since antiquity, but the towel as we know it owes much to the Ottoman hammam, where flat-woven peshtemal towels were used. Looped pile towels from Turkey inspired English manufacturer Christy, which industrialized terry towels in the 1850s. Rectangular terry towels have been the norm ever since.
why_unchanged: A rectangle of absorbent fabric dries the body perfectly, so only fibers and weaves changed.

faqs.question: What is a Turkish towel?
faqs.answer: A Turkish towel or peshtemal is a thin, flat-woven cotton towel used in the hammam, which dries quickly and packs small.

faqs.question: Why are bath towels looped?
faqs.answer: The loops of terry cloth greatly increase surface area, making the towel more absorbent.

faqs.question: Why is Towel Day celebrated on 25 May?
faqs.answer: Fans of Douglas Adams carry a towel on 25 May in tribute to 'The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy', which praises the towel's usefulness.

image.alt: A stack of folded bath towels

name: Triangular bandage

place_of_invention.notes: The Swiss surgeon Mathias Mayor promoted triangular cloths in the 1830s, and Friedrich von Esmarch popularized the printed triangular bandage for first aid in the 1870s; credit is shared.

short_description: A triangle of cloth that can be folded into a sling, pad or binding.
description: The triangular bandage became a first-aid staple after Friedrich von Esmarch included it in field kits and printed illustrated instructions on the cloth itself. It can be used as an arm sling, a head bandage, a pressure pad or a binding for splints. It is still standard in first-aid kits worldwide.
why_unchanged: A single triangle of cloth serves many first-aid purposes, so its shape has never been bettered.

faqs.question: What can a triangular bandage be used for?
faqs.answer: It can serve as an arm sling, a head or hand dressing, a pressure pad, or a tie for securing a splint.

faqs.question: Why were instructions printed on old triangular bandages?
faqs.answer: Esmarch printed diagrams on the cloth so untrained people could apply it correctly in an emergency.

faqs.question: How big is a triangular bandage?
faqs.answer: A common size is roughly 90 by 90 by 127 centimeters.

image.alt: A folded triangular bandage

name: Tweezers

place_of_invention.notes: Copper and bronze tweezers appear in early Egyptian and Mesopotamian sites; similar tools were developed in many ancient cultures.

short_description: A small two-armed tool used to grip and pull tiny objects such as hairs and splinters.
description: Tweezers made of copper or bronze have been found in ancient Egyptian and Mesopotamian sites, used for removing hair and splinters. The Romans used them widely for grooming and in medicine. Modern stainless-steel tweezers have refined tips, but the two springy arms joined at one end are the same.
why_unchanged: Two springy arms joined at one end give fine, controlled grip with no mechanism at all.

faqs.question: How old are tweezers?
faqs.answer: Metal tweezers date back at least 5,000 years to ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia.

faqs.question: Which tip shape is best for eyebrows?
faqs.answer: Slanted tips are the most versatile for brows, while pointed tips are better for splinters and ingrown hairs.

faqs.question: Where does the word 'tweezers' come from?
faqs.answer: It comes from 'tweeze', a small case of instruments, ultimately from the French 'étui'.

image.alt: A pair of slanted stainless-steel tweezers

name: Walking cane

place_of_invention.notes: Walking sticks were used by people everywhere since prehistory; no specific origin can be identified, and the date given is only a placeholder for early evidence.

short_description: A stick with a handle used for support and balance while walking.
description: Walking sticks are among the oldest human tools and appear in ancient Egyptian, Greek and biblical imagery as symbols of authority as well as aids. In 17th–19th century Europe the cane became a fashion accessory for gentlemen. Today canes are mainly mobility aids, but the stick with a crook or handle is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A rigid stick with a handle gives balance and support, which is all that is required.

faqs.question: Which hand should hold a cane?
faqs.answer: Usually the hand opposite the weaker leg, so the cane moves together with that leg.

faqs.question: How tall should a cane be?
faqs.answer: With arms relaxed, the handle should reach the crease of the wrist.

faqs.question: Why were canes fashionable?
faqs.answer: In the 17th–19th centuries an elegant cane signaled status and was part of a gentleman's dress.

image.alt: A wooden walking cane with a curved handle

name: Washcloth

place_of_invention.notes: Pieces of cloth have been used for washing since antiquity; the looped terry fabric used for most washcloths was industrialized in England in the 1850s.

short_description: A small square of absorbent cloth used for washing the face and body.
description: Wiping the body with a damp cloth is an ancient practice. The modern washcloth, a small square of looped terry fabric, became common after English manufacturers developed machine-woven terry cloth in the mid-19th century. It is still a plain square that holds water and soap.
why_unchanged: A small, absorbent square is all that is needed to wet, lather and wipe the skin.

faqs.question: What is a washcloth called elsewhere?
faqs.answer: It is also known as a face cloth, flannel (in the UK) or wash rag.

faqs.question: How often should a washcloth be washed?
faqs.answer: Because damp cloth can grow bacteria, it is best washed after a few uses and allowed to dry fully.

faqs.question: Why are washcloths made of terry cloth?
faqs.answer: Terry's loops increase the surface area, so it holds more water and gently exfoliates.

image.alt: A folded cotton washcloth

name: Wax earplug

place_of_invention.notes: Earplugs of wax are mentioned in antiquity (Odysseus's crew in Homer); Maximilian Negwer began producing Ohropax wax-and-cotton earplugs in 1907.

short_description: A small ball of wax and cotton molded into the outer ear to block noise.
description: In Homer's Odyssey, Odysseus plugs his crew's ears with beeswax to protect them from the Sirens. In 1907 the Berlin pharmacist Maximilian Negwer began selling Ohropax, mouldable balls of wax and cotton wool. These are still produced, alongside foam and silicone earplugs.
why_unchanged: Soft wax molds itself to each ear, so a simple ball gives a custom seal without any design changes.

faqs.question: Who invented wax earplugs?
faqs.answer: Wax was used to plug ears in antiquity, but Maximilian Negwer created the commercial Ohropax earplug in 1907.

faqs.question: Why use wax rather than foam earplugs?
faqs.answer: Wax molds over the ear canal opening and suits people who find foam inside the canal uncomfortable.

faqs.question: What does 'Ohropax' mean?
faqs.answer: It combines German 'Ohr' (ear) with Latin 'pax' (peace).

image.alt: Several wax earplugs

name: White cane

place_of_invention.notes: James Biggs, a Bristol photographer who lost his sight, is credited with painting his cane white in 1921; Guilly d'Herbemont promoted white canes in France in 1931, and US Lions Clubs did so from 1930.

short_description: A long white cane used by blind and visually impaired people for mobility and identification.
description: After losing his sight in an accident in 1921, Bristol photographer James Biggs painted his walking stick white so motorists would notice him. The idea spread in France and the US in the early 1930s, and longer canes for sweeping the ground were developed after the Second World War. The white cane remains an internationally recognized symbol and tool.
why_unchanged: A long, light, highly visible stick both detects obstacles and signals blindness, so its form stays.

faqs.question: Who invented the white cane?
faqs.answer: James Biggs of Bristol is credited with painting his cane white in 1921 to be more visible to traffic.

faqs.question: Why do some white canes have red bands?
faqs.answer: In many countries a red-and-white cane indicates that the user is both deaf and blind.

faqs.question: Is there a White Cane Day?
faqs.answer: Yes; International White Cane Safety Day is observed on 15 October.

image.alt: A folding white cane

name: Amphora

place_of_invention.notes: Archaeologists trace the amphora to Bronze Age Canaanite storage jars on the Levantine coast, in what is now Lebanon, Syria and Israel; the form was later adopted and standardized by Greeks and Romans.

short_description: A two-handled ceramic jar with a narrow neck, used to transport wine, oil and other goods.
description: Amphorae were the shipping containers of the ancient Mediterranean, carrying wine, olive oil and fish sauce by sea. The form grew from Canaanite storage jars and was widely adopted by Greeks, Phoenicians and Romans. Their pointed bases could be packed in sand or ship holds, and similar clay jars are still made for wine today.
why_unchanged: Two handles, a narrow neck and a tapered base solve carrying, sealing and packing, which is why the shape lasted for millennia.

faqs.question: Why do many amphorae have pointed bottoms?
faqs.answer: The pointed base let them be stacked in rows on ships, pushed into sand and used as a third handle for pouring.

faqs.question: What did amphorae carry?
faqs.answer: Mostly wine and olive oil, but also fish sauce, grain, olives and other goods traded around the Mediterranean.

faqs.question: Are amphorae still used?
faqs.answer: Yes. Some winemakers use clay amphorae to ferment and age wine, reviving the ancient method.

image.alt: A terracotta amphora with two handles

name: Barrel

place_of_invention.notes: Roman writers credit Celtic peoples with stave barrels; Herodotus describes palm-wood casks in Mesopotamia earlier, so the precise origin is uncertain.

short_description: A cylindrical wooden container made of bent staves bound by hoops.
description: Wooden barrels were used by Celtic peoples in Gaul and the Alps and were adopted by the Romans, who came to prefer them to fragile clay amphorae. The bulging shape lets a heavy barrel be rolled and pivoted easily. Coopers still build barrels by hand from oak staves and metal hoops in essentially the same way.
why_unchanged: The curved staves and hoops make a strong, rollable, watertight container, which is why coopers still use the ancient design.

faqs.question: Why are barrels bulged in the middle?
faqs.answer: The bulge, called the bilge, lets one person roll and turn a heavy barrel easily and makes the hoops grip tightly.

faqs.question: Who makes barrels?
faqs.answer: Barrels are made by coopers, a traditional craft that still uses many of the same techniques as centuries ago.

faqs.question: Why are wine and whisky aged in oak barrels?
faqs.answer: Oak is strong and watertight and adds flavor and tannins while allowing slow oxidation through the wood.

image.alt: Rows of oak barrels in a cellar

name: Basket

place_of_invention.notes: Basketry impressions in clay from Central Europe are around 27,000 years old, and baskets were made independently all over the world; actual woven baskets rarely survive.

short_description: A container woven from flexible materials such as reeds, willow or grass.
description: Basketry is one of humanity's oldest crafts, predating pottery in many places. Baskets were used for gathering, carrying and storing food, and techniques such as coiling and plaiting appear across all continents. Most baskets are still woven by hand in essentially the same way.
why_unchanged: Weaving flexible fibers produces a light, strong container from local materials, so the technique has not needed to change.

faqs.question: Is basketry older than pottery?
faqs.answer: In many regions, yes. Impressions of woven fibers in fired clay show that weaving was practiced at least 27,000 years ago.

faqs.question: Can baskets be made by machine?
faqs.answer: Very few baskets are machine-made; most are still woven by hand.

faqs.question: What are baskets made from?
faqs.answer: Almost any flexible plant material, including willow, rattan, reed, bamboo, palm leaves and grasses.

image.alt: A handwoven wicker basket

name: Beer mat

place_of_invention.notes: Germany is generally credited with the paperboard beer mat; Robert Sputh of Dresden is often said to have made wood-pulp mats in 1892, while others cite Friedrich Horn in the 1880s.

short_description: A cardboard coaster placed under a beer glass.
description: Felt pads were once used under beer mugs, but they soaked up beer and became unhygienic. In the late 19th century German manufacturers began producing absorbent paperboard mats. The beer mat remains a simple absorbent square or circle.
why_unchanged: An absorbent disk protects tables and is cheap to print, so it hasn't changed.

faqs.question: Who invented the beer mat?
faqs.answer: Germany is generally credited; Robert Sputh of Dresden is often named for wood-pulp mats in 1892, though other early makers are also cited.

faqs.question: What is a beer mat collector called?
faqs.answer: A beer mat collector is called a tegestologist, from the Latin word for a mat or covering.

faqs.question: Why do some people put a beer mat on top of their glass?
faqs.answer: In many German pubs a mat placed on the glass signals that you don't want another round, and it also keeps insects out.

image.alt: A beer glass on a cardboard beer mat

name: Beer stein

place_of_invention.notes: Lidded beer mugs became common in German lands in the 16th century; the claim that lids were required by plague-era hygiene laws is widely repeated but not firmly documented.

short_description: A large lidded beer mug, traditionally made of stoneware.
description: Stoneware mugs became popular in Germany as potters mastered high-fired stoneware. Hinged pewter lids, possibly adopted to keep out insects, became a defining feature. Steins remain associated with German beer culture, especially decorative versions.
why_unchanged: A heavy mug with a hinged lid protects beer and is operated with one thumb, so the form has stayed the same.

faqs.question: What does 'stein' mean?
faqs.answer: It is short for German 'Steinzeugkrug', meaning stoneware jug.

faqs.question: Why do beer steins have lids?
faqs.answer: Lids kept out insects and debris; a popular story links them to hygiene laws during plague outbreaks, but this is not firmly proven.

faqs.question: Is a Maß the same as a stein?
faqs.answer: A Maß is a one-liter glass beer mug used at Oktoberfest; steins are traditionally stoneware with a lid.

image.alt: A decorated stoneware beer stein with a pewter lid

name: Bendy straw

place_of_invention.notes: Joseph B. Friedman patented the flexible drinking straw, with a corrugated hinge section, in 1937.

short_description: A drinking straw with a flexible corrugated joint that bends.
description: Joseph Friedman watched his young daughter struggle to drink from a straight straw at a soda fountain. He inserted a screw into a paper straw, wrapped floss around the threads to create corrugations, and patented the flexible straw in 1937. Hospitals were among its first major customers, and bendy straws still use the same accordion joint.
why_unchanged: An accordion-like section bends without collapsing, so the corrugated joint is unchanged.

faqs.question: Who invented the bendy straw?
faqs.answer: Joseph B. Friedman patented the flexible drinking straw in 1937.

faqs.question: What inspired the bendy straw?
faqs.answer: Friedman saw his daughter struggling to reach a straight straw in a tall glass and invented a bendable one.

faqs.question: Who were the first big users of bendy straws?
faqs.answer: Hospitals, because patients could drink while lying down.

image.alt: Colorful bendy drinking straws in a glass

name: Bento box

place_of_invention.notes: Packed meals of dried rice date back to the 12th century in Japan; the word bento and lacquered lunch boxes are associated with the late 16th-century Azuchi–Momoyama period and became widespread in the Edo period.

short_description: A compartmented Japanese box for a single-portion packed meal.
description: Japanese travelers and workers carried packed meals for centuries, and lacquered boxes for outings appeared in the late 16th century. In the Edo period bento were eaten at the theater and on journeys, and later at schools and offices. Modern bento boxes in plastic or wood keep the lidded, divided layout.
why_unchanged: Separate compartments under a lid keep foods apart and portable, which is all a packed meal needs.

faqs.question: What does bento mean?
faqs.answer: Bento refers to a single-portion packed meal and the box that holds it in Japanese.

faqs.question: What is an ekiben?
faqs.answer: An ekiben is a bento sold at train stations, a tradition that began in the late 19th century.

faqs.question: What is kyaraben?
faqs.answer: Kyaraben, short for 'character bento', is food arranged to look like cartoon characters, often made for children.

image.alt: An open bento box with rice and side dishes

name: Biscuit tin

place_of_invention.notes: Biscuit maker Huntley & Palmers of Reading began selling biscuits in tins in the 1830s, produced by the related tin firm Huntley, Boorne & Stevens; decorated printed tins followed in the 1860s.

short_description: A metal container used to store and sell biscuits.
description: Huntley & Palmers began packaging biscuits in tins to keep them fresh during transport. The tins were made by a firm founded by Joseph Huntley's son, and later were decorated with printed designs. Biscuit tins remain a popular way to store and gift biscuits.
why_unchanged: A lidded metal box keeps biscuits dry and fresh, so it has not changed.

faqs.question: Why are biscuits sold in tins?
faqs.answer: Tins keep biscuits dry and protect them from breaking.

faqs.question: Why do people keep sewing kits in biscuit tins?
faqs.answer: Once empty, the sturdy tins are reused for storage, a popular household habit.

faqs.question: Are vintage biscuit tins collectible?
faqs.answer: Yes, decorative Victorian and Edwardian tins are collectors' items.

image.alt: A decorated biscuit tin

name: Bombilla

place_of_invention.notes: The Guaraní used cane tubes to drink mate; metal bombillas with perforated filter ends spread during the colonial period. Exact dating is uncertain.

short_description: A metal drinking straw with a perforated filter end, used to drink yerba mate.
description: The Guaraní drank mate through tubes of cane, sometimes fitted with woven filters. During the colonial period silversmiths made metal bombillas with perforated bulbs or flattened tips to strain out the leaves. The bombilla remains an essential part of mate drinking in South America.
why_unchanged: A tube with a strainer at the bottom solves the problem of drinking from leaves, so it hasn't changed.

faqs.question: What does bombilla mean?
faqs.answer: It is a Spanish diminutive often translated as 'little pump' or 'little bulb'; in Brazil it is called a bomba.

faqs.question: Should you stir mate with the bombilla?
faqs.answer: No. Moving the bombilla clogs its filter with leaves and is considered poor etiquette among mate drinkers.

faqs.question: What is a bombilla made of?
faqs.answer: Most are stainless steel, silver or nickel silver, with traditional versions also made of cane or bamboo.

image.alt: A metal bombilla in a mate gourd

name: Bota bag

place_of_invention.notes: Leather wine bags have been used in Spain for centuries; their exact age is undocumented.

short_description: A traditional Spanish leather wine bag.
description: The bota is a teardrop-shaped bag of leather lined with pitch or latex for carrying wine. Spaniards squirt wine into their mouths from it, a skill admired at festivals. The form has stayed the same for centuries.
why_unchanged: A soft leather pouch with a nozzle is portable and unbreakable, so it remains unchanged.

faqs.question: How do you drink from a bota?
faqs.answer: Hold it at arm's length and squeeze to send a thin stream into your mouth.

faqs.question: What is a bota lined with?
faqs.answer: Traditionally pitch or resin; modern ones often use latex.

faqs.question: Where is the bota used?
faqs.answer: Especially in Spain at festivals such as San Fermín in Pamplona.

image.alt: A leather bota bag

name: Bottle

place_of_invention.notes: Core-formed glass bottles were made in Mesopotamia and Egypt in the mid-2nd millennium BCE; pottery, gourd and leather bottles are older. Glassblowing in the 1st century BCE made glass bottles common.

short_description: A container with a narrow neck used for storing and pouring liquids.
description: Early glass bottles were small luxury vessels for perfume and oils made in Egypt and Mesopotamia. The invention of glassblowing in the 1st century BCE made bottles cheap and widespread in the Roman world. Machine production in the 20th century made them ubiquitous, but the narrow-necked form is the same.
why_unchanged: A wide body for volume and a narrow neck for pouring and sealing is an ideal combination that has never been improved upon.

faqs.question: When were glass bottles first made?
faqs.answer: Small core-formed glass bottles were made in Egypt and Mesopotamia around 3,500 years ago, long before glassblowing.

faqs.question: Why do bottles have narrow necks?
faqs.answer: A narrow neck makes pouring controlled and lets the bottle be sealed with a small cork or cap.

faqs.question: When did bottles become mass-produced?
faqs.answer: Michael Owens' automatic bottle-making machine of 1903 made glass bottles cheap and abundant.

image.alt: Several glass bottles on a shelf

name: Bowl

place_of_invention.notes: Gourds, shells and wooden bowls likely came first; some of the oldest pottery vessels, from East Asia, date to around 18,000–14,000 years ago, and bowls appear in many independent pottery traditions.

short_description: A round, deep, open vessel used to hold food or liquid.
description: Bowls are among the oldest manufactured objects, made first from natural materials like gourds and wood and then from fired clay. Early pottery traditions in East Asia, Africa and the Near East all produced bowls. The open, rounded form remains universal for soups, grains and mixed dishes.
why_unchanged: A rounded open vessel holds liquids and loose food securely and is easy to make, so the shape never needed improvement.

faqs.question: Is the bowl one of the oldest human-made objects?
faqs.answer: Yes. Bowls were among the earliest forms made once people began firing clay, and wooden or gourd bowls are probably even older.

faqs.question: Why are bowls round?
faqs.answer: A round inner surface has no corners where food gets stuck, distributes heat evenly and is easy to shape by hand or on a wheel.

faqs.question: What is a footed bowl?
faqs.answer: A footed bowl has a small ring or pedestal on its base that raises it slightly, making it more stable and easier to pick up when hot.

image.alt: A set of stacked ceramic bowls

name: Bread clip

place_of_invention.notes: Paxton first cut the clip by hand from plastic to close a fruit bag; his company, Kwik Lok, still makes it.

short_description: A small flat plastic tab with a slot that closes the neck of a plastic bag.
description: Floyd Paxton made the first bread clip in the early 1950s to close a bag of fruit, then built machines to produce and apply them. Bakeries adopted the clips because they are fast to put on and can be reused. Clip colors often indicate the day the bread was baked.
why_unchanged: A flat tab with a notch is fast to apply, reusable and costs a fraction of a cent, so there was nothing to improve.

faqs.question: What do the colors of bread clips mean?
faqs.answer: Many bakeries use a color per day of the week so staff can rotate stock; the code varies by company.

faqs.question: Who invented the bread clip?
faqs.answer: Floyd G. Paxton of Yakima, Washington, in 1952; his company Kwik Lok still produces them.

faqs.question: Why not use a twist tie instead?
faqs.answer: Clips are faster to apply by machine and easier to reopen and reuse by hand.

image.alt: A small plastic bread clip on a bag of bread

name: Bucket

place_of_invention.notes: Leather, bark and wooden stave buckets were used in many ancient cultures; there is no single documented origin.

short_description: An open-topped round container with a handle, used to carry liquids.
description: Buckets have been made from leather, bark, wood and metal since ancient times, notably as wooden stave buckets used by Celtic, Roman and other peoples. They were indispensable for drawing water from wells, milking and firefighting. Today's metal and plastic buckets keep the same tapered cylinder and swinging handle.
why_unchanged: An open container with a bail handle is the simplest way to carry liquid, so its form has stayed essentially the same.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a bucket and a pail?
faqs.answer: The words are generally interchangeable, though 'pail' is sometimes used for smaller buckets.

faqs.question: Why are buckets tapered?
faqs.answer: The taper lets empty buckets nest inside one another and makes them easier to mold or build.

faqs.question: Where does the phrase 'kick the bucket' come from?
faqs.answer: Its origin is uncertain; one theory links it to a beam called a 'bucket' used to hang animals, but none is proven.

image.alt: A metal bucket with a handle

name: Butter dish

place_of_invention.notes: Covered dishes for butter appeared in Europe in the 18th century as table manners and dairy consumption spread; exact origin is undocumented.

short_description: A covered dish for keeping and serving butter.
description: Butter dishes with covers became common in 18th- and 19th-century European households to protect butter from dust and odors. American stick-shaped butter dishes followed the shape of butter sticks. The base and dome or cover remain the same today.
why_unchanged: A base with a cover is all that is needed to protect butter, so the design has not needed to change.

faqs.question: Why use a butter dish?
faqs.answer: A covered dish protects butter from drying out and from absorbing fridge odors.

faqs.question: What is a French butter dish?
faqs.answer: Also called a butter bell, it keeps butter in an inverted cup sealed with water to keep it fresh unrefrigerated.

faqs.question: Why are some butter dishes long and narrow?
faqs.answer: They match the shape of the quarter-pound butter sticks common in the USA.

image.alt: A covered ceramic butter dish

name: Butter knife

place_of_invention.notes: Dedicated butter knives became part of Victorian cutlery sets in the 19th century; exact origin is not documented.

short_description: A small blunt knife used to spread butter.
description: As table settings became more specialized in the 19th century, the butter knife appeared as a blunt, short spreading tool. The master butter knife served butter, while individual butter spreaders were placed at each setting. Both remain the same today.
why_unchanged: A blunt blade spreads soft butter perfectly, so the design has not needed to change.

faqs.question: What's the difference between a master butter knife and a butter spreader?
faqs.answer: The master knife takes butter from the dish, while each guest uses a small spreader.

faqs.question: Why are butter knives blunt?
faqs.answer: They only need to spread soft food, so a blunt edge is safer.

faqs.question: Where does the butter knife go?
faqs.answer: On the bread plate, usually above the forks.

image.alt: A butter knife spreading butter on bread

name: Cake stand

place_of_invention.notes: Footed serving dishes (tazze) were made in Renaissance Europe; the pedestal cake stand became popular in Victorian Britain with afternoon tea.

short_description: A raised plate on a pedestal for displaying cakes.
description: Footed dishes for fruit and sweets existed in Renaissance Europe. The Victorian taste for elaborate cakes and afternoon tea made the cake stand a household item. The plate on a pedestal is still the standard design.
why_unchanged: A raised platform displays a cake and makes slicing easy, so the design has stayed the same.

faqs.question: Why are cakes displayed on stands?
faqs.answer: Raising the cake makes it the centerpiece and makes slicing easier.

faqs.question: What is a tiered cake stand?
faqs.answer: A stand with several stacked plates, often used for afternoon tea.

faqs.question: What is a tazza?
faqs.answer: A shallow footed dish from Renaissance Europe, an ancestor of the cake stand.

image.alt: A glass cake stand holding a cake

name: Calabash bowl

place_of_invention.notes: Bottle gourds were used as containers in Africa, Asia and the Americas from prehistoric times; cut calabash bowls remain especially important in West African households. Dating is approximate.

short_description: A bowl made by cutting a dried gourd in half.
description: Halving a hard-shelled dried gourd produces a light, durable bowl, a technique used since prehistoric times on several continents. In West Africa calabash bowls are used to serve food, carry goods, measure grain and churn milk, and are often carved or pyrographed with designs. They are still made and used in the same way.
why_unchanged: A halved gourd is a ready-made bowl that is light and tough, so there has been nothing to redesign.

faqs.question: What is a calabash?
faqs.answer: A calabash is the hard-shelled fruit of the bottle gourd vine, dried and used as a container; the word is also applied to the unrelated calabash tree's fruit.

faqs.question: How are calabash bowls decorated?
faqs.answer: Artisans carve, scratch or burn patterns into the shell, and some dye or polish the surface.

faqs.question: Are calabashes used for music?
faqs.answer: Yes. Halved gourds form the resonators of instruments such as the kora and balafon, and are played as percussion in West Africa.

image.alt: Carved calabash bowls on display

name: Carafe

place_of_invention.notes: Simple open-mouthed glass vessels for water and wine were made since Roman times; the word carafe entered European languages via Italian and Spanish from Arabic.

short_description: A simple open-necked glass vessel for serving water or wine.
description: Glass serving vessels for water and wine were common in the Roman world, and the term 'carafe' spread in Europe in the 17th century. Carafes are still used in restaurants to serve house wine and water. The simple flared bottle without a stopper remains the same.
why_unchanged: A plain glass vessel with a wide neck is easy to fill and pour, so there has been no reason to change it.

faqs.question: What's the origin of the word carafe?
faqs.answer: It comes through Italian 'caraffa' and Spanish 'garrafa', from Arabic.

faqs.question: Is a carafe the same as a decanter?
faqs.answer: They are similar, but carafes usually lack stoppers and are used for water or everyday wine.

faqs.question: Why do restaurants serve house wine in carafes?
faqs.answer: It allows wine to be served in small quantities from larger containers.

image.alt: A glass carafe of water on a table

name: Champagne flute

place_of_invention.notes: Tall, narrow flute glasses were made in 17th-century Europe for ale and wine; their association with sparkling wine grew in the 18th–19th centuries. Exact origin is uncertain.

short_description: A tall, narrow stemmed glass for sparkling wine.
description: Narrow, tall glasses called flutes were made in the 17th century in England and the Low Countries. As sparkling wine became popular, the flute's shape proved ideal for preserving bubbles. The tall bowl on a stem remains the classic champagne glass today.
why_unchanged: A narrow bowl reduces the surface area so bubbles last longer, which is why the shape endures.

faqs.question: Why are champagne flutes tall and narrow?
faqs.answer: The small surface area slows the escape of bubbles and lets you watch them rise.

faqs.question: What is a champagne coupe?
faqs.answer: A shallow, wide-bowled glass popular in the 19th and early 20th centuries; the story that it was modeled on a royal breast is a myth.

faqs.question: Should you hold a flute by the stem?
faqs.answer: Yes, holding the stem keeps your hand from warming the wine.

image.alt: Two champagne flutes with sparkling wine

name: Chopsticks

place_of_invention.notes: Bronze chopsticks were excavated at Yinxu, the late Shang dynasty capital near Anyang; they may first have been cooking implements before becoming eating utensils.

short_description: A pair of slender sticks held in one hand and used to pick up food.
description: The earliest surviving chopsticks are bronze examples from the Shang dynasty site of Yinxu in China. They were probably first used for cooking and only later became the main eating utensil, spreading to Japan, Korea and Vietnam. Styles differ by country, but the pair of tapered sticks is unchanged.
why_unchanged: Two sticks operated like extended fingers already offer precise, versatile grip, leaving nothing essential to add.

faqs.question: How old are chopsticks?
faqs.answer: The oldest known examples are bronze chopsticks from the Shang dynasty site of Yinxu in China, roughly 3,000 years old.

faqs.question: Why are Korean chopsticks often made of metal?
faqs.answer: Metal chopsticks have a long tradition in Korea; they are durable and easy to clean, and stainless steel is now the most common material there.

faqs.question: Is it rude to stick chopsticks upright in rice?
faqs.answer: In much of East Asia, yes, because chopsticks standing in rice resemble incense sticks used at funerals.

image.alt: A pair of wooden chopsticks resting on a bowl

name: Cork stopper

place_of_invention.notes: Greeks and Romans used cork to seal amphorae; cork stoppers for glass wine bottles became common in 17th-century Europe.

short_description: A plug of cork bark used to seal bottles.
description: Cork from the bark of the cork oak was used in the ancient Mediterranean to seal amphorae and other vessels. With the rise of strong glass wine bottles in 17th-century Europe, cork stoppers became the standard closure. Cork is still harvested in Portugal and Spain and cut into the same simple cylinders.
why_unchanged: Cork is naturally compressible, elastic and watertight, so a simple cylinder of it still seals bottles well.

faqs.question: Where does cork come from?
faqs.answer: Cork is the bark of the cork oak, harvested every nine years or so without cutting down the tree, mainly in Portugal and Spain.

faqs.question: Why is cork good for sealing wine?
faqs.answer: It compresses to fit the neck, expands to seal it and lets in tiny amounts of oxygen that some wines benefit from.

faqs.question: What is 'corked' wine?
faqs.answer: It is wine tainted by a compound called TCA, sometimes found in cork, which gives a musty smell.

image.alt: A pile of natural cork stoppers

name: Crate

place_of_invention.notes: Wooden boxes and slatted containers were used for transport in many ancient societies; no specific origin of the slatted crate is documented.

short_description: A wooden box with open slats used to transport goods such as fruit and bottles.
description: Wooden boxes for carrying goods have been used since antiquity, and slatted crates became standard for transporting produce, bottles and goods. The gaps between slats let air circulate and reduce weight. Although plastic crates are now common, wooden crates are still built the same way.
why_unchanged: A box of slats is light, ventilated, stackable and quick to build, so the basic design remains unchanged.

faqs.question: Why do crates have gaps between the slats?
faqs.answer: The gaps reduce weight, use less wood and allow air to circulate, which keeps fruit and vegetables fresh.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a crate and a box?
faqs.answer: A crate is usually sturdier and has open sides or slats, while a box is fully enclosed.

faqs.question: Are wooden crates reused?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many are reused for shipping or repurposed as furniture and storage.

image.alt: A slatted wooden crate full of apples

name: Cream jug

place_of_invention.notes: Small silver jugs for cream or milk appear in English tea services in the early 18th century as adding milk to tea became fashionable; exact origin is undocumented.

short_description: A small jug for serving milk or cream with tea or coffee.
description: As tea and coffee spread in 18th-century England, small silver jugs for cream and milk became part of tea services. Porcelain versions soon followed. The small spouted jug with a handle remains unchanged.
why_unchanged: A small spout and handle pour a little milk precisely, so the design hasn't needed changing.

faqs.question: Is a creamer the same as a cream jug?
faqs.answer: Yes, in American English the small jug is usually called a creamer, although the word also refers to non-dairy coffee whiteners.

faqs.question: When did people start adding milk to tea?
faqs.answer: The habit became common in Britain during the 18th century, at the same time cream jugs joined tea services.

faqs.question: Why are cream jugs so small?
faqs.answer: Only a splash of milk or cream is needed per cup, and a small jug keeps it fresh and easy to pour precisely.

image.alt: A small porcelain cream jug

name: Crown cork

place_of_invention.notes: William Painter patented the crown cork bottle cap in 1892 and founded the Crown Cork & Seal Company.

short_description: A crimped metal bottle cap lined with a seal.
description: Before the crown cork, bottles were sealed with corks or wire stoppers that often leaked. William Painter's 1892 crimped metal cap sealed carbonated drinks tightly and cheaply. The 21-toothed bottle cap is still used today.
why_unchanged: A crimped metal disk seals pressure cheaply and quickly, so the design hasn't needed to change.

faqs.question: Who invented the bottle cap?
faqs.answer: William Painter of Baltimore patented the crown cork in 1892.

faqs.question: How many teeth does a bottle cap have?
faqs.answer: Modern standard crown caps have 21 teeth.

faqs.question: Why is it called a crown cork?
faqs.answer: Its crimped edge resembles a crown, and early caps were lined with cork.

image.alt: A pile of crimped metal bottle caps

name: Cruet

place_of_invention.notes: Small vessels called cruets were used in the medieval Christian liturgy for wine and water; table cruets for oil and vinegar and cruet stands became common in 17th–18th century Europe.

short_description: A small glass bottle with a stopper for serving oil or vinegar at the table.
description: In medieval Europe small cruets held wine and water during Mass. By the 18th century cruet stands with oil, vinegar and spice containers were a fixture on European tables. Glass cruets with a narrow spout and stopper are still used the same way.
why_unchanged: A small bottle with a narrow spout dispenses oil or vinegar by drops, so the form remains unchanged.

faqs.question: What is a cruet stand?
faqs.answer: A frame holding several cruets and shakers, popular in 18th- and 19th-century dining rooms.

faqs.question: Where does the word cruet come from?
faqs.answer: From Anglo-French 'cruet', a diminutive of the Old French word for pot.

faqs.question: Are cruets used in churches?
faqs.answer: Yes, cruets for water and wine are still used in Catholic and some other services.

image.alt: Two glass cruets of oil and vinegar

name: Cup

place_of_invention.notes: Drinking vessels of horn, wood, gourd and fired clay arose independently in many places; no single origin is known.

short_description: A small open vessel used for drinking.
description: People have shaped small drinking vessels from natural materials since prehistory, and ceramic cups appear widely in Neolithic sites. Ancient civilizations made cups of clay, metal, stone and glass, often with elaborate decoration. The simple open vessel sized for one person remains the basis of every modern cup.
why_unchanged: An open vessel sized for one hand and one drink is all that drinking requires, so its basic form has stayed the same.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a cup and a mug?
faqs.answer: A mug is generally taller, heavier and straight-sided, and is used without a saucer, while a cup is usually smaller and often paired with a saucer.

faqs.question: Why does a 'cup' also mean a unit of measure?
faqs.answer: Cooks used ordinary drinking cups to measure ingredients, and the volume was eventually standardized in recipes.

faqs.question: How old are the oldest cups?
faqs.answer: Ceramic cups are known from Neolithic sites several thousand years old, and cups of wood, horn or gourd were likely used even earlier.

image.alt: A plain ceramic cup on a table

name: Decanter

place_of_invention.notes: Glass serving vessels for wine existed in Roman times; the stoppered glass decanter developed in England after George Ravenscroft's lead crystal of the 1670s.

short_description: A glass vessel used to serve wine or spirits after pouring them from the bottle.
description: Wine was poured into serving vessels in antiquity, but English lead crystal of the late 17th century enabled the classic stoppered decanter. Decanting separated wine from sediment and showed off its color. The wide base and narrow neck design is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A wide body aerates wine and a narrow neck pours cleanly, so the design still works perfectly.

faqs.question: Why decant wine?
faqs.answer: To separate it from sediment and to expose it to air, which can soften young red wines.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a decanter and a carafe?
faqs.answer: Decanters often have stoppers and are used for wine or spirits; carafes are open and often used for water.

faqs.question: Why is lead crystal important for decanters?
faqs.answer: English lead crystal made clear, heavy glass that showed off wine and could be cut decoratively.

image.alt: A crystal decanter filled with red wine

name: Demijohn

place_of_invention.notes: Large bulbous glass bottles encased in wicker were used across Europe by the 18th century; the name is thought to come from French 'dame-jeanne', though its origin is debated.

short_description: A large narrow-necked glass bottle, often wrapped in wicker.
description: Demijohns are large glass bottles used to store and transport wine, oil and other liquids. Their wicker or straw covering protected the glass and made them easier to carry. Home winemakers still use them for fermentation.
why_unchanged: A large glass body with a narrow neck seals easily and stores liquids well, so the form persists.

faqs.question: What is a demijohn used for?
faqs.answer: Today mainly for home winemaking and brewing, as a fermentation vessel.

faqs.question: Why are demijohns covered in wicker?
faqs.answer: The wicker protects the glass from knocks and provides handles for carrying.

faqs.question: Where does the word demijohn come from?
faqs.answer: It probably comes from French 'dame-jeanne' ('Lady Jane'), but the origin is uncertain.

image.alt: A large glass demijohn in a wicker basket

name: Doily

place_of_invention.notes: The word comes from Doiley (or Doyley), a London draper of the late 17th century; the lace doily became popular in the Victorian era.

short_description: A small decorative mat of lace or paper placed under dishes.
description: The word 'doily' is derived from Doiley, a London draper of the late 17th century whose name became attached to light ornamental fabrics. Lace and crocheted doilies became a fixture of Victorian households, placed under vases, teacups and cakes. Paper and fabric doilies are still used in the same way.
why_unchanged: A small lacy mat protects surfaces and dresses up a plate, so its design has remained the same.

faqs.question: Where does the word doily come from?
faqs.answer: It comes from the surname of Doiley, a London draper of the late 17th century.

faqs.question: What are doilies used for?
faqs.answer: They protect furniture from scratches and moisture and decorate plates, especially under cakes and pastries.

faqs.question: Are doilies still used?
faqs.answer: Yes, paper doilies are common in bakeries, and handmade crocheted doilies remain a popular craft.

image.alt: A lace doily under a teacup

name: Drinking horn

place_of_invention.notes: Drinking horns were used by many ancient Eurasian peoples; ornamented examples from Scythian, Thracian and Germanic contexts are well known.

short_description: A cattle horn hollowed out and used as a drinking vessel.
description: Hollow horns of cattle were among the first drinking vessels and were used ceremonially by Scythians, Thracians, Greeks, Germanic peoples and Vikings. Wealthy owners decorated horns with metal mounts. They are still used for celebrations and reenactments.
why_unchanged: A natural horn is already a perfect drinking vessel, so its form has never changed.

faqs.question: Did Vikings really drink from horns?
faqs.answer: Yes, drinking horns are found in Viking-age graves and sagas, though cups and bowls were also used.

faqs.question: Why can't a drinking horn be set down?
faqs.answer: The pointed tip means it must be held or placed in a stand until emptied.

faqs.question: Are drinking horns still used?
faqs.answer: Yes, at festivals, reenactments and some traditional celebrations, such as in Georgia's feasts.

image.alt: A decorated drinking horn on a stand

name: Drinking straw

place_of_invention.notes: A gold-and-lapis drinking tube was found in the Royal Cemetery at Ur, and Sumerian art shows people drinking beer through long tubes. The modern spiral-wound paper straw was patented by Marvin C. Stone in the USA in 1888.

short_description: A thin tube used to sip a drink.
description: Sumerians drank beer through long tubes to avoid sediment floating in the brew, and examples made of precious metals survive from the Royal Cemetery at Ur. For centuries people also used hollow rye stalks. In 1888 Marvin Stone patented the paper drinking straw, and later plastic, metal and plant-based versions kept the same simple tube.
why_unchanged: A hollow tube is the entire design, so changing materials is the only thing left to do.

faqs.question: Why did ancient Sumerians use straws?
faqs.answer: Their beer had husks and sediment floating on top, so drinking through a long tube let them reach the clearer liquid underneath.

faqs.question: Who invented the paper straw?
faqs.answer: Marvin C. Stone patented a spiral-wound paper drinking straw in the United States in 1888.

faqs.question: Why are straws called straws?
faqs.answer: Before paper straws, people commonly used hollow stalks of rye grass, which is literally straw.

image.alt: Several drinking straws in a glass

name: Egg carton

place_of_invention.notes: Newspaper editor Joseph Coyle is credited with inventing a paper egg carton in 1911 to prevent eggs from breaking during delivery.

short_description: A container with individual cups to protect eggs.
description: Joseph Coyle invented a paper carton to stop eggs from breaking. Molded pulp cartons were later developed, but the individual-cell design remains. Egg cartons are used worldwide.
why_unchanged: Separate cups protect each egg, so the design has not needed to change.

faqs.question: Who invented the egg carton?
faqs.answer: Joseph Coyle, a newspaper editor in Smithers, British Columbia, is credited with the paper egg carton in 1911.

faqs.question: Why was the egg carton invented?
faqs.answer: According to the usual account, Coyle wanted to settle a dispute between a farmer and a hotel owner over eggs that kept arriving broken.

faqs.question: Are egg cartons recyclable?
faqs.answer: Molded paper pulp cartons are usually recyclable or compostable, while polystyrene ones are much harder to recycle.

image.alt: A paper pulp egg carton with eggs

name: Egg cup

place_of_invention.notes: Silver egg cups are often said to have been found at Pompeii, but sources vary; egg cups became common in Europe from the 17th–18th centuries.

short_description: A small cup that holds a boiled egg upright for eating.
description: Holders for eating boiled eggs are reported from Roman times, and egg cups became standard in European households from the 18th century. They were made of silver, porcelain, pottery and wood, sometimes with a matching spoon. The small cup sized to hold an egg upright is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A small cup shaped to hold an egg upright is perfectly sized for the task, so there has been no reason to change it.

faqs.question: Did the Romans really use egg cups?
faqs.answer: Egg cups are often said to have been found at Pompeii, but the evidence is debated; they became common in Europe in the 18th century.

faqs.question: Why are egg spoons sometimes not silver?
faqs.answer: Egg yolk tarnishes silver, so egg spoons are often made of bone, horn or gilded metal.

faqs.question: Do people collect egg cups?
faqs.answer: Yes, egg cup collecting is a hobby called pocillovy.

image.alt: A ceramic egg cup holding a soft-boiled egg

name: Ewer

place_of_invention.notes: Jug-shaped pouring vessels with handles and spouts appear in many Bronze Age cultures; the ewer as a basin-and-jug set was common in medieval and early modern Europe.

short_description: A tall jug with a spout, traditionally used for pouring water.
description: Tall pouring vessels with a handle and spout have been made since the Bronze Age, in clay and later in bronze, silver and brass. In medieval and early modern Europe, and across the Islamic world, servants poured water from an ewer over diners' hands into a basin. The tall jug with a spout and handle is unchanged, and ewer-and-basin sets were standard bedroom furniture until running water arrived.
why_unchanged: A tall jug pours a steady stream of water, so the design has stayed the same.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an ewer and a jug?
faqs.answer: An ewer is a jug, usually taller and more decorative, traditionally used for pouring water for washing rather than for drinking.

faqs.question: Why did people wash their hands at the table?
faqs.answer: Before forks were common, people ate with their fingers, so water was poured from an ewer over their hands between courses.

faqs.question: What is an ewer and basin set?
faqs.answer: A matching jug and bowl kept in bedrooms for washing before homes had running water, common in the 18th and 19th centuries.

image.alt: A tall silver ewer

name: Fiasco

place_of_invention.notes: Round-bottomed, straw-covered glass flasks are recorded in Tuscany by the late Middle Ages and appear in Renaissance paintings; the exact origin is uncertain.

short_description: A round-bottomed glass bottle wrapped in straw, traditionally used for Chianti wine.
description: Tuscan glassmakers blew thin, round-bottomed bottles that could not stand on their own, so they were wrapped in straw to protect them and allow them to stand. The fiasco became associated with Chianti wine. It is still made, mostly as a nostalgic package.
why_unchanged: A straw jacket protects a thin round bottle and gives it a flat base, so the design hasn't needed to change.

faqs.question: Why are Chianti bottles wrapped in straw?
faqs.answer: The thin round-bottomed glass needed protection and a flat base, which the straw covering provides.

faqs.question: Is the word 'fiasco' related to failure?
faqs.answer: Yes, in English 'fiasco' means a failure; one theory links it to glassblowers turning flawed pieces into flasks, but the origin is uncertain.

faqs.question: Are fiaschi still used?
faqs.answer: Some Chianti producers still use them, though most switched to standard bottles in the late 20th century.

image.alt: A straw-wrapped Chianti bottle

name: Flat-bottomed paper bag

place_of_invention.notes: Francis Wolle patented a paper bag machine in 1852; Margaret E. Knight patented a machine to make flat-bottomed paper bags in 1871.

short_description: A paper bag with a flat base that stands upright.
description: Margaret Knight designed a machine to fold and glue flat-bottomed paper bags in 1871. The bags could stand on their own and hold more goods than earlier envelope-style bags. They are still used at grocery stores.
why_unchanged: A flat base lets the bag stand upright and hold more, so the design remains unchanged.

faqs.question: Who invented the flat-bottomed paper bag?
faqs.answer: Margaret E. Knight patented a machine to make them in 1871.

faqs.question: Did someone try to steal Knight's idea?
faqs.answer: Yes, Charles Annan claimed it, but Knight won the patent dispute.

faqs.question: Why are flat-bottomed bags better?
faqs.answer: They stand on their own and carry more.

image.alt: A brown paper grocery bag

name: Folding cardboard box

place_of_invention.notes: Robert Gair discovered how to cut and crease paperboard in one operation in 1879, producing pre-cut folding cartons.

short_description: A paperboard box cut and creased to fold flat.
description: Robert Gair discovered that cutting and creasing paperboard in one step made boxes that could be shipped flat and folded. Folding cartons became the standard for packaged goods. The die-cut box design remains the same.
why_unchanged: A box that ships flat and folds quickly is efficient, so its design has stayed the same.

faqs.question: Who invented the folding cardboard box?
faqs.answer: Robert Gair, a Brooklyn paper-bag maker, developed the pre-cut folding carton in 1879.

faqs.question: How was the folding box discovered?
faqs.answer: According to the usual account, a metal rule meant to crease paper bags shifted in the press and cut them instead, giving Gair the idea to cut and crease in one step.

faqs.question: What is the difference between cardboard and corrugated board?
faqs.answer: Corrugated board has a wavy fluted layer between two flat liners, making it much stronger for shipping than plain paperboard.

image.alt: A brown cardboard box

name: Fork

place_of_invention.notes: Bone forks are known from Bronze Age China and cooking forks from ancient Egypt and Rome; the personal table fork spread from Byzantium to Italy around the 11th century and to the rest of Europe by the 17th–18th centuries.

short_description: A handled utensil with two or more tines used to spear and lift food.
description: Large forks were used for cooking and serving long before small personal forks appeared at the table. Table forks were in use among Byzantine elites in late antiquity and reached Venice in the 11th century, where they were initially viewed as an affectation. By the 18th century the four-tined table fork had become standard across Europe.
why_unchanged: A handle with a few pointed tines is the simplest way to pierce and hold food, so only the number and curve of the tines have varied.

faqs.question: When did people start eating with forks in Europe?
faqs.answer: Personal forks reached Italy from Byzantium around the 11th century but only became common across Europe in the 17th and 18th centuries.

faqs.question: Why do modern forks usually have four tines?
faqs.answer: Four tines became standard in the 18th–19th centuries because they hold food better than two or three while still fitting comfortably in the mouth.

faqs.question: Were forks ever considered controversial?
faqs.answer: Yes. Medieval churchmen criticized the fork as an unnecessary luxury, and many Europeans continued to eat with knives, spoons and fingers for centuries.

image.search_query: silver table fork on white background
image.alt: A polished metal dinner fork with four tines

name: Furoshiki

place_of_invention.notes: Wrapping cloths were used in Japan from the Nara period to protect treasures at the Shōsōin repository; the name furoshiki ('bath spread') comes from the Edo period.

short_description: A square Japanese cloth used to wrap and carry goods.
description: Wrapping cloths were used in Japan by the 8th century to protect valuables, including treasures stored at the Shōsōin in Nara. In the Edo period, visitors to public bathhouses wrapped their belongings in a cloth and stood on it while changing, giving rise to the name furoshiki. With a few knots the same square of cloth becomes a bag, a bottle carrier or gift wrapping, and it is now promoted as a reusable alternative to plastic bags.
why_unchanged: A square of cloth can wrap almost any object, so the design has stayed the same.

faqs.question: What does furoshiki mean?
faqs.answer: It means 'bath spread', from the Edo-period habit of wrapping belongings in a cloth at public baths.

faqs.question: How do you tie a furoshiki?
faqs.answer: Most wraps place the object in the center and tie opposite corners together in square knots; dozens of named folds exist for bottles, books and boxes.

faqs.question: Is furoshiki an eco-friendly alternative to bags?
faqs.answer: Yes. Japan's Ministry of the Environment has promoted furoshiki as a reusable alternative to plastic bags and disposable gift wrap.

image.alt: A furoshiki cloth tied around a box

name: Gaiwan

place_of_invention.notes: Lidded tea bowls with saucers developed in China; the gaiwan is generally associated with the Ming dynasty, when steeping loose leaves became common, though some trace earlier lidded cups to the Tang or Song.

short_description: A Chinese lidded tea bowl on a saucer used to brew and drink tea.
description: The gaiwan consists of a bowl, a lid and a saucer, symbolizing heaven, humanity and earth in Chinese tradition. It became popular as loose-leaf tea brewing spread during the Ming dynasty. Tea drinkers still use it to brew and pour tea, holding the lid to strain the leaves.
why_unchanged: A bowl, lid and saucer let one vessel brew, strain and serve tea, so nothing needed to be added.

faqs.question: What does gaiwan mean?
faqs.answer: Gaiwan means 'lidded bowl' in Chinese.

faqs.question: How do you use a gaiwan?
faqs.answer: Steep leaves in the bowl, then tilt the lid slightly to hold back the leaves while pouring tea into cups or drinking directly.

faqs.question: Why is the gaiwan popular with tea enthusiasts?
faqs.answer: Porcelain does not absorb flavors, so one gaiwan can brew any type of tea and let you watch the leaves unfurl.

image.alt: A porcelain gaiwan with lid and saucer

name: Goblet

place_of_invention.notes: Stemmed drinking cups of metal and pottery appear in several Bronze Age cultures; no single origin is known.

short_description: A drinking vessel with a bowl on a stem and foot.
description: Stemmed drinking cups were made by many Bronze Age cultures from clay, silver and gold. In medieval and Renaissance Europe, goblets of precious metal and glass were symbols of wealth. Today's goblets of glass or metal retain the bowl-stem-foot form.
why_unchanged: A raised bowl on a stem is easy to grip and looks dignified, so it has kept its shape since antiquity.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a goblet and a wine glass?
faqs.answer: A goblet usually has a thicker stem and larger bowl, and may be metal; wine glasses are thin-stemmed glass.

faqs.question: Are goblets used in religious ceremonies?
