faqs.question: How was it used in ancient construction?
faqs.answer: Egyptian and other ancient builders hung plumb bobs to check that walls and columns were vertical.

faqs.question: Is it still used?
faqs.answer: Yes, carpenters, surveyors and masons use them to transfer points vertically or check walls.

image.alt: A brass plumb bob hanging on a string

name: Pocket knife

place_of_invention.notes: Folding knives are attested earlier in Iron Age Europe; Roman examples are the first found in large numbers.

short_description: A small knife whose blade folds into its handle so it can be carried safely.
description: Romans carried folding knives with bronze or bone handles, some decorated with animals and gladiators. The pivoting blade that tucks into the handle made a sharp tool safe to keep in a pouch or pocket. Later multi-tool versions added more blades, but the basic folding knife is the same.
why_unchanged: A blade on a pivot that hides inside its own handle solves the problem of carrying a knife, and nothing simpler has been found.

faqs.question: How old is the pocket knife?
faqs.answer: Folding knives date back at least to Iron Age Europe, and the Romans made them widely, around 2,000 years ago.

faqs.question: What is a slipjoint?
faqs.answer: It's the classic pocket-knife mechanism where a spring holds the blade open or closed without locking it.

faqs.question: Are pocket knives legal to carry?
faqs.answer: It depends on the country and blade length; many places allow small non-locking folding knives but restrict larger ones.

image.alt: An open folding pocket knife with a wooden handle

name: Potter's wheel

place_of_invention.notes: Slow-turning wheels (tournettes) appear earlier in the Near East; fast wheels for throwing pots spread from around 3500–3000 BCE.

short_description: A spinning turntable on which clay is shaped into round vessels.
description: The potter's wheel let craftspeople make symmetrical pots far faster than by hand-building with coils. Early wheels were turned by hand or foot; a heavy wheel keeps spinning by momentum while the potter shapes the clay. Modern wheels add an electric motor, but the turning disc and the throwing technique are the same.
why_unchanged: A flat disc that spins at a steady speed is all that's needed to turn a lump of clay into a round vessel.

faqs.question: Is the potter's wheel older than the wheel on carts?
faqs.answer: Most historians think so: the potter's wheel appears in Mesopotamia a few centuries before wheeled vehicles.

faqs.question: What does 'throwing' a pot mean?
faqs.answer: It is the term for shaping clay on a spinning wheel; it comes from an Old English word meaning to twist or turn.

faqs.question: How do kick wheels work?
faqs.answer: The potter pushes a heavy flywheel at foot level with one foot, and its momentum keeps the wheel head turning.

image.alt: Hands shaping clay on a spinning potter's wheel

name: Pulley

place_of_invention.notes: Pulleys for lifting water are often dated to Mesopotamia around this time; evidence is limited, and Greek writers later described compound pulleys.

short_description: A grooved wheel over which a rope runs, used to change the direction of force or lift loads.
description: A pulley lets a rope turn corners and, when combined with other pulleys, reduces the effort needed to lift a load. Early uses included raising water from wells. Pulleys remain essential in cranes, sailboats, elevators and gyms.
why_unchanged: A grooved wheel on an axle is the simplest way to redirect a rope, so there is nothing to change.

faqs.question: Is the pulley a simple machine?
faqs.answer: Yes, it is one of the classical simple machines, together with the lever, wedge, screw, wheel and axle, and inclined plane.

faqs.question: Does a single pulley make lifting easier?
faqs.answer: A single fixed pulley only changes the direction of force; multiple pulleys reduce the force needed.

faqs.question: Where are pulleys used?
faqs.answer: In wells, cranes, elevators, sailing rigging, window blinds and gym machines.

image.alt: A metal pulley with a rope over it

name: Ratchet wrench

place_of_invention.notes: A ratcheting socket wrench patent by J. J. Richardson in 1863 is commonly cited; interchangeable socket sets were popularized later (for example by Snap-on in 1920).

short_description: A handle with a one-way ratchet mechanism that turns interchangeable sockets onto nuts and bolts.
description: The ratchet wrench lets a mechanic turn a nut repeatedly without removing the tool, because the handle swings freely in one direction. A ratcheting socket wrench was patented in the US in 1863, and detachable sockets made it a complete system in the 20th century. Its basic form is unchanged in mechanics' toolboxes.
why_unchanged: A ratchet handle plus snap-on sockets is already the fastest manual way to turn bolts in tight spaces.

faqs.question: Why use a ratchet instead of a regular wrench?
faqs.answer: You can keep turning without lifting the tool off the nut, which is much faster in tight spaces.

faqs.question: How do you reverse a ratchet?
faqs.answer: Most ratchets have a small lever or dial on the head that switches the direction of the free-wheeling action.

faqs.question: What do the drive sizes mean?
faqs.answer: Sizes like 1/4, 3/8 and 1/2 inch refer to the square peg that attaches sockets, with larger drives for heavier work.

image.alt: A ratchet handle with a socket attached

name: Rivet

place_of_invention.notes: Rivets were used in Bronze Age metalwork such as vessels and weapons; they likely appeared independently in many metalworking cultures.

short_description: A metal pin that is hammered or pressed to form a second head, permanently joining parts.
description: A rivet passes through holes in two pieces and is deformed on the other side to lock them together. Bronze Age smiths used rivets to fix blades to handles and assemble vessels. Rivets built steel bridges, ships and aircraft, and still join metal sheets today.
why_unchanged: Deforming a pin to make a second head is a simple, strong permanent joint.

faqs.question: How old are rivets?
faqs.answer: They were used in Bronze Age metalwork thousands of years ago.

faqs.question: Why were rivets used in old bridges and ships?
faqs.answer: Before reliable welding, hot rivets were the strongest way to join steel plates.

faqs.question: What is a pop rivet?
faqs.answer: A blind rivet that can be installed from one side using a special tool.

image.alt: A row of steel rivets on a metal plate

name: Robertson screw

place_of_invention.notes: Patented by P. L. Robertson, whose factory was in Milton, Ontario.

short_description: A screw with a square socket in its head, driven by a matching square-tipped driver.
description: Peter L. Robertson developed the square-drive screw in Canada, reportedly after a slotted screwdriver slipped and cut his hand. The tapered square recess grips the driver firmly, so the screw can even be held on the tip with one hand. It remains especially popular in Canada.
why_unchanged: A tapered square socket gives excellent grip and almost no slipping, so there was nothing to improve.

faqs.question: Why is the Robertson screw so popular in Canada?
faqs.answer: It was invented and manufactured in Canada, and builders there favored it for its grip and speed long before it spread elsewhere.

faqs.question: How do you tell Robertson driver sizes apart?
faqs.answer: They are traditionally color-coded, for example green, red and black handles for the three most common sizes.

faqs.question: Why didn't Ford adopt it widely?
faqs.answer: According to a well-known account, Robertson refused to license the design on Ford's terms, so the carmaker used other screws.

image.alt: Close-up of a square-drive Robertson screw head

name: Roof tile

place_of_invention.notes: Fired clay tiles were used on the 'House of the Tiles' at Lerna; roof tiles were also developed independently in China.

short_description: A fired clay or concrete piece overlapped with others to cover a roof.
description: Roof tiles overlap to shed rain from roofs. Early Bronze Age builders at Lerna in Greece used fired clay tiles, and Greek, Roman and Chinese builders spread their use. Modern tiles follow the same overlapping principle.
why_unchanged: Overlapping tiles shed water efficiently, so the design remains.

faqs.question: How old are roof tiles?
faqs.answer: Clay roof tiles were used at Lerna in Greece around 2500 BCE.

faqs.question: Why are roof tiles curved?
faqs.answer: Curves channel water away and help tiles interlock.

faqs.question: How long do clay tiles last?
faqs.answer: Clay tiles can last for decades or even a century with proper maintenance.

image.alt: Terracotta tiles on a roof

name: Rope

place_of_invention.notes: A fragment of three-ply cord found at Abri du Maras is attributed to Neanderthals about 41,000–52,000 years ago; rope-making likely arose independently in many places.

short_description: Strands of fiber twisted or braided together into a strong, flexible line.
description: Rope twists fibers into strands and then twists strands together, creating strength. A cord fragment found in France attributed to Neanderthals shows the technique is extremely old. Ancient Egyptians made rope from papyrus and palm fibers, and modern ropes use nylon and polyester.
why_unchanged: Twisting fibers together is the basic way to make strong lines, so only the fibers have changed.

faqs.question: How old is rope?
faqs.answer: A cord fragment from Abri du Maras in France is about 41,000 to 52,000 years old and attributed to Neanderthals.

faqs.question: Why are rope strands twisted in opposite directions?
faqs.answer: Alternating twists balance each other so the rope doesn't unravel.

faqs.question: What is the difference between rope and cord?
faqs.answer: Generally, cord is thinner and rope is thicker and stronger.

image.alt: A coil of natural-fiber rope

name: Sandpaper

place_of_invention.notes: Commonly cited as originating in 13th-century China, using crushed shells, seeds and sand glued to parchment; glass paper was later produced industrially in 19th-century Britain.

short_description: Paper or cloth coated with abrasive grit, used to smooth surfaces.
description: Abrasive grit glued to a flexible backing allows smooth sanding of wood, metal and paint. Early versions in medieval China used crushed shells or sand on parchment, and Britain later mass-produced 'glass paper'. Today's sheets use aluminum oxide or silicon carbide but follow the same idea.
why_unchanged: Grit glued to a flexible sheet is already the simplest abrasive tool, so only the grit has changed.

faqs.question: Where was sandpaper invented?
faqs.answer: It is usually traced to 13th-century China, where crushed shells, seeds and sand were glued to parchment.

faqs.question: What do grit numbers mean?
faqs.answer: Higher numbers mean finer grit; around 60–80 is coarse, 120–180 medium, and 220 or more is fine.

faqs.question: Does sandpaper contain sand?
faqs.answer: Rarely today; modern papers use manufactured abrasives such as aluminum oxide or silicon carbide.

image.alt: Sheets of sandpaper in different grits

name: Screwdriver

place_of_invention.notes: Earliest evidence appears in late 15th-century Europe; Germany and France are both proposed as places of origin.

short_description: A hand tool with a shaped tip that fits a screw head and turns it.
description: The screwdriver appeared soon after screws began to be used as fasteners in late medieval Europe. Early screwdrivers had flat blades and were used by armorers, gunsmiths and clockmakers. A shaft with a tip and a handle remains the design, though tip shapes have multiplied.
why_unchanged: A handle and a shaped shaft are all that is needed to transmit twisting force to a screw.

faqs.question: When was the screwdriver invented?
faqs.answer: It appears in Europe in the late 15th century, probably in Germany or France.

faqs.question: Why are there so many tip types?
faqs.answer: Different drive shapes such as slotted, Phillips, square and Torx were developed to transfer more torque or reduce slipping.

faqs.question: Why do thicker handles help?
faqs.answer: A screwdriver works like a wheel and axle: a wider handle lets your hand apply more turning force to the screw.

image.search_query: set of screwdrivers flat and phillips
image.alt: A set of screwdrivers with different tips

name: Sledgehammer

place_of_invention.notes: Heavy stone mauls were used in prehistoric mining (for example at the Great Orme copper mines in Wales); iron sledges became common in the Iron Age. No single origin is known.

short_description: A large, heavy, long-handled hammer swung with both hands.
description: The sledgehammer scales up the ordinary hammer for heavy work such as breaking rock, driving stakes and demolition. Prehistoric miners used large stone mauls to break ore, and iron-headed sledges became widespread once iron working spread. Its design is still simply a heavy head on a long handle.
why_unchanged: Heavy blows only require more mass and a longer lever, which the basic design already provides.

faqs.question: How heavy is a sledgehammer?
faqs.answer: Common sledgehammers have heads of roughly 2 to 9 kg (4 to 20 lb); lighter 'club' or 'lump' hammers are used one-handed.

faqs.question: Where does the name 'sledge' come from?
faqs.answer: It comes from the Old English 'slecg', related to a verb meaning 'to strike'.

faqs.question: How should you swing a sledgehammer safely?
faqs.answer: Keep your feet apart, slide your top hand down the handle as you swing and let the head's weight do the work rather than forcing it with your back.

image.alt: A sledgehammer resting against a broken concrete block

name: Snap-off blade knife

place_of_invention.notes: Yoshio Okada developed the snap-off blade knife in 1956, inspired by broken glass and chocolate bars; his company became OLFA.

short_description: A utility knife with a scored blade whose dull segments can be snapped off.
description: The snap-off blade knife lets users break off a dull segment to reveal a fresh sharp edge. Yoshio Okada invented it in Japan in 1956, and OLFA became a famous maker. It is used in construction, crafts and offices worldwide.
why_unchanged: Snapping off a segment gives an instant sharp edge, which remains the core advantage.

faqs.question: Who invented the snap-off knife?
faqs.answer: Yoshio Okada in Japan in 1956; he founded OLFA.

faqs.question: What inspired the design?
faqs.answer: He was inspired by how glass shards and chocolate bars break along lines.

faqs.question: How do you snap off a blade safely?
faqs.answer: Use the built-in snapper or pliers and dispose of segments in a closed container.

image.alt: A yellow snap-off blade utility knife

name: Speed square

place_of_invention.notes: Albert J. Swanson designed the rafter square and founded Swanson Tool Company in 1925.

short_description: A triangular carpenter's square used for marking angles and rafter cuts.
description: The speed square is a triangle with a lip that hooks on lumber, letting carpenters mark square lines and angles quickly. Albert J. Swanson designed it in 1925. It is now a standard framing tool.
why_unchanged: Its triangular shape is compact and rugged, already ideal for framing work.

faqs.question: Who invented the speed square?
faqs.answer: Albert J. Swanson designed it in 1925 and founded a company to sell it.

faqs.question: What is the 'pivot' point for?
faqs.answer: It lets you rotate the square to mark rafter angles read from the degree scale.

faqs.question: Can it guide a circular saw?
faqs.answer: Yes, carpenters often hold it against a board as a fence for square crosscuts.

image.alt: An aluminum speed square on a board

name: Spirit level

place_of_invention.notes: Melchisédech Thévenot described a bubble level in 1661 correspondence; it came into wider use in the 18th century.

short_description: A tool with a liquid-filled vial containing a bubble that shows when a surface is level.
description: The spirit level uses an air bubble trapped in a slightly curved, liquid-filled vial, which centers when the tool is level. French scientist Melchisédech Thévenot described it in 1661. It replaced the plumb-line A-frame levels used since antiquity.
why_unchanged: A bubble in a vial is a cheap, accurate and power-free indicator of level, so it is still standard.

faqs.question: Why is it called a spirit level?
faqs.answer: The vial is filled with spirit (alcohol), which resists freezing and moves freely.

faqs.question: Who invented the bubble level?
faqs.answer: Melchisédech Thévenot described it in 1661.

faqs.question: How do you check if a level is accurate?
faqs.answer: Place it on a surface, note the bubble, then rotate it 180 degrees; if the bubble position changes, the level needs adjusting.

image.alt: A spirit level with a centered bubble on a shelf

name: Steelyard

place_of_invention.notes: Unequal-arm balances appear in the Greco-Roman world and in Warring States China at roughly the same time.

short_description: A lever scale with one sliding weight that moves along a marked arm.
description: The steelyard hangs the load from a short arm and balances it with a single counterweight slid along a long, graduated arm. Roman markets used bronze steelyards, many of which survive at Pompeii. Market traders in many countries still use the same design today.
why_unchanged: One sliding weight on a marked lever can measure a wide range of loads, so there's no need to carry a full set of weights.

faqs.question: How does a steelyard work?
faqs.answer: It uses the lever principle: a small weight far from the pivot balances a heavy load close to it, and the position of the weight gives the reading.

faqs.question: Why is it called a steelyard?
faqs.answer: The English name likely comes from the Steelyard, the Hanseatic merchants' trading base in medieval London.

faqs.question: Is a steelyard still used today?
faqs.answer: Yes, hand-held steelyards remain common in markets in parts of Asia, Africa and Latin America.

image.alt: A bronze steelyard scale with a hanging hook and counterweight

name: Stepladder

place_of_invention.notes: John H. Balsley patented a folding stepladder in 1862.

short_description: A self-supporting folding ladder with flat steps.
description: The stepladder stands on its own using a hinged support frame and has flat steps. John H. Balsley patented a folding stepladder in 1862. Modern stepladders in aluminum and fiberglass follow the same A-frame design.
why_unchanged: A hinged A-frame is stable and portable, so the design is still standard.

faqs.question: Who invented the stepladder?
faqs.answer: John H. Balsley of Dayton, Ohio, patented the folding stepladder in 1862.

faqs.question: Why shouldn't you stand on the top step?
faqs.answer: Standing on the top reduces stability and increases the risk of falling.

faqs.question: What are spreader bars for?
faqs.answer: They lock the legs open so the ladder doesn't collapse.

image.alt: An aluminum stepladder standing open

name: Tape measure

place_of_invention.notes: Alvin J. Fellows patented a spring-return pocket tape in 1868; James Chesterman of Sheffield had earlier made steel measuring tapes (1829).

short_description: A retractable flexible measuring tape wound inside a case.
description: A tape measure holds a long flexible rule on a reel that winds back inside a small case. Steel measuring tapes were made in England in the early 19th century, and Alvin Fellows patented a spring-return pocket version in 1868. Later improvements added locks and curved blades, but the case-and-reel form is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A reel inside a case makes long measurements portable, and later additions only refined the idea.

faqs.question: Who invented the retractable tape measure?
faqs.answer: Alvin J. Fellows patented a spring-return tape in 1868, building on earlier steel tapes.

faqs.question: Why is the end hook loose?
faqs.answer: The hook moves by its own thickness so measurements are accurate both when hooking an edge and pushing against a surface.

faqs.question: Why is the tape blade curved?
faqs.answer: The curve stiffens the blade so it can extend some distance without bending.

image.alt: A tape measure partly extended on a table

name: Tongue-and-groove pliers

place_of_invention.notes: Introduced by the Champion DeArment Tool Company, maker of the Channellock brand.

short_description: Adjustable pliers with a channel joint that lets the jaws open to several widths.
description: Tongue-and-groove pliers have a pivot that slides between grooved positions, allowing the jaws to grip large pipes and nuts. They were introduced in 1933 by the company that became Channellock. Plumbers often call them 'channel locks' or 'water pump pliers'.
why_unchanged: The channel joint already gives quick, secure size changes, so the design remains the same.

faqs.question: Why are they called water pump pliers?
faqs.answer: They were well suited to tightening packing nuts on the water pumps of early cars.

faqs.question: Who introduced the design?
faqs.answer: It was introduced in 1933 by the Champion DeArment Tool Company, maker of the Channellock brand.

faqs.question: How do you adjust them?
faqs.answer: Open the handles fully, slide the pivot to another groove and close them on the workpiece.

image.alt: Blue-handled tongue-and-groove pliers

name: Torx screw

place_of_invention.notes: Developed by Camcar, a Textron company.

short_description: A screw with a six-pointed star-shaped recess that transmits high torque without slipping.
description: The Torx drive was developed in 1967 to deliver high torque with minimal cam-out on assembly lines. Its six-lobed star shape spreads force evenly and extends the life of both screw and driver bit. It is widely used in cars, electronics and construction screws.
why_unchanged: Its star geometry already solves slipping and stripping, so the shape has stayed the same since 1967.

faqs.question: What does Torx mean?
faqs.answer: It is a trademarked name for the six-lobe drive, generically called a 'star' or 'hexalobular' drive.

faqs.question: Why are Torx screws used in electronics?
faqs.answer: They allow high, controlled torque in small sizes, and tamper-resistant versions with a center pin discourage casual opening.

faqs.question: Can you use an Allen key on a Torx screw?
faqs.answer: Sometimes it will turn, but it fits poorly and can strip the recess, so a proper Torx bit is recommended.

image.alt: Close-up of screws with six-pointed star recesses

name: Try square

place_of_invention.notes: A wooden square was found among the tools in the tomb of Sennedjem at Deir el-Medina; right-angle squares were also used by Roman builders.

short_description: An L-shaped tool used to mark and check right angles.
description: The try square checks that edges and corners are at exactly 90 degrees. Squares were used by Egyptian builders, and one was found with other tools in a workman's tomb at Deir el-Medina. Woodworkers still use the same right-angled design.
why_unchanged: A fixed right angle is all that checking square requires.

faqs.question: Why is it called a 'try' square?
faqs.answer: Because it is used to 'try', meaning test, whether a surface or edge is square.

faqs.question: How do you check a square is accurate?
faqs.answer: Draw a line along its blade, flip it over and draw again; if the lines don't match, it isn't square.

faqs.question: How old are squares?
faqs.answer: Ancient Egyptians used squares over 3,000 years ago.

image.alt: A try square on a wooden board

name: Twist drill bit

place_of_invention.notes: Steven A. Morse developed the twist drill in 1861 and patented it in 1863, founding the Morse Twist Drill company.

short_description: A cylindrical drill bit with spiral flutes that clear chips while cutting.
description: The twist drill bit has helical flutes that carry chips out of the hole as it cuts. Steven A. Morse invented it in the 1860s, and it soon became the standard bit for metal and wood. Today almost every drill bit in a household toolbox follows his design.
why_unchanged: Spiral flutes cut and clear chips at once, so later changes were only to materials and point angles.

faqs.question: Who invented the twist drill?
faqs.answer: Steven A. Morse of Massachusetts invented it in 1861 and patented it in 1863.

faqs.question: Why do drill bits have spiral grooves?
faqs.answer: The flutes channel chips out of the hole and let coolant or air reach the cutting edges.

faqs.question: What is the typical point angle?
faqs.answer: General-purpose bits commonly have a 118-degree point, while harder metals often use 135 degrees.

image.alt: A set of steel twist drill bits

name: Vernier caliper

place_of_invention.notes: Pierre Vernier invented the vernier scale in 1631; Joseph R. Brown of Brown & Sharpe is credited with the first practical machinist's vernier caliper in 1851.

short_description: A sliding caliper with a vernier scale that allows precise readings to fractions of a millimeter.
description: The vernier caliper combines a sliding jaw with Pierre Vernier's 17th-century auxiliary scale to make precise measurements. Joseph R. Brown produced an affordable machinist's version in 1851, which helped standardize manufacturing. Digital calipers now exist, but the vernier version is still widely used.
why_unchanged: The vernier scale gives high precision with no electronics, so the classic design remains.

faqs.question: How do you read a vernier scale?
faqs.answer: Read the main scale at the zero mark, then find the vernier line that aligns exactly with a main-scale line to get the fractional value.

faqs.question: Who invented the vernier scale?
faqs.answer: French mathematician Pierre Vernier described it in 1631.

faqs.question: What can a vernier caliper measure?
faqs.answer: Outside dimensions, inside diameters with the small upper jaws, and depths with the rod at the end.

image.alt: A stainless steel vernier caliper measuring a bolt

name: Wall plug

place_of_invention.notes: John Joseph Rawlings developed the fiber wall plug in 1911, sold under the Rawlplug brand.

short_description: A sleeve inserted into a drilled hole in masonry that expands to grip a screw.
description: The wall plug lets screws hold firmly in brick, concrete and plaster. John Joseph Rawlings invented an early version made of fiber in 1911, and the brand name Rawlplug became widely used. Modern plugs are plastic, but the sleeve-in-a-hole design is the same.
why_unchanged: An expanding sleeve is the simplest way to anchor a screw in masonry, so the idea remains.

faqs.question: Who invented the wall plug?
faqs.answer: John Joseph Rawlings developed it in London in 1911.

faqs.question: How does a wall plug work?
faqs.answer: As the screw enters, the plug expands and presses against the sides of the hole.

faqs.question: What size plug should I use?
faqs.answer: Match the plug to the drill bit and screw size listed on the packaging.

image.alt: Plastic wall plugs with screws

name: Warded lock

place_of_invention.notes: Roman locksmiths made warded locks and keys in iron and bronze; they were widespread in the Roman Empire.

short_description: A lock with internal obstructions (wards) that only a correctly shaped key can bypass.
description: The warded lock uses fixed ridges inside the lock that block keys without matching notches. Romans used warded locks widely, and they remained the main European lock type through the medieval period. Simple warded locks are still found in cheap padlocks and antique furniture.
why_unchanged: Its simplicity makes it cheap and durable for low-security uses, so it was never redesigned.

faqs.question: How does a warded lock work?
faqs.answer: Fixed obstacles inside the lock block any key that does not have matching cuts.

faqs.question: Is a warded lock secure?
faqs.answer: Not very; skeleton keys cut away to avoid the wards can open many warded locks.

faqs.question: What is a skeleton key?
faqs.answer: A key cut down to a minimal shape that can bypass the wards of many locks.

image.alt: An antique warded lock with an iron key

name: Wedge

place_of_invention.notes: Wedge-shaped tools have been used since the Stone Age; no single origin can be identified.

short_description: A tapered piece of material driven into a gap to split or lift.
description: The wedge is one of the simple machines, converting a blow on its wide end into strong sideways force. Prehistoric people used stone, antler and wood wedges to split wood and stone. Splitting wedges of steel are still used for firewood and quarry work.
why_unchanged: A taper multiplies force by its geometry alone, so the shape cannot be improved.

faqs.question: Why is the wedge a simple machine?
faqs.answer: It converts force on its wide end into greater force at right angles, splitting or lifting objects.

faqs.question: How were wedges used in ancient quarries?
faqs.answer: Workers drove wedges into lines of holes to split large stone blocks.

faqs.question: Is an axe a wedge?
faqs.answer: Yes, the head of an axe works as a wedge attached to a handle.

image.alt: A steel splitting wedge driven into a log

name: Whetstone

place_of_invention.notes: Stones were used to sharpen tools throughout prehistory; perforated whetstones are common finds from the Bronze Age. No single origin exists.

short_description: A flat abrasive stone used to sharpen and hone the edges of blades and tools.
description: Whetstones have sharpened knives, axes and chisels since prehistory. Natural sandstone and fine-grained stones were used for millennia, while modern stones may be synthetic ceramics or diamond plates. The technique of drawing a blade across a flat abrasive surface is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A flat abrasive surface is the basic requirement for sharpening, and nothing simpler works better.

faqs.question: Does 'whetstone' mean it must be wet?
faqs.answer: No; 'whet' is an old word meaning to sharpen. Many stones are used with water or oil, but the name doesn't refer to wetness.

faqs.question: What angle should I sharpen at?
faqs.answer: Many kitchen knives use about 15 to 20 degrees per side; chisels and plane blades are often around 25 to 30 degrees.

faqs.question: Why do whetstones need flattening?
faqs.answer: Stones wear unevenly over time, and a dished stone produces rounded edges.

image.alt: A knife being sharpened on a whetstone

name: Windlass

place_of_invention.notes: Herodotus mentions wooden windlasses used to tighten the cables of Xerxes' bridge over the Hellespont in 480 BCE; the device may be older.

short_description: A horizontal drum turned by a crank or handle that winds a rope or chain to lift or pull loads.
description: A windlass winds a rope around a drum using a crank, giving great pulling force. It was used in antiquity to tighten bridge cables, lift water from wells and raise building materials. Windlasses are still used for anchors, wells and winches.
why_unchanged: A drum and a crank turn a small force into a large pull, a principle that cannot be improved.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a windlass and a capstan?
faqs.answer: A windlass has a horizontal drum, while a capstan has a vertical drum.

faqs.question: What did ancient windlasses do?
faqs.answer: They lifted water and building materials and tightened ropes, such as the cables of Xerxes' Hellespont bridge described by Herodotus.

faqs.question: Are windlasses still used?
faqs.answer: Yes, especially on boats for raising anchors and in traditional wells.

image.alt: A wooden windlass with crank over a well

name: Wire rope

place_of_invention.notes: Wilhelm Albert, a mining official, developed wire rope for mine hoisting in 1834.

short_description: Rope made of twisted steel wires, used for lifting and supporting heavy loads.
description: Wire rope twists strands of metal wire together like fiber rope, giving great strength and flexibility. Wilhelm Albert developed it for German mines in 1834 to replace chains and hemp ropes that failed. It is now used in cranes, elevators, bridges and cable cars.
why_unchanged: The twisted-wire design delivers strength and flexibility, so it remains the standard.

faqs.question: Who invented wire rope?
faqs.answer: Wilhelm Albert developed it in the Harz mining region of Germany in 1834.

faqs.question: Why was wire rope needed?
faqs.answer: Chains and hemp ropes broke too often in deep mine shafts.

faqs.question: Where is wire rope used?
faqs.answer: In elevators, cranes, suspension bridges, ski lifts and ships.

image.alt: Close-up of a twisted steel wire rope

name: Wood screw

place_of_invention.notes: Metal screws used as fasteners appear in Europe in the 15th century; the screw principle itself is much older (Greek and Roman presses).

short_description: A threaded metal fastener that cuts its own path into wood when turned.
description: Although the screw thread was known in antiquity for presses and water-lifting, using small metal screws as fasteners began in late medieval Europe. Early screws were filed by hand and expensive until 18th- and 19th-century machines made them cheap and pointed. The helical thread around a shank with a slotted head remains the standard.
why_unchanged: A helical thread converts turning into strong clamping force, which no simpler shape can match.

faqs.question: When were screws first used to fasten things?
faqs.answer: Metal screws used as fasteners appear in 15th-century Europe, for example in armor and firearms.

faqs.question: Why are screws stronger than nails in some jobs?
faqs.answer: The thread grips the wood along its length, so screws resist pulling out much better and can clamp parts tightly together.

faqs.question: Why do some wood screws have a smooth upper shank?
faqs.answer: The unthreaded portion lets the top board slide down freely so the screw pulls the two pieces tightly together.

image.alt: Close-up of brass slotted wood screws

name: Wrench

place_of_invention.notes: Fixed wrenches (spanners) for nuts and bolts appear in Europe as threaded fasteners spread, used on armor, firearms and machinery; no single origin is documented.

short_description: A hand tool with a fixed jaw or ring that grips and turns nuts and bolts.
description: Wrenches developed in late medieval and early modern Europe as threaded fasteners spread. Early examples were forged to fit specific nuts on guns, armor and machines. The open-end and box-end wrench still consists of a shaped opening on a lever handle.
why_unchanged: A jaw that fits a nut plus a handle for leverage is all that turning a bolt requires.

faqs.question: Is it called a wrench or a spanner?
faqs.answer: Americans usually say 'wrench', while British English says 'spanner' for fixed tools and often 'wrench' for adjustable ones.

faqs.question: Why are open-end wrench heads angled?
faqs.answer: The roughly 15-degree angle lets you flip the wrench over to keep turning a nut in tight spaces.

faqs.question: What is a combination wrench?
faqs.answer: It has an open end on one side and a closed ring on the other, both for the same size of nut.

image.alt: A row of steel combination wrenches

name: Backgammon board

place_of_invention.notes: Backgammon belongs to the ancient 'tables' family; the Roman game tabula and the Persian nard are close ancestors, and the exact origin is debated.

short_description: A board of 24 triangular points on which two players race 15 checkers each using dice.
description: Backgammon descends from tables games played in the Roman world and in Sasanian Persia, where the game of nard was described in a 6th-century text. Its board of 24 points arranged in four quarters became widespread across the Middle East and Europe. The doubling cube, added in the 1920s in New York, is the only major modern addition.
why_unchanged: The race-and-block mechanics depend on the 24-point layout, so the board has stayed the same for well over a millennium.

faqs.question: How old is backgammon?
faqs.answer: Its direct ancestors, such as Roman tabula and Persian nard, were played at least 1,500 years ago. Even older Near Eastern race games share the idea of moving pieces by dice.

faqs.question: What is the doubling cube?
faqs.answer: It is a die marked 2 to 64 introduced in the 1920s that lets players raise the stakes during a game.

faqs.question: How many checkers does each player use?
faqs.answer: Each player has 15 checkers that must all be moved home and borne off to win.

image.search_query: backgammon board with checkers and dice
image.alt: An open backgammon board with checkers and dice

name: Ball

place_of_invention.notes: The oldest surviving rubber balls come from El Manatí, Mexico (c. 1600 BCE); balls of leather, cloth and other materials were made in many ancient cultures.

short_description: A round object for throwing, kicking, bouncing or rolling in play and sport.
description: Balls are found in almost every culture, and the oldest surviving rubber balls, from El Manatí in Mexico, are about 3,600 years old. Ancient Egyptians, Greeks and Romans made balls of leather, linen and inflated bladders. Modern sports use specialized balls, but a simple sphere remains the most universal toy.
why_unchanged: A sphere rolls and bounces in every direction equally, which is exactly what play requires.

faqs.question: What are the oldest known balls?
faqs.answer: Rubber balls from El Manatí in Mexico, dating to about 1600 BCE, are among the oldest surviving ones.

faqs.question: Did ancient Mesoamericans play ball games?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Mesoamerican ballgame was played with a heavy rubber ball for thousands of years.

faqs.question: Why do balls bounce?
faqs.answer: Elastic materials compress on impact and then spring back, pushing the ball away from the surface.

image.alt: A red rubber ball on a playground

name: Barbell

place_of_invention.notes: Globe barbells were used in 19th-century European gymnasiums, such as Hippolyte Triat's in Paris; plate-loading barbells spread in the early 20th century. No single inventor is known.

short_description: A long bar with weights on each end, lifted with both hands.
description: Barbells developed in 19th-century Europe from wooden wands and dumbbells, with early versions using hollow globes filled with sand or shot. Strongmen popularized them in music halls, and plate-loading bars appeared around 1900. The Olympic barbell, standardized in the 20th century, keeps the same bar-and-weights design.
why_unchanged: A straight bar with balanced weights is the most efficient way to load two-handed lifts.

faqs.question: How heavy is an Olympic barbell?
faqs.answer: The standard men's Olympic bar weighs 20 kg and the women's 15 kg.

faqs.question: What were early barbells like?
faqs.answer: Many had hollow globes at each end that could be filled with sand or lead shot to change the weight.

faqs.question: What lifts use a barbell?
faqs.answer: Common lifts include the squat, bench press, deadlift, snatch and clean and jerk.

image.alt: A loaded barbell on a gym floor

name: Billiard cue

place_of_invention.notes: The cue developed from the butt end of the earlier billiard mace in the late 17th century; the leather tip is credited to François Mingaud in the early 19th century.

short_description: A long tapered stick used to strike balls in billiards, pool and snooker.
description: Billiards was first played by pushing balls with a mace, a stick with a broad head. In the late 17th century players began striking with the narrow butt end, which became the cue. The leather tip and chalk added in the early 19th century allowed spin, giving the cue the form it has today.
why_unchanged: A straight tapered shaft with a small tip is the most precise way to strike a ball, so the design has stayed.

faqs.question: Where does the word cue come from?
faqs.answer: It comes from the French 'queue', meaning tail, referring to the narrow end of the old mace.

faqs.question: Why do players chalk the tip?
faqs.answer: Chalk increases friction between tip and ball, preventing miscues and allowing spin.

faqs.question: Who added the leather tip?
faqs.answer: The French player François Mingaud is credited with popularizing the leather cue tip in the early 19th century.

image.search_query: billiard cue and balls on table
image.alt: A wooden billiard cue resting on a pool table

name: Bocce ball

place_of_invention.notes: Ball-throwing games toward a target were played in ancient Greece and Rome; bocce in its modern form developed in Italy. Claims of ancient Egyptian origin are speculative.

short_description: A heavy ball rolled toward a small target ball in the game of bocce.
description: Games of tossing balls toward a target were played in ancient Rome and spread throughout the Empire. In Italy they became bocce, played on dirt or grass courts with eight large balls and a small target called the pallino. Bocce is still played in parks and clubs around the world with the same equipment.
why_unchanged: A weighted ball rolled at a target needs no further refinement.

faqs.question: What is the pallino?
faqs.answer: The pallino is the small target ball that players try to get their bocce balls closest to.

faqs.question: How many balls are in a bocce set?
faqs.answer: A standard set has eight bocce balls, four per team, plus the pallino.

faqs.question: Is bocce the same as pétanque?
faqs.answer: They are related, but pétanque uses hollow steel balls thrown from a standing circle, while bocce balls are rolled on a court.

image.alt: Red and green bocce balls near a small white pallino

name: Boomerang

place_of_invention.notes: Wooden boomerangs from Wyrie Swamp are about 10,000 years old; an even older ivory throwing stick is known from Obłazowa Cave in Poland. The returning type is associated with Aboriginal Australians.

short_description: A curved, wing-shaped throwing stick, some types of which return to the thrower.
description: Throwing sticks are among humanity's oldest tools, and the oldest preserved Australian boomerangs, from Wyrie Swamp, date back roughly 10,000 years. Aboriginal Australians made both returning boomerangs, used for play and sport, and heavier non-returning ones for hunting. Today sport boomerangs are thrown in competitions for accuracy, distance and catching.
why_unchanged: Its aerofoil arms and spin create the returning flight, and that shape cannot be simplified further.

faqs.question: Do all boomerangs come back?
faqs.answer: No. Many traditional boomerangs were made for hunting and fly straight; only the lighter returning type comes back.

faqs.question: Why does a boomerang return?
faqs.answer: Its spinning, wing-shaped arms create uneven lift that makes it turn in a circle and come back to the thrower.

faqs.question: How old is the boomerang?
faqs.answer: Australian boomerangs are about 10,000 years old, and throwing sticks elsewhere are even older.

image.alt: A carved wooden boomerang

name: Bow and arrow

place_of_invention.notes: Holmegaard bows from Denmark (c. 7000 BCE) are among the oldest complete bows; arrow shafts from Stellmoor, Germany are older, and stone points suggest bow use in Africa more than 60,000 years ago.

short_description: A flexible stave with a string that launches arrows, used today for sport archery.
description: The bow and arrow is one of the oldest human inventions, with complete wooden bows surviving from Mesolithic Denmark and evidence of earlier use in Africa. It was a key hunting and war tool for millennia before becoming a sport. Modern archery uses longbows, recurves and compound bows, but the stave-and-string principle is unchanged.
why_unchanged: Storing energy in a bent stave and releasing it through a string is the essence of the bow and cannot be simplified.

faqs.question: How old is the bow and arrow?
faqs.answer: Complete bows survive from about 9,000 years ago, and stone points from Africa suggest bows were used more than 60,000 years ago.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a longbow and a recurve bow?
faqs.answer: A longbow has straight limbs, while a recurve's tips curve away from the archer to store more energy.

faqs.question: Is archery an Olympic sport?
faqs.answer: Yes. Recurve archery has been in every Summer Olympics since 1972.

image.alt: A wooden recurve bow with arrows

name: Bowling pin

place_of_invention.notes: Ninepins (Kegeln) is documented in medieval Germany; objects from an Egyptian grave of about 3200 BCE have been interpreted as a bowling game, but this is debated.

short_description: A bottle-shaped wooden pin set up in groups to be knocked down by a rolled ball.
description: Games of knocking down pins with a ball were widespread in medieval Europe, especially the German ninepins. Ten-pin bowling developed in the United States in the 19th century and the pin was standardized by bowling organizations. Modern pins are hard maple coated in plastic, but the narrow-necked, wide-bellied shape is unchanged.
why_unchanged: The tall, bottle-like profile makes pins topple and scatter in an exciting way, so the shape has endured.

faqs.question: How heavy is a bowling pin?
faqs.answer: A regulation ten-pin bowling pin weighs about 1.4 to 1.6 kg and stands 38 cm tall.

faqs.question: Why did bowling switch from nine to ten pins?
faqs.answer: A popular story says ten pins were adopted in the US to get around laws banning ninepins, but evidence for this is thin.

faqs.question: Is bowling an ancient game?
faqs.answer: Pin games are documented in medieval Europe, and some researchers think similar games existed in ancient Egypt.

image.alt: Ten white bowling pins with red stripes

name: Building blocks

place_of_invention.notes: John Locke recommended lettered dice or blocks for teaching children in 1693; Friedrich Froebel popularized geometric wooden block sets in Germany in the 1830s.

short_description: Simple wooden cubes and shapes that children stack and arrange.
description: Wooden blocks have long been used as educational toys; philosopher John Locke suggested lettered blocks for teaching the alphabet in 1693. In the 1830s German educator Friedrich Froebel, founder of the kindergarten, made sets of geometric blocks a central part of early education. Plain wooden blocks are still among the most common toys for young children.
why_unchanged: Plain geometric shapes encourage open-ended building, so they never needed to be redesigned.

faqs.question: Why are blocks good for children?
faqs.answer: Stacking blocks builds motor skills, spatial reasoning and early maths concepts.

faqs.question: Who popularized building blocks?
faqs.answer: Friedrich Froebel, founder of the kindergarten, made block sets a key teaching tool in the 1830s.

faqs.question: What are unit blocks?
faqs.answer: Unit blocks are hardwood blocks sized in exact proportions, developed by Caroline Pratt in the early 20th century.

image.alt: A stack of plain wooden building blocks

name: Checkers set

place_of_invention.notes: Draughts likely arose in southern France by combining the older game of alquerque with a chessboard; exact dating is uncertain.

short_description: A checkered board with 24 round, flat pieces used to play checkers (draughts).
description: Checkers, called draughts in Britain, is thought to have developed in medieval France when players moved alquerque-style captures onto a chessboard. The compulsory-capture rule was added in the 16th century, and the game has been played with the same board and disc-shaped pieces ever since. Variants include the 10x10 international draughts popular in Europe and Africa.
why_unchanged: Flat stackable discs on a squared board are all the game needs, including the ability to crown a piece by stacking.

faqs.question: Is checkers the same as draughts?
faqs.answer: Yes. Americans call it checkers and British players call it draughts; the standard game uses an 8x8 board and 12 pieces per side.

faqs.question: How is a king made in checkers?
faqs.answer: When a piece reaches the opponent's back row, another piece is stacked on top to show it can now move backwards.

faqs.question: Has checkers been solved?
faqs.answer: Yes. In 2007 a computer program called Chinook proved that perfect play from both sides leads to a draw.

image.alt: A checkers board with red and black disc pieces

name: Chess set

place_of_invention.notes: Chess descends from the Indian game chaturanga; it passed through Persia (shatranj) and its modern rules settled in southern Europe around 1475.

short_description: A checkered 8x8 board with 32 pieces for the strategy game of chess.
description: Chess emerged in India around the 6th century as chaturanga, was adopted in Persia as shatranj and spread to Europe through the Islamic world. By the late 15th century the queen and bishop gained their modern powers, giving the game its current form. The familiar Staunton piece design was introduced in 1849 and remains the tournament standard.
why_unchanged: The 64-square board and two armies of 16 pieces have defined the game for over 500 years, so the set has no reason to change.

faqs.question: Where was chess invented?
faqs.answer: Chess is generally traced to India around the 6th century CE. It then spread through Persia and the Arab world to Europe.

faqs.question: What are Staunton chess pieces?
faqs.answer: Staunton is the standard piece design introduced in 1849 and named after English player Howard Staunton. It is required in most official tournaments.

faqs.question: Why is the queen the most powerful piece?
faqs.answer: The queen gained her long-range moves in Europe in the late 15th century, a change that made the game faster and more aggressive.

image.alt: A wooden chess set arranged on a checkered board

name: Chinese checkers board

place_of_invention.notes: The game was published by Ravensburger in 1892 as Stern-Halma, a star-shaped variant of Halma (invented in 1883 by George Howard Monks); it was renamed Chinese checkers in the US in the 1920s.

short_description: A six-pointed star board with holes and marbles or pegs, used in a race game.
description: Despite its name, Chinese checkers was invented in Germany, published by Ravensburger in 1892 as Stern-Halma. It was based on Halma, an American game by George Howard Monks. The name Chinese checkers was a 1920s US marketing choice, and the star-shaped board is unchanged.
why_unchanged: The six-pointed star with its triangular corners is the game, so the board has stayed the same.

faqs.question: Is Chinese checkers from China?
faqs.answer: No. It was invented in Germany in 1892 and given its name in the US in the 1920s.

faqs.question: How many people can play?
faqs.answer: It can be played by two, three, four or six players.

faqs.question: What is the goal?
faqs.answer: The goal is to move all your pieces into the opposite point of the star.

image.alt: A star-shaped Chinese checkers board with marbles

name: Cribbage board

place_of_invention.notes: Cribbage is credited to the poet Sir John Suckling, who developed it from the older game of noddy; the pegging board was used for scoring.

short_description: A long board with rows of holes and pegs used to keep score in cribbage.
description: Cribbage was developed in England in the early 17th century, traditionally credited to poet Sir John Suckling. Its distinctive scoring board, with pegs moved along rows of holes, makes counting points quick and visible. The game and board are still played the same way, notably by sailors and in pubs.
why_unchanged: Moving pegs along holes is a fast, error-proof way to keep score, so the board never changed.

faqs.question: Who invented cribbage?
faqs.answer: It is credited to the English poet Sir John Suckling in the early 17th century.

faqs.question: Why does cribbage use a board?
faqs.answer: The board lets players record frequent small scores quickly with pegs instead of writing them down.

faqs.question: Is cribbage popular in the navy?
faqs.answer: Yes. It is a long tradition in the US submarine force, where a historic board is passed to the oldest serving submarine.

image.alt: A wooden cribbage board with metal pegs

name: Croquet set

place_of_invention.notes: Croquet emerged in Ireland in the 1830s–1850s and was brought to England in the early 1850s; a game called paille-maille is an earlier relative.

short_description: Wooden mallets, balls, hoops and a peg used to play the lawn game of croquet.
description: Croquet developed in Ireland and became a sensation in England in the 1860s, played on lawns by men and women together. Players use mallets to strike balls through hoops in a set order. The mallets, balls and wire hoops in today's sets are essentially the same as in Victorian times.
why_unchanged: Mallets, balls and hoops are the complete game, and their simple forms have stayed.

faqs.question: Where was croquet invented?
faqs.answer: Croquet developed in Ireland and was brought to England in the 1850s.

faqs.question: What is a croquet stroke?
faqs.answer: It is the shot where you place your ball against another and strike it so both move.

faqs.question: Was croquet an Olympic sport?
faqs.answer: Yes. It was played at the 1900 Paris Olympics, and roque, a variant, in 1904.

image.search_query: croquet set mallets balls hoops lawn
image.alt: Croquet mallets and coloured balls on a lawn

name: Cup-and-ball

place_of_invention.notes: The bilboquet was fashionable in 16th-century France, notably at the court of Henri III; similar catching toys exist in many Indigenous cultures.

short_description: A handle with a cup on top and a ball tied by a string, tossed up and caught in the cup.
description: Cup-and-ball toys, called bilboquet in French, became a fashion at the French court in the 16th century and remained popular across Europe. Indigenous peoples of the Americas and the Arctic made similar catching toys from bone and hide. The design of a stick, a cup and a tethered ball is still sold everywhere.
why_unchanged: A stick, cup and tethered ball are the simplest catching challenge possible.

faqs.question: What is a bilboquet?
faqs.answer: Bilboquet is the French name for cup-and-ball, a toy popular at the French court in the 1500s.

faqs.question: How do you play cup-and-ball?
faqs.answer: You swing or flick the ball up and try to catch it in the cup or on a spike.

faqs.question: Is kendama the same thing?
faqs.answer: Kendama is a Japanese relative with extra cups and a spike, allowing many more tricks.

image.search_query: wooden cup and ball toy bilboquet
image.alt: A wooden cup-and-ball toy

name: Curling stone

place_of_invention.notes: The oldest known curling stone, the Stirling Stone, bears the date 1511; curling is also depicted in 16th-century Flemish paintings.

short_description: A heavy polished granite stone with a handle slid along ice toward a target.
description: Curling originated in Scotland, where the oldest known stone is dated 1511. Early stones were rough river rocks; handles and standardized shapes came later. Today's stones are made of granite from Ailsa Craig in Scotland or from Wales, and they keep the same rounded shape with a handle on top.
why_unchanged: A heavy, smooth stone that glides and curls on ice is the whole game, so its form is unchanged.

faqs.question: How heavy is a curling stone?
faqs.answer: A stone weighs up to about 19.96 kg (44 lb).

faqs.question: Where does curling granite come from?
faqs.answer: Most Olympic stones are made of granite from Ailsa Craig, an island off Scotland, or from Trefor in Wales.

faqs.question: Why do curlers sweep?
faqs.answer: Sweeping slightly warms the ice, helping the stone travel farther and curl less.

image.alt: A red-handled granite curling stone on ice

name: Dartboard

place_of_invention.notes: The standard 'clock' numbering is often credited to Brian Gamlin in 1896, but his existence is unverified; Thomas William Buckle (c. 1913) is another claimant.

short_description: A round target divided into numbered segments with doubles, trebles and a bullseye.
description: The standard clock-face dartboard numbering, which places high numbers beside low ones to punish inaccuracy, was in use by the early 20th century. Early boards were made from elm and had to be soaked to heal the holes, until sisal-fibre bristle boards took over from the 1930s. The board's layout of 20 segments, double and treble rings and bullseye remains standard worldwide.
why_unchanged: The numbering scheme balances risk and reward so well that it has been kept unchanged for over a century.

faqs.question: Why are the numbers on a dartboard in that order?
faqs.answer: The order places high and low numbers next to each other so that inaccurate throws are penalized.

faqs.question: What is a bristle dartboard made of?
faqs.answer: Bristle boards are made of compressed sisal fibres, which close up after a dart is pulled out.

faqs.question: How high is a dartboard hung?
faqs.answer: The centre of the bullseye is placed 1.73 metres (5 feet 8 inches) above the floor.

image.alt: A bristle dartboard with three darts in the treble twenty

name: Darts

place_of_invention.notes: Darts as a pub game developed in late 19th-century England; a popular story links it to archers throwing cut-down arrows, but this is unproven.

short_description: Small weighted, flighted arrows thrown by hand at a target board.
description: Throwing short arrows at a target became a popular English pub game in the late 19th century, and darts with wooden barrels and feather flights were common by the early 1900s. Modern darts use tungsten barrels and plastic flights, but the shape of point, barrel, shaft and flight is the same. Darts is now a major televised sport.
why_unchanged: A weighted point at the front and stabilizing flights at the back are what make a dart fly straight.

faqs.question: Where did the game of darts begin?
faqs.answer: Darts as we know it developed in English pubs in the late 19th century.

faqs.question: Why are modern darts made of tungsten?
faqs.answer: Tungsten is very dense, so the barrel can be slim yet heavy, allowing darts to cluster tightly on the board.

faqs.question: What are flights for?
faqs.answer: Flights stabilize the dart in the air, much like the feathers on an arrow.

image.alt: Three darts with colourful flights

name: Diabolo

place_of_invention.notes: The diabolo (kongzhu) was known in China for centuries and was described by Europeans in the 1790s; the modern Western name and form date to Gustave Philippart in France around 1906.

short_description: An hourglass-shaped spool spun and tossed on a string tied between two hand sticks.
description: The diabolo originated in China, where it is known as kongzhu and often made with hollow ends that whistle. Europeans encountered it in the late 18th century, and French engineer Gustave Philippart developed the modern diabolo around 1906, sparking a craze. The two-cup spool and string on hand sticks are still used for juggling and circus tricks.
why_unchanged: The hourglass spool balances naturally on a string, which makes the design perfect as it is.

faqs.question: Where does the diabolo come from?
faqs.answer: It originated in China, where it is called kongzhu.

faqs.question: Why do some Chinese diabolos whistle?
faqs.answer: Their hollow ends have slits that make a humming sound as they spin.

faqs.question: What does diabolo mean?
faqs.answer: The name was coined in France and is often linked to Greek words meaning 'to throw across'.

image.alt: A red diabolo spinning on a string between two sticks

name: Dice

place_of_invention.notes: Some of the oldest cubic dice come from Shahr-e Sukhteh (Iran) and Indus Valley sites; earlier games used animal knucklebones as lots.

short_description: Small cubes marked with one to six pips, rolled to generate random numbers in games.
description: Six-sided dice have been found at Bronze Age sites in Iran and the Indus Valley, and they spread across the ancient world as tools for gambling, games and divination. Opposite faces on most standard dice add up to seven, a convention already common in antiquity. Today they are used in board games, casino games and tabletop role-playing.
why_unchanged: A cube is the simplest fair shape to roll, so nothing about the basic form needed improving.

faqs.question: How old are dice?
faqs.answer: Cubic dice date back at least to around the mid-3rd millennium BCE, with finds in Iran and the Indus Valley. Earlier people cast animal knucklebones in a similar way.

faqs.question: Why do opposite sides of a die add up to seven?
faqs.answer: It is a long-standing convention that balances the pips around the cube. Many ancient dice already followed it, though not all did.

faqs.question: Why are casino dice sharp-cornered and transparent?
faqs.answer: Precision casino dice are made with sharp edges and clear material so that they roll fairly and can be checked for hidden weights.

image.alt: Several white six-sided dice with black pips

name: Discus

place_of_invention.notes: The discus was part of the ancient Olympic pentathlon, traditionally introduced in 708 BCE.

short_description: A heavy disc thrown for distance in athletics.
description: The discus throw was part of the ancient Greek pentathlon, and Myron's sculpture the Discobolus made the event iconic. Ancient discuses were made of stone, bronze or lead and varied in size. The modern discus, a wooden or plastic disc with a metal rim, keeps the same flat, lens-like shape.
why_unchanged: A flat lens-shaped disc flies stably when spun, so its shape needs no change.

faqs.question: How heavy is a discus?
faqs.answer: The men's discus weighs 2 kg and the women's 1 kg.

faqs.question: What is the Discobolus?
faqs.answer: It is a famous ancient Greek statue by Myron, around 450 BCE, showing an athlete about to throw a discus.

faqs.question: Was the discus in the first modern Olympics?
faqs.answer: Yes. It was contested at the 1896 Athens Games and won by Robert Garrett of the US.

image.alt: A discus resting on a track field

name: Doll

place_of_invention.notes: Wooden 'paddle dolls' from Middle Kingdom Egypt are often cited; whether some ancient figurines were toys or ritual objects is debated.

short_description: A small model of a human figure used as a plaything.
description: Doll-like figures are among the oldest toys, with wooden and clay examples from ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome, although some may have had religious purposes. Roman children played with jointed dolls of bone and ivory. Rag, porcelain, celluloid and vinyl dolls followed, but the human figure has remained the core of the toy.
why_unchanged: A child-sized human figure meets the same need for imaginative play in every era.

faqs.question: What are the oldest known dolls?
faqs.answer: Some of the oldest are wooden figures from ancient Egypt around 2000 BCE, though their purpose is debated.

faqs.question: Did Roman children have jointed dolls?
faqs.answer: Yes. Jointed dolls of bone, ivory and wood have been found in Roman children's graves.

faqs.question: What is a rag doll?
faqs.answer: A rag doll is a soft doll made of cloth and stuffing, often homemade, and is one of the most widespread types.

image.alt: An old-fashioned cloth doll

name: Dominoes

place_of_invention.notes: Chinese dominoes are recorded around the 12th–13th centuries; European dominoes appeared in Italy in the 18th century, possibly independently.

short_description: Rectangular tiles each divided into two ends marked with pips, used in matching games.
description: Dominoes appear in Chinese sources from the Song dynasty and were closely related to dice. European dominoes surfaced in 18th-century Italy and France and spread quickly, with the standard double-six set of 28 tiles. They are used both for matching games and, famously, for toppling in long chains.
why_unchanged: Each tile simply records a pair of dice results, a perfect and unchanging way to encode the game.

faqs.question: How many tiles are in a domino set?
faqs.answer: A standard double-six set has 28 tiles, one for each possible pair of numbers from blank to six.

faqs.question: Where do dominoes come from?
faqs.answer: They are first recorded in China around the 12th to 13th centuries, and appeared in Europe in the 18th century.

faqs.question: What is the domino effect?
faqs.answer: It is the chain reaction seen when one falling tile knocks over the next; the term is used for any cascading series of events.

image.alt: A set of black dominoes with white pips

name: Dreidel

place_of_invention.notes: The dreidel is a Jewish adaptation of the teetotum, a lettered spinning top played in Europe; exact dating is uncertain.

short_description: A four-sided spinning top with Hebrew letters, played during Hanukkah.
description: The dreidel adapts the European teetotum, a spinning top with letters on its sides used in gambling games. Jewish communities replaced the letters with the Hebrew nun, gimel, hei and shin, later read as 'a great miracle happened there'. It is spun during Hanukkah, with players winning or giving coins, nuts or chocolate.
why_unchanged: A four-sided top that lands on a random face is all the game needs.

faqs.question: What do the letters on a dreidel mean?
faqs.answer: They stand for 'Nes Gadol Haya Sham', meaning 'a great miracle happened there'; in Israel the last letter is pe for 'here'.

faqs.question: How do you play dreidel?
faqs.answer: Each player spins in turn and, depending on the letter, takes nothing, all, half, or puts in to the pot.

faqs.question: Where did the dreidel come from?
faqs.answer: It is adapted from the teetotum, a lettered top played in Europe for centuries.

image.alt: A wooden dreidel with Hebrew letters

name: Dumbbell

place_of_invention.notes: The term 'dumb bell' appears in early 18th-century England; ancient Greek athletes used hand weights called halteres.

short_description: A short bar with a weight at each end, lifted with one hand for strength training.
description: Ancient Greek athletes trained with handheld weights called halteres, and by the early 18th century the English used weighted 'dumb bells'. The name is thought to come from bell-ringing practice devices that made no sound. Today's dumbbells, made of iron, rubber or chrome, keep the same handle-and-weights form.
why_unchanged: A handle with balanced weights on either side is the simplest effective design for one-handed lifting.

faqs.question: Why is it called a dumbbell?
faqs.answer: The name is thought to come from bell-ringing practice devices that were 'dumb', meaning silent.

faqs.question: Did ancient athletes use dumbbells?
faqs.answer: Ancient Greeks used similar hand weights called halteres, especially for the long jump.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a dumbbell and a barbell?
faqs.answer: A dumbbell is short and held in one hand, while a barbell is a long bar held with both hands.

image.alt: A pair of iron dumbbells on a gym floor

name: Etch A Sketch

place_of_invention.notes: André Cassagnes invented 'L'Écran Magique' in the late 1950s; the Ohio Art Company licensed it and released it as Etch A Sketch in 1960.

short_description: A drawing toy with two knobs that move a stylus to scrape lines on a grey screen.
description: French electrician André Cassagnes invented the drawing screen in the late 1950s and showed it at the 1959 Nuremberg Toy Fair. The Ohio Art Company bought the rights and released it in 1960 as Etch A Sketch, which became a best-seller. Turning the knobs moves a stylus that scrapes aluminium powder off the glass, and shaking it erases the picture.
why_unchanged: Its two-knob mechanism is the toy's defining challenge, so the design has stayed the same.

faqs.question: How does an Etch A Sketch work?
faqs.answer: A stylus behind the glass scrapes off aluminium powder, leaving dark lines, and shaking re-coats the screen.

faqs.question: Who invented it?
faqs.answer: French inventor André Cassagnes created it; Ohio Art released it in 1960.

faqs.question: Why is it hard to draw curves?
faqs.answer: Each knob only moves the stylus horizontally or vertically, so curves need both turned together.

image.alt: A red Etch A Sketch with a drawing on the screen

name: Flip book

place_of_invention.notes: John Barnes Linnett patented the flip book in 1868 under the name kineograph.

short_description: A small book of pictures that seem to move when the pages are flipped quickly.
description: The flip book was patented in 1868 by John Barnes Linnett as the kineograph, meaning 'moving picture'. Each page shows a slightly different drawing, so flipping through them creates animation. It remains a popular craft and souvenir, and is one of the simplest forms of animation.
why_unchanged: A stack of sequential pictures already produces animation, so nothing needed changing.

faqs.question: Who invented the flip book?
faqs.answer: John Barnes Linnett patented it in 1868 as the kineograph.

faqs.question: How many pages does a flip book need?
faqs.answer: Even 10 to 20 pages can show a short movement, but more pages make it smoother.

faqs.question: Can you make your own?
faqs.answer: Yes. Drawing a slightly changing image in the corner of a notebook's pages is a classic way to make one.

image.alt: A hand flipping the pages of a flip book

name: Flying disc

place_of_invention.notes: Morrison and Warren Franscioni sold the plastic Flyin-Saucer in 1948; Wham-O bought the design and named it Frisbee in 1957.

short_description: A plastic disc with a curved lip that glides when thrown with a spin.
description: After years of tossing metal pie tins and cake pans, Walter Frederick Morrison and Warren Franscioni produced a plastic flying disc in 1948. Morrison's improved Pluto Platter was bought by Wham-O, which renamed it Frisbee in 1957 after the Frisbie Pie Company tins. The disc is used in casual play and in sports like ultimate and disc golf.
why_unchanged: The rounded lip and spin-stabilized shape already provide excellent flight, so the design has remained.

faqs.question: Why is it called a Frisbee?
faqs.answer: The name was taken from the Frisbie Pie Company, whose pie tins students used to throw before plastic discs existed.

faqs.question: Who invented the flying disc?
faqs.answer: Walter Frederick Morrison, with Warren Franscioni, created the first plastic flying disc in 1948.

faqs.question: Why does a flying disc fly so well?
faqs.answer: Its curved upper surface generates lift, and spinning keeps it stable in the air.

image.alt: A plastic flying disc in mid-air

name: Go board

place_of_invention.notes: Go is mentioned in Chinese texts from around the 6th–4th centuries BCE; early boards were 17x17 before the 19x19 grid became standard.

short_description: A grid board with black and white stones used for the territory game Go.
description: Go, known as weiqi in China and baduk in Korea, is among the oldest board games still played, with literary references dating to the first millennium BCE. Players place black and white stones on the intersections of a grid to surround territory. The 19x19 board has been standard for well over a thousand years, and Japanese go boards are often thick blocks of kaya wood.
why_unchanged: Stones on a simple grid already give near-infinite strategic depth, so the equipment never needed refinement.

faqs.question: How old is Go?
faqs.answer: Go is mentioned in Chinese writings from roughly 2,500 years ago, making it one of the oldest board games still played in its original form.

faqs.question: Why are stones placed on the lines and not in the squares?
faqs.answer: In Go, the intersections are the playing points, which is why a 19x19 board has 361 positions.

faqs.question: What made Go famous in AI history?
faqs.answer: In 2016 the program AlphaGo defeated top professional Lee Sedol, a milestone many experts had expected to be a decade away.

image.search_query: go board with black and white stones
image.alt: A wooden Go board with black and white stones

name: Golf tee

place_of_invention.notes: George Franklin Grant patented a wooden tee in 1899; the Reddy Tee of 1921 popularized it. Golfers previously used small piles of sand.

short_description: A small peg pushed into the ground to hold a golf ball for the first shot of a hole.
description: Before tees, golfers built small mounds of damp sand to raise the ball. Boston dentist George Franklin Grant, one of the first African American graduates of Harvard's dental school, patented a wooden tee in 1899. The peg-with-a-cup design is the same today, though tees are now also made of plastic and bamboo.
why_unchanged: A peg with a small cup is the simplest way to raise a ball off the ground.

faqs.question: What did golfers use before tees?
faqs.answer: They made small mounds of wet sand to raise the ball.

faqs.question: Who invented the golf tee?
faqs.answer: George Franklin Grant, a Boston dentist, patented the wooden golf tee in 1899.

faqs.question: Can you use a tee for every shot?
faqs.answer: No. Under the rules of golf a tee may only be used for the first stroke on each hole, from the teeing area.

image.alt: Wooden golf tees with a golf ball

name: Hacky sack

place_of_invention.notes: The footbag game was created by John Stalberger and Mike Marshall in 1972; Hacky Sack is a trademark now owned by Wham-O.

short_description: A small bean bag kept in the air with the feet in the game of footbag.
description: John Stalberger and Mike Marshall developed the hacky sack in 1972 as a fun way to exercise an injured knee. The small, soft bag filled with pellets became a playground and campus staple in the 1980s. Similar foot-juggling games exist in many cultures, such as Southeast Asian sepak takraw and Chinese jianzi.
why_unchanged: A small soft bag that doesn't bounce away is exactly what foot juggling needs.

faqs.question: Who invented the hacky sack?
faqs.answer: John Stalberger and Mike Marshall created it in Oregon in 1972.

faqs.question: What is footbag?
faqs.answer: Footbag is the generic name for games played with a small bag kept aloft using the feet.

faqs.question: What is the goal of hacky sack?
faqs.answer: In the casual 'circle' game, players pass the bag around without letting it touch the ground or using their hands.

image.alt: A crocheted hacky sack on grass

name: Hand puppet

place_of_invention.notes: Glove puppetry spread across Europe from the Italian Pulcinella tradition in the 17th century; Chinese glove puppetry is also centuries old.

short_description: A puppet worn on the hand, with fingers moving its head and arms.
description: Glove puppets became popular street entertainment in 17th-century Europe, with characters such as Italy's Pulcinella and Britain's Mr Punch. In China, glove puppetry (budaixi) developed in Fujian and remains a traditional art. Hand puppets of cloth and felt are still widely used in children's play, theatre and television.
why_unchanged: A hollow figure worn over the hand gives direct, expressive control, which needs no improvement.

faqs.question: How does a glove puppet work?
faqs.answer: The puppeteer's index finger moves the head while the thumb and another finger move the arms.

faqs.question: Who is Mr Punch?
faqs.answer: Mr Punch is a British glove-puppet character derived from the Italian Pulcinella, first recorded in England in 1662.

faqs.question: Are hand puppets used in education?
faqs.answer: Yes. Teachers and therapists use them to help children express feelings and practise language.

image.alt: A colourful felt hand puppet

name: Hobby horse

place_of_invention.notes: Plutarch tells of the Spartan king Agesilaus riding a stick horse with his children; stick horses appear in many cultures and periods.

short_description: A stick with a horse's head at one end that a child 'rides' between the legs.
description: Stick horses are among the oldest pretend toys, with ancient anecdotes describing adults playing with them alongside children. They appear in medieval and Renaissance paintings of children's games. The modern version, a stuffed or wooden horse head on a pole, is unchanged and has even inspired the hobbyhorsing sport in Finland.
why_unchanged: A stick and a horse's head are all imaginative riding requires.

faqs.question: How old is the hobby horse?
faqs.answer: Stick horses go back to antiquity; Plutarch tells of the Spartan king Agesilaus riding one with his children.

faqs.question: Where does 'hobby' come from?
faqs.answer: The word 'hobby' originally meant a small horse, and riding a hobby horse came to mean pursuing a favourite pastime.

faqs.question: What is hobbyhorsing?
faqs.answer: It is a modern Finnish sport in which riders perform dressage and jumping courses on hobby horses.

image.alt: A child riding a hobby horse with a stuffed head

name: Hockey puck

place_of_invention.notes: The first organized indoor ice hockey game in Montreal in 1875 used a flat wooden puck instead of a ball; vulcanized rubber pucks followed soon after.

short_description: A flat disc of hard rubber struck with sticks in ice hockey.
description: Ice hockey was first played with balls, but the 1875 indoor game at Montreal's Victoria Skating Rink used a flat wooden disc that would not bounce into spectators. Rubber pucks followed, and the standard puck is now 3 inches across and 1 inch thick. They are frozen before games to reduce bouncing.
why_unchanged: A flat rubber disc slides smoothly and stays low on the ice, so it has never needed redesign.

faqs.question: Why are hockey pucks frozen before games?
faqs.answer: Freezing makes the rubber harder and less bouncy, so the puck slides more predictably.

faqs.question: How big is a hockey puck?
faqs.answer: A standard puck is 3 inches (7.6 cm) in diameter, 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick and weighs about 170 g.

faqs.question: Why did hockey switch from a ball to a puck?
faqs.answer: A flat puck stays on the ice and is less likely to fly into spectators.

image.alt: A black hockey puck on ice

name: Hoop and stick

place_of_invention.notes: Hoop rolling is shown on Greek vases and described by ancient writers; it was also known in ancient Egypt and Rome.

short_description: A large hoop rolled along the ground and kept moving by striking it with a stick.
description: Children in ancient Greece rolled hoops guided by a short stick, a game depicted on painted vases and later popular in Rome. Hoop trundling remained a common street game in Europe and North America into the early 20th century. Wooden or metal hoops are still used in traditional games and school celebrations.
why_unchanged: A simple ring and a stick are all the game needs, so the toy has never been redesigned.

faqs.question: How do you play hoop and stick?
faqs.answer: You set the hoop rolling and tap or push it with the stick to keep it upright and steer it.

faqs.question: How old is hoop rolling?
faqs.answer: It was already a common game in ancient Greece and Rome more than 2,000 years ago.

faqs.question: Is it related to the hula hoop?
faqs.answer: Both use a large hoop, but the hula hoop is spun around the body, whereas the trundling hoop is rolled along the ground.

name: Hula hoop

place_of_invention.notes: Wham-O, founded by Richard Knerr and Arthur 'Spud' Melin, launched the plastic hula hoop in 1958; hoops of rattan, grapevine and wood were used for exercise and play since antiquity.

short_description: A light plastic hoop twirled around the waist, limbs or neck.
