description: People have spun and rolled hoops since ancient times, but Wham-O's plastic hula hoop, launched in 1958, created a worldwide craze with tens of millions sold within months. The name comes from the hip movements of Hawaiian hula dancing. Today hoops are used in fitness, dance and circus performance.
why_unchanged: A light, round tube is all that is needed to keep the hoop spinning, so the design remained.

faqs.question: Who made the first plastic hula hoop?
faqs.answer: The Wham-O company introduced it in 1958, though people had used hoops of natural materials for thousands of years.

faqs.question: Why is it called a hula hoop?
faqs.answer: The name refers to the hip movements of Hawaiian hula dancing.

faqs.question: Can hula hooping be exercise?
faqs.answer: Yes. Weighted fitness hoops are used for cardio and core workouts.

image.alt: A person spinning a colourful hula hoop

name: Hurley

place_of_invention.notes: Hurling is described in early Irish law and legend; claims that it is thousands of years old are traditional and hard to date precisely.

short_description: A curved ash stick with a flat blade used to play hurling and camogie.
description: The hurley, or camán, is the stick used in hurling, an Irish field game mentioned in early medieval Irish law texts and legends. It is traditionally carved from a single piece of ash, with the grain following the curve of the blade. Its shape has barely changed, though metal bands and protective grips have been added.
why_unchanged: Carving a curved blade from the root end of ash gives a strong, flexible stick that needs no redesign.

faqs.question: What wood is a hurley made from?
faqs.answer: Hurleys are traditionally made from ash, using the curve where the trunk meets the root.

faqs.question: What is the ball called?
faqs.answer: The hurling ball is called a sliotar, a leather ball with raised stitching.

faqs.question: Is hurling fast?
faqs.answer: Yes. It is often called one of the fastest field games, with the sliotar struck at well over 100 km/h.

image.alt: A wooden ash hurley with a sliotar ball

name: Ice skates

place_of_invention.notes: Bone skates were used in northern Europe for millennia; research suggests they may have originated in Finland. Steel-edged skates developed in the Netherlands in the 13th–14th centuries.

short_description: Boots or frames fitted with blades for gliding over ice.
description: The earliest skates were animal bones strapped to the feet, used in northern Europe at least 4,000–5,000 years ago. Dutch craftsmen introduced sharpened metal blades in the late Middle Ages, allowing skaters to push off and glide. Today's figure, hockey and speed skates refine the same blade-under-boot design.
why_unchanged: A narrow blade under the foot is what allows gliding on ice, and that principle cannot change.

faqs.question: What were the first ice skates made of?
faqs.answer: They were made of flattened animal bones strapped to the feet.

faqs.question: Why do ice skates glide?
faqs.answer: A thin layer of water and loosely bound molecules at the ice surface reduces friction under the blade.

faqs.question: Why do figure skates have toe picks?
faqs.answer: The serrated toe pick helps figure skaters grip the ice for jumps and spins.

image.alt: A pair of ice skates on a frozen pond

name: Indian clubs

place_of_invention.notes: Club swinging derives from much older Persian and Indian exercise traditions (meel, jori); British soldiers brought the practice to Britain in the 19th century.

short_description: Bottle-shaped wooden clubs swung in patterns for strength and flexibility.
description: Indian clubs come from traditional exercise clubs used by wrestlers in India and Persia. British soldiers stationed in India adopted them and introduced club swinging to Britain in the 19th century, where it became a popular form of exercise. Indian clubs even appeared at the 1904 and 1932 Olympics and are now enjoying a revival.
why_unchanged: A weighted club swung in circles works the shoulders and grip in a way that needs no redesign.

faqs.question: Where do Indian clubs come from?
faqs.answer: They come from traditional exercise clubs used in India and Persia, adopted by the British in the 19th century.

faqs.question: Were Indian clubs an Olympic sport?
faqs.answer: Yes. Club swinging was an Olympic gymnastics event in 1904 and 1932.

faqs.question: What are they good for?
faqs.answer: Swinging clubs improves shoulder mobility, grip strength and coordination.

image.alt: A pair of wooden Indian clubs

name: Jack-in-the-box

place_of_invention.notes: Spring-loaded surprise boxes are recorded in 16th-century Europe; a legend links the toy to the medieval English priest John Schorne, but this is folklore.

short_description: A box from which a figure on a spring pops up when the lid opens.
description: The jack-in-the-box, a figure that springs out of a box when the lid is released, has been a European toy since at least the 16th century. Later versions added a crank that plays a tune, such as 'Pop Goes the Weasel', before the lid flies open. The surprise of the pop-up figure has kept the design unchanged.
why_unchanged: Its entire appeal is the sudden spring-loaded surprise, which needs no improvement.

faqs.question: How does a jack-in-the-box work?
faqs.answer: A coiled spring under the figure is held down by the lid; when the latch releases, the spring pushes the figure out.

faqs.question: What tune do they usually play?
faqs.answer: Many crank-operated versions play 'Pop Goes the Weasel', with the figure popping out on the 'pop'.

faqs.question: How old is the toy?
faqs.answer: Jack-in-the-boxes have been made in Europe since at least the 1500s.

image.alt: A jack-in-the-box with a clown figure popping out

name: Jacks

place_of_invention.notes: Jacks descends from knucklebones (astragali), played in ancient Greece and Rome and elsewhere; metal six-pointed jacks with a rubber ball are a later version.

short_description: Small pointed pieces tossed and picked up between bounces of a ball.
description: Jacks developed from knucklebones, a game played with sheep ankle bones across the ancient world, notably in Greece and Rome. Players toss the pieces, then pick up one, two or more at a time while a ball or another piece is in the air. Modern sets use six-pointed metal or plastic jacks and a small rubber ball.
why_unchanged: Small pieces that can be scattered and grabbed are all the game needs, so its essence is unchanged.

faqs.question: How do you play jacks?
faqs.answer: You scatter the jacks, bounce the ball, pick up a set number of jacks and catch the ball before it bounces twice.

faqs.question: Where does jacks come from?
faqs.answer: It comes from knucklebones, an ancient game played with small animal bones.

faqs.question: What are 'onesies' and 'twosies'?
faqs.answer: They are the rounds of the game where you pick up the jacks one at a time, then two at a time, and so on.

image.search_query: metal jacks and rubber ball game
image.alt: Metal jacks and a red rubber ball on a table

name: Javelin

place_of_invention.notes: The javelin throw was part of the ancient Olympic pentathlon, traditionally said to have been introduced in 708 BCE; throwing spears are far older.

short_description: A light spear thrown for distance in track and field athletics.
description: Spears have been thrown since prehistoric times, but the javelin as a sport entered the ancient Olympic pentathlon, traditionally in 708 BCE. Greek athletes used a leather thong wrapped around the shaft to add spin. The modern javelin, standardized in the 20th century, is still a long pointed shaft with a grip.
why_unchanged: A balanced pointed shaft is the most efficient shape for a thrown projectile.

faqs.question: How heavy is an Olympic javelin?
faqs.answer: The men's javelin weighs 800 g and the women's 600 g.

faqs.question: When did the javelin become a sport?
faqs.answer: It was part of the ancient Olympic pentathlon, traditionally from 708 BCE.

faqs.question: Why was the javelin redesigned in 1986?
faqs.answer: Throws were getting dangerously long, so the centre of gravity was moved forward to shorten flights; the overall shape stayed the same.

image.alt: An athlete about to throw a javelin

name: Jianzi

place_of_invention.notes: Shuttlecock kicking is traditionally traced to the Han dynasty; clear records date from later periods, so early dating is uncertain.

short_description: A weighted shuttlecock with feathers that is kept in the air by kicking.
description: Jianzi is a traditional Chinese game in which players keep a feathered shuttlecock in the air using their feet and body. It is traditionally said to date back about 2,000 years and is popular across Asia, with versions such as Vietnam's đá cầu. The shuttle, made of feathers fixed to a weighted base, is unchanged.
why_unchanged: Feathers on a weighted disc make a slow, stable target for kicking, so no improvement was needed.

faqs.question: How do you play jianzi?
faqs.answer: Players keep the shuttlecock in the air with their feet and body, without using their hands.

faqs.question: How old is jianzi?
faqs.answer: It is traditionally traced to the Han dynasty, about 2,000 years ago.

faqs.question: Is jianzi a competitive sport?
faqs.answer: Yes. Shuttlecock sport has international federations and competitions, especially in Asia and Europe.

image.alt: A colourful feathered jianzi shuttlecock

name: Jigsaw puzzle

place_of_invention.notes: London engraver and mapmaker John Spilsbury is credited with the first 'dissected maps' in the 1760s.

short_description: A picture cut into interlocking pieces that must be reassembled.
description: The jigsaw puzzle began in the 1760s when John Spilsbury mounted maps on wood and cut them along country borders as teaching aids. Puzzles became a popular pastime, and in the early 20th century interlocking pieces and die-cut cardboard made them cheap to mass-produce. The name comes from the jigsaw or fretsaw used to cut wooden puzzles.
why_unchanged: Cutting a picture into pieces that fit back together is the whole idea, and it needs no improvement.

faqs.question: Who invented the jigsaw puzzle?
faqs.answer: John Spilsbury, a London mapmaker, is credited with making the first ones in the 1760s as geography teaching aids.

faqs.question: Why is it called a jigsaw puzzle?
faqs.answer: Wooden puzzles were cut with a jigsaw or fretsaw, which gave the toy its name.

faqs.question: What is the best strategy to solve one?
faqs.answer: Most people sort the edge pieces first, build the border, and then group the remaining pieces by colour.

image.alt: A partly completed jigsaw puzzle

name: Juggling balls

place_of_invention.notes: A wall painting in a Middle Kingdom tomb at Beni Hasan shows women juggling balls; juggling also appears in other ancient cultures.

short_description: Small soft balls tossed in patterns by jugglers.
description: One of the earliest depictions of juggling, from a tomb at Beni Hasan in Egypt, shows women tossing several balls. Juggling with balls has been a street and circus skill in many cultures since then. Modern juggling balls are typically beanbags of leather or fabric that do not roll away when dropped.
why_unchanged: A small ball that fits in the hand and lands softly is all juggling needs.

faqs.question: How old is juggling?
faqs.answer: A tomb painting from ancient Egypt, around 4,000 years old, shows women juggling balls.

faqs.question: Why are juggling balls filled with beans or seeds?
faqs.answer: Bean-bag balls do not bounce or roll away when dropped, making practice easier.

faqs.question: What is the basic juggling pattern?
faqs.answer: The three-ball cascade, where balls are thrown in alternating arcs from hand to hand, is the first pattern most people learn.

image.alt: Three colourful juggling balls

name: Juggling clubs

place_of_invention.notes: Juggling clubs developed from Indian clubs in late 19th-century American vaudeville and circus; the performer DeWitt Cook is often credited with early club juggling.

short_description: Bottle-shaped clubs thrown and caught in spinning patterns by jugglers.
description: Juggling clubs developed in the late 19th century when performers adapted exercise clubs, known as Indian clubs, for throwing. Early clubs were solid wood; later ones were hollow and lighter. Modern clubs use plastic bodies around a wooden or fibreglass core but keep the classic bottle shape.
why_unchanged: The weighted bulb and handle create a predictable spin, which is ideal for juggling.

faqs.question: Where did juggling clubs come from?
faqs.answer: They were adapted from Indian exercise clubs by 19th-century entertainers.

faqs.question: Why do clubs spin in the air?
faqs.answer: Jugglers release them with a flick so that they rotate once or more before being caught by the handle.

faqs.question: What is passing?
faqs.answer: Passing is juggling clubs between two or more people, a popular group activity.

image.alt: Three white juggling clubs

name: Jump rope

place_of_invention.notes: Rope skipping appears in European sources by the 17th century; claims of ancient Egyptian or Chinese origin are often repeated but poorly documented.

short_description: A length of rope swung over the head and under the feet while the jumper skips over it.
description: Skipping over a swinging rope is an old children's game across many cultures, documented in Europe from at least the early modern period. It became a playground staple in the 19th century and later a key training tool for boxers. Double Dutch, using two ropes turned in opposite directions, is a popular team version.
why_unchanged: A rope with optional handles is all that skipping requires, so the object has stayed the same.

faqs.question: Why do boxers use jump ropes?
faqs.answer: Skipping builds footwork, coordination and endurance in a small space, which is why it is a classic boxing exercise.

faqs.question: What is Double Dutch?
faqs.answer: It is a game in which two people turn two ropes in opposite directions while one or more jumpers skip between them.

faqs.question: How long should a jump rope be?
faqs.answer: A common rule is that the handles should reach about the armpits when you stand on the middle of the rope.

image.alt: A jump rope with wooden handles

name: Jungle gym

place_of_invention.notes: Lawyer Sebastian Hinton designed the climbing frame and patented it in the early 1920s; he named it the Junglegym.

short_description: A climbing frame of interconnected bars for children's play.
description: Sebastian Hinton designed the jungle gym around 1920, inspired by a bamboo frame his father, mathematician Charles Howard Hinton, built to teach children three-dimensional thinking. He patented it as the Junglegym, and the first one was installed at a school in Winnetka, Illinois. Its grid of climbing bars remains a playground fixture.
why_unchanged: A lattice of bars gives endless climbing routes, so the structure has never needed to change.

faqs.question: Who invented the jungle gym?
faqs.answer: Sebastian Hinton invented and patented it in the early 1920s.

faqs.question: What inspired the jungle gym?
faqs.answer: His father's bamboo frame, used to teach children to think in three dimensions.

faqs.question: What do people in Britain call it?
faqs.answer: In Britain it is usually called a climbing frame.

image.alt: Children climbing a metal jungle gym

name: Kaleidoscope

place_of_invention.notes: Brewster invented the kaleidoscope in 1816 and patented it in 1817.

short_description: A tube of mirrors that creates symmetrical patterns from loose coloured pieces as it is rotated.
description: Scottish physicist Sir David Brewster invented the kaleidoscope in 1816 while studying light polarization, and patented it in 1817. It became a huge craze, with hundreds of thousands sold in a few months, many by copiers. The basic design of angled mirrors inside a tube with a chamber of coloured objects is still used today.
why_unchanged: The optical principle of reflecting mirrors at fixed angles is complete in itself, so there was nothing to change.

faqs.question: Who invented the kaleidoscope?
faqs.answer: Sir David Brewster invented it in Scotland in 1816 and patented it in 1817.

faqs.question: What does the word mean?
faqs.answer: It comes from Greek words meaning 'beautiful form' and 'to look at'.

faqs.question: How does a kaleidoscope make patterns?
faqs.answer: Two or more mirrors set at an angle reflect a small group of objects many times, producing a symmetrical image.

image.alt: A brass kaleidoscope tube

name: Kendama

place_of_invention.notes: Cup-and-ball toys reached Japan in the Edo period; the modern kendama with three cups and a spike was patented as the 'Nichigetsu Ball' by Hamaji Egusa in 1919.

short_description: A Japanese skill toy with a handle, two side cups, a base cup, a spike and a ball on a string.
description: Kendama developed from the cup-and-ball toys that reached Japan in the 18th century. In 1919 Hamaji Egusa created the modern design with a cross-piece, three cups and a spike, and the town of Hatsukaichi in Hiroshima is still a centre of production. Kendama has become a worldwide hobby with competitions and trick videos.
why_unchanged: Its arrangement of cups and spike allows countless tricks, so the 1919 design has remained the standard.

faqs.question: What are the parts of a kendama?
faqs.answer: It has a handle (ken) with a spike, two side cups, a bottom cup, and a ball (tama) with a hole.

faqs.question: Who created the modern kendama?
faqs.answer: Hamaji Egusa designed it in Hiroshima in 1919, calling it the Nichigetsu Ball.

faqs.question: What is the hardest basic trick?
faqs.answer: Spiking the ball onto the ken's point, called tome-ken, is a classic challenge.

image.alt: A wooden kendama with a red ball

name: Kettlebell

place_of_invention.notes: The Russian word girya appears in a dictionary of 1704; similar handled weights were used in other cultures, including ancient Greece.

short_description: A cast-iron ball with a handle, swung and lifted for strength and conditioning.
description: Kettlebells, known in Russia as girya, were originally used as counterweights in markets and became popular for strength training and feats in the 18th and 19th centuries. They are lifted, swung and pressed in dynamic movements that work the whole body. Kettlebell sport (girevoy sport) is a recognized discipline today.
why_unchanged: A weight with an offset handle is ideal for swinging movements, so the simple cast design has remained.

faqs.question: Where do kettlebells come from?
faqs.answer: They are associated with Russia, where the word girya is recorded from the early 1700s.

faqs.question: What is a kettlebell swing?
faqs.answer: It is a hip-driven movement where the bell is swung between the legs and up to chest height.

faqs.question: How are kettlebells weighed traditionally?
faqs.answer: Traditional Russian kettlebells are measured in poods; one pood is about 16 kg.

image.alt: A black cast-iron kettlebell

name: Kite

place_of_invention.notes: Chinese tradition credits the philosophers Mozi and Lu Ban with early kites; the attribution is legendary rather than documented.

short_description: A light frame covered with fabric or paper that flies on the wind at the end of a line.
description: Kites are traditionally said to have been invented in China around the 5th century BCE, first made of wood and silk and later of bamboo and paper. They were used for signalling and measuring as well as play, and spread across Asia and later to Europe. Kites also played a role in science, including Benjamin Franklin's famous electricity experiment.
why_unchanged: A light sail held at an angle by a tethered line is the core aerodynamic principle, and it has not changed.

faqs.question: Who invented the kite?
faqs.answer: Chinese tradition credits the philosophers Mozi and Lu Ban around the 5th century BCE, though this is legend rather than record.

faqs.question: How does a kite stay in the air?
faqs.answer: Wind pushing against the angled surface creates lift, while the line holds the kite in place.

faqs.question: Were kites used for anything besides fun?
faqs.answer: Yes. They have been used for military signalling, weather measurements and early aviation research.

image.alt: A colorful diamond kite flying in a blue sky

name: Lawn bowl

place_of_invention.notes: The Southampton Old Bowling Green is said to have been in use since 1299; earlier ball games were played in Europe, but lawn bowls developed in Britain.

short_description: A biased ball rolled toward a small white jack in the game of lawn bowls.
description: Lawn bowls has been played in England since the Middle Ages, and the Southampton Old Bowling Green claims use since 1299. The bowls are not perfect spheres but are shaped with a bias so they curve as they slow down. Modern bowls are made of composite rather than lignum vitae wood, but the biased shape is unchanged.
why_unchanged: Its bias, which makes the bowl curve, is the essence of the game, so the shape has not changed.

faqs.question: Why do lawn bowls curve?
faqs.answer: They are shaped with a bias, slightly flatter on one side, which makes them curve as they slow down.

faqs.question: What is the target called?
faqs.answer: The small white or yellow ball is called the jack.

faqs.question: Is the Drake story true?
faqs.answer: Legend says Sir Francis Drake finished a game of bowls before facing the Spanish Armada in 1588, but it is not well documented.

image.alt: Dark lawn bowls on a grass green near a white jack

name: Mahjong tiles

place_of_invention.notes: Mahjong developed from earlier Chinese card games in the mid-to-late 19th century; legends attributing it to Confucius are myths.

short_description: A set of 144 engraved tiles of suits, honours and flowers used in the game of mahjong.
description: Mahjong emerged in 19th-century China from older card games and spread rapidly, reaching the West in the 1920s, when it became a craze in America. The game uses tiles in three suits, plus winds, dragons and flowers. Sets made of bone and bamboo have given way to plastic, but the tiles are unchanged in design.
why_unchanged: The tile set encodes the game's rules, so changing it would mean changing the game.

faqs.question: How many tiles are in a mahjong set?
faqs.answer: A standard Chinese set has 144 tiles, including flowers and seasons.

faqs.question: Was mahjong invented by Confucius?
faqs.answer: No. That is a popular legend; historians date the game to 19th-century China.

faqs.question: Is mahjong solitaire the same game?
faqs.answer: No. Mahjong solitaire is a matching puzzle that uses the tiles, while real mahjong is a four-player game of sets.

image.alt: Mahjong tiles arranged on a green table

name: Mancala board

place_of_invention.region: Horn of Africa (Aksumite Ethiopia and Eritrea)
place_of_invention.notes: Some of the oldest secure mancala boards come from Aksumite sites; older claims from the Near East are disputed.

short_description: A board of rows of pits in which seeds or stones are sown around in a counting game.
description: Mancala is a family of 'sowing' games in which players pick up seeds from one pit and drop them one by one into following pits. Boards carved into stone have been found at Aksumite sites in Ethiopia and Eritrea, and the games spread throughout Africa, the Middle East and Asia under names such as oware, bao and congkak. Many boards are still simply rows of hollows in wood or even in the ground.
why_unchanged: Rows of cups and a handful of seeds are the whole game, so there was nothing to improve.

faqs.question: What does mancala mean?
faqs.answer: The word comes from Arabic naqala, meaning to move, and is used as a family name for hundreds of sowing games.

faqs.question: How do you play mancala?
faqs.answer: Players take all the seeds from one pit and sow them one at a time into the next pits, capturing seeds according to the rules of the local variant.

faqs.question: Do you need a board to play?
faqs.answer: No. Many people play by scooping pits into the ground and using pebbles or seeds.

image.alt: A carved wooden mancala board with pits holding seeds

name: Marbles

place_of_invention.region: Ancient Egypt and the Indus Valley
place_of_invention.notes: Small clay and stone balls interpreted as marbles are known from Egypt, Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley; their use as toys is likely but not always certain.

short_description: Small hard spheres flicked with the thumb in a variety of children's games.
description: Small balls of clay, stone and polished pebbles have been found in ancient Egypt, the Indus Valley and Mesopotamia, and Roman writers describe games with nuts that work like marbles. Clay marbles were mass-produced in the 19th century, and German glassmakers popularized swirled glass marbles from the 1840s. The game of knocking marbles out of a ring is still played in tournaments today.
why_unchanged: A small sphere rolls and collides predictably, so the toy is already perfect in its simplest form.

faqs.question: How old are marbles?
faqs.answer: Small balls likely used as marbles date back thousands of years to Egypt and the Indus Valley. Glass marbles became common only in the 19th century.

faqs.question: What is a 'shooter'?
faqs.answer: A shooter is a slightly larger marble that a player flicks with the thumb to knock other marbles out of the ring.

faqs.question: Where does the phrase 'losing your marbles' come from?
faqs.answer: It is an early 20th-century American expression; one idea links it to the distress of a child losing a prized marble collection.

image.alt: A handful of colorful glass marbles

name: Marionette

place_of_invention.notes: String-operated figures are mentioned by Xenophon and other Greek writers; articulated figures are also known from ancient Egypt, and marionette traditions developed independently in Asia.

short_description: A puppet controlled from above by strings attached to a wooden control bar.
description: String puppets were known in ancient Greece, where writers described figures moved by strings, and similar traditions developed in India, China and Southeast Asia. In Europe, marionette theatre flourished from the Renaissance onward, especially in Italy and Central Europe. The marionette still has jointed limbs worked by strings from a hand-held control.
why_unchanged: Jointed limbs controlled by strings from above produce lifelike movement, so the design has endured.

faqs.question: Where does the word marionette come from?
faqs.answer: It is from French, meaning 'little Mary', possibly from medieval figures of the Virgin Mary.

faqs.question: How many strings does a marionette have?
faqs.answer: Simple ones have around nine strings, while complex figures can have dozens.

faqs.question: Is marionette theatre recognized as heritage?
faqs.answer: Yes. Czech and Slovak puppetry is on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.

image.alt: A wooden marionette hanging from its strings

name: Matryoshka doll

place_of_invention.notes: The first set was carved by Vasily Zvyozdochkin and painted by Sergey Malyutin around 1890–1892, reportedly inspired by a Japanese nesting doll.

short_description: A set of hollow wooden dolls of decreasing size that nest inside each other.
description: The matryoshka was created in Russia in the early 1890s by woodturner Vasily Zvyozdochkin and painter Sergey Malyutin, probably inspired by a Japanese nesting figure. The first set, a girl in a headscarf holding a rooster, had eight dolls and won a medal at the 1900 Paris Exposition. Matryoshkas are still turned from linden wood and hand-painted.
why_unchanged: The nested shells are the whole idea, so the shape cannot change without losing it.

faqs.question: What does matryoshka mean?
faqs.answer: It comes from the Russian name Matryona, a traditional name associated with a mother figure.

faqs.question: How many dolls are in a set?
faqs.answer: Typical sets have five to ten pieces, but some record sets contain dozens.

faqs.question: Who made the first matryoshka?
faqs.answer: Vasily Zvyozdochkin carved and Sergey Malyutin painted the first set in the early 1890s.

image.alt: A set of painted Russian nesting dolls in a row

name: Medicine ball

place_of_invention.notes: The term 'medicine ball' is recorded in the late 1880s; weighted balls of stuffed skins are said to have been used much earlier, but evidence is anecdotal.

short_description: A heavy, soft-sided ball thrown and caught for strength and conditioning.
description: Weighted balls for exercise became popular in late 19th-century American gymnasiums under the name medicine ball, 'medicine' meaning health. Stories of ancient Persian wrestlers or Hippocrates using stuffed animal skins are frequently repeated but hard to verify. Today medicine balls are made of leather, rubber or vinyl and used in athletic training and rehabilitation.
why_unchanged: A heavy ball that can be thrown and caught safely needs no further refinement.

faqs.question: Why is it called a medicine ball?
faqs.answer: 'Medicine' was used in the sense of something good for health.

faqs.question: What are medicine balls used for?
faqs.answer: They are thrown, caught and lifted to build power, core strength and coordination.

faqs.question: Did Herbert Hoover play with one?
faqs.answer: Yes. President Hoover and his staff played a medicine-ball game, later called Hooverball, at the White House.

image.alt: A leather medicine ball on a gym floor

name: Nine men's morris board

place_of_invention.notes: Morris boards are well attested in the Roman world; an Egyptian board from Kurna (c. 1400 BCE) is often cited but its dating is disputed.

short_description: A board of three nested squares joined at the midpoints, used for a game of forming rows of three.
description: Nine men's morris, a strategy game where players form 'mills' of three pieces, was widely played in the Roman Empire and medieval Europe. Boards were carved into church benches, castle stones and cloister seats. The game is still sold with the same board of three concentric squares and 24 points.
why_unchanged: The 24-point board is the game itself, so its layout has never needed to change.

faqs.question: How do you win nine men's morris?
faqs.answer: You win by reducing your opponent to two pieces or leaving them with no legal moves.

faqs.question: What is a mill?
faqs.answer: A mill is a row of three of your pieces, which lets you remove one of your opponent's pieces.

faqs.question: Is it mentioned in literature?
faqs.answer: Yes. Shakespeare refers to 'the nine men's morris' in A Midsummer Night's Dream.

image.alt: A wooden nine men's morris board with black and white pieces

name: Pachisi board

place_of_invention.notes: Pachisi is associated with the Mughal emperor Akbar, whose courtyard at Fatehpur Sikri has a giant board; the game itself is likely older. Ludo is a simplified version patented in England in 1896.

short_description: A cross-shaped board for a race game played with cowrie shells and pieces.
description: Pachisi is a traditional Indian race game played on a cross-shaped board, often of embroidered cloth, with moves determined by tossed cowrie shells. It is famously linked to the Mughal emperor Akbar, who is said to have played it with people as living pieces on a courtyard board. Western versions such as Ludo and Parcheesi keep the same cross-shaped track.
why_unchanged: The cross-shaped track is the heart of the game and has been kept by every variant.

faqs.question: What does pachisi mean?
faqs.answer: It comes from the Hindi word for twenty-five, the highest throw of the cowrie shells.

faqs.question: Is Ludo the same game?
faqs.answer: Ludo is a simplified English version, patented in 1896, using a die instead of shells.

faqs.question: Did Akbar really play with human pieces?
faqs.answer: Tradition says so, and a giant board survives in the courtyard of Fatehpur Sikri.

image.alt: A cross-shaped embroidered pachisi board with pieces

name: Parallel bars

place_of_invention.notes: Friedrich Ludwig Jahn introduced parallel bars at his open-air gymnasium in Berlin around 1811–1812.

short_description: Two parallel horizontal rails on uprights used for gymnastic swings and supports.
description: German educator Friedrich Ludwig Jahn, the father of the Turnen gymnastics movement, introduced parallel bars at his Hasenheide training ground in Berlin in the early 19th century. The apparatus became a core part of men's artistic gymnastics. Modern bars use fiberglass-reinforced wooden rails, but the layout of two raised parallel rails is the same.
why_unchanged: Two rails at shoulder width are exactly what support and swinging exercises require.

faqs.question: Who invented the parallel bars?
faqs.answer: Friedrich Ludwig Jahn introduced them in Berlin in the early 1800s.

faqs.question: Are parallel bars an Olympic event?
faqs.answer: Yes. Parallel bars are one of the six apparatus in men's artistic gymnastics.

faqs.question: How high are competition parallel bars?
faqs.answer: The rails are set roughly 2 metres above the floor, and the distance between them can be adjusted for each gymnast.

image.alt: Wooden gymnastics parallel bars in a gym

name: Pétanque boule

place_of_invention.notes: Pétanque was created in 1907 in La Ciotat, traditionally credited to Jules Lenoir, whose rheumatism prevented the running start of jeu provençal; steel boules became standard in the 1920s.

short_description: A hollow steel ball thrown toward a small wooden jack in the game of pétanque.
description: Pétanque was born in 1907 in La Ciotat, France, when players adapted the game of jeu provençal so that they could throw from a standing position. The name comes from the Provençal for 'feet anchored'. Hollow steel boules, introduced in the 1920s, have remained the standard ever since.
why_unchanged: A hollow metal ball of set weight and size is ideal for throwing and knocking, so the boule has stayed the same.

faqs.question: Where was pétanque invented?
faqs.answer: It was invented in La Ciotat, near Marseille, in 1907.

faqs.question: What is the small ball called?
faqs.answer: The small target ball is called the cochonnet, meaning 'piglet', or the jack.

faqs.question: Are boules solid?
faqs.answer: No. Competition boules are hollow steel, weighing between 650 and 800 grams.

image.alt: Steel pétanque boules near a small wooden jack on gravel

name: Pick-up sticks

place_of_invention.notes: The game, known as Mikado in much of Europe, was popular in the 19th century; claims of an ancient Chinese origin are unverified.

short_description: A bundle of thin sticks dropped in a pile and removed one by one without moving the others.
description: Pick-up sticks, also called Mikado or spillikins, became a popular parlour game in 19th-century Europe and America. Players drop a bundle of sticks and then take turns removing one at a time without disturbing the others. Sticks are coloured or banded to show their point value.
why_unchanged: A handful of thin sticks is all the game needs, and its challenge depends on that simplicity.

faqs.question: What is Mikado?
faqs.answer: Mikado is the European name for pick-up sticks, in which the highest-scoring stick is called the Mikado.

faqs.question: What is the rule if another stick moves?
faqs.answer: If any other stick moves while you are picking one up, your turn ends.

faqs.question: What is another old name for the game?
faqs.answer: In Britain it was traditionally called spillikins or jackstraws.

image.alt: Coloured pick-up sticks scattered on a table

name: Pinwheel

place_of_invention.notes: Pinwheels appear in European art from at least the 16th–17th centuries; Chinese windmill toys (fengche) also have a long history. The origin is unknown.

short_description: A wheel of curled vanes on a stick that spins when blown or held in the wind.
description: The pinwheel, or paper windmill, has been a children's toy for centuries, appearing in early modern European paintings of children at play. Similar toys have long been sold at festivals in China. It is made by cutting a square into folded vanes and pinning the centre to a stick so that wind turns it.
why_unchanged: Folded vanes on a free axle are the simplest wind turbine, and the toy has never needed more.

faqs.question: How do you make a pinwheel?
faqs.answer: Cut a square from the corners toward the centre, fold every other point to the middle and pin it loosely to a stick.

faqs.question: Why does a pinwheel spin?
faqs.answer: Wind pushes against the angled vanes, creating a turning force around the pin.

faqs.question: Is a pinwheel related to a windmill?
faqs.answer: Yes. It works on the same principle as a windmill or wind turbine, in miniature.

image.alt: A colourful pinwheel spinning on a stick

name: Playground slide

place_of_invention.notes: The slide at Wicksteed Park, installed in the early 1920s, is often called the oldest surviving playground slide; earlier slides existed in US playgrounds.

short_description: A smooth inclined chute that children climb up to and slide down.
description: Playground slides appeared in the early 20th century as public playgrounds spread in Britain and the United States. One of the oldest surviving examples was built by Charles Wicksteed for his park in Kettering, England. Modern slides are made of plastic or stainless steel, but the ladder-and-chute design is unchanged.
why_unchanged: A ladder and a smooth slope are all a slide needs, and gravity does the rest.

faqs.question: Where is the oldest playground slide?
faqs.answer: The slide at Wicksteed Park in England, from the early 1920s, is often called the oldest surviving one.

faqs.question: Why are some slides made of plastic?
faqs.answer: Plastic stays cooler in the sun than metal and can be moulded into tubes and spirals.

faqs.question: Why can slides give you a static shock?
faqs.answer: Friction between clothing and plastic builds up static electricity as you slide.

image.alt: A metal slide in a children's playground

name: Playing cards

place_of_invention.notes: A Chinese text of the 9th century mentions a 'leaf game'; cards reached Europe through the Mamluk world in the 1370s.

short_description: A deck of printed cards with suits and ranks, used for countless games of chance and skill.
description: Playing cards are generally traced to Tang dynasty China, where paper and woodblock printing made them possible. They travelled west through the Islamic world and appeared in Europe in the late 14th century, where suits eventually settled into the French hearts, diamonds, clubs and spades. A standard deck of 52 cards plus jokers is now used worldwide.
why_unchanged: A stack of identical-backed, thin, printable cards is already the ideal format for shuffling and dealing.

faqs.question: Where were playing cards invented?
faqs.answer: Most historians place their origin in China around the 9th century, during the Tang dynasty. They reached Europe by the 1370s.

faqs.question: Why does a deck have 52 cards?
faqs.answer: The 52-card deck of four suits with 13 ranks became standard in Europe by the 15th and 16th centuries. Popular theories linking it to weeks of the year are later inventions.

faqs.question: Where did the French suits come from?
faqs.answer: Hearts, diamonds, clubs and spades were adopted in France in the late 15th century because the simple shapes were cheap to print with stencils.

image.search_query: deck of playing cards fanned out
image.alt: A fanned-out deck of playing cards showing the four suits

name: Pogo stick

place_of_invention.notes: Early spring-stilt patents include George H. Herrington (US, 1891); George Hansburg patented a design in 1919, and Max Pohlig and Ernst Gottschall patented one in Germany around 1920. Credit is disputed.

short_description: A spring-loaded pole with footrests that lets the rider bounce upright.
description: Spring-loaded jumping sticks were patented in the late 19th century, and the pogo stick took its familiar form around 1919–1920 in the US and Germany. It became a popular fad in the 1920s and again in later decades. Modern extreme pogo sticks use air or elastomer springs but keep the same pole, handlebars and foot pegs.
why_unchanged: A pole with a spring, handles and footrests is all bouncing requires.

faqs.question: Who invented the pogo stick?
faqs.answer: Several inventors patented similar devices; George Hansburg in the US and Max Pohlig and Ernst Gottschall in Germany are most often credited.

faqs.question: Why is it called pogo?
faqs.answer: The name is often linked to the German inventors Pohlig and Gottschall, combining the first letters of their surnames.

faqs.question: How high can you jump on a pogo stick?
faqs.answer: Extreme pogo athletes using powerful springs have cleared bars more than three metres high.

image.alt: A metal pogo stick with foot pegs

name: Pull toy

place_of_invention.notes: Clay animals on wheels are known from Indus Valley cities and Mesopotamia; wheeled animal figures also appear in pre-Columbian Mexico.

short_description: A toy on wheels, often an animal, that a child pulls along by a string.
description: Small clay animals with wheels, likely pulled by strings, have been found in Indus Valley cities such as Mohenjo-daro and in Mesopotamia. Wheeled clay figures also appear in ancient Mexico, a culture that did not otherwise use the wheel for transport. Wooden pull-along ducks, dogs and trains remain classic toddler toys.
why_unchanged: A figure on wheels with a string is the simplest moving toy, so it has never changed.

faqs.question: How old are pull toys?
faqs.answer: Wheeled clay animals from the Indus Valley and Mesopotamia are around 4,500 years old.

faqs.question: Why are pull toys good for toddlers?
faqs.answer: They encourage walking and give children a sense of control as the toy follows them.

faqs.question: Did ancient Mexicans have wheeled toys?
faqs.answer: Yes. Wheeled animal figures have been found in pre-Columbian Mexico.

image.alt: A wooden pull-along duck toy on wheels

name: Punching bag

place_of_invention.notes: Greek boxers and pankratiasts trained with a hanging leather bag called the korykos; the modern heavy bag became standard in 19th-century boxing gyms.

short_description: A heavy hanging bag struck repeatedly to train punches.
description: Ancient Greek athletes trained by striking a korykos, a leather sack filled with sand, flour or seeds hung at chest height. Boxing gyms of the 19th century adopted canvas and leather heavy bags filled with sawdust or rags. Modern bags use synthetic leather and textile fill, but they still hang from a chain and absorb blows the same way.
why_unchanged: A heavy, cushioned hanging target is all striking practice requires.

faqs.question: Did ancient athletes use punching bags?
faqs.answer: Yes. Greek boxers trained with a leather bag called the korykos.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a heavy bag and a speed bag?
faqs.answer: A heavy bag builds power, while a small speed bag rebounds quickly to train timing and hand speed.

faqs.question: What are punching bags filled with?
faqs.answer: Typical fillings are textile scraps, sand or foam, chosen for weight and softness.

image.alt: A leather punching bag hanging in a boxing gym

name: Quoits

place_of_invention.notes: Quoits is mentioned in English sources from the 14th century; it may have developed from horseshoe throwing or ancient discus throwing.

short_description: Rings of metal, rope or rubber thrown to land over or near a peg.
description: Quoits, a game of tossing rings at a pin, has been played in England since at least the late Middle Ages and remains a traditional pub and village sport in Britain. Rope quoits became a popular deck game on ocean liners, and ring toss is a fairground classic. The ring and peg format has not changed.
why_unchanged: A ring and a target peg form a perfect throwing game, needing nothing more.

faqs.question: How do you score in quoits?
faqs.answer: Points go to rings that encircle the peg, called ringers, or land closest to it.

faqs.question: Is quoits related to horseshoes?
faqs.answer: Yes. The American game of horseshoes is closely related and probably shares origins with quoits.

faqs.question: Where is quoits still played?
faqs.answer: Traditional quoits leagues remain in parts of Britain, especially northern England, Wales and Scotland.

image.alt: Metal quoits lying around a peg in clay

name: Rocking horse

place_of_invention.notes: Wooden rocking horses on bow rockers are known from 17th-century England; the safety-stand version was patented in the US in the late 19th century.

short_description: A toy horse mounted on curved rockers or a swinging stand that a child can ride.
description: Rocking horses developed from earlier hobby horses and became popular children's toys in 17th-century England, carved from wood on bow-shaped rockers. In the Victorian era they were often dappled and fitted with real hair manes and tails. A swinging safety stand was introduced in the late 19th century, but the horse itself kept its familiar form.
why_unchanged: A rideable horse figure that rocks back and forth needs nothing more than its curved base.

faqs.question: When did rocking horses appear?
faqs.answer: They became common in England in the 17th century, developing from earlier hobby horses and barrel horses.

faqs.question: Why are many rocking horses dappled grey?
faqs.answer: Dapple grey horses were fashionable in Victorian Britain, and Queen Victoria's liking for them is often credited.

faqs.question: What is a safety stand?
faqs.answer: It is a frame on which the horse swings on metal hangers, which takes up less room and is less likely to tip than bow rockers.

image.alt: A dapple grey wooden rocking horse

name: Rubber duck

place_of_invention.notes: Rubber toys became possible after vulcanization; rubber ducks appeared in the late 19th century, and Peter Ganine patented a well-known floating duck design in 1949. No single inventor is credited.

short_description: A small yellow duck-shaped bath toy that floats.
description: Rubber ducks appeared in the late 19th century after vulcanized rubber made it possible to mould toys. The familiar floating yellow duck was popularized in the 20th century, helped by sculptor Peter Ganine's 1949 patent and later by Sesame Street's Ernie song 'Rubber Duckie' in 1970. Most modern ducks are made of vinyl rather than rubber.
why_unchanged: A buoyant, cheerful duck shape does its job perfectly, so it has never needed to change.

faqs.question: Why are rubber ducks yellow?
faqs.answer: Yellow is cheerful and resembles a duckling, and it became the classic colour.

faqs.question: Are rubber ducks really made of rubber?
faqs.answer: Most modern ones are made of vinyl, though the name stuck.

faqs.question: What is rubber duck debugging?
faqs.answer: It is a programming technique of explaining code line by line to a rubber duck to find mistakes.

image.alt: A yellow rubber duck floating in water

name: Rubik's Cube

place_of_invention.notes: Ernő Rubik built the first prototype in 1974 and patented it in Hungary in 1975.

short_description: A 3x3x3 twisting puzzle cube whose coloured faces must be restored.
description: Hungarian architecture professor Ernő Rubik created the cube in 1974 as a tool to teach spatial thinking. Released internationally in 1980, it became one of the best-selling toys in history. The 3x3x3 mechanism of a core, centres, edges and corners is the same as Rubik's original.
why_unchanged: The internal mechanism and colour scheme were complete from the start, so only manufacturing quality has changed.

faqs.question: Who invented the Rubik's Cube?
faqs.answer: Hungarian professor Ernő Rubik invented it in 1974.

faqs.question: How many positions does the cube have?
faqs.answer: A standard Rubik's Cube has about 43 quintillion possible positions.

faqs.question: What is God's number?
faqs.answer: It is the maximum number of moves needed to solve any position, proven in 2010 to be 20.

image.alt: A scrambled Rubik's Cube showing coloured faces

name: Seesaw

place_of_invention.notes: The English word 'see-saw' is recorded in the 1600s; the Korean seesaw game neolttwigi is also centuries old.

short_description: A long board balanced on a central pivot that two riders tip up and down.
description: A plank balanced on a pivot is one of the simplest playground devices, known in Europe at least since the 17th century and in Korea as the traditional standing seesaw game neolttwigi. It became a standard fixture of playgrounds in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Its fun comes from a simple lever: when one side goes down, the other goes up.
why_unchanged: A lever on a fulcrum is the whole toy, so its form cannot be simplified.

faqs.question: What is another name for a seesaw?
faqs.answer: In parts of the US it is called a teeter-totter.

faqs.question: What physics does a seesaw demonstrate?
faqs.answer: It is a lever: a lighter rider can balance a heavier one by sitting farther from the pivot.

faqs.question: What is neolttwigi?
faqs.answer: It is a traditional Korean game in which players stand on the ends of a board and bounce each other high into the air.

image.alt: Two children on a playground seesaw

name: Shot put

place_of_invention.notes: Stone-putting contests are ancient in Scotland and Ireland, and medieval soldiers are said to have thrown cannonballs; the metal shot became standard in the 19th century.

short_description: A heavy metal ball pushed from the shoulder for distance in athletics.
description: Putting heavy stones is an ancient strength contest in Scotland and Ireland, still seen at Highland games. With the arrival of cannon, iron balls became a popular substitute, and standardized metal shots were used in 19th-century British athletics. The event's ball and putting style are unchanged in modern athletics.
why_unchanged: A dense sphere is the simplest weight for a pushing throw, so the shot has stayed the same.

faqs.question: How heavy is a shot?
faqs.answer: The men's shot weighs 7.26 kg (16 lb) and the women's 4 kg.

faqs.question: Why is it 'put' and not thrown?
faqs.answer: Rules require the shot to be pushed from the shoulder rather than thrown with a straight arm.

faqs.question: What is the stone put?
faqs.answer: It is a traditional Scottish Highland games event using a natural stone instead of a metal ball.

image.alt: A metal shot put ball on a throwing circle

name: Shuttlecock

place_of_invention.notes: Games with feathered shuttlecocks existed in ancient China, Japan, India and Greece; battledore and shuttlecock was popular in 17th-century England, and badminton emerged in the 1870s.

short_description: A cone of feathers set in a rounded cork base, hit back and forth with rackets in badminton.
description: Feathered shuttlecocks were used in battledore and shuttlecock, a children's game popular in early modern Europe, and similar games existed for centuries in Asia. Badminton took shape in the 1870s and was named after Badminton House in England. Top-level shuttlecocks are still made from 16 goose feathers set in a cork base.
why_unchanged: Feathers fixed in a weighted base create a high-drag projectile that always flies cork first, which nothing has bettered.

faqs.question: How many feathers does a shuttlecock have?
faqs.answer: A standard feather shuttlecock has 16 overlapping feathers.

faqs.question: Why does a shuttlecock always turn cork first?
faqs.answer: The heavy cork base and high-drag feather skirt make it flip so that the base leads.

faqs.question: How fast can a shuttlecock travel?
faqs.answer: Off a professional smash it can exceed 400 km/h, though it slows down very quickly.

image.alt: A white feather shuttlecock with a cork base

name: Skis

place_of_invention.notes: Ski fragments from Vis I near Lake Sindor (Russia) date to around 6000 BCE; rock carvings in Norway and claims from China's Altai region are also cited.

short_description: Long, narrow boards attached to boots for gliding over snow.
description: Skis were invented thousands of years ago for travel and hunting in snowy northern lands, with ancient fragments found in Russia and Scandinavia. Norwegian innovations in the 19th century turned skiing into a sport. Modern skis use composite materials and shaped sidecuts, but remain long boards bound to the feet.
why_unchanged: Spreading weight on long, smooth boards is the essential solution for travelling over snow.

faqs.question: How old are skis?
faqs.answer: The oldest ski fragments are about 8,000 years old, found in northern Russia.

faqs.question: Where did skiing become a sport?
faqs.answer: Skiing as a sport developed in 19th-century Norway, especially the Telemark region.

faqs.question: Why are skis curved up at the front?
faqs.answer: The upturned tip helps the ski ride over the snow instead of digging in.

image.alt: A pair of skis standing in the snow

name: Sled

place_of_invention.notes: Fragments of sledge runners from Finland date to the Mesolithic; sleds were likely used across northern regions.

short_description: A vehicle on runners for sliding over snow and ice.
description: Sleds are among the oldest vehicles, with runner fragments from Mesolithic Finland and long use across the Arctic for transport. Children's sleds for sliding downhill became popular in the 19th century, including the steerable Flexible Flyer patented in 1889. The basic deck on runners has stayed the same.
why_unchanged: A platform on smooth runners is the most efficient way to glide over snow.

faqs.question: How old is the sled?
faqs.answer: Sled runner fragments from Finland are around 9,000 years old, making sleds one of the oldest vehicles.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a sled and a toboggan?
faqs.answer: A sled has runners, while a toboggan has a flat bottom that rests directly on the snow.

faqs.question: What was the Flexible Flyer?
faqs.answer: It was a steerable sled patented by Samuel Leeds Allen in 1889, which became a classic American toy.

image.alt: A wooden sled with metal runners in the snow

name: Slingshot

place_of_invention.notes: Y-shaped slingshots depended on vulcanized rubber, patented by Charles Goodyear in 1844; no single inventor is known.

short_description: A Y-shaped frame with elastic bands and a pouch used to shoot small projectiles.
description: The slingshot became possible after vulcanized rubber was developed in the 1840s, which made strong, durable elastic bands. By the second half of the 19th century boys in America and Europe were making them from forked branches. Modern sport slingshots use metal frames and flat latex bands but keep the same fork-and-pouch design.
why_unchanged: A fork, two bands and a pouch are the minimum needed, so the form has not changed.

faqs.question: How is a slingshot different from a sling?
faqs.answer: A sling is an ancient weapon made of cords and a pouch swung by hand, while a slingshot uses a forked frame and elastic bands.

faqs.question: When was the slingshot invented?
faqs.answer: It appeared in the mid-19th century after vulcanized rubber made strong elastic bands possible.

faqs.question: Is there a slingshot sport?
faqs.answer: Yes. Target shooting with slingshots is a recognized hobby with clubs and competitions.

image.alt: A wooden Y-shaped slingshot with rubber bands

name: Slinky

place_of_invention.notes: Naval engineer Richard James conceived the toy in 1943 after watching a spring fall; it went on sale in 1945 and was patented in 1947.

short_description: A pre-compressed helical spring toy that 'walks' down stairs.
description: Richard James got the idea for the Slinky in 1943 while working with tension springs for ships. With his wife Betty, who chose the name, he sold the first 400 in Gimbels department store in Philadelphia in 1945, all within 90 minutes. The steel coil design has remained essentially unchanged.
why_unchanged: A coiled spring of the right size walks down stairs on its own, so the toy needed nothing more.

faqs.question: Who invented the Slinky?
faqs.answer: Naval engineer Richard James invented it in 1943; his wife Betty named it.

faqs.question: Why does a Slinky walk down stairs?
faqs.answer: Gravity and momentum transfer the coils one end over the other in a wave-like motion.

faqs.question: How long is a Slinky's wire?
faqs.answer: The original steel Slinky uses about 80 feet (24 m) of wire.

image.alt: A metal Slinky walking down steps

name: Snakes and ladders board

place_of_invention.notes: The game derives from Indian moral games such as gyan chaupar; the earliest surviving boards are from the 18th century, and claims of a 13th-century origin are not well documented. It reached England in the 1890s.

short_description: A numbered grid board with ladders that lift players up and snakes that send them down.
description: Snakes and ladders comes from Indian games such as gyan chaupar, where ladders represented virtues and snakes vices. British colonists brought it to England in the late 19th century, and Milton Bradley sold it in the US as Chutes and Ladders from 1943. The board of 100 squares with snakes and ladders is still sold in the same form.
why_unchanged: A numbered race track with shortcuts and setbacks needs nothing more to be fun.

faqs.question: Where did snakes and ladders come from?
faqs.answer: It came from Indian games that taught moral lessons, with ladders as virtues and snakes as vices.

faqs.question: What is Chutes and Ladders?
faqs.answer: It is the American version launched by Milton Bradley in 1943, with chutes instead of snakes.

faqs.question: Is there any skill in the game?
faqs.answer: No. Moves are decided entirely by dice, which makes it ideal for young children.

image.alt: A colourful snakes and ladders board with dice

name: Snow globe

place_of_invention.notes: Erwin Perzy of Vienna is credited with the first commercial snow globes around 1900; glass globes with snow appeared earlier, notably at the 1878 Paris Exposition.

short_description: A clear globe of liquid containing a scene and particles that swirl like snow when shaken.
description: Water-filled globes with floating 'snow' were shown at the 1878 Paris Exposition, and around 1900 Viennese instrument maker Erwin Perzy began making them commercially. Shaking the globe makes white particles swirl and drift down over a small scene. Snow globes are still popular souvenirs and holiday decorations.
why_unchanged: A sealed globe of liquid and drifting particles is the whole effect, so the design has endured.

faqs.question: Who made the first snow globe?
faqs.answer: Erwin Perzy of Vienna is often credited with the first commercial snow globes around 1900.

faqs.question: What is the snow made of?
faqs.answer: Early makers experimented with various fine white particles; modern globes use small plastic flakes.

faqs.question: Why does the snow fall slowly?
faqs.answer: Glycerin or other additives thicken the liquid, slowing the particles.

image.alt: A snow globe with a winter village scene

name: Snowshoes

place_of_invention.notes: Snowshoes are believed to have originated in Central Asia; one of the oldest surviving examples, from the Italian Alps, dates to around 3800 BCE.

short_description: Wide frames worn under the boots to spread weight and keep from sinking into snow.
description: Snowshoes spread a walker's weight over a larger area so they do not sink into deep snow. They are thought to have originated in Central Asia, and one of the oldest examples, found in the Alps, is nearly 6,000 years old. Indigenous peoples of North America developed many refined designs of wooden frames laced with rawhide.
why_unchanged: Distributing body weight over a large area is the whole principle, so the shape has persisted.

faqs.question: How do snowshoes work?
faqs.answer: They spread your weight over a larger surface, so you stay on top of deep snow instead of sinking.

faqs.question: How old are snowshoes?
faqs.answer: One of the oldest known pairs, from the Italian Alps, is about 5,800 years old.

faqs.question: Who developed traditional snowshoe designs?
faqs.answer: Indigenous peoples of North America created many styles, such as the bear paw and the long-tailed Ojibwe shoe.

image.alt: Traditional wooden snowshoes laced with rawhide

name: Spinning top

place_of_invention.notes: Clay tops are reported from early Mesopotamian sites; tops were invented independently in many cultures.

short_description: A toy that spins on a point, balancing by gyroscopic motion until it slows down.
description: Spinning tops are among the oldest known toys, with clay examples from ancient Mesopotamia and later finds from Egypt, Greece, China and the Americas. They are set spinning by twisting a stem, pulling a string or whipping them. The physics of angular momentum keeps a fast top upright until friction slows it down.
why_unchanged: A weighted body with a central point is all a top needs to spin, so its shape has never had to change.

faqs.question: Why does a spinning top stay upright?
faqs.answer: Its angular momentum resists changes in its orientation, so it remains balanced while spinning fast enough.

faqs.question: How old is the spinning top?
faqs.answer: Tops date back several thousand years, with ancient examples from Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece and China.

faqs.question: How do you launch a string top?
faqs.answer: You wind a string tightly around the top, then throw it forward while pulling the string back so it unwinds and spins the top.

image.alt: A painted wooden spinning top on a table

name: Spirograph

place_of_invention.notes: British engineer Denys Fisher developed the toy in the early 1960s and launched it in 1965; mathematical gear-drawing devices existed earlier.

short_description: A set of plastic gears and rings used to draw looping geometric patterns.
description: Engineer Denys Fisher created the Spirograph and introduced it at the 1965 Nuremberg International Toy Fair. By placing a pen in a hole in a toothed wheel and rolling it inside or around a ring, users draw curves called hypotrochoids and epitrochoids. The set of gears and rings is essentially the same today.
why_unchanged: Toothed wheels rolling in rings produce the patterns mechanically, so the design needed no change.

faqs.question: Who invented the Spirograph?
faqs.answer: British engineer Denys Fisher invented it and launched it in 1965.

faqs.question: What curves does a Spirograph draw?
faqs.answer: It draws mathematical curves called hypotrochoids and epitrochoids.

faqs.question: Why do some patterns close quickly and others take many loops?
faqs.answer: It depends on the ratio of teeth between the wheel and the ring; the more complex the ratio, the more loops before the pattern repeats.

image.alt: Coloured Spirograph patterns on paper with plastic gears

name: Stilts

place_of_invention.notes: Stilts are mentioned in ancient Greek sources and also have long traditions in China and Africa; the origin is unknown.

short_description: A pair of poles with footrests that raise the walker above the ground.
description: Stilts have been used for play, work and performance since antiquity, with references in ancient Greece and long traditions in China and Africa. In 19th-century France, shepherds of the Landes region walked on stilts to cross marshy ground. Today they appear in circuses, parades and as children's toys.
why_unchanged: A pole with a step is the simplest way to extend the leg, so no redesign was ever needed.

faqs.question: Why did shepherds use stilts?
faqs.answer: Shepherds in the marshy Landes region of France used tall stilts to cross wet ground and watch their flocks.

faqs.question: Are stilts used in performances?
faqs.answer: Yes. Stilt walkers are a traditional part of carnivals, circuses and street festivals around the world.

faqs.question: Are stilts still used for work?
faqs.answer: Yes. Drywall installers and plasterers often wear strap-on stilts to reach ceilings.

image.alt: A child walking on wooden stilts

name: Swing

place_of_invention.notes: A clay figurine of a woman on a swing from Hagia Triada, Crete (c. 1450 BCE) is an early depiction; swings appear in many ancient cultures.

short_description: A seat hung from ropes or chains that moves back and forth like a pendulum.
description: Swinging is shown in Minoan art from Crete and in ancient Greek vase painting, where it was associated with festivals. Swings are found across cultures, from India's festival swings to European garden swings. Playground swings with chains and rubber seats became common in the 20th century.
why_unchanged: A seat on two suspension lines is all a pendulum ride requires.

faqs.question: How old is the swing?
faqs.answer: A Minoan figurine from about 1450 BCE shows a person on a swing, and swings were well known in ancient Greece.

faqs.question: How do you swing higher without a push?
faqs.answer: Pumping your legs and leaning at the right moments shifts your centre of mass, adding energy to each swing.

faqs.question: What physics explains a swing?
faqs.answer: A swing behaves like a pendulum, trading height for speed and back again.

image.alt: A wooden swing hanging from a tree

name: Table football

place_of_invention.notes: Harold Searles Thornton filed a British patent in 1921 (granted 1923); other claimants include Lucien Rosengart in France and Alejandro Finisterre in Spain.

short_description: A table game with rows of rotating rods holding player figures that kick a ball.
description: Harold Searles Thornton patented table football in Britain in the early 1920s, reportedly inspired by matchbox players. The game spread across Europe in the following decades and became known as foosball in the US. It still uses the same layout of eight rods with fixed figures over a pitch.
why_unchanged: Rods with fixed figures turned by handles are the game's entire mechanism, so its design endures.

faqs.question: Who invented table football?
faqs.answer: Harold Searles Thornton patented it in Britain in the early 1920s, though others also claim it.

faqs.question: Why is it called foosball?
faqs.answer: The name comes from the German 'Fußball', meaning football.

faqs.question: Is spinning the rods allowed?
faqs.answer: In most official rules, spinning the rod more than 360 degrees before or after striking is not allowed.

image.alt: A foosball table with red and blue players

name: Tangram

place_of_invention.notes: Tangram books were published in China in the early 19th century (1813 is often cited); the puzzle reached Europe and America soon after.

short_description: A dissection puzzle of seven flat pieces arranged to form silhouettes.
description: The tangram is a Chinese puzzle of seven pieces: five triangles, a square and a parallelogram, cut from a single square. It became a craze in Europe and America in the early 19th century after ships brought puzzle books from China. The pieces are unchanged, and thousands of figures can be made from them.
why_unchanged: Seven pieces cut from one square already offer endless shapes, so nothing has been changed.

faqs.question: How many pieces does a tangram have?
faqs.answer: A tangram has seven pieces, called tans: five triangles, a square and a parallelogram.

faqs.question: Where does the tangram come from?
faqs.answer: It originated in China and was popularized in the early 19th century.

faqs.question: What are the rules?
faqs.answer: All seven pieces must be used, laid flat, and must not overlap.

image.alt: Seven wooden tangram pieces arranged as a square

name: Teddy bear

place_of_invention.notes: Morris Michtom in Brooklyn and the Steiff company in Germany both produced toy bears in 1902–1903, and both are credited.

short_description: A soft stuffed toy bear, usually jointed and covered in plush fabric.
description: The teddy bear was named after US President Theodore Roosevelt after a 1902 hunting incident and cartoon. In the same years Morris Michtom of Brooklyn and Richard Steiff of the German Steiff company each created stuffed bears independently. The toy became an instant craze and remains a classic comfort object for children worldwide.
why_unchanged: A soft, huggable bear is valued for comfort rather than function, so its basic form has endured.

faqs.question: Why is it called a teddy bear?
faqs.answer: It is named after President Theodore 'Teddy' Roosevelt, who in 1902 refused to shoot a bear tied up for him on a hunt.

faqs.question: Who made the first teddy bear?
faqs.answer: Morris Michtom in the US and the Steiff company in Germany both made stuffed bears around 1902–1903, and both are credited.

faqs.question: Why do some old teddy bears have humps?
faqs.answer: Early bears, especially Steiff models, were designed to look like real bears with long snouts and shoulder humps.

image.alt: A brown jointed teddy bear sitting upright

name: Thaumatrope

place_of_invention.notes: The thaumatrope was popularized in 1825 by physician John Ayrton Paris; its invention has also been attributed to William Henry Fitton and Charles Babbage.

short_description: A disc with a picture on each side that seems to merge into one image when spun on strings.
description: The thaumatrope was a popular Victorian optical toy, introduced in London in 1825. Spinning the disc by its strings makes the images on each side, such as a bird and a cage, appear combined. It is still made as a simple craft and demonstrates the persistence of vision.
why_unchanged: A two-sided disc on strings is the simplest possible optical illusion device.

faqs.question: How does a thaumatrope work?
faqs.answer: As the disc spins quickly, the eye merges the two images into one.

faqs.question: What is the classic thaumatrope image?
faqs.answer: A bird on one side and a cage on the other, which together show the bird inside the cage.

faqs.question: Who invented it?
faqs.answer: John Ayrton Paris popularized it in 1825, though others have been credited.

image.alt: A thaumatrope disc showing a bird and a cage

name: Tiddlywinks

place_of_invention.notes: Joseph Assheton Fincher filed a patent for the game in 1888.

short_description: Small plastic discs flicked into a cup by pressing their edge with a larger disc.
description: Tiddlywinks was patented in England in 1888 by Joseph Assheton Fincher and became a Victorian parlour craze. Players press a large disc, the squidger, on the edge of a small wink to flip it into a pot. Cambridge University students revived it as a competitive sport in 1955, with complex rules still played today.
why_unchanged: Flipping a disc by pressing its edge works perfectly, so the winks, squidger and pot are unchanged.

faqs.question: What is a squidger?
faqs.answer: A squidger is the larger disc used to press on the edge of a wink and flip it.

faqs.question: Who invented tiddlywinks?
faqs.answer: Joseph Assheton Fincher patented the game in England in 1888.

faqs.question: Is there competitive tiddlywinks?
faqs.answer: Yes. Organized by associations in Britain and the US, the competitive game began at Cambridge University in 1955.

image.alt: Coloured tiddlywinks discs around a small cup

name: Toboggan

place_of_invention.notes: The toboggan was developed by Indigenous peoples of northern North America for transport; the word comes from an Algonquian language (likely Mi'kmaq). Dating is uncertain.

short_description: A long, flat-bottomed sled with a curled front, without runners.
description: Indigenous peoples of what is now Canada used toboggans made of bent wood boards to haul goods over deep snow. The flat bottom spreads weight so the sled rides on soft snow rather than sinking in. In the 19th century tobogganing became a popular winter sport, and wooden toboggans are still made in the traditional style.
why_unchanged: Thin boards curled at the front glide over soft snow perfectly, so the design never changed.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a toboggan and a sled?
faqs.answer: A toboggan has a flat bottom that sits on the snow, while a sled is raised on runners.

faqs.question: Where does the word toboggan come from?
faqs.answer: It comes from an Algonquian language of eastern Canada, probably Mi'kmaq.

faqs.question: Why does the front curl up?
faqs.answer: The curled front lets the toboggan ride over snow instead of ploughing into it.

image.alt: A wooden toboggan with a curled front in the snow

name: Toy balloon

place_of_invention.notes: Michael Faraday made rubber balloons for hydrogen experiments in 1824; Thomas Hancock sold do-it-yourself toy balloon kits in 1825. Earlier balloons were made of animal bladders.

short_description: A thin rubber bag inflated with air or helium, used for play and decoration.
description: Before rubber, people inflated animal bladders and intestines for play. In 1824 scientist Michael Faraday made the first rubber balloons for his experiments with hydrogen, and toy kits followed the next year. Latex balloons were mass-produced in the 20th century, but the inflatable rubber skin is the same concept.
why_unchanged: A stretchy, sealed skin that holds air is the whole object, so it has stayed the same.

faqs.question: Who invented the rubber balloon?
faqs.answer: Michael Faraday made the first rubber balloons in 1824 for experiments with hydrogen.

faqs.question: Why do helium balloons float?
faqs.answer: Helium is lighter than air, so the balloon is pushed upward by the surrounding air.

faqs.question: Why do balloons stick to walls after rubbing?
faqs.answer: Rubbing gives the balloon a static charge, which attracts it to neutral surfaces.

image.alt: A bunch of colourful rubber balloons

name: Toy soldier

place_of_invention.notes: Flat tin figures were mass-produced in Nuremberg from the 18th century (notably by the Hilpert family); William Britain introduced hollow-cast lead soldiers in London in 1893. Military figurines are much older.

short_description: A small figure of a soldier, made of tin, lead or plastic, used for play and collecting.
description: Military figurines are known from ancient Egypt, but mass-produced tin soldiers began in 18th-century Germany, especially Nuremberg. In 1893 William Britain introduced hollow-cast lead soldiers, which made them cheaper and hugely popular. Plastic figures largely replaced metal ones after World War II, but the small standing soldier is the same toy.
why_unchanged: A small figure that can be lined up into armies is all imaginative war play requires.

faqs.question: Where were toy soldiers first mass-produced?
faqs.answer: Tin soldiers were mass-produced in Nuremberg, Germany, from the 18th century.

faqs.question: Why did metal soldiers disappear?
faqs.answer: Lead was found to be toxic, and cheaper plastic figures took over after the 1950s.

faqs.question: What is The Steadfast Tin Soldier?
faqs.answer: It is a fairy tale by Hans Christian Andersen, published in 1838, about a one-legged toy soldier.

image.alt: A row of painted toy soldiers

name: Trampoline

place_of_invention.notes: George Nissen and Larry Griswold built their first trampoline around 1934–1936 at the University of Iowa; Nissen later trademarked the name.

short_description: A sheet of strong fabric stretched over a frame by springs, used for bouncing.
description: Gymnast George Nissen and coach Larry Griswold built the first modern trampoline in the 1930s, inspired by the safety nets of trapeze artists. Nissen's company sold it for military pilot training and gymnastics, and he trademarked the name from the Spanish 'trampolín' (diving board). Trampolining became an Olympic sport in 2000.
why_unchanged: A taut bed suspended on springs from a frame is the simplest way to store and return bouncing energy.

faqs.question: Who invented the trampoline?
faqs.answer: George Nissen and Larry Griswold built the first modern trampoline in Iowa in the 1930s.

faqs.question: Is trampolining an Olympic sport?
faqs.answer: Yes. It has been part of the Olympic Games since Sydney 2000.

faqs.question: Where does the name come from?
faqs.answer: Nissen took it from the Spanish word 'trampolín', meaning diving board.

image.alt: A round trampoline in a garden

name: Whip top

place_of_invention.notes: Whipping tops were known in ancient Greece and Rome (Virgil's Aeneid compares a character to a top whipped by boys) and in ancient Egypt and China; the origin is unknown.

short_description: A top kept spinning by lashing it with a small whip.
description: The whip top is spun by hand or by a cord, then kept going by striking its side with a small whip. It was a familiar children's toy in ancient Greece and Rome, and versions are known from Egypt, China and medieval Europe. Wooden whip tops are still played with in parts of Asia and Europe.
why_unchanged: A simple top and whip work perfectly together, so the toy has stayed the same for over two thousand years.

faqs.question: How do you keep a whip top spinning?
faqs.answer: You strike its side with a short whip, which adds spin every time.

faqs.question: How old is the whip top?
faqs.answer: It was known in ancient Greece and Rome and appears in Virgil's Aeneid.

faqs.question: Is the whip top still played?
faqs.answer: Yes. It is a traditional game in China and parts of Europe and Asia.

image.alt: A wooden whip top with a small whip

name: Yo-yo

place_of_invention.notes: A Greek vase of about 440 BCE shows a boy with a yo-yo, and terracotta disks survive; similar toys may have existed in China. The modern name was popularized in the 1920s USA.

short_description: Two joined discs with a string wound around the axle that spin down and climb back up.
description: Ancient Greek vase paintings and clay discs show that yo-yos were played with around 2,500 years ago. The toy was popular in 18th-century Europe as the bandalore, and the name yo-yo was brought to the United States by Filipino-American Pedro Flores, who began manufacturing them in 1928. Later Donald Duncan's company turned it into a worldwide craze.
why_unchanged: Two discs on an axle with a string are the whole mechanism, and that design already works perfectly.

faqs.question: How old is the yo-yo?
faqs.answer: There is evidence of yo-yo-like toys in ancient Greece around 500 BCE, making it one of the oldest toys.

faqs.question: Where does the name yo-yo come from?
faqs.answer: It was popularized by Pedro Flores in 1920s California; the word is generally linked to the Philippines.

faqs.question: What is a 'sleeper'?
faqs.answer: A sleeper is the basic trick where the yo-yo stays spinning at the bottom of the string before being called back up.

image.alt: A classic wooden yo-yo with its string

name: Zoetrope

place_of_invention.notes: William George Horner described the device, which he called the daedaleum, in 1834; it was patented as the zoetrope in the US by William E. Lincoln in 1867.

short_description: A spinning drum with slits that creates the illusion of motion from a strip of pictures.
description: The zoetrope was invented in 1834 by British mathematician William George Horner, who called it the daedaleum. When the drum is spun, viewers look through the slits at a strip of sequential images, which appear to move. It became a popular Victorian toy and helped lay the foundations of cinema.
why_unchanged: Its slit-and-drum principle is the essence of the illusion, so it has never needed to change.

faqs.question: How does a zoetrope work?
faqs.answer: The slits act like a shutter, showing each image briefly so the brain blends them into motion.

faqs.question: Who invented the zoetrope?
faqs.answer: William George Horner invented it in 1834, calling it the daedaleum.

faqs.question: Is the zoetrope linked to cinema?
faqs.answer: Yes. It is one of the optical toys that led to motion pictures.

image.alt: A Victorian zoetrope drum with picture strip
